It carries semi-abelian schemes G and G^∨ that extend the universal abelian scheme and its dual, and a homomorphism λ: G → G^∨ that extends the polarization. Only its normalization enters the models below, so a normal model built as P2 builds X_par is enough.
- Finiteness of S^tor_{K^pK_p,Q} → ∏_{i=1}^r A^tor_{g,d_i,Q} for suitable cone decompositions. The paper assumes this. The map itself (conjugation followed by level change) comes from C3.
- Normality, properness and Z_p-flatness of S^tor_{K^pK_p}. Over the interior it is S_{K^pK_p}.
- The variant over Z_p^cycl: S^tor_{K^pK_p,Z_p^cycl}, the normalization of ∏_{i=1}^r A^tor_{g,d_i} × Spec Z_p^cycl in S^tor_{K^pK_p,Q_p^cycl}.
  - It is normal and flat over Z_p^cycl but not noetherian, and its interior is S_{K^pK_p,Z_p^cycl}.
  - Its map to S^tor_{K^pK_p} ×_{Spec Z_p} Spec Z_p^cycl is in general not an isomorphism (the toroidal form of Remark 3.4.22).
  - The paper does not say whether Z_p^cycl means Z_p[ζ_{p^∞}] or its p-adic completion. If it means Z_p[ζ_{p^∞}], the model is the inverse limit of the normalizations over the rings Z_p[ζ_{p^m}]; locally its ring is the union of theirs.
- No irreducible component of the special fibre lies in the boundary (sourceIssues E67).

Layer G2 (§4.1.1, p. 41). Let n ≥ 1 (sourceIssues E64), and let K_{p,n} be the Iwahori subgroup of level p^n.
- S^tor_{K^pK_{p,n}} is the normalization of ∏_{i=0}^g A^tor_{g,d_i} × Spec Z_p in S^tor_{K^pK_{p,n},Q_p}. Here d_0 = 1 and d_i = p^{n(g−i)} for 1 ≤ i ≤ g, so A_{g+i} has polarization degree d_i² (sourceIssues E65). The cone decompositions must make S^tor_{K^pK_{p,n},Q_p} → ∏_{i=0}^g A^tor_{g,d_i,Q_p} finite; the paper says only "We construct similarly".
- The chain, as printed: "By [FC90], I, prop. 2.7, we have a chain of isogenies of semi-abelian schemes A = A_g → A_{g+1} → ⋯ → A_{2g} → A_1 → ⋯ → A_g = A where the total map A → A is multiplication by p^n."
- A = A_g is the pullback of G from the factor A^tor_{g,d_0}, and A_{g+i} is the pullback of G from the factor A^tor_{g,d_i}.
- A_1, …, A_{g−1} come from no factor. Over the interior A_j ≅ A_{2g−j}^∨, so take for A_j the pullback of G^∨ from the factor A^tor_{g,d_{g−j}}.
- Faltings–Chai I, Prop. 2.7 (C4) then extends every map of the chain uniquely, and the composite is still p^n.
- For 1 ≤ i ≤ 2g, define Gr_i on all of S^tor_{K^pK_{p,n}} as the kernel of the map in the chain whose target is A_i. Over the interior this is ShimuraVarietiesHondaTatePartII's Gr_i: H_i modulo the term before it in the flag, whose order is g+1, …, 2g, 1, …, g, with 0 before H_{g+1} (sourceIssues E66).
- Prove that Gr_i is quasi-finite and flat. Along the boundary it is not finite in general (sourceIssues E67).
- Remark 4.1.2 (p. 41), as printed: "When n = 1, S^tor_{K^pK_{p,1}} is the usual integral model of Iwahori level." ShimuraVarietiesHondaTatePartII proves the interior form: it identifies S_{K^pK_{p,1}} with the Iwahori lattice-chain moduli. Deduce the toroidal form here. The interior of S^tor_{K^pK_{p,1}} is that moduli space, and by the uniqueness in Faltings–Chai I, Prop. 2.7, the chain above extends its universal chain of isogenies.

Imports:
- "Toroidal compactifications and boundary geometry" (ShimuraCompactifications) C0–C5: C3 for the generic-fibre maps, C4 for Faltings–Chai I, Prop. 2.7, and C5 for the good-level models and their normalizations at higher p-level.
- "Complex Shimura varieties and canonical models, Part II: integral models and reduction" (ShimuraVarietiesHondaTatePartII), which keeps A_{g,d}, the interior models over Z_p and Z_p^cycl, the flag H_i, Gr_i over the interior, and the interior form of Remark 4.1.2 (S_{K^pK_{p,1}} is the Iwahori lattice-chain moduli).
- "Siegel and PEL moduli problems" (PELModuli) M4–M5.
- "Shimura data, Hermitian domains, and adelic level structures" (ShimuraData) D5.

Consumers (none of them is imported):
- "Hida and Coleman families, period modules, and family L-functions, Part II: higher Hida and higher Coleman theory for coherent cohomology" (HigherHidaAndColemanTheory). It keeps the blow-up, the normalized level-K_{p,1,n} model over Z_p(ζ_{p^n}), C^tor_t, and D_i, which it defines from this layer's Gr_i.
- "Automorphic bundles and classical automorphic forms, Part II: integral coherent cohomology and Hecke-equivariant perfect complexes" (IntegralCoherentHeckeComplexes).
- "Igusa varieties, compactified period fibers and torsion concentration, Part II: ordinary Igusa formal schemes of Siegel varieties" (IgusaVarietiesAndTorsionConcentrationPartIISiegelOrdinary). It keeps IG^tor and its open immersion into the p-adic completion of S^tor_{K^pK_p,Z_p^cycl}.

Tests:
- Take K = K^pK_p ⊆ G(Ẑ) = K_{(1,…,1)}, r = 1, d_1 = 1, δ_1 = (1, …, 1), and cone decompositions for which S^tor_{K,Q} → S^tor_{K^pG(Z_p),Q} → A^tor_{g,1,Q} is finite. Then the model is C5's normalization of S^tor_{K^pG(Z_p)} in S^tor_{K,Q_p}, which is imported, not rebuilt.
- For g = n = 1, at the cusp with H_2 = μ_p, Gr_1 = ker(Tate(q^p) → Tate(q)) has order p off q = 0 and is trivial on it.
- For g = 2 and n = 1, use the map to X_Kli(p) that keeps H_3 and forgets H_4 (for compatible cone decompositions). Along it, A → A_1 → A, of degrees p³ and p, is the pullback of P3's Klingen chain G → G' → G.
routes.reason:
"Toroidal compactifications and boundary geometry" (ShimuraCompactifications) compactifies PEL moduli integrally at good level in C5 and normalizes that model at higher p-level. It does not plan three things that Boxer–Pilloni use (§3.4.23, p. 40; §4.1.1, p. 41):
- a toroidal compactification over Z_p of de Jong's A_{g,d} with p | d;
- the normalization models S^tor_{K^pK_p} built from these compactifications, over Z_p and over Z_p^cycl;
- the extension of the Iwahori isogeny chain to semi-abelian schemes over the boundary of these models, with the kernels Gr_i as quasi-finite flat group schemes.

This is new mathematics in the direction of ShimuraCompactifications, so it belongs in a Part II (PROTOCOL 15). That Part II has already been proposed. PAPER-FARB-KISIN-WOLFSON-24 proposed ShimuraCompactificationsPartIIHodgeTypeIntegralBoundary for the integral boundary beyond C5, and PAPER-MAULIK-SHANKAR-TANG-22 joined it. PAPER-PILLONI-20 widened it to Klingen and paramodular level for GSp4, using the same normalization method.

The Siegel datum is of Hodge type. §3.4.19 follows Lan and Madapusi Pera, whose normalization construction the joined briefs already use. So this paper joins that proposal and extends Pilloni's layers to every genus and every level at p, instead of opening a rival Part II. The normalization theorem is then stated once for all four briefs.

The interior models, A_{g,d}, and the flag and Gr_i over the interior stay with "Complex Shimura varieties and canonical models, Part II: integral models and reduction" (ShimuraVarietiesHondaTatePartII). This route imports that roadmap, which leaves the toroidal models and Gr_i on the boundary to this one, so integral compactifications keep one owner.

The models are not planned inside a consumer, because several consumers use them and some of those consumers are upstream of others. The Igusa Part II takes the toroidal Z_p^cycl model from here. HigherHidaAndColemanTheory builds its blow-up, its level-K_{p,1,n} model and D_i on these models. The route imports none of its consumers, so no cycle arises.

routes.title: Igusa varieties, compactified period fibers and torsion concentration, Part II: ordinary Igusa formal schemes of Siegel varieties
routes.brief:
Starts where Igusa varieties, compactified period fibers and torsion concentration (IgusaVarietiesAndTorsionConcentration), its first prerequisite, stops. Its Igusa stages (IG.0–IG.3) treat only the split unitary datum of Caraiani–Scholze's non-compact paper, with Igusa varieties over central leaves in characteristic p; it has no Siegel datum and no finite-level Igusa formal schemes over Z_p. This Part II builds the ordinary Igusa tower of the Siegel varieties of G = GSp_{2g}, for every g ≥ 1 and every prime p, as p-adic formal schemes over Z_p, with finite levels, partial toroidal compactifications and open embeddings into integral models. Source: §3.4 (pp. 35–40) of G. Boxer and V. Pilloni, "Higher Hida theory for Siegel modular forms", Invent. Math. 244 (2026), 45–141, doi:10.1007/s00222-025-01393-2. "p. N" is a page of the authors' version of 5 November 2025; sourceIssues numbers are PAPER-BOXER-PILLONI-26's. The other Part II of the same parent, Igusa varieties, compactified period fibers and torsion concentration, Part II: compact unitary Shimura varieties (IgusaVarietiesAndTorsionConcentrationPartIICompactUnitary), proposed by PAPER-CARAIANI-SCHOLZE-17, goes in a different direction (compact unitary data and torsion concentration); the two Part IIs share no layer and neither imports the other. PAPER-CARAIANI-SCHOLZE-17's source route would widen IG.0–IG.1 only to compact PEL data of type (A)/(C), which excludes the Siegel datum. If that widening is accepted and written for PEL data with good reduction at p, compact or not (the open Igusa variety of b, its quasi-isogeny description and the structure of Aut(X̃_b) do not use compactness), this Part II builds on IG.0–IG.1 for those three objects and proves only their b_ord instance over Z_p. Otherwise layers 1 and 2 build them for b_ord.

Setting. P = P_µ is the stabiliser of ⟨e_{g+1},…,e_{2g}⟩, M = M_µ its Levi, U_P its unipotent radical, Φ^{+,M} the roots of U_P (pp. 33–34). K^p ⊆ G(A_f^p) is neat (p. 34), except in Lemma 3.4.20, where K^p_δ contains −1 and both sides are formal algebraic stacks. As in the paper, 𝔍𝔊 denotes the formal Igusa schemes, 𝓘𝓖 their adic generic fibres, 𝓢 the adic Siegel varieties, and 𝔄, 𝔖 the p-adic completions of the integral models.

Final results as printed, then corrections.
- Lemma 3.4.3 (p. 36). "The group J_ord is a representable formal group scheme over Spf Z_p. We have J_ord = M_µ(Q_p) ⋉ U_{J_ord} where M(Q_p) is a locally profinite group viewed as a locally constant formal group scheme over Spf Z_p, and U_{J_b} = µ̃_{p^∞} ⊗_{Q_p} Sym² Q_p^g, where µ̃_{p^∞} is the universal cover of µ_{p^∞}. The action of M(Q_p) on U_{J_b} is given by the usual action of M(Q_p) on Sym² Q_p^g ≃ U_P(Q_p)."
- Lemma 3.4.8 (p. 37). For compact open K_{p,P} ⊆ P′(Q_p), its schematic closure \overline{K_{p,P}} in J_ord "is a profinite flat group scheme over Spec Z_p. Its generic fiber is K_{p,P}."
- Proposition 3.4.9 (p. 37). For compact open K′_{p,P} ⊆ K_{p,P} ⊆ P′(Q_p): (1) the fpqc quotient 𝔍𝔊_{K^pK_{p,P}} of 𝔍𝔊_{K^p} by \overline{K_{p,P}} exists as a p-adic formal scheme; (2) 𝔍𝔊_{K^p} → 𝔍𝔊_{K^pK_{p,P}} is a \overline{K_{p,P}}-torsor for the fpqc topology; (3) 𝔍𝔊_{K^pK_{p,P}} is smooth of finite type over Z_p; (4) the fpqc quotient 𝔍𝔊_{K^pU_{K_{p,P}}} of 𝔍𝔊_{K^p} by \overline{U_{K_{p,P}}} exists as a p-adic formal scheme; (5) 𝔍𝔊_{K^pU_{K_{p,P}}} → 𝔍𝔊_{K^pK_{p,P}} "is a profinite étale map with group M_{K_{p,P}}"; (6) J_ord induces an action of T̂_{K_{p,P}} on 𝔍𝔊_{K^pU_{K_{p,P}}}, whose formal completions at closed points are homogeneous spaces under T̂_{K_{p,P}}; (7) 𝔍𝔊_{K^pU_{K′_{p,P}}} → 𝔍𝔊_{K^pU_{K_{p,P}}} is finite flat and equivariant along the isogeny T̂_{K′_{p,P}} → T̂_{K_{p,P}}, and 𝔍𝔊_{K^pK′_{p,P}} → 𝔍𝔊_{K^pK_{p,P}} is finite flat.
- Proposition 3.4.16 (p. 39). For a K^pG(Z_p)-admissible cone decomposition Σ (§3.4.15): "The space 𝔍𝔊^tor_{K^p,Σ} carries an action of P′(Z_p), extending the action on 𝔍𝔊_{K^p}. For any K_{p,P} ⊆ P′(Z_p), the categorical quotient of 𝔍𝔊^tor_{K^p,Σ} by K_{p,P} exists and is denoted by 𝔍𝔊^tor_{K^pK_{p,P},Σ}."
- §3.4.17 (p. 39). Over Z_p^cycl, with Z_p(1) = Z_p fixed, there is a P(Q_p)-equivariant map 𝓘𝓖_{K^p,Z_p^cycl} → 𝓢_{K^p} × Spa(Q_p^cycl, Z_p^cycl) whose induction to G(Q_p) is injective and G(Q_p)-equivariant. For x ∈ G(Q_p), K_p ⊆ G(Q_p) compact open and K_{p,P} = P(Q_p) ∩ xK_px^{−1}, it induces an open immersion 𝓘𝓖_{K^pK_{p,P},Z_p^cycl} → 𝓢_{K^pK_p} × Spa(Q_p^cycl, Z_p^cycl).
- Lemma 3.4.20 (p. 40). "We have 𝔄^ord_{g,δ} = 𝔍𝔊_{K_{δ,P}} where K_{δ,P} = K^p_δ(K_{δ,p} ∩ P(Q_p))."
- Lemma 3.4.24 (p. 40). The map of §3.4.17 "comes from an open immersion of formal schemes" 𝔍𝔊_{K^pK_{p,P},Z_p^cycl} ↪ 𝔖_{K^pK_p,Z_p^cycl}, the p-adic completion of the normalization of ∏_i A_{g,d_i} × Spec Z_p^cycl in S_{K^pK_p,Q_p^cycl}, for any auxiliary choice of (d_i, δ_i, K ↪ K_{δ_i}) as in §3.4.19. For suitable cone decompositions it extends to the toroidal models, and in general it does not descend over Z_p (Remark 3.4.25).

Corrections the design job applies:
- E55: X_ord's summands are ordered inconsistently. Put the étale part first throughout: X_ord = (Q_p/Z_p)^g ⊕ (µ_{p^∞})^g, λ_can accordingly, b_ord = diag(Id_g, p^{−1}Id_g) = µ(p)^{−1}, Aut(X̃_ord) block lower triangular, so Aut_symp(X̃_ord) lies in P and Hom(X̃_et, X̃_m) is the U_P block; swap (x, y) in the proof of Proposition 3.4.9 and in Remark 3.4.18 likewise. Alternatively keep the printed order and make the swap explicit where M(Q_p) embeds in J_ord and in §3.4.17.
- E56: U_{J_ord} for U_{J_b} in Lemma 3.4.3.
- E58: in the exact sequence of closures and in Proposition 3.4.9(5), the group is the image K_{p,P}/U_{K_{p,P}} of K_{p,P} in M(Q_p). It equals M_{K_{p,P}} = K_{p,P} ∩ M(Q_p) when K_{p,P} = M_{K_{p,P}} ⋉ U_{K_{p,P}}, which holds for all K_{p,P} when p > 2 and can fail when p = 2.
- E59: add the Z_p^cycl form of Proposition 3.4.9(1)–(3) for every compact open K ⊆ P(Q_p), Galois-stable or not: 𝔍𝔊_{K^pK,Z_p^cycl} exists and is smooth, hence normal, as the quotient of 𝔍𝔊_{K^pK_1} ×_{Spf Z_p} Spf Z_p^cycl by a free action of the finite constant group K/K_1. Here U_K = K ∩ U_P(Q_p), M_1 is an open subgroup of K ∩ M(Q_p) that is normal in the image of K in M(Q_p), and K_1 = M_1 ⋉ U_K is open and normal in K and comes from P′(Q_p). In the analogue of (5) the group is the image of K in M(Q_p). §3.4.17 and Lemma 3.4.24 need this for general x and K_p.
- E63: the A_{g,δ} imported from ShimuraVarietiesHondaTatePartII, which owns its definition, its ordinary locus and the decomposition, must be the locus where the kernel of the polarization is fppf-locally, not étale-locally, ∏ Z/δ_iZ × µ_{δ_i}. The schematic closure of A_{g,δ,Q} does not work instead. Then Lemma 3.4.20 holds, and 𝔄^ord_{g,d} = ∐_δ 𝔄^ord_{g,δ} holds on underlying spaces; for g ≥ 2 it is in general not an equality of formal schemes (it fails for g = 2, d = p²).
- Misprints: (3) follows from (6) with (5), not from (4) (E60); the Raynaud quotient is of 𝔍𝔊_{K^pP′(Z_p)_n} by \overline{K_{p,P}}/\overline{P′(Z_p)_n} (E61); P′(Z_p) for P(Z_p) in §3.4.15 and the proof of Proposition 3.4.16 (E62).

Layers.
1. The ordinary p-divisible group and its symmetries (pp. 35–37). X_ord, λ_can, b_ord; J_ord = Qisog_symp(X_ord) = Aut_symp(X̃_ord); Lemma 3.4.3; J^an_ord and its exact sequences; P′(Q_p) ⊆ J^an_ord, generated by M(Q_p) and U_P(Q_p)(1), identified with P(Q_p) over Q_p^cycl; Remark 3.4.4. Level groups: J^int_ord and P′(Z_p) = M(Z_p) ⋉ U_P(Z_p)(1) (Remark 3.4.6), U_{K_{p,P}}, M_{K_{p,P}}, the splitting for p > 2 (Remark 3.4.7), schematic closures (footnote 3), Lemma 3.4.8, the sequence of closures, and T̂_{K_{p,P}} = (µ̃_{p^∞} ⊗ Sym² Z_p^g)/\overline{U_{K_{p,P}}}, a formal torus.
2. Igusa formal schemes (pp. 35–38). 𝔍𝔊_{K^p} as the moduli of (A, λ, η^p, j), its quasi-isogeny formulation, and the right action j ↦ j∘g of J_ord. The Frobenius-limit construction: 𝔍𝔊_{K^pP′(Z_p)} is the ordinary locus of the p-adic Siegel moduli space at level K^pG(Z_p); 𝔍𝔊_{K^pU_P(Z_p)(1)} is the pro-étale torsor of (x, y, c) with (x^D, y^D)∘λ∘(x, y) = cλ_can (footnote 4); the canonical Frobenius lifts F (quotient by A[p]^m) on 𝔍𝔊_{K^pP′(Z_p)} and 𝔍𝔊_{K^pU_P(Z_p)(1)}, finite flat because the base is smooth, and 𝔍𝔊_{K^p} = lim_{×F} 𝔍𝔊_{K^pU_P(Z_p)(1)}. Proposition 3.4.9; Remarks 3.4.10–3.4.11 (completed local rings; (x_α) ↦ (x_α^{p^{n_α}})).
3. Variants and Hecke correspondences (pp. 38–39). 𝔍𝔊 over Z_p^cycl (§3.4.12), with E59. Include the Z_p^cycl form of Proposition 3.4.9(7), finite flatness of 𝔍𝔊_{K^pK′,Z_p^cycl} → 𝔍𝔊_{K^pK,Z_p^cycl}, for all compact open K′ ⊆ K ⊆ P(Q_p). For g ∈ M(Q_p), the correspondence 𝔍𝔊_{K^pK_{p,P}} ← 𝔍𝔊_{K^p(gK_{p,P}g^{−1}∩K_{p,P})} → 𝔍𝔊_{K^pK_{p,P}} with finite flat projections; any g ∈ P(Q_p) over Z_p^cycl (Remark 3.4.14). Their operators on cohomology are built downstream.
4. Partial toroidal compactifications (p. 39). For K^pG(Z_p)-admissible Σ: the ordinary locus of the toroidal compactification, the torsor of isomorphisms µ_{p^∞}^g → A[p^∞]^m with c ∈ Z_p^× (the connected part extends over the boundary), 𝔍𝔊^tor_{K^p,Σ} as a Frobenius limit containing 𝔍𝔊_{K^p} as an open, Proposition 3.4.16, its Z_p^cycl form for every open K ⊆ P(Z_p) (the proof uses no Galois stability), and a definition of 𝔍𝔊^tor_{K^pK,Z_p^cycl} for a general compact open K ⊆ P(Q_p): conjugate K into P(Z_p) by an element of M(Q_p), as in the proof of Lemma 3.4.8, and transport Σ. The toroidal extension of Lemma 3.4.24 uses this. Also 𝔍𝔊_{K^pK_{p,P}} ↪ 𝔍𝔊^tor_{K^pK_{p,P},Σ}, and refinement by boundary blow-ups (Lan 2017), with the Frobenius lifts extended over the boundary, and the independence of coherent cohomology from Σ applied from ShimuraCompactifications C3.
5. Comparison with Siegel varieties (pp. 39–40). §3.4.17, Remark 3.4.18, Lemma 3.4.20, with 𝔍𝔊_{K^p_δ(K_{δ,p}∩P(Q_p))} defined as a formal algebraic stack (the stack quotient of 𝔍𝔊_{K′^pK_{p,P}} by K^p_δ/K′^p for a neat normal open K′^p ⊆ K^p_δ), and with the observation that K_{δ,p} ∩ P(Q_p) = (K_{δ,p} ∩ M(Q_p)) ⋉ (K_{δ,p} ∩ U_P(Q_p)) is Galois-stable, hence a compact open subgroup of P′(Q_p). Lemma 3.4.24 with its toroidal extension, Remark 3.4.25.

Imports, never re-planned: Shimura data, Hermitian domains, and adelic level structures (ShimuraData) D5: GSp_{2g}, P, M, U_P, Φ^{+,M}. Reductive bundles, B(G) and Newton strata (BunGAndNewtonStrata) BG0: B(G), the σ-centralizer J_b and its inner-Levi description, applied to the b_ord of layer 1 to show that its σ-centralizer is M, whose Q_p-points are the M(Q_p) of Lemma 3.4.3. This σ-centralizer is not the paper's J_{b_ord} := J_ord (§3.4.2), which is the formal group M(Q_p) ⋉ U_{J_ord}. Finite flat group schemes and integral p-adic Hodge theory (FiniteFlatGroupsAndIntegralPadicHodgeTheory) R07.1–R07.2: p-divisible groups, Dieudonné modules, Raynaud's flat closures. Hodge–Tate theory, canonical subgroups, and automorphic period maps (HodgeTateAndCanonicalSubgroups) T0 and T2: universal covers and their representability (PAPER-CARAIANI-SCHOLZE-17's source route); at T0 also the Hasse invariant of a BT_1 (PAPER-PILLONI-20's source route), whose invertibility locus is the ordinary locus. The Hasse invariant is taken from T0, never from SiegelModularFormsModPn. Abelian Schemes And Arithmetic Moduli (AbelianSchemesAndArithmeticModuli) A4: Serre–Tate theory, and Katz's coordinates, which this paper's source route adds there: the deformation space over W(k) of a polarized ordinary abelian variety over a perfect field k, with trivialized étale and multiplicative parts, is a formal torus isomorphic to Ĝ_m ⊗ Sym² Z_p^g, compatibly with Frobenius. Layer 2 identifies this torus with T̂_{P′(Z_p)} and proves that it acts simply transitively on the completions of 𝔍𝔊_{K^pU_P(Z_p)(1)} (proof of Proposition 3.4.9(6)); neither object belongs to A4. Scheme, stack, cohomology and intersection foundations (SchemeAndStackFoundations) SF.1: quotients by free actions of finite locally free group schemes. Siegel and PEL moduli problems (PELModuli) M2: the smooth moduli space over Z_p of abelian schemes with a prime-to-p polarization and neat level K^p, at level K^pG(Z_p), and its universal abelian scheme. Toroidal compactifications and boundary geometry (ShimuraCompactifications) C3–C5, with independence of the cone decomposition. Adic Spaces PartII (AdicSpacesPartII), stage AdicSpacesPartII:R2: adic generic fibres of formal schemes. Shimura towers and perfectoid representability (PerfectoidShimuraVarieties) S1: 𝓢_{K^p}, 𝓢^tor_{K^p,Σ}. Complex Shimura varieties and canonical models, Part II: integral models and reduction (ShimuraVarietiesHondaTatePartII): A_{g,d}, A_{g,δ} (with E63), K_δ and the normalization models over Z_p and Z_p^cycl. Toroidal compactifications and boundary geometry, Part II: integral boundary charts of Hodge type (ShimuraCompactificationsPartIIHodgeTypeIntegralBoundary): their toroidal versions. It imports neither HigherHidaAndColemanTheory nor SiegelModularFormsModPn.

Consumers: Hida and Coleman families, period modules, and family L-functions, Part II: higher Hida and higher Coleman theory for coherent cohomology (HigherHidaAndColemanTheory), which keeps Lemmas 4.1.7 and 4.3.6 (the descents of Lemma 3.4.24 to Z_p and to Z_p(ζ_{p^n}), the latter with E86), Proposition 4.2.4 and §5, and reuses this tower where its genus-two Klingen towers meet the ordinary locus. Algebraic modular forms, reduction and Serre weights, Part II: Siegel modular forms of genus two modulo p^n (SiegelModularFormsModPn) should import the g = 2 instance for its p-adic Siegel modular forms; PAPER-PILLONI-20's brief for it would otherwise build that tower there.

Acceptance tests:
- g = 1: J_ord = (Q_p^×)² ⋉ µ̃_{p^∞}, T̂_{P′(Z_p)} = Ĝ_m, and Remark 3.4.11 reads x ↦ x^{p^n}.
- Hida's cover Isom(µ_{p^n}^g, A[p^n]^m) of the ordinary locus is 𝔍𝔊_{K^pK_{p,P}} for K_{p,P} the preimage in P′(Z_p) of the elements of M(Z_p) acting trivially on µ_{p^n}^g.
- E55: z = diag(1_g, p·1_g) acts by p on U_P, by p^{−1} on the opposite unipotent radical, and by p on Hom(X̃_et, X̃_m) exactly in the étale-first order.
- E58: for p = 2, g = 1, K = K_0 ∪ g_0K_0 with K_0 = {(a 0; c d) : a ≡ d ≡ 1 mod 4, c ≡ 0 mod 2} and g_0 = (1 0; −1 −1), K ∩ M(Q_p) is torsion-free while the image of K in M(Q_p) contains diag(1, −1).
- E59: for g = 1, p odd, x = 1 and K_p = {γ ∈ GL_2(Z_p) : γ_11, γ_22 ∈ 1+pZ_p, γ_12 ∈ p²Z_p, γ_21 ≡ (γ_11−1)/p mod p}, the group K_p ∩ P(Q_p) is neither Galois-stable nor a semidirect product, yet its Igusa variety over Z_p^cycl is smooth.
- E63 (g = 1, d = p, δ = (p)): K_{δ,p} ∩ P(Q_p) = {(a 0; c d) : a, d ∈ Z_p^×, c ∈ p^{−1}Z_p} is diag(1, p)-conjugate to P(Z_p), so 𝔍𝔊_{K_{δ,P}} is the whole ordinary locus of 𝔄_{1,p}. With the fppf definition, 𝔄^ord_{1,(p)} is that whole ordinary locus (A_{1,(p)} is A_{1,p} minus the supersingular points), and Lemma 3.4.20 holds. The étale-local condition holds at every ordinary closed point of the special fibre but not at its generic point, so it cuts out no locally closed substack.
routes.reason: Section 3.4 builds the ordinary Igusa tower of GSp_{2g} over Z_p. It has five parts: the polarized ordinary p-divisible group and its group J_ord of symplectic self-quasi-isogenies; the level groups of P′(Q_p) and their flat closures; the finite-level Igusa formal schemes of Proposition 3.4.9; their Hecke correspondences and partial toroidal compactifications; and the open embeddings into integral Siegel models (Lemmas 3.4.20 and 3.4.24). This is Igusa geometry, the direction of IgusaVarietiesAndTorsionConcentration, but no layer of that roadmap covers it. IG.0–IG.3 are restricted to the split unitary datum of Caraiani–Scholze's non-compact paper and to central leaves in characteristic p. PAPER-CARAIANI-SCHOLZE-17's pending widening reaches only compact PEL data, with neither Siegel partial compactifications nor Z_p-integral finite levels, and its compact unitary Part II goes in another direction. HodgeTateAndCanonicalSubgroups T5 builds Igusa torsors only for Hilbert varieties; PAPER-PILLONI-20's source route adds Siegel material there (ω_G^mod), but no Igusa tower. The additions therefore form a Part II of that roadmap rather than a source route. Nothing here is specific to higher Hida theory, and the tower cannot live in HigherHidaAndColemanTheory: SiegelModularFormsModPn, which is upstream of that roadmap, needs the genus-two tower, and one owner must serve both. The integral-model Part IIs, ShimuraVarietiesHondaTatePartII and ShimuraCompactificationsPartIIHodgeTypeIntegralBoundary, stay upstream because they supply the models the tower embeds into.

(p. 23). Part (i) of Theorem 8.13, the analytic ring (B,R)■, is imported from SolidAnalyticRings (Light condensed mathematics, solid abelian groups and analytic rings) SA.3. 'Theorem 9.17' covers f^!R = ω_{X/R}[d] (pp. 23–24); beside 'Theorem 9.18' add discreteness of p̄^!F̄ for proper p̄ and p̄^!(F̄ ⊗ L) = p̄^!F̄ ⊗ p̄^*L (p. 17). 'The key computation' gives j_! for Spec A[1/f] (p. 15). Corrections: sourceIssues E23 (shifts), E24 (coherent extension in Proposition 2.3.5), E26 (p̄^!F̄ bounded below, uniformly in twists), E35 (base change of f^! along Tor-independent squares), E40 (j_! in the triangles), E43 (U ⊆ Z scheme-theoretically), E45 (F bounded below in Lemma 2.10.1(4)). D3 ('Construct the parabolic stabilizing the Hodge filtration and the compact dual as a flag variety') owns the Kostant combinatorics of general (G, µ), with M_µ the Levi of P_µ (sourceIssues E1): ^MW, the minimal-length representatives of W_M\W, characterised by wX⋆(T)^+ ⊆ X⋆(T)^{+,M}, equivalently w^{−1}Φ^+_M ⊆ Φ^+ (sourceIssues E52); X⋆(T)^{M_µ,+} = ∪_{w∈^MW} wX⋆(T)^+ (p. 3); the longest element w_{0,M} of W_M (p. 3) and the involution w ↦ w_{0,M}ww_0 of ^MW (p. 5); the Bruhat stratification P\G = ⊔_{w∈^MW} C_w with ℓ(w) = dim C_w and w′ ≤ w iff C_{w′} ⊆ C̄_w (p. 34), over Z, since it is used over Z_p and F_p; Schubert varieties X_w, opposite Schubert varieties X^w and Y_w = ∪_{w′≥w} C_{w′} (sourceIssues E116); and [BP21] Lemma 3.1.2, X^w ⊆ Y_w (p. 60). It imports the Bruhat decomposition from tauceti:TauCetiRoadmap/ReductiveGroups (Reductive algebraic groups), Layer 7, and the split reductive group scheme over Z with its base change from Layer 9 of the same roadmap, since Layer 7 works over a field. D5 ('all Siegel data', 'compact duals') gains the GSp_{2g} coordinates of §3.1 (p. 34) for every g: B ⊆ P, Φ^+ = Φ^+_M ⊔ Φ^{+,M}, ρ, ρ_nc; the two dominant cones; W as permutations with w(i) + w(2g+1−i) = 2g+1, W_M, and ^MW (Definition 1.3.1, p. 3), given by w^{−1}(g+1) ≺ ⋯ ≺ w^{−1}(2g) for the order g+1 ≺ ⋯ ≺ 2g ≺ 1 ≺ ⋯ ≺ g (sourceIssues E53); the sequence (w_1, …, w_g) and its meaning on C_w. The GSp_4 data at D5 become the case g = 2. PotentialAutomorphyInfrastructure (Reusable infrastructure for potential automorphy over CM fields) should import general ^MW from D3. Source to add: Boxer–Pilloni, Higher Coleman theory (arXiv:2110.10251), Lemma 3.1.2.

L2 ('General qcqs scheme compactification'; 'Construct common refinements'; 'Missing approximation, schematic closure, compactification and derived-coefficient lemmas are owned here') receives the category of compactifications of §2.1.1 (p. 7), as PAPER-ZAVYALOV-25 did for strict morphisms. It gains: strict maps ξ, those with ξ^⋆X = X (p. 7); Lemma 2.1.4, a map out of a compactification in which X is dense is strict; Lemma 2.1.5, compactifications whose boundary is an effective Cartier divisor are cofinal, with strict maps; Lemma 2.1.6, compactifications over which a given finite locally free sheaf extends to a locally free sheaf are cofinal, with strict maps. The layer must prove cofilteredness completely, including the equaliser of two parallel maps, a closed subscheme containing X that is again a compactification (sourceIssues E14). Corrections: in Lemma 2.1.5 blow up X̄, not X, at the ideal of the boundary (sourceIssues E13); Lemma 2.1.6's proof must be repaired, because Tag 0ESN requires scheme-theoretic density and constant rank (sourceIssues E12). One repair first replaces X̄ by the disjoint union of the scheme-theoretic closures of the constant-rank pieces of X and then applies Tag 0ESN. The other uses flattening by blow-up (Raynaud–Gruson, Theorem 5.2.2; Stacks Tag 0815) with centre disjoint from X. It imports Rees-algebra blow-ups from AlgebraicModuliForArithmeticGeometry (Algebraic moduli and representability for arithmetic geometry) R09.7a and coherent extension from SchemeAndStackFoundations (Scheme, stack, cohomology and intersection foundations) SF.0. Flattening by blow-up is planned in L5, but L5 depends on L2 through ClassicalAdicEtaleCohomology (The classical analytic cohomology inputs to diamonds) H1 and H5, so if the second repair is used, L2 must prove flattening by blow-up and L5 import it. Already a source: the Stacks Project; this paper cites its Tags 0F41 and 02OS (p. 7), and Tag 0815 is needed if flattening is used. Source to add, if flattening is used: Raynaud–Gruson, Critères de platitude et de projectivité (Invent. Math. 13, 1971), Théorème 5.2.2.

SF.0 ('Construct schemes, quasi-coherent modules ...'; 'State flat ... hypotheses as properties of named morphisms') receives two statements: every coherent sheaf on an open subscheme of a noetherian scheme extends to a coherent sheaf, and coherent sheaves on a noetherian scheme are pseudo-coherent (proof of Lemma 2.1.6, p. 7; Remark 2.3.3, p. 16); and Tor-independence of X → S and S′ → S, meaning Tor_i^{O_{S,s}}(O_{X,x}, O_{S′,s′}) = 0 for i > 0, equivalently O_{X×_S S′} = O_X ⊗^L_{O_S} O_{S′}, implied by flatness of either map (pp. 12, 22–23). The layer must state Tor-independence as a property of a cartesian square: the second base change formula needs X and C both Tor-independent from S′ over S (sourceIssues E35). SF.1 ('Prove effective fpqc/fppf descent for the required objects, algebraic-space quotients') receives the quotient of a (formal) scheme by a free action of a finite locally free group scheme with every orbit in an affine open: the fppf quotient exists and the map to it is a torsor (proof of Proposition 3.4.9, p. 38; Raynaud 1967). It is applied to the quotient of IG_{K^pP′(Z_p)_n} by the finite flat group scheme formed by the closure of K_{p,P} modulo that of P′(Z_p)_n (sourceIssues E61). SF.2 ('construct sheaf cohomology') receives the commutation of cohomology on quasi-compact quasi-separated schemes with filtered colimits of quasi-coherent sheaves (Stacks Tag 01FF; pp. 16–17). Source to add: Raynaud, Passage au quotient par une relation d'équivalence plate (1967). Already a source: the Stacks Project; this paper cites its Tags 0G41 and 01FF (pp. 7, 16).

SA.3 receives four general statements of §2, and part (i) of a theorem that §2 cites. Under 'Propositions 5.3.3, 5.3.7 and 5.3.12 (complete modules for finitely generated ideals)': the affine core of Lemma 2.9.3 (pp. 27–28), M ⊗_{R■} R̂^I = lim_n M ⊗ R/I^n for pseudo-coherent M ∈ D(R■); the paper is also a source for the planned Lemma 2.9.2 (p. 27), that R̂^I is an idempotent R■-algebra. Under 'The pre-analytic and analytic structures (A,S)■ (Definition 5.5.4)': part (i) of Clausen–Scholze's Theorem 8.13, which is cited on pp. 12 and 18: for maps R → B of finitely generated Z-algebras, (B,R)■ with (B,R)■[S] = R■[S] ⊗_R B is analytic; and the passage from M ∈ D(A■) with an endomorphism T to D((A[T],A)■) (§2.4.1, p. 18). As footnote 2 suggests, the layer must build it ∞-categorically: D((A[T],A)■) is equivalent to the ∞-category of pairs (M, T), realised by M ⊗_A A[X] → M ⊗_A A[X] with differential X − T in degrees −1 and 0 (sourceIssues E23, E28). Next to 'D(Z[T]■) as a localisation of D((Z[T],Z)■)': A[[T]] ⊗^L_{(A[T],A)■} A[T,T^{−1}]■ = 0 (pp. 18, 24; sourceIssues E38), so M^ord = 0 for every (A[[T]],A)■-module. Under 'Finite-type algebras (RC §5.3)': Lemma 2.6.4 (p. 21), N ⊗^L_{A■} M = N ⊗^L_{B■} (B ⊗^L_A M) for a map A → B of finitely generated Z-algebras, M a complex of discrete A-modules, N ∈ D(B■). The sheaf form of Lemma 2.9.3 and its RΓ formula belong to AnalyticStacks (Six-functor formalisms and analytic stacks) AS.3. Already a source: Scholze (with Clausen), Lectures on Condensed Mathematics (2019), which this paper cites as Clausen–Scholze; this paper uses its Lecture VIII (Theorem 8.13), which the roadmap does not yet read.

CC.3 covers the duality between admissible and perfect complexes, under 'Establish biduality only in its compact/discrete or admissible category' and 'Prove its module structure over O[[K₀]] for a compact open K₀'. It receives Definition 1.4.1 (p. 4): a complex in D(Z_p[T′(Z_p)]) is admissible of amplitude [a, b] if it is represented by a bounded complex in degrees [a, b] with terms C^0(T′(Z_p), Z_p)^{n_i}; Remark 1.4.2 (p. 5): its Z_p-dual is a perfect Λ′-complex of amplitude [−b, −a], where Λ′ = Z_p[[T′(Z_p)]]; and the anti-equivalence in the proof of Lemma 5.4.2 (p. 57): i(M) = Hom_{Z_p}(M, Z_p) takes admissible complexes to perfect Λ-complexes, and with j(M) = (M ⊗̂_{Z_p} Λ)^{T(Z_p)} the composite j ∘ i^{−1} is Hom_Λ(−, Λ). The layer must state these for a profinite group G, with T′(Z_p) and T(Z_p) as instances, proved degreewise from the identification of the Z_p-dual of C(G, Z_p) with Z_p[[G]] (PadicMeasuresIwasawaAlgebras (P-adic measures, completed group algebras, and characteristic ideals) L1). On the admissible side the terms must be direct summands of C(G, Z_p)^{n_i}, because projective Z_p[[G]]-modules need not be free when G is not pro-p. For pro-p G, such as T′(Z_p), Z_p[[G]] is local and the terms are C(G, Z_p)^{n_i}, as in Definition 1.4.1. It must use the completed tensor product: the identity RHom_{T′(Z_p)}(1, C^0(T′(Z_p), Z_p) ⊗̂_{Z_p} Λ) = Λ[0] in the proof of Lemma 5.4.1 (p. 56) fails for the algebraic one (sourceIssues E9). It must fix the action of T(Z_p) on Λ as t ↦ [t] and say which Λ-module structure the dual carries, contragredient or transpose, which differ by the involution [t] ↦ [t^{−1}]; the specialisation statements depend on these conventions (sourceIssues E110), and the Λ-adic Serre duality of Theorem 5.5.2 (p. 57) also needs the twist by the involution induced by t ↦ w_0t^{−1} (sourceIssues E7). Perfect complexes come from DeformationAndDerivedPatchingAlgebra (Commutative algebra for deformation theory and patching) P7. Source to add: this paper, §1.4 and §5.4.

T0 ('Extend that same API to the generic-fibre Tate modules ...'; 'Extend the local construction to semi-abelian degeneration charts') holds Fargues's degree (routed there from Pilloni 2020) and gains, from §4.1.8 (p. 41) and §4.2.7 (p. 44): a finite flat group scheme H, generically étale over a p-adic base, has an effective Cartier divisor D_H with complement the étale locus, D_H + D_{H^D} = V(p^h) for H of order p^h, and over a complete rank-one valuation ring with v(p) = 1, D_H = (x) and deg H = v(x). From the proof of Proposition 4.2.8 (p. 45), beside the additivity and monotonicity along generic isomorphisms routed here from Pilloni (2020): a generic isomorphism u: H_1 → H_2 has deg H_1 = deg H_2 exactly when u is an isomorphism. Pages 45–46: deg G[p^m] = m·dim G; a BT_n of dimension d has degree nd; 0 ≤ deg H ≤ h, with the extremes exactly for H étale and H multiplicative. The layer must also treat an isogeny f of semi-abelian schemes over a normal Z_p-flat base such that f is étale after inverting p; its kernel is in general only quasi-finite and flat at the boundary. It defines the divisor of f as the zero locus of det Lie(f), proves that this is an effective Cartier divisor, additive under composition, and equal to Fargues's divisor of ker f where ker f is finite. The Siegel identity D_i + D_{2g+1−i} = V(p^n) is then proved with the divisors D_i in HigherHidaAndColemanTheory (Hida and Coleman families, period modules, and family L-functions, Part II: higher Hida and higher Coleman theory for coherent cohomology) (sourceIssues E67). The corrected proofs of Corollary 4.2.10 and Proposition 4.2.15 use the equality case (sourceIssues E77). Already added as a source by the Pilloni (2020) extraction: Fargues, La filtration de Harder–Narasimhan des schémas en groupes finis et plats (Crelle 645, 2010); this paper uses §2 Déf. 3, §2 Lemme 3 and §3 Cor. 3.

R09.7a ('Construct blowups by the Rees algebra with their projective universal property, affine charts') receives Proposition-construction 4.1.11 (p. 42): for effective Cartier divisors D_1, D_2 on a scheme X̄ and the blow-up p : X̃ → X̄ along the ideal generated by O(−D_1) and O(−D_2), there are effective Cartier divisors D′_1, D′_2 on X̃ with disjoint supports and p^*D_1 + D′_2 = p^*D_2 + D′_1, given locally by the degree-one sections x′_i of O(1). The layer must state it for arbitrary schemes, outside the characteristic-zero scope of the resolution algorithm. A0-extension ('Extend proper-flat coherent cohomology and base change beyond curves') already receives from the Pilloni (2020) extraction f^! for lci maps, fundamental classes, and the fundamental class of a finite flat map as its trace. This paper adds the case of Fakhruddin–Pilloni's Proposition 2.6 used in the proof of Proposition 4.3.11 (p. 48), for quasi-finite lci maps of relative dimension 0 between schemes smooth over Z_p: p_1^!O is an invertible sheaf in degree 0, there is a fundamental class O → p_1^!O, and where p_1 is finite flat it is the trace. In the application the open sets are the complements of ∪_i D_i ∩ D_{2g+1−i} (sourceIssues E88). Its comparison with the solid f^! of AnalyticStacks (Six-functor formalisms and analytic stacks) AS.3 belongs where both are used, not here. Sources to add: Fakhruddin–Pilloni, Hecke operators and the coherent cohomology of Shimura varieties (2021), Proposition 2.6; this paper, §4.1.10.

AF.1 ('Define relative Lie algebra cochains Hom_K(∧^q(g/k),V)') and AF.4 ('Define algebraic highest weights, infinitesimal characters and cohomological representations') receive Harris's genus-g statement, Theorem 1.3.8 (p. 4): for κ ∈ X⋆(T)^{M_µ,+} and w ∈ C(κ) there is a non-degenerate limit of discrete series π_∞(κ, w) of G(R), determined by κ and w, such that π_∞(κ, w) ⊗ V_κ has (p_µ, K_∞)-cohomology in degree ℓ(w). AF.4 also receives C(κ) = {w ∈ ^MW : w^{−1}w_{0,M}(κ + ρ) ∈ X⋆(T)^−_Q} (p. 48), with its non-emptiness and the independence of w^{−1}w_{0,M}(κ + ρ) from w ∈ C(κ), as the antidominant cone is a fundamental domain for W. The layer must add (p_µ, K_∞)-cohomology relative to the parabolic p_µ, not only (g, K)-cohomology, for GSp_{2g}; PAPER-PILLONI-20 and PAPER-CALEGARI-GERAGHTY-20 asked for it for GSp_4. Corrections: the degree ℓ(w) does not determine π_∞(κ, w); drop the uniqueness claim (sourceIssues E5); the introduction's definition of C(κ) must be read in X⋆(T)_Q, as on p. 48 (sourceIssues E3). AF.4 imports ^MW and w_{0,M} from ShimuraData (Shimura data, Hermitian domains, and adelic level structures) D3, and ρ and the GSp_{2g} cones from D5. The GSp_4 cases and chambers already routed to AF.1 and AF.4 become g = 2 instances. Already a source, added by PAPER-CALEGARI-GERAGHTY-20: Harris, Automorphic forms and the cohomology of vector bundles on Shimura varieties (1990); this paper uses its Theorem 3.4.

P7 ('construct minimal representatives over local rings'; 'Prove derived Nakayama'; 'Define perfectness through local finite-projective resolutions') receives two statements. Lemma 2.6.6 (pp. 21–22): over a local ring A, a complex M⁰ → M¹ → M² of finite free modules that is exact modulo m_A is exact, with ker(d₀) a direct summand of M⁰, Im(d₀) of M¹ and Im(d₁) of M² (sourceIssues E33 corrects the second). It is the step of the minimal-complex theory behind the perfectness criterion Lemma 2.6.7 (p. 22), which is planned here and for which the paper is also a source. From the proof of Proposition 2.3.13 (p. 17): for a pseudo-coherent P and a filtered system E_n all in D^{≥a} for one fixed a, Hom(P, colim E_n) = colim Hom(P, E_n), by replacing P with a perfect complex that agrees with it in the relevant degrees. The layer must state the uniform lower bound as a hypothesis; checking it is the step missing from that proof (sourceIssues E26). P7 states the ring form. The form on a noetherian scheme used in Proposition 2.3.13 is derived where it is used, from the ring form and the commutation of cohomology with filtered colimits in SchemeAndStackFoundations (Scheme, stack, cohomology and intersection foundations) SF.2. The layer must state Lemma 2.6.6 for an arbitrary local ring, as the paper does, and the colimit statement for a pseudo-coherent complex over any ring, beyond its setting of complete noetherian local O-algebras. Source to add: this paper, §2.3.12 and §2.6.5.

C3 ('Prove the structure-sheaf pushforward and the normality statements used to compare sections under refinements. Where higher direct images are required, make their vanishing a separate theorem') receives Proposition 7.5 of Lan (2017), which §3.4.15 (p. 39) invokes: for a refinement Σ′ of Σ, the toroidal compactification for Σ′ is obtained by blowing up along the boundary, and coherent cohomology (of the canonical and subcanonical extensions) does not depend on the cone decomposition. The paper applies it to the partial toroidal compactifications IG^tor_{K^pK_{p,P},Σ} of the ordinary Igusa formal schemes. The layer must state the vanishing of higher direct images locally on the target through the toroidal charts, so that it applies to integral models at deep level and to partial toroidal compactifications of ordinary Igusa varieties. C4 ('Construct semi-abelian schemes, their character groups, extensions of abelian schemes by tori, biextensions') receives Faltings–Chai I, Proposition 2.7: over a normal noetherian base, a homomorphism of semi-abelian schemes given over a dense open subscheme extends uniquely; hence so does a quasi-isogeny (§4.1.1, p. 41; Lemma 4.2.2, p. 43). The layer must note that the kernel of an extended isogeny is quasi-finite and flat but in general not finite at the boundary (sourceIssues E67). Consumers: ShimuraCompactificationsPartIIHodgeTypeIntegralBoundary (Toroidal compactifications and boundary geometry, Part II: integral boundary charts of Hodge type), IgusaVarietiesAndTorsionConcentrationPartIISiegelOrdinary (Igusa varieties, compactified period fibers and torsion concentration, Part II: ordinary Igusa formal schemes of Siegel varieties) and HigherHidaAndColemanTheory (Hida and Coleman families, period modules, and family L-functions, Part II: higher Hida and higher Coleman theory for coherent cohomology). Already a source: Faltings–Chai, Degeneration of abelian varieties; this paper uses I, Proposition 2.7. Source to add: Lan, Integral models of toroidal compactifications with projective cone decompositions (IMRN 2017), Proposition 7.5.

A4 ('Prove the Serre–Tate equivalence for deformations of abelian schemes with endomorphism and polarization structures') receives Katz's Serre–Tate local moduli, used in the proof of Proposition 3.4.9 (p. 38): the deformation space of a polarised ordinary abelian variety over a perfect field k, with trivialised étale and multiplicative parts of its p-divisible group, is a formal torus, with its canonical Frobenius. The Pilloni (2020) extraction routed the genus-two case here and asked for the general statement; this paper needs every genus g. The layer must state it for all g with the polarisation, so that the formal torus is the torus of symmetric maps, Ĝ_m ⊗ Sym² Z_p^g in the paper's coordinates; the proposed IgusaVarietiesAndTorsionConcentrationPartIISiegelOrdinary (Igusa varieties, compactified period fibers and torsion concentration, Part II: ordinary Igusa formal schemes of Siegel varieties) applies it to the simply transitive action of T̂_{P′(Z_p)} ≅ Ĝ_m ⊗ Sym² Z_p^g on formal completions of Igusa varieties. That identification uses the étale-first ordering of X_ord (sourceIssues E55). Already a source, added by the Pilloni (2020) extraction: Katz, Serre–Tate local moduli, Lecture Notes in Math. 868 (1981), 138–202.

The layer's 'Construct trace for finite locally free algebras and finite étale analytic maps, its base-change and composition laws, and its compatibility with algebraic trace' covers the algebraic statement used in the proof of Lemma 2.6.11 (p. 22): if B → C is finite étale and Spec C → Spec B is surjective, the trace Tr_{C/B} : C → B is surjective, so some c₀ ∈ C has Tr(c₀) = 1. The layer must add this surjectivity for faithfully flat finite étale algebras over an arbitrary ring, as a property of the algebraic trace it compares with. This creates a link from the layer to IntegralCoherentHeckeComplexes (Automorphic bundles and classical automorphic forms, Part II: integral coherent cohomology and Hecke-equivariant perfect complexes), which uses it to show that r_⋆O_Y is locally projective over O_X[G] for a finite étale Galois cover r : Y → X with group G. LI.3's 'abelian and exact categories, resolutions, derived functors, spectral sequences' covers the homological input of the proof of Theorem 2.9.7 (p. 28): a finite chain A_{d−1}^• → ⋯ → A_{−1}^• of maps of bounded above complexes can be replaced, up to homotopy equivalence, by bounded above complexes in which every map A_i^• → A_{i−1}^• is a termwise split injection (Stacks Tag 014M), so that A_{−1}^• becomes a finitely filtered complex whose spectral sequence (Stacks Tag 012M) is the Cousin spectral sequence. The layer must add this replacement lemma for finite chains, proved with mapping cylinders, next to the spectral sequence of a filtered complex, which it already plans (the paper cites Stacks Tag 012M for it). Its consumer is the Cousin spectral sequence of AnalyticStacks (Six-functor formalisms and analytic stacks) AS.3. No correction is needed. Already a source: the Stacks Project; this paper cites its Tags 014M and 012M on p. 28.

IHG.2 ('For a Hecke action on a bounded perfect complex define its finite image algebras ... Prove localization decompositions over complete coefficient rings ... and finite generation') receives the finiteness used in the proof of Lemma 2.4.3 (p. 18): for a noetherian ring A and bounded complexes M, N of finitely generated A-modules, Hom_{D(A)}(M, N) is a finitely generated A-module, so the A-subalgebra of End_{D(A)}(M) generated by one endomorphism T is finite; and D(A), having countable direct sums, is idempotent complete (Bökstedt–Neeman), so every idempotent e of End_{D(A)}(M) splits, M ≅ eM ⊕ (1 − e)M. sourceIssues.printed: "We fix a point h ∈ 𝓗_g corresponding to a map h : Res_{ℂ/ℝ}(𝔾_m) → G_ℝ. We let µ be the Hodge cocharacter associated to h, P_µ be the Siegel parabolic of G associated to µ, and M_µ be the unipotent radical of P_µ."
sourceIssues.correction: "… and M_µ be the Levi of P_µ." Here M_µ is the Levi subgroup containing T, which is the centralizer of µ. With µ(z) = diag(Id_g, z·Id_g) it is isomorphic to GL_g × 𝔾_m. This is how §3.1, p. 33 defines it.
sourceIssues.reason:
The page image confirms the printed sentence word for word: "M_µ be the unipotent radical of P_µ". Every other use of M_µ in the paper, including the next sentences, treats it as the Levi of P_µ.

(i) p. 2: "Let us fix a maximal torus and a Borel T ⊆ B ⊆ P_µ ⊆ G. Let Rep(M_µ) be the category of finite dimensional algebraic representations of M_µ. Irreducible representations are labeled by M_µ-dominant weights κ ∈ X⋆(T)^{M_µ,+}. The tower of Shimura varieties carries a natural M_µ-torsor". The unipotent radical of the Siegel parabolic is the commutative vector group Sym² of dimension g(g+1)/2. In characteristic 0 its only irreducible algebraic representation is the trivial one, and it contains no maximal torus of G. So a labelling by dominant weights of T makes no sense for it. The automorphic vector bundles ω^κ come from representations of the Levi GL_g × 𝔾_m.

(ii) p. 2, §1.2: "the unipotent subgroup of the Borel of M_µ(ℤ_p)". This only makes sense if M_µ is reductive.

(iii) p. 3, §1.3: "W_M be the Weyl group of M_µ". Also ^MW is the set of minimal length representatives of W_M\W.

(iv) p. 4, §1.3.7: K_∞ ⊆ G(ℝ), the stabilizer of h, "is a real form of M_µ". K_∞ is compact modulo centre (a unitary group in g variables, with similitudes). It is a real form of GL_g × 𝔾_m, never of a unipotent group.

(v) §3.1, p. 33 sets up the notation correctly: "Let M_µ = M be the Levi and U_P be the unipotent radical." It also gives dominance "for the Levi M" as k_1 ≥ ⋯ ≥ k_g and says "W_M be the Weyl group of the Levi M". p. 36 says "We recall that M = M_µ is the Levi of P_µ = P."

So the words "unipotent radical" in §1.1 are a slip for "Levi". The paper's own conventions do not support the printed reading. Because §3 re-defines M_µ correctly and all proofs and results use it as the Levi, the slip affects nothing beyond this sentence of the introduction.

sourceIssues.locator: §1.2 (Hida theory), last sentence of the paragraph beginning "In [Pil20], we considered the case g = 2", p. 2. The 2024 preprint does not contain this sentence: its §1.2 says only "Results in this direction have already appeared in [Pil20], [BCGP21], [LPSZ19], [BP20] for g = 1 and g = 2". The whole paragraph describing the complex M^0 → M^1 of [Pil20], this sentence included, was added in the revision.
sourceIssues.printed: In the current paper we show that the modules M^0 and M^1 actually extend over the entire weight space : they are higher Hida theories for H^0 and H^1 (interpolating regular weight cohomology).
sourceIssues.correction: Replace the sentence with one that says only what the paper proves: "In the current paper we construct higher Hida theories for H^0 and H^1 over the entire weight space. These are the complexes M^•_w for w = Id and for the element w_1 of length one of ^MW (§5.2, §5.4). They interpolate ordinary H^0 and H^1 in the regular weights with C(κ) = {Id}, resp. {w_1} (Corollary 4.5.5, Proposition 1.4.7). In the singular weights ω^{(k,2)} we have C(κ) = {Id, w_1}. There the Cousin spectral sequence (Theorem 4.5.2) computes the ordinary part of H^0 and H^1 at Iwahori level from their specialisations, which is the role that M^0 → M^1 plays in [Pil20]." The claim that the complex of [Pil20] is itself a restriction of M^•_Id and M^•_{w_1} should either be dropped or be stated and proved separately. Such a statement would have to pass from Iwahori level to Klingen level (see the reason).
sourceIssues.reason:
The sentence on p. 2 says that the paper shows that the terms M^0 and M^1 of the complex of [Pil20], which is built along the one-variable line of weights ω^{(k,2)}, extend over the whole weight space. The body never states or proves such a comparison. [Pil20] is cited in the body only twice, and neither citation concerns its complex M^0 → M^1. On p. 56, in the proof of Theorem 5.3.5, the ordinary cohomology of a kernel vanishes "as in [Pil20], sect. 10.7". On p. 63, in the proof of Proposition 6.2.13, the proof says "Compare with [Pil20], sect. 10.7". The weights ω^{(k,2)} and the singular line never reappear after p. 2.

The best defence is to read the sentence loosely, and in that sense the intended content is proved. The complexes M^•_Id and M^•_{w_1} are defined over Λ = Z_p[[T(Z_p)]] (§5.2, §5.4). They specialise in every locally algebraic weight (Theorem 5.3.5, Remark 5.4.3), and they interpolate regular-weight H^0 and H^1 (Corollary 4.5.5, Proposition 1.4.7). For κ = (k,2) we have C(κ) = {Id, w_1}, and the Cousin spectral sequence (Theorem 4.5.2) builds the ordinary H^0 and H^1 from their two specialisations. The notions of ordinarity also agree on Hecke parameters. By [Pil20] (the discussion of the T-operator before its §7.1), for r = 2 ordinarity for the Klingen operator diag(p², p, p, 1) is equivalent to Newton = Hodge, i.e. α_p β_p is a unit. That is also the condition of Definition 1.3.5.

The literal claim still needs an argument that is not formal and that the paper does not give. The objects differ as follows:
- **Level and ordinary projector.** [Pil20] works at Klingen level with the projector of the single operator U. The present paper works at (deep) Iwahori level with the T^{++}(Q_p)-ordinary projector.
- **Coefficients and support.** [Pil20] uses a sheaf F^κ over Z_p[[Z_p^×]] on the p-rank ≥ 1 locus, and its two terms come from the ordinary locus and from local cohomology along the p-rank-one locus. The paper uses Igusa towers with the support conditions of §§4–5.

The levels really do give different answers. Take an unramified π_p with slopes (0, 0, k+1, k+1) and α_p ≠ β_p:
- On the Klingen invariants of π_p (dimension 4), the Klingen U has eigenvalues proportional to α_pβ_p, α_pγ_p, β_pδ_p and γ_pδ_p. Only the first is a unit, so π_p contributes once to the complex of [Pil20].
- The stabiliser of the singular ν+ρ has order 2, so π_p has two characters that are ordinary in weight κ (orderings (α, β, γ, δ) and (β, α, δ, γ)). So π_p contributes twice to the Iwahori-level abutment.

Hence the specialisations of M^•_Id and M^•_{w_1} along the line are not literally the terms of the complex of [Pil20]. At best that complex is a Klingen-level descent or direct factor of them, which the paper does not construct.

The paper also proves only that M^•_{w_1,cusp} has amplitude [0, 1] (Proposition 5.6.3). So even its restriction to the line is not shown to be a module in degree 1, as M^1 is in [Pil20].

Consequences: the passage is used nowhere later in the paper. No numbered statement and no proof depends on it, and Theorems 1.4.3, 1.4.8 and 4.5.2 are unaffected. The rewording given in the correction describes accurately what the paper proves, and it is the minimal fix. The kind is a gap because the sentence asserts a comparison with the complex of [Pil20] that is nowhere proved; it affects nothing because no later statement or proof uses it.

review.reason: Confirmed as a gap. The sentence printed at the end of §1.2 is `In the current paper we show that the modules $M^0$ and $M^1$ actually extend over the entire weight space : they are higher Hida theories for $H^0$ and $H^1$', and those $M^0,M^1$ are the terms of the two-step complex of [Pil20]. sourceIssues.printed: We define C(κ) = {w ∈ ^MW, −w^{−1}w_{0,M}(κ + ρ) ∈ X^⋆(T)^+}. We let ν + ρ = −w^{−1}w_{0,M}(κ + ρ) for any w ∈ C(κ).
sourceIssues.correction: C(κ) = {w ∈ ^MW : −w^{−1}w_{0,M}(κ + ρ) ∈ X^⋆(T)^+_Q}. The dominance condition has to be read in X^⋆(T)_Q. This is how the body defines the set on p. 48: "C(κ) = {w ∈ ^MW, w^{−1}w_{0,M}(κ+ρ) ∈ X^⋆(T)^−_Q}".
sourceIssues.reason: The paper's coordinates (§3.1, pp. 33–34) are X^⋆(T) = {(k_1,…,k_g;k) ∈ Z^g×Z : Σk_i ≡ k mod 2}. Roots are trivial on the centre, so they have k = 0. Computing directly from the Borel of p. 34 gives ρ = (−1,−2,…,−g; 0), which is dominant for 0 ≥ k_1 ≥ … ≥ k_g. Because Σρ_i = −g(g+1)/2, ρ lies in X^⋆(T) exactly when g ≡ 0 or 3 mod 4. Take κ ∈ X^⋆(T). For every u ∈ W, uρ − ρ lies in the root lattice, and 2ρ ∈ X^⋆(T). Hence −w^{−1}w_{0,M}(κ+ρ) ≡ ρ modulo X^⋆(T). So when g ≡ 1 or 2 mod 4, which includes g = 1 and g = 2, this element is never in X^⋆(T). On p. 34, X^⋆(T)^+ is a subset of X^⋆(T), so the set as printed is empty. For example, when g = 1 we have ρ = (−1;0), and w = 1 gives (1−k_1; −k), whose coordinate sum 1−k_1+k is odd. That contradicts the next sentence ("If ν+ρ is regular, then the set C(κ) contains a unique element") and Remark 1.4.5 (#C(κ) = 1). With the rational dominant cone, as on p. 48, everything is consistent: ν = −w^{−1}w_{0,M}(κ+ρ) − ρ is integral, as Theorem 1.4.3(5) requires. The intended meaning is clear from p. 48.

sourceIssues.reason: On p. 2, colim_K RΓ(S^tor_{K,Σ}, ω^κ) is the colimit over all compact open K ⊆ G(A_f), a complex of smooth G(A_f)-representations. Take its Jacquet module with respect to B ⊆ G(Q_p), then T_{K_p}-invariants and the ordinary part. The result is a smooth G(A_f^p)-representation, namely colim_{K^p} RΓ(S^tor_{K^pK_p}, ω^κ)^{ord}. The colimit over K'_p with K^p fixed is admissible. With K^p fixed, the display is the standard identity (the canonical lifting of Casselman). The intended meaning is clear.

sourceIssues.locator: §1.3.7, Theorem 1.3.8, p. 4. The January 2024 preprint has the same statement as Theorem 1.3.7 (§1.3.6, p. 3 of the preprint), with (𝔭, K∞) in place of (𝔭_µ, K∞). The mistake was therefore already in the preprint and was not fixed in the revision.
sourceIssues.printed: Theorem 1.3.8 ([Har90], thm. 3.4). Let κ ∈ X⋆(T)^{Mµ,+} and w ∈ C(κ). There exists a unique non degenerate limit of discrete series representation π∞(κ, w) of G(R), with the property that π∞(κ, w) ⊗ Vκ has (𝔭_µ, K∞)-cohomology in degree ℓ(w).
sourceIssues.correction:
Drop the claim that the cohomological degree characterises the representation. A correct form: "Let κ ∈ X⋆(T)^{Mµ,+} and w ∈ C(κ). There is a non-degenerate limit of discrete series π∞(κ, w) of G(R), determined by κ and w, such that π∞(κ, w) ⊗ Vκ has (𝔭_µ, K∞)-cohomology in degree ℓ(w)." Here κ fixes the Harish-Chandra parameter λ = −w_{0,M}(κ + ρ). The element w fixes the Weyl chamber w·C⁺, where C⁺ is the dominant chamber; the closure of w·C⁺ contains λ. π∞(κ, w) is the representation of G(R) induced from the limit of discrete series of G(R)^+ with these data. The degree ℓ(w) alone determines π∞(κ, w) only when no other element of C(κ) of the same length gives a different representation. For G(R) = GSp_{2g}(R) this fails for every g ≥ 4.

In the other direction, distinct elements of C(κ) give distinct limits of discrete series of G(R)^+, but not necessarily distinct representations of GSp_{2g}(R). The elements w and w_{0,M} w w_0 give the same representation of G(R) whenever both lie in C(κ). This happens exactly when κ = −w_{0,M}κ − 2ρ_nc on the derived group. The simplest case is g = 1 in weight one: the weight-one limit of discrete series of GL_2(R) contributes to both H^0 and H^1.
sourceIssues.reason:
Conventions of §3.1 (pp. 33–34). X⋆(T)^+ is given by 0 ≥ k_1 ≥ … ≥ k_g, and Mµ-dominance by k_1 ≥ … ≥ k_g. The positive roots are e_i − e_j and −e_i − e_j (i < j) and −2e_i, with simple roots −2e_1 and the e_i − e_{i+1}. So ρ = (−1, −2, …, −g) on the derived group. The roots of M are the e_i − e_j, W_M = S_g, and d = g(g+1)/2. Put λ = −w_{0,M}(κ + ρ). The definition on p. 3 then reads C(κ) = {w ∈ ^MW : w(ν + ρ) = λ}. Since κ + ρ is strictly decreasing, λ is regular for the roots of M. So every w ∈ W with w(ν + ρ) = λ lies in ^MW, and C(κ) is a coset of the stabiliser of ν + ρ.

Counterexample for g = 4. Take κ = (3,3,3,3; k) with k even; this is parallel weight 3. Then κ + ρ = (2, 1, 0, −1), λ = (1, 0, −1, −2) and ν + ρ = (0, −1, −1, −2). The stabiliser of ν + ρ is generated by the reflections in −2e_1 and e_2 − e_3 and has order 4. So C(κ) has four elements:
- x ↦ (−x_2, x_1, x_3, x_4), of length 2;
- w: x ↦ (−x_2, −x_1, x_3, x_4), of length 3;
- w′: x ↦ (−x_3, x_1, x_2, x_4), of length 3;
- x ↦ (−x_3, −x_1, x_2, x_4), of length 4.
Each sends ν + ρ to λ and maps the dominant cone into the Mµ-dominant cone. The positive roots made negative are −e_1 − e_2, −2e_1, −2e_2 for w, and e_1 − e_3, e_2 − e_3, −2e_3 for w′. So ℓ(w) = ℓ(w′) = 3.

Identify the compact Cartan of K∞ with T, so that the compact roots are the roots of M. As in [Har90], each u ∈ C(κ) corresponds to the limit of discrete series π(λ, uC⁺) of G(R)^+ with Harish-Chandra parameter λ and chamber uC⁺. Here π(λ, uC⁺) ⊗ Vκ has (𝔭_µ, K∞)-cohomology in degree ℓ(u) and in no other degree. π(λ, uC⁺) is non-degenerate because λ is regular for every compact root. By Knapp–Zuckerman, π(λ, wC⁺) ≅ π(λ, w′C⁺) would require an element of W_K = W_M that fixes λ and carries wC⁺ to w′C⁺. Since λ is M-regular, that element is trivial, so the two representations of G(R)^+ are inequivalent.

The same holds for G(R) = GSp_8(R). K∞ lies in G(R)^+, which has index 2. An element δ of similitude −1 normalises K∞ and inverts its compact Cartan. Hence δπ(λ, uC⁺) ≅ π(λ*, w_{0,M}uw_0·C⁺) with λ* = −w_{0,M}λ = (2, 1, 0, −1), which is not W_M-conjugate to λ. So each π(λ, uC⁺) induces to an irreducible representation of G(R) whose restriction to G(R)^+ is π(λ, uC⁺) ⊕ δπ(λ, uC⁺). The inductions for w and w′ are non-isomorphic, because π(λ, w′C⁺) is neither π(λ, wC⁺) nor δπ(λ, wC⁺).

For u = w or w′, the δ-constituent belongs to the Serre-dual weight κ* = −w_{0,M}κ − 2ρ_nc = (2,2,2,2) and to the element w_{0,M}uw_0 ∈ C(κ*), of length 10 − 3 = 7. Its cohomology is against V_{κ*}, and it has none against Vκ, because its parameter λ* is not W_M-conjugate to λ. So G(R) has two non-isomorphic non-degenerate limits of discrete series, each with (𝔭_µ, K∞)-cohomology against Vκ in degree 3 = ℓ(w) = ℓ(w′), and in that degree only. This contradicts the uniqueness asserted in the theorem.

If instead the parameter attached to κ is normalised as κ + ρ = λ*, each π(λ, uC⁺) is replaced by its δ-conjugate, and the representations of G(R) are the same. The weights (2,2,2,2) and (2,2,2,0) give further examples for g = 4: in each, C(κ) has lengths 6, 7, 7, 8 and λ ≠ −w_{0,M}λ.

Every g ≥ 4. Take κ = (3,3,3,3,0,…,0; k) with k even. Then ν + ρ = (0, −1, −1, −2, −5, −6, …, −g) and λ = (g, …, 6, 5, 1, 0, −1, −2). The stabiliser of ν + ρ is generated by the commuting simple reflections in −2e_1 and e_2 − e_3. So C(κ) is m times this group of order 4, with m of minimal length in the coset, and its lengths are ℓ(m), ℓ(m) + 1, ℓ(m) + 1, ℓ(m) + 2. For example they are 7, 8, 8, 9 for g = 5. Since −2 is an entry of λ and 2 is not, λ* is not W_M-conjugate to λ, and the argument above applies unchanged.

Small g.
- For g ≤ 2 the lengths on ^MW (0, 1, resp. 0, 1, 2, 3) are pairwise distinct, so the question does not arise.
- For g = 3 the lengths on ^MW are 0, 1, 2, 3, 3, 4, 5, 6. The two elements of length 3 are x ↦ (−x_2, −x_1, x_3) and x ↦ (−x_3, x_1, x_2). Both lie in C(κ) only when ν + ρ = (0, b, b) with b < 0. Then λ = (−b, 0, b) = −w_{0,M}λ. An example is κ = (2,2,2), where C(κ) has lengths 2, 3, 3, 4.
- The involution w ↦ w_{0,M} w w_0 of ^MW has no fixed points, because w_0 = −1 is central in W and w_{0,M} ≠ w_0. So in this case it exchanges the two elements of length 3. Their limits of discrete series of G(R)^+ are δ-conjugate, and together they form one irreducible representation of GSp_6(R). For κ = (2,2,2), Blattner's formula gives their lowest K-types as (1, 1, −2) and (2, −1, −1), and x ↦ −w_{0,M}x exchanges them.
So for G(R) = GSp_{2g}(R) the uniqueness holds for g ≤ 3 and fails for every g ≥ 4. For G(R)^+ or Sp_{2g}(R) it already fails for g = 3.

The paper itself allows several elements of C(κ) of the same length. Theorem 1.4.3(5) (p. 5) and Theorem 4.5.2 (p. 51) sum over the w ∈ C(κ) of a given length (ℓ(w) = a, resp. ℓ(w) = p).

Classification. The uniqueness is a substantive claim, false as printed, and not a slip whose intended meaning is clear from context; so this is an error. What is false is the numbered Theorem 1.3.8 itself, so the error affects a stated result. Its reach ends there. Theorem 1.3.8 is a recollection in the introduction, and limits of discrete series appear nowhere else in the paper. The sentence after it (π_f ↪ colim_K H^{ℓ(w)}) is indexed by w ∈ C(κ) and does not use uniqueness. The same holds for the Cousin spectral sequence (Theorem 1.4.3(5), Theorem 4.5.2). So no proof in the paper depends on the uniqueness, and the main results are unaffected.

review.reason: Confirmed as printed, and the uniqueness clause is what fails. Theorem 1.3.8 asserts a *unique* non-degenerate limit of discrete series $\pi_\infty(\kappa,w)$ whose tensor with $V_\kappa$ has $(\mathfrak p_\mu,K_\infty)$-cohomology in degree $\ell(w)$, so it characterises the representation by the degree alone. Two elements of $C(\kappa)$ of equal length give two representations with cohomology in the same degree, and conversely $w$ and $w_{0,M}ww_0$ can give the same representation of $G(\R)$ while being distinct in $^MW$; the finding's smallest instance, the weight-one limit of discrete series of $\mathrm{GL}_2(\R)$ contributing to both $H^0$ and $H^1$, is the familiar one. The repair is to drop `unique' and say that $\pi_\infty(\kappa,w)$ is determined by $\kappa$ and $w$ — which is what the rest of the paper uses, since it always names both.

sourceIssues.locator: §1.3.7 (Archimedean representation theory and limits of discrete series), the paragraph after Theorem 1.3.8, p. 4. The 2024 preprint has the same text in §1.3.6, after Theorem 1.3.7, p. 3.
sourceIssues.printed: Let π = π∞(κ, w) ⊗ πf be an automorphic representation. Then πf ↪ colimK H^{ℓ(w)}(S^{tor}_{K,Σ}, ω^κ) ⊗ ℂ. When w = Id, π∞(κ, Id) is a holomorphic limit of discrete series and the representation π is generated by holomorphic modular forms.
sourceIssues.correction: Add the word "cuspidal": "Let π = π∞(κ, w) ⊗ πf be a cuspidal automorphic representation. Then πf ↪ colim_K H^{ℓ(w)}(S^{tor}_{K,Σ}, ω^κ) ⊗ C." This is the standard statement from Harris: cusp forms of ∂̄-cohomology type give classes in the coherent cohomology of the canonical extension. The failure only happens when ℓ(w) ≥ 1. For w = Id, a holomorphic automorphic form of moderate growth is a section of ω^κ over the toroidal compactification, and H^0 is left exact. So the degree-0 case, and the following sentence about w = Id, hold for every automorphic π.
sourceIssues.reason:
The paper sets G = GSp_{2g}, and nothing in this recollection excludes g = 1. Take g = 1, so G = GL_2. M_µ is then the torus, ^M W = {Id, w_0}, and ℓ(w_0) = 1. Fix k ≥ 3 and the weight κ with ω^κ = ω^{2−k} in classical notation. Then C(κ) = {w_0}, and π∞(κ, w_0) is the antiholomorphic discrete series D_k^- (after matching the central character by a twist). This is the representation that computes H^1(X, ω^{2−k}) by Dolbeault cohomology.

(1) A non-cuspidal π of this type exists. A holomorphic Eisenstein series of weight k (for example E_4 at level SL_2(ℤ), or a weight-k Eisenstein series of level Γ_1(N)) generates the automorphic representation D_k^+ ⊗ πf. At every unramified ℓ, πf has the component Ind(|·|^{(k−1)/2}, |·|^{−(k−1)/2}), up to a twist; this is irreducible because k − 1 ≠ ±1. Its T_ℓ eigenvalue is 1 + ℓ^{k−1}, so the normalized Satake parameters are {ℓ^{(k−1)/2}, ℓ^{−(k−1)/2}}. The complex conjugate of this Eisenstein series, twisted by a power of |ν| if needed, generates an automorphic representation π' = D_k^- ⊗ π'_f. Here π'_f is a twist of the contragredient of πf, so its Satake parameters at ℓ still have ratio of absolute value ℓ^{±(k−1)}. Hence π' has the form π∞(κ, w_0) ⊗ π'_f, with π' automorphic but not cuspidal.

(2) Such a π'_f cannot occur in H^1. On the compactified modular curve, Kodaira–Spencer gives Ω^1 = ω^2(−D). Serre duality then gives H^1(X_K, ω^{2−k})^∨ ≅ H^0(X_K, ω^k(−D)) = S_k(K), compatibly with Hecke correspondences up to a twist by a character. So colimK H^1(X_K, ω^{2−k}) ⊗ ℂ is a character twist of the smooth dual of colimK S_k(K) ⊗ ℂ = ⊕ σ_f, the sum over cuspidal σ of weight k. Every irreducible subrepresentation is therefore σ_f^∨ ⊗ χ for a cuspidal σ. At unramified ℓ, its Satake parameters have ratio of absolute value 1: this follows from Deligne's theorem, or already from the Hecke bound |a_ℓ| = O(ℓ^{k/2}) against ℓ^{k−1} for large ℓ, since k ≥ 3. So π'_f does not embed into colimK H^1(S^{tor}_K, ω^κ) ⊗ ℂ, and the printed statement fails for w = w_0.

For w = Id the non-cuspidal statement does hold, because holomorphic Eisenstein series lie in H^0(X, ω^k) for the canonical extension. That is presumably why the slip goes unnoticed in the next sentence. The statement is an introductory recollection and is not used later in the paper, so no result depends on it. As printed, the statement is false for non-cuspidal π. Counterexample: take g = 1 and G = GL2, so that M_µ = T, ^MW = W = {1, s} and ℓ(s) = 1. Take k = 4 (any k ≥ 3 works). Let κ be the weight with ω^κ = ω^{2−k} = ω^{−2} in classical notation, with the matching similitude component. Then ν + ρ is regular and C(κ) = {s}. The representation π∞(κ, s) of Theorem 1.3.8 is the antiholomorphic discrete series of weight k (or the full discrete series D_k, if G(R)-representations are meant). Now take the automorphic representation π generated by the complex conjugate of the level-one Eisenstein series E_4 (or by E_4 itself, in the G(R) reading). Its archimedean component is π∞(κ, s). Its finite part πf is unramified everywhere, with T_ℓ-eigenvalue 1 + ℓ^3, so the ratio of its Satake parameters at ℓ is ℓ^{±3}. The hypothesis of the sentence is therefore satisfied.

On the other side, look at the compactified modular curve with the canonical extension. There Ω^1 = ω^2(−D) (Kodaira–Spencer), so Serre duality gives H^1(X_K, ω^{2−k}) ≅ H^0(X_K, ω^k(−D))^∨ = S_k(K)^∨, compatibly with Hecke operators. Hence colim_K H^1(X_K, ω^{2−k}) ⊗ C is, up to a twist by a character, the smooth dual of the space of weight-k cusp forms. Every irreducible subrepresentation of it is a twist of the contragredient of the finite part of a cuspidal representation. For such a representation the ratio of Satake parameters at unramified ℓ has absolute value 1 (Deligne), and neither twisting nor taking contragredients changes that. So πf does not embed, and does not even occur as a subquotient; this was checked by direct computation of the Satake ratios above.

Attempted defences, none of which works:
(a) The paper never defines "automorphic representation" as cuspidal. In §1.1 it refers to [Su24] for computing coherent cohomology by automorphic forms, which suggests general automorphic forms.
(b) That comparison does not rescue the claim. (p,K)-cohomology is not left exact in positive degree, so a subrepresentation π of the space of automorphic forms need not inject on H^{ℓ(w)}; the example above is exactly such a case.
(c) The citation [Har90, thm. 3.4] supports only the archimedean statement (Theorem 1.3.8). The embedding is Harris's result for cusp forms.
The intended meaning is almost certainly "cuspidal", and with that word added the sentence is correct. As printed, though, it is a false statement, not a slip that the context repairs.

Consequences: the sentence is part of an introductory "we recall" paragraph and has no proof. Nothing later in the paper refers to §1.3.7, Theorem 1.3.8 or this embedding. The main results (Theorem 1.4.3, Proposition 1.4.7, Theorem 1.4.8, and §§4–6) are about the ordinary parts of coherent cohomology and do not use it. The proposed correction is right and minimal. Restricting to w = Id would also make the sentence true, but "cuspidal" is the intended form.

sourceIssues.printed: Theorem 1.4.8 (Serre duality 5.5.1). There is a perfect pairing M^•_w ⊗_Λ M^•_{w_{0,M}ww_0,cusp} → Λ[−d], for which the adjoint of t ∈ T(Q_p) is w_0t^{−1} and the adjoint of [K_ℓgK_ℓ] is [K_ℓg^{−1}K_ℓ] for any prime ℓ ≠ p such that K_ℓ = G(Z_ℓ) and g ∈ G(Q_ℓ). sourceIssues.correction: Twist the Λ-structure of the second factor by the involution ι of Λ = Z_p[[T(Z_p)]] induced by t ↦ w_0t^{−1}. Equivalently, ⟨λx, y⟩ = ⟨x, ι(λ)y⟩ = λ⟨x, y⟩, so that M^•_{w_{0,M}ww_0,cusp} ≅ ι^*RHom_Λ(M^•_w, Λ)[−d]. The adjoint of t ∈ T(Q_p) is w_0t^{−1}, as printed. In the compatibility clause, the first factor is specialized at ν and the second at ν∘ι: the weights (κ, χ) and (−w_{0,M}κ − 2ρ_nc, w_0χ^{−1}) of Theorem 5.5.1. The same reading should be given to the unsubscripted ⊗ of Theorem 5.5.2.

So the pairing cannot be both Λ-balanced and have adjoint w_0t^{−1}.

3. The paper's own finite-level statement gives the same conclusion. Theorem 5.5.1 (p. 57) pairs RΓ_w(K^p, κ, χ) with RΓ_{w_{0,M}ww_0}(K^p, −w_{0,M}κ − 2ρ_nc, w_0χ^{−1}, cusp). Here κ = −w_{0,M}w(ν_alg + ρ) − ρ (p. 56). Using w_{0,M}ρ = −ρ_c + ρ_nc and w_0ρ = −ρ, the partner weight corresponds to the character ν' = (−w_0ν_alg)·(w_0χ^{−1}) = ν∘ι. This was checked by direct computation for g = 1, 2, 3 and every w in the Weyl group. On the centre, ν' = ν^{−1}. A Λ-bilinear pairing M ⊗_Λ N → Λ[−d] specializes at ν to a pairing of the two specializations at the same ν, which is not the classical duality.

4. The correction is consistent with both facts. Under ι, ⟨λ_z x, y⟩ = ⟨x, λ_{ι(z)}y⟩ = ⟨x, (w_0z^{−1})y⟩, and the specialization of ι^*N at ν equals the specialization of N at ν∘ι. The formula ι(t) = c(t)^{−1}t for GSp_{2g} was also checked by direct computation. 1. How T(Z_p) acts. Both factors are defined in the same way (p. 5; §5.4, p. 56): M^•_w = RHom_{T(Z_p)}(1, RΓ_w(K^p) ⊗̂_{Z_p} Λ), where T(Z_p) acts diagonally, and M^•_{w,cusp} is defined in the same way. T(Q_p) acts through its action on RΓ_w(K^p). This is the action used in every "T(Q_p)-equivariant" statement and in the diamond operators of Proposition 1.4.7. On the diagonal invariants, t ∈ T(Z_p) acting on the first factor is the same as multiplication by the unit [t]^{−1} ∈ Λ. So on M^•_w and on M^•_{w',cusp} (w' = w_{0,M}ww_0), every t ∈ T(Z_p) ⊂ T(Q_p) acts by the same scalar of Λ.

2. What a Λ-balanced pairing forces. If the pairing is balanced over Λ with these structures, then ⟨[t]^{−1}x, y⟩ = ⟨x, [t]^{−1}y⟩, so each t ∈ T(Z_p) is its own adjoint.

3. Why this contradicts the adjoint clause. Use the conventions of §3.1 (p. 33): W is the set of permutations w with w(i) + w(2g+1−i) = 2g+1, and T = {diag(t_i) : t_i t_{2g+1−i} = c}. Then w_0 is i ↦ 2g+1−i, so w_0(t) = c(t)t^{−1} and w_0t^{−1} = c(t)^{−1}t. For a scalar z ∈ Z(Z_p) we get w_0z^{−1} = z^{−1} ≠ z. Combining step 2 with the stated adjoint gives ⟨x, ([z] − [z]^{−1})y⟩ = 0 for all x, y. Since the pairing is perfect, [z]^2 − 1 would annihilate the cohomology of M^•_{w',cusp}. Its specializations would then vanish at every weight ν with ν(z)^2 ≠ 1. By Proposition 1.4.7 (the cuspidal case), these specializations are classical ordinary coherent cohomology, which is nonzero in weights with nontrivial central weight. For example, take g = 1, w = Id and w' = w_0: the specializations are Serre-dual to ordinary cusp forms, whose central characters vary with the weight.

4. The paper's own Theorem 5.5.1 (p. 57) points the same way. It pairs weight (κ, χ) of w with weight (−w_{0,M}κ − 2ρ_nc, w_0χ^{−1}) of w'. Write κ = −w_{0,M}w(ν+ρ) − ρ and use w_{0,M}ρ = ρ_nc − ρ_M and −w_0ρ = ρ. Then −w_{0,M}κ − 2ρ_nc = −w_{0,M}w'(ν'+ρ) − ρ with ν' = −w_0ν, that is, ν'(t) = ν(w_0t^{−1}). This identity was checked by direct computation for all w ∈ W when g = 1, 2, 3. The finite part matches as well: χ' = w_0χ^{−1} = χ∘ι. So the dual factor is the specialization of M^•_{w'} at ν∘ι, not at ν. In the coordinates of §3.1, ι fixes the k_i and changes k to −k. A ⊗_Λ pairing specializes both factors at the same point, so it can agree with Theorem 5.5.1, as the last sentence of Theorem 1.4.8 claims, only at weights that are trivial on the centre.

5. The defence fails. The Λ-structure on M^• is fixed by its definition, and nothing in the paper twists it on the second factor. A reading in which T(Z_p) acts trivially on M^• contradicts the T(Q_p)-action the paper uses. Theorem 5.5.1, the specialized statement, is correct. The proof of Theorem 5.5.2 "as in the previous theorem" produces the ι-twisted pairing, so the fix is the twist.

6. What depends on it. Remark 5.6.2 and the length-two case in the proof of Proposition 5.6.3 (p. 58, "prove the dual statement for the non-cuspidal cohomology") use the duality only for amplitudes, checked at all residual characters. ι^* is an exact autoequivalence of perfect Λ-complexes: it preserves amplitude and permutes the residual characters. So these arguments are unaffected. Remark 6.2.18 uses the duality of Lemma 5.4.2, not Serre duality. The Hecke operators t ∉ T(Z_p) and the prime-to-p adjoints are unaffected. Only the statement of Theorem 1.4.8, and the unsubscripted Theorem 5.5.2 if read as Λ-bilinear, needs correcting.

sourceIssues.reason:
(1) The coefficient field in Proposition 1.4.7. The left-hand side of the display is over ℚ_p(ζ_{p^n}). On the right-hand side, however, the exponent n is printed on ζ_p (ζ_p^n) instead of in the subscript. Read literally, ζ_p^n is the n-th power of a primitive p-th root of unity. Then ℚ_p(ζ_p^n) ⊆ ℚ_p(ζ_p): it equals ℚ_p(ζ_p) if p ∤ n and ℚ_p if p | n. For n ≥ 2 this field is strictly smaller than ℚ_p(ζ_{p^n}), which has degree p^{n−1}(p−1) over ℚ_p. The two sides of the stated equality would then not have the same scalars. The field is meant to be ℚ_p(ζ_{p^n}) on both sides: χ takes values in ℤ_p(ζ_{p^n})^×, and on the same page Theorem 1.4.3(4) and (5) and Remark 1.4.6 all extend scalars to ℚ_p(ζ_{p^n}). This slip does not recur in Remark 5.4.3 on p. 57, where the coefficients are correctly printed as ℤ_p(ζ_{p^n}).

(2) The weight κ in Proposition 1.4.7 and Remark 5.4.3. Both passages form κ = −w_{0,M}w(ν + ρ) − ρ from ν = ν_{alg}χ.

The sheaf ω^κ is defined only for an algebraic weight κ ∈ X^⋆(T)^{M,+} (§5.3.1, p. 55; compare Theorem 1.4.3(4), p. 5). Likewise, the notation RΓ_w(K^p, κ, χ) is introduced on p. 56 only for κ formed from the algebraic part ν_{alg}. But ν = ν_{alg}χ is a character of T(ℤ_p) with values in ℤ_p(ζ_{p^n})^×, and it is the restriction of an algebraic character only when χ is trivial. The reason is that a character of T that is algebraic and has finite order on the Zariski-dense subgroup T(ℤ_p) is trivial. So for χ ≠ 1 the printed κ is only locally algebraic. Then ω^κ is not defined, and κ is not a weight for which RΓ_w(K^p, κ, χ) has been given a meaning.

The finite-order part χ is already accounted for elsewhere. In Proposition 1.4.7 it enters through the χ-isotypic part [χ]. In Remark 5.4.3 it enters through the definition RΓ_w(K^p, κ, χ) = RHom_{T(ℤ_p)}(ν, RΓ_w(K^p) ⊗ ℤ_p(ζ_{p^n})).

The paper states the intended formula in its definitions at the end of §5.3, p. 56: "Let ν = ν_{alg}χ : T(ℤ_p) → ℤ_p(ζ_{p^n})^×, with ν_{alg} ∈ X^⋆(T) and χ a finite order character. Let κ = −w_{0,M}w(ν_{alg}+ρ)−ρ." In the regular-weight case, Theorem 1.4.3(4) applies the same formula to an algebraic ν ∈ X^⋆(T)^+. In the 2024 preprint, the corresponding definition (p. 54) also read κ = −w_{0,M}w(ν + ρ) − ρ. The revision corrected it to ν_{alg} there, but not in Proposition 1.4.7 or in Remark 5.4.3.

Both slips are notational, and the intended statements are clear from p. 56 and from Theorem 1.4.3. The rest of the paper takes κ algebraic and treats χ separately, for instance in Proposition 6.2.6 (p. 61) and Theorem 6.2.9 (p. 62). Nothing later uses the misprinted forms. These are therefore misprints, and the mathematics is unaffected.

sourceIssues.locator: §2.1.1, proof of Lemma 2.1.6, p. 7. The 2024 preprint (also p. 7) has a different proof. It takes "an arbitrary extension of 𝒢 to X̄ by [Sta22], TAG 01PE", performs "a suitable blow-up X̄′" and cites [RG71], thm. 5.2.2 (flattening by blow-up), whose hypotheses hold here.
