sourceIssues.printed: Lemma 2.1.6. Let 𝓕 be a locally free sheaf of finite rank over X. The set of compactifications (j_X : X ↪ X̄) with the property that 𝓕 extends to a locally free sheaf over X̄ is cofinal among compactifications, with maps being strict maps. Proof. Let X̄ be a compactification. We can take a coherent 𝓕̄ extension of 𝓕 to X̄ by [Sta22], Tag 0G41, and then perform a suitable blow-up so that the strict transform of 𝓕̄ is locally free by [Sta22], Tag 0ESN.
sourceIssues.correction: Replace the reference to Tag 0ESN by flattening by blow-up (Raynaud–Gruson [RG71], Thm. 5.2.2 = [Sta22], Tag 0815), applied to 𝓕̄ on X̄ with U = X. This is what the 2024 preprint cites. It gives a U-admissible blow-up X̄′ → X̄ (centre disjoint from X) after which the strict transform of 𝓕̄ is flat and of finite presentation, hence finite locally free, and restricts to 𝓕 on X. Because the centre misses X, the map X̄′ → X̄ is an isomorphism over X and hence strict. Alternatively, Tag 0ESN can be kept after one preparatory step. Replace X̄ by the disjoint union of the scheme-theoretic closures in X̄ of the finitely many open-and-closed pieces X_r ⊂ X on which 𝓕 has constant rank r. This map is strict, and X_r is scheme-theoretically dense in its closure. Then blow up the r-th Fitting ideal on each piece. Passing first to a compactification with Cartier boundary (Lemma 2.1.5) is another way to get density, but the constant-rank splitting is still needed.
sourceIssues.reason:
Tag 0ESN is Lemma 31.36.3 of the Stacks Project. It reads: "Let X be a scheme. Let 𝓕 be a finitely presented O_X-module. Let U ⊂ X be a scheme theoretically dense open such that 𝓕|_U is finite locally free of constant rank r." It then concludes that the blow-up in the r-th Fitting ideal is U-admissible and that the strict transform is locally free of rank r. In the proof, X̄ is an arbitrary compactification, and Definition 2.1.2 asks only for a proper X̄ with an open immersion of X. So X need not be scheme-theoretically dense, or even dense, in X̄. Also, 𝓕 is only locally free "of finite rank", so its rank may vary from one connected component of X to another. The proof does not reduce to the case covered by the lemma, and without these hypotheses the lemma's conclusion fails. Two examples over S = Spec k, checked by direct computation:
(i) Density. Take X = A¹, X̄ = P¹ ⊔ Spec k[ε]/(ε²), 𝓕 = O_X, and 𝓕̄ = O_{P¹} on the first piece and k = k[ε]/(ε) on the second. The module k is cyclic, so Fit_1(𝓕̄) = O_X̄. The blow-up in Fit_1 is therefore the identity, and the strict transform is 𝓕̄ itself, which is not locally free at the extra point.
(ii) Constant rank. Take X = A¹ ⊔ A¹, X̄ = P¹ ⊔ P¹, 𝓕 = O ⊔ O², and 𝓕̄ = (O ⊕ k_∞) ⊔ (O² ⊕ k_∞). Here X is scheme-theoretically dense. Fit_1(𝓕̄) is zero on the second P¹, so blowing it up deletes that component and the blow-up is not X-admissible. Fit_2(𝓕̄) is the unit ideal on the first P¹, so blowing it up leaves O ⊕ k_∞ there, which is not locally free.
So the cited lemma does not give the asserted step for an arbitrary compactification. The lemma itself is true: repair (a) or the routine reductions in (b) prove it. Strictness is not a separate problem. Once a blow-up with centre disjoint from X is available (Tag 0ESN(1), or U-admissibility in Raynaud–Gruson), strictness is immediate, and Lemma 2.1.4 also gives it once X is dense. Stacks Tag 0ESN (Divisors, Lemma 31.36.3) reads: "Let X be a scheme. Let 𝓕 be a finitely presented O_X-module. Let U ⊂ X be a scheme theoretically dense open such that 𝓕|_U is finite locally free of constant rank r. Then the blowup of X in the rth Fitting ideal of 𝓕 is U-admissible [and] the strict transform 𝓕′ ... is locally free of rank r ...". The proof applies it with U = X inside an arbitrary compactification X̄. Neither hypothesis is checked there, and neither holds in general.

(a) Density. X need not be scheme-theoretically dense in X̄, and without density the conclusion can fail. Example: let X̄ be P¹_k with an embedded point at ∞, with local ring k[t,e]/(te, e²) there. Let X = X̄ − {∞} = A¹ and 𝓕 = O_X. The coherent extension 𝓕̄ = O_X̄/(e) has Fit₁(𝓕̄) = O_X̄, so the Fitting-ideal blow-up is the identity. The strict transform is then 𝓕̄ itself, which is killed by e ≠ 0 and has fibre k at ∞, so it is not locally free there. Blowing up the reduced point ∞ does remove the embedded point and makes the pull-back O_{P¹}. So a suitable blow-up exists, but not by the cited lemma as stated.

(b) Constant rank. The lemma assumes 𝓕 has finite rank, not constant rank, and X may be disconnected. Example: two P¹'s meeting in a point, with X the complement of the node. If 𝓕 has rank 1 on one component of X and rank 2 on the other, then Tag 0ESN does not apply for any single r.

Defence considered. The statement of Lemma 2.1.6 is true, and both defects are easy to repair. The preceding Lemma 2.1.5 produces Cartier boundary, and the complement of an effective Cartier divisor is scheme-theoretically dense ([Sta22], Tag 07ZU). Taking scheme-theoretic closures of the constant-rank pieces is a strict map. Strictness is automatic once a result of this kind applies: part (1) of Tag 0ESN (or the U-admissibility in Raynaud–Gruson) puts the centre off X, so the blow-up is an isomorphism over X. Part (3) (K|_U = 0) shows that the strict transform restricts to 𝓕. The word "suitable" does not supply these steps, and the proof does not mention them. So this is a genuine but minor gap in the proof, not an error in the statement.

Consequences. Lemma 2.1.6 is used only in the proof of Theorem 2.7.4 (p. 24), together with Lemmas 2.1.12 and 2.1.30. That proof needs a strict map so that Lemma 2.1.29 transfers the dynamic structure. Both repairs above give strict maps, so Theorem 2.7.4 and everything after it is unaffected.

History. The 2024 preprint's proof reads "perform a suitable blow-up X̄′ and take the strict transform to find an extension ... which is locally free ([RG71], thm. 5.2.2)". Raynaud–Gruson flattening needs neither density nor constant rank. The preprint's Lemma 2.1.6 also did not claim strictness. The revision added the strictness clause, replaced [RG71] by Tag 0ESN, and dropped [RG71] from the bibliography.

The proof of Lemma 2.1.6 extends $\mathcal F$ coherently and then blows up `so that the strict transform of $\bar{\mathcal F}$ is locally free' by a Stacks tag. The tag cited, 0ESN, is stated for a finitely presented module together with a *scheme-theoretically dense* open over which it is finite locally free *of constant rank*; the lemma provides neither, since Definition 2.1.2 does not require $X$ dense in $\bar X$ and a locally free sheaf on a disconnected $X$ need not have constant rank. sourceIssues.locator: §2.1, proof of Lemma 2.1.5, p. 7
sourceIssues.printed: "We have D = V(ℐ). We let X̄′ be the blow-up of X at the ideal ℐ. Then by [Sta22], Tag 02OS, X ↪ X̄′ is a compactification mapping to X ↪ X̄."
sourceIssues.correction: "We let X̄′ be the blow-up of X̄ at the ideal ℐ." The blow-up should be of the compactification X̄, not of the open subscheme X.
sourceIssues.reason: On the page image, the bar is on X̄′ but not on the X in "the blow-up of X", while the surrounding sentences do distinguish X from X̄ ("the closed complement of X in X̄", "mapping to X ↪ X̄"). So this is not a text-layer artefact. In this proof, X is the open subscheme, D is the closed complement X̄ \ X with its reduced structure, and ℐ is the ideal sheaf in O_X̄ with D = V(ℐ). This matches the sentence just before Lemma 2.1.5, which takes ℐ as "a sheaf of ideals in O_X̄". Taken literally, the printed sentence does not work: ℐ is not an ideal sheaf of O_X, and its restriction to X is the unit ideal O_X. So "the blow-up of X at ℐ" is either undefined or equal to X itself, which is generally not proper. The cited result fits only the corrected reading. Stacks Tag 02OS (Lemma 31.33.4) states: "Let X be a scheme. Let Z ⊂ X be a closed subscheme. The blowing up b : X′ → X of Z in X has the following properties: 1. b|_{b⁻¹(X∖Z)} : b⁻¹(X∖Z) → X∖Z is an isomorphism, 2. the exceptional divisor E = b⁻¹(Z) is an effective Cartier divisor on X′, …". Apply this to the ambient scheme X̄ with Z = D. Then b : X̄′ → X̄ is an isomorphism over X̄ \ D = X, so X embeds as an open subscheme of X̄′. Also X̄′ \ X = b⁻¹(D) is an effective Cartier divisor. X̄′ is proper over S because it is projective over the noetherian scheme X̄, which is proper over S. X is dense in X̄′ because it is the complement of an effective Cartier divisor, so Lemma 2.1.4 gives strictness, exactly as the proof goes on to say. The intended argument is therefore clear and correct once the bar is restored. Lemma 2.1.5 and everything that relies on it are unaffected.

sourceIssues.locator: §2.1.1, the paragraph after Definition 2.1.2, p. 7; also Lemma 2.1.13, p. 8, and Lemma 2.1.32, p. 10. The 2024 preprint has the same omission. sourceIssues.printed:
p. 7 (§2.1.1, after Definition 2.1.2): "Compactifications of X form a category, with maps ξ : (j_X : X ↪ X̄) → (j′_X : X ↪ X̄′) being given by maps of S-scheme ξ : X̄ → X̄′, extending the identity of X. Moreover, the category is cofiltered: given compactifications X̄ and X̄′ we may take the closure of the diagonal X in X̄ ×_S X̄′."
p. 8, Lemma 2.1.13: "The category of compactifications of (C, X, p1, p2) is cofiltered, with maps being strict maps: if (C̄, X̄, p̄1, p̄2) and (C̄′, X̄′, p̄′1, p̄′2) are two compactifications, there exists a compactification (C̄″, X̄″, p̄″1, p̄″2) with strict maps (C̄″, X̄″, p̄″1, p̄″2) → (C̄, X̄, p̄1, p̄2) and (C̄″, X̄″, p̄″1, p̄″2) → (C̄′, X̄′, p̄′1, p̄′2). Proof. We can take X̄″ to be the closure of X in X̄ × X̄′ and C̄″ to be the closure of C in C̄ × C̄′."
p. 10, Lemma 2.1.32: "The category of dynamic (resp. strict dynamic, resp. compact dynamic) compactifications of (C, X, p1, p2, ) where maps are non strict maps is cofiltered: if (C̄, X̄, p̄1, p̄2, D+, D−) and (C̄′, X̄′, p̄′1, p̄′2, D′+, D′−) are two dynamic (...) compactifications, there exists a dynamic (...) compactification (C̄″, X̄″, p̄″1, p̄″2, D″+, D″−) with maps (C̄″, ...) → (C̄, X̄, p̄1, p̄2, D+, D−), (C̄″, ...) → (C̄′, X̄′, p̄′1, p̄′2, D′+, D′−)."
sourceIssues.correction:
The fix is to add the equalizer condition for parallel maps. Let ξ1, ξ2 : X̄ ⇉ X̄′ be two maps of compactifications. Let E ⊆ X̄ be their equalizer, the pull-back of the diagonal of X̄′ ×_S X̄′ along (ξ1, ξ2).
- E is a closed subscheme, because X̄′ is separated over S.
- X ⊆ E, because ξ1∘j_X = ξ2∘j_X = j′_X.
- E ∩ X = X, so X is open in E.
Hence E is a compactification, and E ↪ X̄ is a strict map with ξ1|_E = ξ2|_E. Equivalently, one can use the scheme-theoretic closure X̄″ of X in X̄. Since j_X is quasi-compact, X is scheme-theoretically dense in X̄″. Two maps to the separated X̄′ that agree on X therefore agree on X̄″.

For compactifications of correspondences (Lemma 2.1.13), take the equalizers E_C ⊆ C̄ and E_X ⊆ X̄ of the two components. Then p̄_i maps E_C into E_X. Also E_C ×_{E_X×E_X} (X×X) = E_C ×_{C̄} C = C. So (E_C, E_X) is a compactification with a strict map to (C̄, X̄) that equalizes the two maps.

For dynamic compactifications (Lemma 2.1.32), pull D± back to E_X. By Lemma 2.1.29 the result is dynamic (resp. strict dynamic, resp. compact dynamic), and the inclusion is a strict map.

Non-emptiness holds by Remark 2.1.3 and Lemma 2.1.11. For dynamic compactifications it is the standing assumption of §2.5.
sourceIssues.reason:
At all three places the paper claims "cofiltered", but the argument only builds a common refinement of two objects. The second axiom of a cofiltered category, equalizing parallel maps, is never addressed.
This axiom is not automatic. Definition 2.1.2 does not require X to be dense in X̄; Lemma 2.1.4 adds density as a separate hypothesis. So maps of compactifications need not be unique. Example: X = A^1_k over a field k, X̄ = P^1_k ⊔ Spec k and X̄′ = P^1_k, with X embedded in the P^1 component of X̄. Proper over k: yes. A map X̄ → X̄′ extending the identity of X must be the identity on the P^1 component, since X is dense there and P^1 is separated. The extra point, however, may go to any k-point of P^1. So there are distinct parallel maps ξ1 ≠ ξ2 (for example, sending the point to 0 or to ∞). Such a pair is equalized, for example, by the closed immersion of the P^1 component, but that needs an argument.
The argument above (the equalizer is a closed subscheme containing X, and the inclusion is strict) was checked directly, and it goes through in all three settings. So the claims are true as stated.
The omission touches no stated result. The later uses rely only on common refinements: §2.5.6 (p. 20), "By lemma 2.1.13, we can therefore assume that (C̄, X̄, p̄1, p̄2) = (C̄′, X̄′, p̄′1, p̄′2)". The same holds for the remark after Theorem 2.5.1 (p. 19), "(recall that the category of strict dynamic compactifications is cofiltered by lemma 2.1.32)". The equalizer axiom is what makes identifications obtained through different refinements agree. A cofiltered category, in the standard sense, satisfies three conditions:
1. it is non-empty;
2. any two objects receive maps from a common object;
3. any two parallel maps are equalized by some map into their source.

The sentence on p. 7 establishes only condition 2, and so do the glosses after the colons in Lemmas 2.1.13 and 2.1.32.

Condition 3 is not automatic. Definition 2.1.2 does not require X to be dense in X̄, and Lemma 2.1.4 adds density as a separate hypothesis. So maps of compactifications need not be unique. Example over a field k: take X = A^1, X̄ = P^1 ⊔ Spec k and X̄′ = P^1. A map X̄ → X̄′ extending the identity of X may send the extra point to any k-point of P^1. Parallel strict maps also exist. Take X̄′ = P^1 ⊔ P^1, with X in the first copy. The extra point may go to ∞ or to any k-point of the second copy. With C = X, p1 = p2 = id and C̄ = X̄, the same happens in the categories of Lemma 2.1.13.

The best defence is that the glosses show the authors use "cofiltered" to mean only condition 2. Under that reading, all three statements are proved correctly. The closure of X in X̄ ×_S X̄′ is a compactification with strict maps to both factors, since the graph of j′_X is closed in X × X̄′.

However, the property is used only once, in the remark on p. 19: "The theorem implies that the ordinary cohomology depends only on the data (C, X, p1, p2) (recall that the category of strict dynamic compactifications is cofiltered by lemma 2.1.32) … We simply denote it by RΓ(X, F)^{C−ord}". Section 2.5.6 (p. 20) uses Lemma 2.1.13 only for common refinements. Common refinements show that two choices give quasi-isomorphic complexes. They do not show that the quasi-isomorphism is independent of the maps chosen. Those maps are built from pull-backs along ξ (Lemma 2.2.7, Proposition 2.2.11), so a priori they depend on ξ. Condition 3 closes the gap. Let e : E → C′ be a strict map that equalizes ξ1, ξ2 : C′ ⇉ C. Then e*ξ1* = e*ξ2*, and e* is a quasi-isomorphism by Theorem 2.5.1(3). Hence ξ1* = ξ2* on ordinary cohomology, given the evident compatibility of these quasi-isomorphisms with composition. So the paper asserts the property, needs it for the canonical identification it uses, and does not prove it. That makes this a genuine but minor gap.

The missing condition holds by the equalizer argument in the correction. Direct verification confirms each step: E is closed, contains X, and meets X in X; E_C ×_{E_X×E_X} (X×X) = C; Lemma 2.1.29 applies to the strict inclusion. Condition 1 holds for schemes and for correspondences. For dynamic compactifications it can fail. Example over a field: X = A^1 and C = A^1 ⊔ A^1, with (p1, p2) given by x ↦ (x, 0) on the first copy and x ↦ (0, x) on the second. This correspondence has no dynamic compactification: a boundary point can lie in neither D+ nor D−. But §2.5 assumes that a strict dynamic compactification exists.

Lemmas 2.1.13 and 2.1.32 are cited only on pp. 10, 19 and 20, and no other argument uses condition 3. The stated results stand, and the proposed fix is correct and minimal.

Cofilteredness of a category needs both the common-refinement axiom and the equalizing of parallel maps, and at §2.1.1, Lemma 2.1.13 and Lemma 2.1.32 only the first is argued. sourceIssues.printed: Example 2.1.21. Let S = Spec F_p. We consider the Frobenius correspondence. Namely, C̄ = X̄, and we let p_2 = F : X̄ → X̄ be the Frobenius map and p_1 : X̄ → X̄ be the identity. Then for any closed subscheme D, we have p̄⋆_2 D = p p̄⋆_1 D, so D is strictly contracted.
sourceIssues.correction: Replace "we have p̄⋆_2 D = p p̄⋆_1 D" by "we have p̄⋆_1 D ≤ (1/p) p̄⋆_2 D". The reason: write D = V(I). Then p̄⋆_1 D = D, and p̄⋆_2 D = F⋆D = V(I^{[p]}), where I^{[p]} is the ideal generated by the p-th powers of local sections of I. Since I^{[p]} ⊆ I^p, Definition 2.1.15(2), applied with 1/p = 1/p (numerator 1, denominator p), gives p̄⋆_1 D ≤ (1/p) p̄⋆_2 D. So D is strictly contracted, with s = 1/p. The equality p̄⋆_2 D = p p̄⋆_1 D, meaning I^{[p]} = I^p, holds when D is locally principal. It fails in general, although it can hold for some other D. One can also note that p̄⋆_2 D ≤ s' p̄⋆_1 D holds for every rational s' > p, but not for s' = p.
sourceIssues.reason:
The printed text on p. 9 matches the quotation above. The paper writes p̄⋆D for the preimage (fibre product) of a closed subscheme, as with ξ⋆X on p. 7. So p̄⋆_1 D = V(I), and p̄⋆_2 D = F⋆D has ideal F^{-1}(I)·O = I^{[p]}. The paper defines multiples nD only for locally principal subschemes, through O(−nD). The natural meaning of p·p̄⋆_1 D is V(I^p).

The equality fails as soon as D is not locally principal. Take D = V(x, y), the origin of A^2 over F_p, or a closed F_p-point of P^2, where the local computation is the same. Then F⋆D = V(x^p, y^p). The monomial x^{p−1}y has total degree p, so it lies in (x, y)^p. It is not divisible by x^p or by y^p, so it does not lie in (x^p, y^p). Hence V(I^{[p]}) ≠ V(I^p).

The equality also fails in the weaker two-sided sense of the preorder ≤ of Definition 2.1.15(2). The relation p̄⋆_2 D ≤ p·p̄⋆_1 D would need (x, y)^{pb} ⊆ (x^p, y^p)^b for some b ≥ 1. But x^{pb−1}y lies in (x, y)^{pb} and in none of the generators x^{pi}y^{p(b−i)}. This was checked by direct computation for p = 2, 3, 5, 7 and b = 1, …, 4, and it holds for all p and b by the divisibility argument just given.

Only the inequality p̄⋆_1 D ≤ (1/p) p̄⋆_2 D is needed for strict contraction (Definition 2.1.19(5)). It holds because (I^{[p]})^1 ⊆ I^p. So the conclusion of the example is correct. Nothing in the paper cites Example 2.1.21, and the later uses of Frobenius (§3.4, pp. 38–39) do not rely on it. The error is confined to this illustrative example.

One refinement to the proposed correction: the equality can hold for some D that are not locally principal. For example, take I = (x, y) in F_p[x, y]/(x, y)^2; there I^p = 0 = I^{[p]}. So "holds when D is locally principal, but not in general" is more accurate than "holds only for locally principal D". The printed text on p. 9 is as quoted. The paper writes p̄⋆D for the scheme-theoretic pull-back of a closed subscheme (compare ξ⋆X on p. 7 and the pull-backs of Cartier divisors in Lemma 2.1.29). For the graph of Frobenius, p̄⋆_1 D = V(I) and p̄⋆_2 D = F^{-1}(D) = V(I^{[p]}). The paper defines a multiple nD of a closed subscheme only when D is locally principal, through O(−nD) (§2.1.14, p. 8). Otherwise the only scaled notion is the relation "D ≤ sD′" of Definition 2.1.15(2): D = V(I), D′ = V(I′), s = a/b and (I′)^a ⊆ I^b.

Defence considered. Under every reading the paper supports, the printed equality is false once D is not locally principal.
(i) As ideals, the equality reads I^{[p]} = I^p. Take D = V(x, y), the origin in A^2 over F_p, or a closed F_p-point of P^2, where the local picture is the same. Then x^{p−1}y lies in (x, y)^p but not in (x^p, y^p).
(ii) Read as a two-sided relation in the preorder of Definition 2.1.15(2), the equality needs p̄⋆_2 D ≤ p·p̄⋆_1 D. That means (x, y)^{pb} ⊆ (x^p, y^p)^b for some b ≥ 1. But the monomial x^{pb−1}y lies in (x, y)^{pb}, while ⌊(pb−1)/p⌋ + ⌊1/p⌋ = b − 1 < b, so it does not lie in (x^p, y^p)^b. Checked by direct computation for p = 2, 3, 5, 7 and all b ≤ 29, and the argument covers all p and b.
(iii) The most charitable reading is asymptotic. I^{[p]} is a reduction of I^p: every product of p generators has its p-th power in (I^{[p]})^p. So p̄⋆_2 D ≤ s′ p̄⋆_1 D holds for every s′ > p. For I = (x, y), checked by direct computation, the least admissible exponent ratio is (pb + p − 1)/b, which tends to p. So the equality is true "up to ε". The paper never defines such an equivalence, however, and at s = p the relation fails.
Locally principal D (I = (f) locally) do satisfy I^{[p]} = (f^p) = I^p, and that is presumably the case the authors had in mind. The example, though, says "for any closed subscheme D".

The conclusion survives. Strict contraction (Definition 2.1.19(5)) needs only p̄⋆_1 D ≤ s p̄⋆_2 D for some 0 < s < 1. Here s = 1/p works because I^{[p]} ⊆ I^p. (The correspondence is admissible because the graph of F is a closed immersion, X̄ being separated.)

Consequences. Nothing in the paper cites Example 2.1.21. Strict contraction is established later only in Lemma 4.4.2 (p. 50), by a direct local computation with generators of Cartier divisors. The Frobenius lifts of §3.4 (pp. 38–39) play no role in any contraction argument. So the error is confined to this illustrative example.

sourceIssues.locator: §2.1, proof of Lemma 2.1.17(3), second diagram, bottom-left vertex, p. 9
sourceIssues.printed: In the second commutative diagram of the proof of Lemma 2.1.17 (p. 9), the top row reads "A --a^k f^q--> A --f^{(k−1)q−k′q′}--> A". The vertical arrows are labelled "(f′)^{k′p′}", "f^{(k−1)q}" and "f^{k′q′}". The bottom row reads "A(f′)^{kp′} ⟶ A(f)^{(k−1)q} ⟶ A(f)^{k′q′}". The diagram is introduced by the sentence "We now let k′ = k p/p′ (for k large enough and divisible by p′). The above diagram yields the new diagram:"
sourceIssues.correction: The bottom-left vertex should read A(f′)^{k′p′}, which equals A(f′)^{kp}. It should not read A(f′)^{kp′}.
sourceIssues.reason:
The proof sets s = p/q and s′ = p′/q′, and then defines k′ = kp/p′, so k′p′ = kp. The second diagram is said to be obtained from the first. The first diagram's left column is the multiplication map A → A(f′)^{kp}, given by (f′)^{kp}. In the second diagram that arrow is correctly relabelled "(f′)^{k′p′}", which is again (f′)^{kp}. Its target must therefore be the ideal A(f′)^{k′p′} = A(f′)^{kp}. The printed vertex A(f′)^{kp′} is a different ideal in general: kp′ = k′p′ only if p = p′. The printed vertex also contradicts the arrow label directly beneath it.

I checked the rest of the diagram by direct computation. First, (k−1)q = k′q′ · (p′q/(pq′)) · ((k−1)/k) ≥ k′q′ for k large, because p′q/(pq′) = s′/s > 1. So the right square, with f^{(k−1)q} = f^{k′q′} · f^{(k−1)q−k′q′}, commutes. Second, the left square commutes because (f′)^{kp} = a^k f^q f^{(k−1)q}. The bottom row therefore gives A(f′)^{k′p′} → A(f)^{k′q′}. This matches the next sentence, "We now change p′ to k′p′ and q′ to k′q′", and the conclusion O_X̄(−p′D′) → O_X̄(−q′D) with the ratio still equal to s′.

The rendered page and a zoomed image both show the superscript as kp′, so this is not an artefact of the text layer. The slip is confined to one vertex label. The arrow label, the ratios, the renaming and the conclusion of Lemma 2.1.17(3) are all correct as printed, so nothing downstream depends on the misprint.

sourceIssues.printed: There exists a dynamic (resp. strict dynamic, resp. compact dynamic) compactification 𝒞′ = (C̄′, X̄′, p̄′₁, p̄′₂, D′₊, D′₋) and a strict map 𝒞′ → 𝒞 with the property that D′₊ and D′₋ are Cartier divisors on X̄′ and p̄⋆_i D′₊, p̄⋆_i D′₋ for i = 1, 2 are Cartier Divisors in 𝒞′.
sourceIssues.correction: … D′₊ and D′₋ are Cartier divisors on X̄′, and (p̄′_i)⋆D′₊, (p̄′_i)⋆D′₋ for i = 1, 2 are Cartier divisors on C̄′.
sourceIssues.reason: D′₊ and D′₋ are subschemes of X̄′. They can only be pulled back along the maps p̄′_i : C̄′ → X̄′, which the statement itself names inside 𝒞′. The unprimed p̄_i go from C̄ to X̄ and cannot be applied to D′±. "In 𝒞′" should be "on C̄′", because 𝒞′ denotes the whole tuple and not a scheme. The proof gives the corrected statement. X̄′ is the blow-up of X̄ along 𝒥𝒥 (the product of the ideals of D₊ and D₋), so the pullbacks D′± are Cartier. C̄′ is the blow-up of C̄″ = C̄ ×_{X̄×X̄} (X̄′ × X̄′) along the union of the four pulled-back divisors, so the ideal of that union becomes invertible on C̄′. A product of ideals is invertible only if each factor is, so each of the four pullbacks is Cartier on C̄′. The proof also writes p̄⋆_i for the unnamed projections C̄″ → X̄′, so the dropped prime is a notational slip. The intended statement is unambiguous.

sourceIssues.printed: "Proof. We let X̄′′ and C̄′′ be compactifications of X′ and C′. We let X̄′ be the closure of X′ in X̄′′ × X̄ and C̄′ be the closure of C′ in C̄′′ × C̄. We claim that X̄′ ×_X̄ X = X′. Indeed, the natural map X′ → X̄′ ×_X̄ X is both an open immersion and a proper map (since X′ → X is assumed to be proper). Similarly, we see that C̄′ ×_C̄ C = C′. We thus deduce that C′ = C̄′ ×_{X̄′×X̄′} X′ × X′. We have a diagram:" This is followed by a displayed diagram with C̄′ at the top, arrows p̄′2 and p̄′1 from C̄′ to the two copies of X̄′, a vertical arrow t : C̄′ → C̄, arrows p̄2, p̄1 : C̄ → X̄, and r : X̄′ → X̄ on both sides.
sourceIssues.correction:
Replace the first sentence with: "We let (C̄″, X̄″, p̄″1, p̄″2) be a compactification of the correspondence (C′, X′, p′1, p′2), which exists by Lemma 2.1.11."

Keep X̄′ and C̄′ as the closures of X′ and C′ in X̄″ × X̄ and C̄″ × C̄. Let t : C̄′ → C̄ be the second projection. Define p̄′i : C̄′ → X̄′ as the restriction of p̄″i × p̄i : C̄″ × C̄ → X̄″ × X̄. The rest of the proof then goes through unchanged, because p̄i ∘ t = r ∘ p̄′i.

An equivalent fix, following the pattern of the proof of Lemma 2.1.11: take C̄′ to be the closure of C′ in C̄″ × C̄ × X̄′ × X̄′, and let t, p̄′1, p̄′2 be the projections.
sourceIssues.reason:
The printed page matches the quoted text. The gap is real under the paper's own conventions.

**Why the maps are missing.** In Definition 2.1.2, a compactification of C′ is just a proper scheme containing C′ as an open subscheme. The paper uses the phrase "compactifications of X and C" in exactly this sense in the proof of Lemma 2.1.11 (p. 8). There it takes the closure of C in C̄′ × X̄ × X̄ precisely so that the projections p̄1 and p̄2 exist. In the proof of Lemma 2.1.34 the closure is taken only in C̄′′ × C̄. That space carries t : C̄′ → C̄ but no map to X̄′. So the arrows p̄′1 and p̄′2 in the displayed diagram are never constructed. The earlier sentence "C′ = C̄′ ×_{X̄′×X̄′} X′ × X′" already assumes these arrows exist.

**Counterexample: the maps can fail to exist.**
- Work over a field. Let X = C = X′ = C′ = A², with every map the identity.
- Let X̄ = C̄ = P² and p̄1 = p̄2 = id. Then C̄ ×_{X̄×X̄} (X × X) = A².
- Let D+ be the line at infinity and D− = ∅. This is a dynamic compactification.
- Choose X̄′′ = P¹ × P¹ and C̄′′ = P².
- Then X̄′ is the closure of the graph of the rational map P² ⇢ P¹ × P¹, [x:y:z] ↦ ([x:z],[y:z]). This is P² blown up at [1:0:0] and [0:1:0].
- C̄′ is the diagonal of P² × P², so it is P².
- A morphism C̄′ → X̄′ extending the identity of A² would give a morphism P² → P¹ × P¹ extending this rational map. The rational map is undefined at [1:0:0]: near that point it is (y,z) ↦ [y:z]. So no such morphism exists.

**The correction works.** Checked directly:
- C′ is open and dense in the new C̄′.
- C′ → C̄′ ×_C̄ C is an open immersion and is proper, because C′ → C is proper. Hence C̄′ ×_C̄ C = C′.
- X̄′ ×_X̄ X = X′, so (r × r)⁻¹(X × X) = X′ × X′.
- Using p̄i ∘ t = r ∘ p̄′i: C̄′ ×_{X̄′×X̄′} (X′ × X′) = t⁻¹(C̄ ×_{X̄×X̄} (X × X)) = t⁻¹(C) = C′.
- r⁻¹(D+ ∪ D−) = X̄′ \ X′.
- Pullbacks of (strict or compact) expansion and contraction go through t exactly as printed.

**Effect.** Only the proof is affected; the statement of Lemma 2.1.34 is true. The lemma is used in the proof of Theorem 5.1.4 (p. 53), which remains valid. **The printed text is as quoted.** The proof never builds the arrows p̄′1 and p̄′2 in its diagram, and with the choices as printed they need not exist.

**Defences tried.**
- (i) Could "compactifications of X′ and C′" mean a compactification of the correspondence (C′, X′, p′1, p′2)? The paper's usage does not support this. Definition 2.1.2 defines a compactification of a scheme. The proof of Lemma 2.1.11 (p. 8) uses the same phrase, "Let X̄ and C̄′ be compactifications of X and C", in exactly that sense: there the two compactifications are unrelated. That is why the proof then takes the closure of C in C̄′ × X̄ × X̄, so that the projections p̄1 and p̄2 exist. By contrast, when the proof of Lemma 2.1.13 (p. 8) takes closures in C̄ × C̄′ and X̄ × X̄′, both factors are already compactifications of correspondences, with maps between them.
- (ii) Could the arrows exist anyway? Not in general. The closure C̄′ ⊂ C̄″ × C̄ maps to C̄ and to C̄″, but nothing given maps C̄″ to X̄″, so nothing maps C̄′ to X̄′.

**Counterexample.** It satisfies the lemma's hypotheses in the dynamic case.
- Work over a field. Let X = C = X′ = C′ = A², with all maps the identity.
- Take the dynamic compactification C̄ = X̄ = P², p̄1 = p̄2 = id, D+ = ∅, D− = the line at infinity. Then D+ is expanded, D− is contracted, and X̄ \ X = D− ∪ D+.
- Choose X̄″ = P¹ × P¹ ⊃ A² and C̄″ = P². Then C̄′ is the diagonal of P² × P², isomorphic to P².
- Any p̄′i compatible with the correspondence must be the identity on A². Compose it with X̄′ → X̄″ = P¹ × P¹ and then with the second projection. This gives a morphism P² → P¹ extending (x, y) ↦ y, which is not constant.
- But every morphism P² → P¹ is constant, since two distinct fibres would be disjoint curves in P².
- So the diagram in the proof does not exist for this admissible choice. The same failure breaks the step "C′ = C̄′ ×_{X̄′×X̄′} X′ × X′" and the pull-back step (p̄′2)⋆D′+ ≤ s(p̄′1)⋆D′+, since both need p̄′i with p̄i ∘ t = r ∘ p̄′i.

**Why the correction works.** Checked directly.
- Both sides of p̄″i ∘ j_{C′} = j_{X′} ∘ p′i agree, and p̄i ∘ j_C ∘ (C′ → C) = j_X ∘ (X′ → X) ∘ p′i. So (p̄″i × p̄i) maps C′ into X′. Hence it maps the schematic closure C̄′ into the closed subscheme X̄′, and p̄i ∘ t = r ∘ p̄′i holds by construction.
- The map C′ → C̄′ ×_C̄ C is an open immersion. It is proper because C′ → C is proper. So C̄′ ×_C̄ C = C′.

Let r be such that (√0_V)^r = (0). We see that for all l ≥ 0,
(p̄⋆₂(t̂₁, ⋯, t̂_{d′}))^q + √0_V)^l ⊆ (p̄⋆₂(t̂₁, ⋯, t̂_{d′}))^{q(l−r)}.
sourceIssues.correction: ((p̄⋆₂(t̂₁, ⋯, t̂_{d′}))^q + √0_V)^l ⊆ (p̄⋆₂(t̂₁, ⋯, t̂_{d′}))^{q(l−r)}. Optionally, say "for all l ≥ r", or state that non-positive powers of an ideal mean the unit ideal.
sourceIssues.reason: The display has two opening and three closing parentheses, so the outer parenthesis before p̄⋆₂ is missing. The inclusion is correct once it is restored. Write J = p̄⋆₂(t̂₁, …, t̂_{d′}) and N = √0_V with N^r = 0. Then (J^q + N)^l = Σ_{k=0}^{min(l,r−1)} J^{q(l−k)}N^k ⊆ J^{q(l−r+1)} ⊆ J^{q(l−r)} for l ≥ r. For 0 ≤ l < r the exponent q(l − r) is negative. With the usual reading of a non-positive power as the whole ring, the inclusion is trivial there, so "for all l ≥ 0" does no harm, and only large l is used on p. 12 ("For l large enough, pl < q(l−r)"). The same missing parenthesis is in the 2024 preprint. There the exponent was printed as ql − r, which does not hold in general: for A = k[x, ε]/(ε³), J = (x), N = (ε), q = 2, r = 3, the term ε²x^{2l−4} lies in (J² + N)^l but not in (x^{2l−3}). The revision corrected the exponent to q(l − r) but left the parenthesis unbalanced.

Conventions. Definition 2.2.4 (p. 12) defines two groups: RΓ_{D₊,D₋}(X̄, ℱ) = RΓ(X̄, (j₊)⋆(j₋)!ℱ) and RΓ_{D₋,D₊}(X̄, ℱ) = RΓ(X̄, (i₋)!(i₊)⋆ℱ). In each, the first subscript is the outer operation and the second is the inner one. The D₊-type set always carries ⋆ and the D₋-type set always carries !. The sheaf must be given on X̄ \ (D₊ ∪ D₋). By Remark 2.2.5 (p. 12), a sheaf on a larger open can be used after restricting it.

Lemma-construction 2.2.6 (p. 12) gives maps RΓ_{D₊,D₋} → RΓ_{D′₊,D′₋} and RΓ_{D₋,D₊} → RΓ_{D′₋,D′₊}. It assumes D′₋ ⊆ D₋ and D₊ ⊆ D′₊, and it needs the sheaf on X̄ \ (D′₋ ∪ D₊). That open contains both X̄ \ (D₊ ∪ D₋) and X̄ \ (D′₊ ∪ D′₋). The construction involves only the complementary opens, so inclusions of the underlying sets are enough.

Definition 2.1.24 (p. 9) requires D₊ to be expanded and D₋ to be contracted. By Definition 2.1.19(1) and (4) (p. 9), this means p̄⋆₂D₊ ⊆ p̄⋆₁D₊ and p̄⋆₁D₋ ⊆ p̄⋆₂D₋. These inclusions are set-theoretic (Remark 2.1.20). Take X = X̄ \ (D₊ ∪ D₋) and C = C̄ ×_{X̄×X̄} (X × X), as in Definition 2.1.9 (p. 7). Then C = C̄ \ (p̄⋆₁D₊ ∪ p̄⋆₂D₋). Proposition 2.10.4(2) (p. 30) takes C to be exactly this open, and the proof's chain C → C̄ \ p̄⋆₁D₊ → C̄ assumes it. The sheaves live on the following opens:
- p⋆₂ℱ on p̄₂⁻¹(X) = C̄ \ (p̄⋆₂D₊ ∪ p̄⋆₂D₋);
- p!₁ℱ on p̄₁⁻¹(X) = C̄ \ (p̄⋆₁D₊ ∪ p̄⋆₁D₋);
- T only on C.

The first diagram is correct. Its three opens are p̄₂⁻¹(X), C and p̄₁⁻¹(X). Both of its Lemma 2.2.6 steps satisfy the hypotheses: the first uses p̄⋆₂D₊ ⊆ p̄⋆₁D₊, and the second uses p̄⋆₁D₋ ⊆ p̄⋆₂D₋. Each sheaf is given where it is needed.

The printed second diagram is not correct. Both middle terms RΓ_{p̄⋆₁D₋,p̄⋆₂D₊} use the open U = C̄ \ (p̄⋆₁D₋ ∪ p̄⋆₂D₊). This open contains both p̄₁⁻¹(X) and p̄₂⁻¹(X), and in general it is strictly larger than C. The first arrow does satisfy the inclusion hypotheses of Lemma 2.2.6, but it needs p⋆₂ℱ on U, and p⋆₂ℱ is given only on p̄₂⁻¹(X). The middle arrow would need T on U. The last Lemma 2.2.6 arrow would likewise need p!₁ℱ on U. U is strictly larger than p̄₂⁻¹(X), and so also than C, as soon as p̄⋆₂D₋ is not contained in p̄⋆₁D₋ ∪ p̄⋆₂D₊. Nothing in the hypotheses rules this out.

Example. Work over S = Spec 𝔽₃; §2.2 assumes that all schemes are of finite type over ℤ. Take X̄ = C̄ = ℙ¹, p̄₁ = id, p̄₂(z) = z², D₊ = {∞} and D₋ = {1}. As sets, p̄⋆₁D₊ = p̄⋆₂D₊ = {∞} and p̄⋆₁D₋ = {1} ⊆ p̄⋆₂D₋ = {1, −1}. So (C̄, X̄, p̄₁, p̄₂, D₊, D₋) is a dynamic correspondence. Put X = ℙ¹ \ {1, ∞} and C = p̄₁⁻¹(X) ∩ p̄₂⁻¹(X) = ℙ¹ \ {1, −1, ∞}. Then the data form a dynamic compactification (Definition 2.1.26, p. 10) of the correspondence (C, X, p₁, p₂), where p₁ is the inclusion and p₂(z) = z². The printed middle open U = ℙ¹ \ {1, ∞} contains −1, where neither p⋆₂ℱ nor T is given.

The printed second row is exactly the first row with D₊ and D₋ interchanged in every subscript. That moves the index 1 onto D₋ and the index 2 onto D₊, which is the wrong way round.

With the corrected indices, the middle terms RΓ_{p̄⋆₂D₋,p̄⋆₁D₊} live on C̄ \ (p̄⋆₂D₋ ∪ p̄⋆₁D₊) = C. Both uses of Lemma 2.2.6 are then legitimate. The first uses p̄⋆₂D₊ ⊆ p̄⋆₁D₊ with the sheaf on p̄₂⁻¹(X). The second uses p̄⋆₁D₋ ⊆ p̄⋆₂D₋ with the sheaf on p̄₁⁻¹(X). The endpoints must be RΓ_{D₋,D₊}(X̄, ℱ), since Definition 2.2.4 defines these groups on X̄ and the proposition's own sentence names RΓ_{D₋,D₊}(X̄, ℱ).

The proof says it does "the first case". The sentence of the statement names RΓ_{D₋,D₊} first. But the proof's Lemma 2.2.7 pair and its construction of the middle map both belong to the first diagram, for RΓ_{D₊,D₋}. Its Lemma 2.2.6 pair and its middle map, however, are the terms of the printed second diagram: they carry that diagram's supports (p̄⋆₁D₋, p̄⋆₂D₊), and the middle map even has that diagram's C in place of C̄. The construction that follows belongs to the first case. On the chain C → C̄ \ p̄⋆₁D₊ → C̄, j_{C,−} extends by zero across p̄⋆₂D₋, and j_{C,+} pushes forward across p̄⋆₁D₊. By Definition 2.2.4 and Remark 2.2.5, (j_{C,+})⋆(j_{C,−})! therefore computes RΓ_{p̄⋆₁D₊,p̄⋆₂D₋}(C̄, ·). This is the middle term of the first diagram, not the printed RΓ_{p̄⋆₁D₋,p̄⋆₂D₊}(C, ·). The corrected outer maps are exactly the ones Lemma 2.2.6 provides, by the two inclusions above.

The later use agrees with the correction. The proof of Proposition 2.10.3 (p. 30) treats the RΓ_{D₋,D₊} case using only the composite RΓ_{p̄⋆₂D₋,p̄⋆₂D₊}(C̄, p⋆₂ℱ) → RΓ_{p̄⋆₁D₋,p̄⋆₁D₊}(C̄, p!₁ℱ). It factors this composite through cohomology of C̄ \ (p̄⋆₁D₊)° with support in the closed set C̄ \ ((p̄⋆₂D₋)° ∪ (p̄⋆₁D₊)°). This set is the formula for C with interiors. Like the corrected row, it pairs p̄⋆₂ with D₋ and p̄⋆₁ with D₊. No later result uses the misprinted intermediate terms. The January 2024 preprint has the same statement and proof (pp. 13–14).

Kind and reach. The intended construction is clear from the first diagram, from the proof's own chain of immersions and from its later use, so this is a misprint. Part of it is in the statement. As printed, the second diagram of Proposition 2.2.10 is not defined: its middle terms live on an open where p⋆₂ℱ and T are not given. So it affects a stated result. The endpoints of both diagrams and the intended endomorphism T_𝒞 are unchanged.

On p. 8, a map of compactifications (C̄, X̄, p̄1, p̄2) → (C̄′, X̄′, p̄′1, p̄′2) consists of maps C̄ → C̄′ and X̄ → X̄′ that are the identity on C and X and make the obvious diagrams commute. Definition 2.1.28 (p. 10) writes a map of dynamic compactifications as ξ: 𝒞′ → 𝒞 with D′± ⊇ ξ⋆D±, and calls it strict when D′± = ξ⋆D±. So the stated map 𝒞 → 𝒞′ is a pair ξ: C̄ → C̄′, ξ: X̄ → X̄′ with the following properties:
- p̄′i∘ξ = ξ∘p̄i;
- D± = ξ⋆D′±;
- ξ⁻¹(X) = X, so ξ: X̄ → X̄′ is strict in the sense of p. 7. This follows from the previous property, because X̄ \ X = D+ ∪ D− and X̄′ \ X = D′+ ∪ D′− (Definition 2.1.26, p. 10).
Both maps ξ are proper, since they are maps between proper S-schemes.

2. The primes in column 3 are a slip. D′+ and D′− are closed subschemes of X̄′, but p̄1 and p̄2 map C̄ to X̄. So (p̄1)⋆D′+ and (p̄2)⋆D′− are not defined. Every other subscript in the bottom row uses D±. In particular, column 4, RΓ_{(p̄1)⋆D+,(p̄2)⋆D−}(C̄, (p̄1)^!𝓕), is reached from column 3 by the map induced by T. So the unprimed entry is exactly the pull-back of the top-row entry above it, which is what the equality in column 3 asserts.

3. The four columns marked ‖ are correct.
- Columns 1 and 6: the open part is X̄ \ (D+ ∪ D−) = X (Definition 2.1.26, p. 10).
- Columns 3 and 4: the open part is C̄ \ ((p̄1)⋆D+ ∪ (p̄2)⋆D−). D+ is expanded and D− is contracted (Definitions 2.1.19 and 2.1.24, p. 9). So (p̄2)⋆D+ ⊆ (p̄1)⋆D+ and (p̄1)⋆D− ⊆ (p̄2)⋆D− as sets. Over these open parts ξ is the identity, so Lemma 2.2.8 (p. 14) gives the equalities.

4. Column 2 is a pull-back, and it points down. Here the open part is U = p̄2⁻¹(X). It is the preimage of U′ = (p̄′2)⁻¹(X) ⊆ C̄′. U contains C but can be larger, and ξ: U → U′ is proper but need not be an isomorphism. Since p̄′2∘ξ = ξ∘p̄2 and ξ is the identity on X, we have ξ⋆(p̄′2)⋆𝓕 = (p̄2)⋆𝓕. So Lemma 2.2.7 (p. 13) gives a pull-back from the C̄′-term to the C̄-term, which is ↓.
Lemma 2.2.7 gives a map ↑ only as a trace. A trace would need the sheaf ξ^!(p̄′2)⋆𝓕 on U, and this is not (p̄2)⋆𝓕 in general. For example, take X̄′ = X̄ with ξ the identity and D′± = D±. Let C̄ be the blow-up of C̄′ at a closed point of U′ \ C near which C̄′ is a smooth surface. This is a strict map of dynamic compactifications: the expanded and contracted conditions pull back, and C = C̄ ×_{X̄×X̄} (X × X) still holds because the centre is not in C. Near the exceptional curve E we have ξ^!(p̄′2)⋆𝓕 = (p̄2)⋆𝓕 ⊗ 𝒪(E). For a nonzero locally free 𝓕 the two sheaves differ: (p̄2)⋆𝓕 is trivial on E, because p̄2 contracts E, while 𝒪(E) restricts to 𝒪(−1) on E.

sourceIssues.correction:
The paper's own conventions are the standard ones: K[1]^i = K^{i+1}, and cone(K → L) has K in degree −1 and L in degree 0. Under them the shifts change as follows.
(1) p. 15: lim_n F̄(−nD) = cone(∏_n F̄(−nD) → ∏_n F̄(−nD))[−1]. This is the fibre of (m_n) ↦ (m_n − m_{n+1}), with H^0 = lim and H^1 = lim^1.
(2) p. 15: j_!M = M ⊗_{(A[X],A)■} (A((X^{−1}))/A[X])[−1]. This is the cited definition ([CSb], Lecture VIII, Observation 8.11). The same [−1] belongs in the "Moreover" display and in the first line of the display on p. 16.
(3) p. 16: j_!M = cone(M̄[[X^{−1}]]X^{−1} →^{1−Xf} M̄[[X^{−1}]]X^{−1})[−1]. This is the fibre of 1 − Xf. For M̄ a module, it is a two-term complex in degrees 0 and 1.
(4) p. 18: M is quasi-isomorphic to cone(M ⊗_A A[X] →^{X−T} M ⊗_A A[X]), with no shift. For M a module, that is the two-term complex M ⊗_A A[X] → M ⊗_A A[X] with differential X − T, in degrees −1 and 0.
To fix the p. 15 display alone, replace [1] by [−1]. For the proof of Proposition 2.3.2 to be right line by line, (2) and (3) are also needed. Fixing (1) and (3) without (2) leaves the step from the first to the second line of the p. 16 display off by one shift. The statement of Proposition 2.3.2 is unchanged, with lim the usual derived limit, and so is every later result.
sourceIssues.reason:
Conventions. The paper does not state its conventions for shifts or cones. It grades cohomologically throughout (H^i, and amplitudes such as [0, ℓ(w)] in Theorem 1.4.3, p. 5). It uses the standard conventions: K[1]^i = K^{i+1}, and cone(φ: K → L) has K in degree −1 and L in degree 0. Three passages show this.
- Theorem 1.4.8 (p. 5) gives a pairing into Λ[−d] and says it is compatible with classical Serre duality. Classical Serre duality pairs H^i with H^{d−i} through a trace map on H^d. So Λ[−d] sits in degree d. The same reading applies to the pairings into Z_p(ζ_{p^n})[−d] and Λ[−d] in Theorems 5.5.1–5.5.2 (p. 57).
- In the proof of Proposition 2.3.5 (p. 16), the cone of the levelwise surjection (M, ·f) → (f^nM), whose kernels are the M[f^n], is written (lim_n M[f^n])[1]. So a surjection with kernel K has cone K[1], with the kernel in degree −1.
- Remark 2.9.4 (p. 28) writes the triangle j_!j*F → F → î_*î*F as lim_n I^n ⊗ F → F → lim_n F ⊗ O_X/I^n. This is R lim applied to the levelwise triangles I^n ⊗ F → F → F ⊗ O_X/I^n. So it needs the limit of the constant system F to be F, in degree 0. It also identifies j_!j*F with lim_n I^n ⊗ F with no shift, which is what Proposition 2.3.2 intends.
With these conventions, let φ: P → Q be a map of modules in degree 0. Then cone(φ) has H^{−1} = ker φ and H^0 = coker φ. cone(φ)[1] lives in degrees −2 and −1. The fibre cone(φ)[−1] has ker φ in degree 0 and coker φ in degree 1.

(1) p. 15. The derived limit of an inverse system (P_n) is the fibre of (m_n) ↦ (m_n − m_{n+1}) on ∏P_n, with H^0 = lim and H^1 = lim^1. Read literally, the printed formula gives (R lim)[2].
Example: take the constant system A with identity transitions. The map on ∏A has kernel the constant sequences, which is ≅ A. It is surjective: put m_1 = 0 and m_{n+1} = m_n − b_n. So cone(∏ → ∏) is A in degree −1, and the printed cone(∏ → ∏)[1] is A in degree −2. The limit is A in degree 0. Even if "cone" is read as the fibre, the printed [1] puts A in degree −1.
Geometric check: X̄ = P^1 over a field k, D = ∞, F̄ = O. For n ≥ 1, H^0(P^1, O(−n)) = 0 and H^1(P^1, O(−n)) has dimension n − 1, with surjective transition maps. So lim_n RΓ(P^1, O(−n)) is concentrated in degree 1, as H^1_c(A^1, O) ≅ k((T^{−1}))/k[T] should be. The printed formula would put it in degree −1.
The printed formula also contradicts how lim is used afterwards. In the proof of Proposition 2.3.5, Mittag-Leffler gives H^i(X̄, j_!F) = lim_n H^i(X̄, I^nF̄) in the same degree i.

(2) p. 15. The cited definition carries the shift.
- [CSb], Lecture VIII, Observation 8.11 defines j_! as M ↦ M ⊗^L (A_∞/A)[−1], with A = Z[T] and A_∞ = Z((T^{−1})).
- Observation 8.12 applies this to products: j_!(∏_I A) = ∏_I (A_∞/A)[−1].
- For A = R[T], the proof of Proposition 11.4 in Lecture XI has f_!M = M ⊗^L_{(A,R)■} R((T^{−1}))/R[T][−1], and f^!R = RHom_R(R((T^{−1}))/R[T], R)[1] ≅ R[T][1].
The shift is forced. A((X^{−1})) is an idempotent (A[X],A)■-algebra that becomes 0 in (A[X],A[X])■. So j_!M is the fibre of M → M ⊗ A((X^{−1})). Since A[X] → A((X^{−1})) is injective, this fibre is M ⊗ (A((X^{−1}))/A[X])[−1]. Over a field this is the compactly supported cohomology of the affine line, k((X^{−1}))/k[X] in degree 1. The formula quoted "by definition" on p. 15 drops the [−1].

(3) p. 16. Put N = M̄[[X^{−1}]]X^{−1} = ∏_{n≥1} M̄X^{−n}. X acts by (Xm)_n = m_{n+1}, since the X^0 term dies in A((X^{−1}))/A[X]. So (1 − Xf)(Σ m_n X^{−n}) = Σ (m_n − f m_{n+1}) X^{−n}.
Locally F̄(−nD) = M̄, with multiplication by f as the transition maps. So 1 − Xf is exactly the map (m_n) ↦ (m_n − m_{n+1}) of the p. 15 display. Its kernel is lim(⋯ →^f M̄ →^f M̄) and its cokernel is lim^1.
Xf − 1 has constant term −1, so it is a nonzerodivisor on A[X]. Hence A[X]/(Xf − 1) ≃ [A[X] →^{Xf−1} A[X]] in degrees −1 and 0. So N ⊗_{(A[X],A)■} A[X]/(Xf − 1) ≃ cone(N →^{1−Xf} N), up to the sign of the differential, with no shift. The printed second equality therefore does not follow even from the printed first line: it adds a spurious [1].
With the [−1] from (2), j_!M = cone(1 − Xf)[−1]. Its H^0 is the limit and its H^1 is lim^1, so j_!M = R lim_n F̄(−nD), which is Proposition 2.3.2.
Example: take A = M̄ = k[f] over a field k. The system k[f] ←^f k[f] ←^f ⋯ has lim 0 and lim^1 = k[[f]]/k[f]. So j_!O sits in degree 1, as the [−1] predicts.

(4) p. 18. X − T is injective on M ⊗_A A[X] = M[X]: compare leading coefficients in X. Its cokernel is M, via Σ m_i X^i ↦ Σ T^i m_i, and X acts on it as T. This works degreewise when M is a complex. So cone(X − T) ≃ M, while the printed cone(X − T)[1] ≃ M[1].

No single convention makes all four passages correct.
- Reversing the direction of [1] makes (1) and (3) correct. But it contradicts the Λ[−d] duality and the cone (lim_n M[f^n])[1] in the proof of Proposition 2.3.5.
- Reading "cone" as the fibre makes (4) correct. It also makes the last step on p. 16 agree with the printed line before it. But it contradicts the proof of Proposition 2.3.5, and it leaves (1) in degrees −1 and 0.
- On pp. 15–16, cone(…)[1] seems to be meant as the two-term complex in degrees 0 and 1. Read that way, the p. 18 formula gives M[−1].
- A homological grading is ruled out by the paper's cohomological notation.
- The j_! formula misquotes [CSb] under every convention.
Still, the intended meaning of each passage is clear. (1), (2) and (4) recall standard facts, and their wording says so ("We recall", "By definition ([CSb])", "the quasi-isomorphic"). (3) is the step that is to be matched with (1) to give Proposition 2.3.2. Every slip is in a shift: a [−1] is dropped in (2), and [1] stands in place of [−1] in (1) and (3) and in place of no shift in (4). So these are misprints.

Consequences: none. The p. 15 display is used only in the proof of Proposition 2.3.2, where the final display on p. 16 is matched against it. As printed, each side is its true value shifted by [2]. The printed values are cone(1 − Xf)[1] and cone(∏ → ∏)[1], and the true values are cone(1 − Xf)[−1] and cone(∏ → ∏)[−1]. So the printed comparison still gives the right identification j_!F ≅ lim_n F̄(−nD). With the corrected shifts the computation proves Proposition 2.3.2, and Remark 2.9.4 (p. 28) agrees with it. Later uses of Proposition 2.3.2 need only its statement, with lim the ordinary derived limit: Corollary 2.3.4 and Proposition 2.3.5 (p. 16), Corollary 2.3.11 (p. 17), and the proof of Proposition 2.7.2 (p. 23). The p. 18 sentence serves only to view M as an object of D((A[T],A)■) before Definition 2.4.2. The text says that the replacement is quasi-isomorphic to M, and the shift plays no role later. No stated result changes.

The paper's own conventions in §2.3 settle the point. In §2.3.1 (p. 15), j : X → X̄ is the open immersion with X̄ \ X = D, 𝓕 lives on X, and \overline{𝓕} is a chosen object on X̄ with j^*\overline{𝓕} = 𝓕. Proposition 2.3.2 gives j_!𝓕 = lim_n \overline{𝓕}(−nD) as an object on X̄. So j_!𝓕 is a sheaf on X̄, and its cohomology is taken on X̄. Corollary 2.3.4 writes RΓ(X̄, j_!𝓕), and the proof of 2.3.5 ends "hence H^i(X̄, j_!𝓕) = lim_n H^i(X̄, 𝓘^n \overline{𝓕})" (image checked).

Read literally, H^i(X, j_!𝓕) would mean cohomology on the open X of j^*j_!𝓕 = 𝓕, which is H^i(X, 𝓕). That is not the intended group. Remark 2.3.6 identifies the right-hand side with Hartshorne's cohomology with compact support, which is not the ordinary cohomology of 𝓕 on the non-proper X. The X without a bar is therefore a genuine misprint, not an artefact of the text layer. The plain 𝓕 on the right-hand side is a second, smaller slip of the same kind.

The argument is sound once corrected. The cone of the map of inverse systems is controlled by the systems M[f^n], which stabilise, so lim \overline{𝓕}(−nD) → lim 𝓘^n\overline{𝓕} is a quasi-isomorphism. Since X̄ is proper over an artinian ring, the H^i(X̄, 𝓘^n\overline{𝓕}) are finite A-modules, so the system is Mittag-Leffler and the limit passes to cohomology. This proves the corrected statement.

Nothing later cites Proposition 2.3.5. Its label and Hartshorne's [Har72] occur only here and in the bibliography, so no later result or proof is affected.

sourceIssues.printed:
Corollary 2.3.14. Assume that we have maps p̄⋆₂𝒪_X̄(D₊) → p̄⋆₁𝒪_X̄(D₊) and p̄⋆₂𝒪_X̄(−D₋) → p̄⋆₁𝒪_X̄(−D₋). For all k₊, k₋ ≥ 0 and n as in proposition 2.3.13, the cohomological correspondence T induces maps:
RΓ(X̄, 𝓕̄(−nD₋ − k₋D₋ + k₊D₊)) → RΓ(X̄, 𝓕̄(nD₊ − k₋D₋ + k₊D₊))
which induce, after passing to the limit and colimit as in corollary 2.3.11, the map T_𝒞 of proposition 2.2.10.
Proof. We have maps p̄⋆₂𝒪_X̄(k₊D₊ − k₋D₋) → p̄⋆₁𝒪_X̄(k₊D₊ − k₋D₋). We simply twist the cohomological correspondence of proposition 2.3.13 to obtain the desired map in cohomology. □
sourceIssues.correction:
Add a compatibility hypothesis. Let α₊: p̄⋆₂O_X̄(D₊) → p̄⋆₁O_X̄(D₊) and α₋: p̄⋆₂O_X̄(−D₋) → p̄⋆₁O_X̄(−D₋) be the given maps. Let s₊: O_X̄ → O_X̄(D₊) be the dual of the structure map O_X̄(−D₊) → O_X̄, and let t₋: O_X̄(−D₋) → O_X̄ be the structure map. Require
α₊ ∘ p̄⋆₂s₊ = p̄⋆₁s₊ and p̄⋆₁t₋ ∘ α₋ = p̄⋆₂t₋.
Equivalently, both maps lie over the maps to O_C̄. Locally they are induced by the ideal inclusions p̄⋆₁I₊ ⊆ p̄⋆₂I₊ and p̄⋆₂I₋ ⊆ p̄⋆₁I₋.

The map at level (k₊, k₋) is the map of Proposition 2.3.13 twisted by α₊^{⊗k₊} ⊗ α₋^{⊗k₋}. Under this hypothesis it commutes with the transition maps of Corollary 2.3.11. Also, α₊ and α₋ restrict to the identity on C, under the trivialisations given by s₊ and t₋, so the twisted map restricts to T on C. The level maps therefore induce T_C.

The maps from Lemma 2.1.17 used in Lemma 2.5.3 satisfy the hypothesis, because the diagram in Lemma 2.1.17(3) commutes with the maps to the ideals.

Pullback and trace are natural, so the question can be settled on C̄.

To pass to the colimit over k₊ and the limit over k₋, these maps must commute with the transition maps 𝓕̄(k₊D₊ − …) → 𝓕̄((k₊+1)D₊ − …), induced by s₊, and 𝓕̄(… − (k₋+1)D₋) → 𝓕̄(… − k₋D₋), induced by t₋. A counterexample, checked by direct computation. Take S = Spec k with k a field. Let (C, X, p₁, p₂) = (𝔸¹, 𝔸¹, id, id), compactified by (ℙ¹, ℙ¹, id, id), with D₊ = {∞} and D₋ = ∅, where 𝒪(−D₋) = 𝒪 → 𝒪 is the identity. This is a dynamic compactification in the sense of Definition 2.1.26: the maps are proper, D₊ is expanded, D₋ is contracted, and X̄ \ X = D₊ ∪ D₋. Take 𝓕 = 𝒪_X, T = id, 𝓕̄ = 𝒪_ℙ¹ and n = 0. (a) Let α₊ = 0 and α₋ = id. The maps at every level k₊ ≥ 1 are zero, so they induce the zero map on k[x], not T_𝒞 = id.

(b) Let α₊ = λ·(canonical map) with λ ∈ k^×, λ ≠ 1. The level-k₊ map is λ^{k₊}·id on H⁰(ℙ¹, 𝒪(k₊)). Follow the section 1 ∈ H⁰(𝒪). Applying the level-0 map and then the transition gives 1; applying the transition and then the level-1 map gives λ. So the maps are not a morphism of direct systems and induce no map on the colimit.

In both cases the conclusion of the corollary fails, so the printed statement is false for arbitrary maps. It holds once the compatibility above is added. Restricted to C, compatible maps are the identity under the identification 𝒪(±D±)|_C = 𝒪_C, so the twisted maps restrict to T.

The intended maps are the natural ones: the proof speaks of "the" twisted maps, and Lemma 2.1.17(3) explicitly provides diagrams compatible with the maps to the ideals. The corollary is not cited by number elsewhere. The same twisting is carried out in the proofs of Lemma 2.5.3 and Proposition 2.5.4 with the canonical maps of Lemma 2.1.17, which satisfy the condition. So no later result is affected; only the corollary's statement needs the extra hypothesis. **Why the hypothesis is too weak.** To pass to lim over k₋ and colim over k₊, the level maps must form a map of systems. So they must commute with the transition maps F̄(aD₊ − bD₋) → F̄((a+1)D₊ − bD₋), which come from s₊, and F̄(aD₊ − (b+1)D₋) → F̄(aD₊ − bD₋), which come from t₋.

For the twisted maps this holds when α₊ ∘ p̄⋆₂s₊ = p̄⋆₁s₊ and p̄⋆₁t₋ ∘ α₋ = p̄⋆₂t₋. It fails in general, and the printed hypothesis asks nothing of the maps. That hypothesis is even vacuous, since the zero maps always exist.

**Why the charitable reading fails.** Under the paper's own conventions "maps" cannot silently mean "the canonical maps". By §2.1.14, O_X̄(−D) is a chosen invertible sheaf with a map to O_X̄, and it is not unique. Moreover, Lemma 2.1.17 says "canonical" explicitly where it means it; Corollary 2.3.14 has no such qualifier.

**Counterexample (checked by direct computation).** Take:
- S = X = X̄ = C = C̄ = Spec Z, with p₁ = p₂ = id;
- D₊ = D₋ = ∅, with O(−D±) = O → O the identity (allowed by §2.1.14);
- F = O and T = id, so n = 0;
- α₊ = −1 and α₋ = 1.

The twisted level map on RΓ(Spec Z, O) = Z is multiplication by (−1)^{k₊}, while all transition maps are the identity. So the level maps do not form a map of systems, and nothing is induced on the colimit. Yet T_C is the identity.

A non-degenerate version of the same example:
- X̄ = C̄ = P¹_Z and X = C = A¹_Z;
- D₊ = ∞ and D₋ = ∅;
- α₊ = −1.

On H⁰(P¹, O(k)) the level map is (−1)^k. The transition map is multiplication by the section vanishing at ∞, which is injective. The two paths around the square differ by 2ι(f) ≠ 0.

Taking α₊ = 0 also fails: the level maps vanish for k₊ ≥ 1 but not for k₊ = 0.

The proof ("We simply twist …") does not address any of this. With compatible maps, the remaining identification of the limit map with T_C through Corollary 2.3.11 and Lemma 2.2.7 is routine but also unwritten.

**Consequences.** Corollary 2.3.14 is never cited later.
- §2.5.2 says it "improve[s] on the results of section 2.3.12" and redoes the construction. Lemma 2.5.3 twists the map of Proposition 2.3.13 by the maps p̄⋆₂O(qD₊) → p̄⋆₁O(pD₊) and p̄⋆₂O(−pD₋) → p̄⋆₁O(−qD₋) given by Lemma 2.1.17. These lie over the ideal inclusions, so they are compatible. The proof of Proposition 2.5.4 ("The endomorphism T of each of the complexes is given by going around the diagram once") uses exactly this compatibility, and it holds there.
- The same unqualified hypothesis, "we have maps (p″₂)⋆O_{X″}(D₊) → (p″₁)⋆O_{X″}(D₊) and (p″₂)⋆O_{X″}(−D₋) → (p″₁)⋆O_{X″}(−D₋)", recurs in Theorem 2.11.4(3), p. 32. Its proof on p. 33 ("by assumption, the map T on the limit factors as maps …") uses the twisted maps in the same way and needs the same compatibility. In part (4), which is the part applied later, the maps come from Lemmas 2.5.3 and 2.1.17 and are compatible.

The main results are therefore unaffected. The statement of Corollary 2.3.14 as printed needs the added hypothesis, and so does the parallel hypothesis in Theorem 2.11.4(3).

sourceIssues.correction:
The proof should also say that the targets p̄!₁𝓕̄(nD_C) = p̄!₁𝓕̄ ⊗ 𝒪_C̄(nD_C) are uniformly bounded below. By Definition 2.1.24 the map p̄₁ is proper, so Rp̄₁⋆ has cohomological amplitude in [0, d] on quasi-coherent complexes for some d. For a discrete K in D^{<−d} this gives Hom(K, p̄!₁𝓕̄) = Hom(Rp̄₁⋆K, 𝓕̄) = 0, since 𝓕̄ is a sheaf in degree 0. Taking K to be a truncation of p̄!₁𝓕̄ (which the paper states is discrete) shows p̄!₁𝓕̄ ∈ D^{≥−d}. Twisting by a line bundle keeps this bound for every n.

The factorization then follows from a standard fact. On the noetherian (hence qcqs) scheme C̄, Hom(P, −) commutes with filtered colimits of quasi-coherent complexes that are uniformly bounded below, for any pseudo-coherent P. To see this, choose a perfect Q → P whose cone lies in D^{≤−d−2}, which approximation by perfect complexes allows on a qcqs scheme. Then Hom(P, E) = Hom(Q, E) for every E in D^{≥−d}, including the colimit, and Q is compact. The same holds in D(𝒪_{C̄,■}): all the objects are discrete, discrete objects are closed under colimits, and the embedding is fully faithful.

The proposed correction is right and minimal. Its extra claim that p̄!₁𝓕̄ has coherent cohomology is true but not needed. When 𝓕̄ is locally free, as for the sheaves ω^κ used later, p̄⋆₂𝓕̄ is perfect and hence compact, and the sentence holds as written.

sourceIssues.correction:
The proposed repair is right, and it is essentially the minimal one.

1. Framework. Take D(A■) and D(O_{X,■}) to be the stable ∞-categories. Clausen–Scholze's Theorem 9.8, which the paper cites for D(O_{X,■}), is itself ∞-categorical, and the triangulated category is its homotopy category.

2. Definition 2.4.2. D((A[T],A)■) is the ∞-category of A[T]-module objects in D(A■). A[T] is the free associative A-algebra on one generator, so D((A[T],A)■) is equivalent to the ∞-category of pairs (M, T) with T an endomorphism of M. So M^ord is functorial in (M, T), and the cone of X − T realises this equivalence. With the standard cone, the displayed shift [1] should be dropped.

3. Lemma 2.4.4. Read "the action is induced by actions on each M_{i,j}" as follows: the T_{i,j} form an endomorphism of the diagram (M_{i,j}) in the ∞-category, i.e. a diagram I × J → D((A[T],A)■), and T is its colimit–limit. The forgetful functor to D(A■) preserves limits and colimits, so the first line of the proof and part (1) then hold as printed. Parts (2) and (3) follow as written.

4. Applications. Each application must supply this coherence. In §2.5 it does.
- The sheaves F(k₊D₊ − k₋D₋) and their transition maps form a diagram of coherent sheaves, so the diagram is canonically coherent.
- The operators of Lemma 2.5.3 and Corollary 2.3.14 are one morphism p̄⋆₂F(−nD₋) → p̄!₁F(nD₊) in D(O_{C̄,■}), tensored with maps of invertible sheaves and composed with transition maps, followed by the adjunction unit and the trace. All of these are natural transformations.
- With the colimit–limit of Corollary 2.3.11 taken in the ∞-category, the operators therefore form an endomorphism of the diagram.

The same holds for the later uses (Theorem 2.7.4, p. 24; p. 53).

One refinement to the proposed wording: the operators are not maps of sheaves, since p̄!₁F is a complex. They are a single morphism twisted by maps of invertible sheaves.
sourceIssues.reason:
The paper says it works in "a triangulated category of solid O_X-modules" (p. 12). Footnote 2 admits that turning an endomorphism into an A[T]-module is not canonical there. The following checks show exactly what survives in the triangulated setting and what does not.

(a) Objects survive. Let T be an endomorphism of M in D(A■). By adjunction, X − T : M ⊗_A A[X] → M ⊗_A A[X] is a well-defined morphism of D((A[X],A)■). So its cone is determined up to isomorphism, and so is M^ord ≅ cone(X − T on M ⊗_{A■} A[X^{±1}]■). Definition 2.4.2 therefore makes sense for objects, though not canonically or functorially.

(b) Invertibility statements survive. Let f : M → N commute with T in the homotopy category. Apply Hom(−, Ñ) to the triangle M ⊗ A[X] → M ⊗ A[X] → M̃. This shows that f lifts to a morphism M̃ → Ñ in D((A[T],A)■), but only up to morphisms that the forgetful functor kills. Every object Ñ of D((A[T],A)■) is the cone of T ⊗ 1 − 1 ⊗ T on N ⊗_A A[T]. So such a morphism factors through the connecting map, and by adjunction a composite of two of them is zero. Lifts are therefore unique modulo an ideal of square zero, and whether a lift becomes invertible on ordinary parts does not depend on the lift chosen. So this step of Lemma 2.4.4(2) and Proposition 2.5.4 (p. 20) holds even in the triangulated setting: T invertible on ordinary parts forces the horizontal maps, the vertical maps and T′ to be invertible.

(c) The colimit–limit step does not survive. The step that fails is "We have that M = colim_i lim_j M_{i,j} in D((A[T],A)■)" (proof of Lemma 2.4.4). In a triangulated category, colimits and limits of diagrams exist only up to non-unique isomorphism. Endomorphisms T_{i,j} that commute with the transition maps up to homotopy do not determine the induced endomorphism of the colimit–limit: for a sequential colimit it is unique only modulo lim¹ Hom(M_i[1], M). Nor do they give a diagram in D((A[T],A)■) whose colimit–limit is (M, T). The paper gives no such lift, and footnote 2 concerns only the non-uniqueness of the cone. Lemma 2.4.4(1) needs the lift, and (2) and (3) use (1). Through (1) the lift is needed by Proposition 2.5.4 and Theorem 2.5.1 (pp. 19–20; "canonically quasi-isomorphic" also needs it), by Theorem 2.7.4 (p. 24) and by p. 53.

The defence succeeds only in the ∞-categorical setting, which the cited source supplies. There:
- modules over the induced analytic ring (A[T],A)■ are A[T]-modules whose underlying A-module is A■-complete, since completeness is tested by adjunction against A■[S];
- modules over the free algebra A[T] are exactly objects with an endomorphism.
So the paper's lemma holds for coherent diagrams, and §2.5 produces coherent diagrams, as explained in the correction. No stated result changes. But the paper declares a triangulated framework, and in footnote 2 the authors say that an ∞-categorical treatment "might be desirable". So the step as printed is asserted without adequate proof: a genuine gap in the proofs.

Preprint. The text of January 2024, p. 17, has only "Let T be an operator acting on M so that we can view M as an object of D((A[T],A)■)", with no justification and no footnote. The gap is therefore already there. The revision added the cone construction and footnote 2, which flag the problem but do not resolve it.

sourceIssues.printed: Definition 2.4.5: "Let M, N ∈ D(A■). A map T : M → N is said to have finite rank if it has a factorization M → C → N where C is a complex whose cohomology groups are finite A-modules." Proof of Lemma 2.4.6: "Let M → C → M be a factorization of T, where C is a complex with finite cohomology. We can also think of T as an endomorphism of C by composing the arrows of the factorization of T. It is clear that the induced map M^ord → C^ord is a quasi-isomorphism, since it factors T. But H^i(C^ord) is a direct factor of H^i(C) by lemma 2.4.3." Lemma 2.4.3 (p. 18) begins: "Assume that A is an artinian local ring and that M is a bounded complex of finite A-modules equipped with an action of an operator T. ...". Its proof begins: "We consider the algebra B generated by T in End(M). This is a finite A-algebra."
sourceIssues.correction:
Lemma 2.4.6 is true as stated. Only the justification of the last step has to change: Lemma 2.4.3 covers bounded complexes, and C need not be bounded.

Replacement for the last step. Every cohomology group of C is a finite A-module, so it is discrete. An object of D(A■), or of D((A[T],A)■), whose cohomology groups are all discrete is itself discrete: the natural map to it from the discrete complex of its underlying values is an isomorphism on every H^i. So C, with the action of T_C, is a discrete complex of A[T]-modules. The functor − ⊗_{(A[T],A)■} A[T,T^{-1}]■ preserves colimits and sends A[T] to A[T,T^{-1}]. Discrete complexes of A[T]-modules are generated from A[T] by colimits and shifts. So on discrete complexes this functor is the ordinary localization − ⊗^L_{A[T]} A[T,T^{-1}]. Case (2) of the proof of Lemma 2.4.3 uses the same fact. This localization is exact, so H^i(C^ord) = H^i(C) ⊗_{A[T]} A[T,T^{-1}]. Since H^i(C) has finite length and T acts A-linearly on it, this is the Fitting summand of H^i(C) on which T is bijective. It is a direct factor of H^i(C), and its complement is the summand on which T is nilpotent. Hence H^i(M^ord) ≅ H^i(C^ord) is a finite A-module.

The step can also be proved with the paper's own lemmas. For a ≤ b, the truncation τ^{[a,b]}C is a bounded complex with finite cohomology on which T_C acts, so Lemma 2.4.3 applies to it. For a ≤ i ≤ b it gives H^i((τ^{[a,b]}C)^ord) = the T-bijective summand of H^i(C). D(A■) is left complete, because countable products of solid A-modules are exact. Filtered colimits are exact. So C = colim_b lim_a τ^{[a,b]}C. Lemma 2.4.4(1) then gives C^ord = colim_b lim_a (τ^{[a,b]}C)^ord. In each degree i these systems are eventually constant, so H^i(C^ord) is the T-bijective summand of H^i(C).

Adding "bounded" to Definition 2.4.5 would also make the proof correct as written. But the proof of Proposition 2.10.3 (p. 30) would then need F to be bounded, and that proposition assumes only that F has coherent cohomology groups.
sourceIssues.reason:
The proof of Lemma 2.4.3 needs a bounded complex. It uses that the A-subalgebra B of End(M) generated by T is finite over A, so that B is a product of local algebras. Definition 2.4.5 puts no boundedness condition on C. The paper says "bounded" explicitly when it means it: in Lemma 2.4.3, Lemma 2.4.4(3) and Theorem 2.5.1(2). The paper's own use of the definition also allows unbounded C. In the proof of Proposition 2.10.3 (p. 30), the finite rank of T_C comes from factoring the map RΓ_{p̄₂^⋆D₋,p̄₂^⋆D₊}(C̄, p₂^⋆F) → RΓ_{p̄₁^⋆D₋,p̄₁^⋆D₊}(C̄, p₁^!F) through RΓ_{C̄∖(p̄₂^⋆D̊₋ ∪ p̄₁^⋆D̊₊)}(C̄∖p̄₁^⋆D̊₊, p₂^⋆F). There F ∈ D(O_{X,■}) is only assumed to have coherent cohomology groups, and Lemma 2.10.1(4) gives only finite cohomology groups. When F is unbounded, this complex is in general unbounded too.

For unbounded C the finiteness used in the proof of Lemma 2.4.3 fails, even within the hypotheses of Lemma 2.4.6. Under the convention of §2.2, schemes are of finite type over Z, so an artinian local A is a finite ring. Take A = k = F_p (any field works). Let C = ⊕_{n≥1} (k[x]/(x^n))[n], with T_C acting as multiplication by x on the n-th summand. Every H^i(C) is finite. Since T_C = T_C∘id, T_C is a finite-rank endomorphism of M = C. D(k) → D(k■) is fully faithful, and over a field Hom_{D(k)}(V[n], W[m]) = 0 for n ≠ m. Each summand is compact. Hence End(C) = ∏_n End_k(k[x]/(x^n)). A polynomial that kills T_C is divisible by x^n for every n, so it is zero. Thus B ≅ k[x], which is not finite over k, and the argument of Lemma 2.4.3 cannot start. Taking C = ⊕_{n≥1} (k[x]/(f_n))[n], with f_n pairwise distinct monic irreducible polynomials other than x, gives an example in which T_C is invertible.

The assertion made in the step is nevertheless true, by the argument in the correction. In the first example, H^i(C) ⊗_{A[T]} A[T,T^{-1}] = 0 for all i, so C^ord = 0. The earlier steps of the proof are sound for unbounded C as well. Write a : M → C and b : C → M, with b∘a = T_M and a∘b = T_C. On ordinary parts, a has the left inverse T_M^{-1}∘b and the right inverse b∘T_C^{-1}, so M^ord → C^ord is an isomorphism. So the step is asserted without adequate justification, but it is not false, and Lemma 2.4.6 holds as stated.

The gap is confined to this proof. No later proof cites Lemma 2.4.6 or Proposition 2.10.3. The finiteness of ordinary cohomology in Theorem 2.5.1(2) and Proposition 2.5.4 (pp. 19–20) comes from Lemma 2.4.4 applied to the bounded complexes RΓ(X̄, F̄(k₊D₊ − k₋D₋)).

So only the D₋ map has lost its sign. The displayed formula on the next line confirms the correction. Start from T : p̄⋆₂F̄(−nD₋) → p̄!₁F̄(nD₊). Tensor with the k₊-th power of the D₊ map and the k₋-th power of the corrected D₋ map, using p̄!₁(F ⊗ L) = p̄!₁F ⊗ p̄⋆₁L for L invertible. The source becomes F̄(k₊qD₊ − (n + pk₋)D₋) and the target F̄((pk₊ + n)D₊ − qk₋D₋), exactly as printed. With the sign as printed, the target would instead carry +qk₋D₋. After it, compose with the map that relaxes the poles along D₊ from p(k₊ + 1) + n to k₊q. This gives the printed T : p̄⋆₂F̄((k₊+1)qD₊ − k₋qD₋) → p̄!₁F̄(k₊qD₊ − (k₋+1)qD₋). sourceIssues.locator: §2.5.6 (Independence on the choice of a dynamic compactification; proof of Theorem 2.5.1(3)), p. 20
sourceIssues.printed: "We can therefore consider three strict dynamic correspondences (C̄, X̄, p̄1, p̄2) with divisors (D+, D−), (D′+, D′−), (D′+ ∪ D+, D′− ∪ D−). This reduces us to consider the case that D′+ ⊇ D+ and D′− ⊇ D−. We can first treat the case that D′+ ⊇ D+ and D′− = D− and then the case D′+ = D+ and D′− ⊆ D−. We therefore concentrate on the case D′+ ⊇ D+ and D′− = D− as the other is similar."
sourceIssues.correction: "… and then the case D′+ = D+ and D′− ⊇ D−." The inclusion sign in the second sub-case should be reversed.
sourceIssues.reason: The page image of p. 20 shows the printed sign is "⊆", so this is not a text-layer artefact. The sentence just before it reduces to the case D′+ ⊇ D+ and D′− ⊇ D−. That is exactly the case where the identity of (C̄, X̄, p̄1, p̄2) is a map C′ → C in the sense of Definition 2.1.28 (p. 10). That definition requires D′+ ⊇ ξ⋆D+ and D′− ⊇ ξ⋆D−, and Theorem 2.5.1(3) is stated for such maps. The natural way to split this case into two steps is to pass through the intermediate pair (D′+, D−). The first step, (D+, D−) against (D′+, D−), is the printed first case: D′+ ⊇ D+ and D′− = D−. The second step, (D′+, D−) against (D′+, D′−), keeps D+ fixed and enlarges the minus-divisor. So it is the case D′+ = D+ and D′− ⊇ D−. Read literally, the printed second case "D′− ⊆ D−" lies inside the reduced case (D′− ⊇ D−) only when D′− = D−, so it would be empty. The printed text makes sense only if one silently swaps which compactification carries the primes in the second step. The next sentence keeps the original naming ("concentrate on the case D′+ ⊇ D+ and D′− = D−"), so no such swap is intended. The sign is therefore a slip. It is harmless. What is being proved is that two ordinary cohomologies are quasi-isomorphic, and that statement is symmetric in C and C′, so either inclusion gives the same case after renaming. The second case is also never written out ("the other is similar"). The argument that is written out uses only D′+ ⊇ D+ with D′− = D−: it uses D′+ ≤ aD+ + bD− and the chain of maps with k+ ≥ m and k− ≥ m + bk+. That argument is unaffected. Theorem 2.5.1(3), and its later uses (Proposition 2.6.2 on p. 21, and the definitions in §4 that rely on independence of the compactification), do not depend on the sign.

sourceIssues.printed: Remark 2.6.3. Our assumption that 𝓕 is A-flat is only used to make sure that 𝓕 ⊗_A M is again a coherent sheaf (and in particular is bounded below) so that RΓ(X, 𝓕 ⊗_A M)^{C−ord} is a well defined notion. The assumption that M is a discrete A-module is crucial.
sourceIssues.correction: … only used to make sure that 𝓕 ⊗^L_A M is again a coherent sheaf, namely 𝓕 ⊗_A M (and in particular is bounded below) …
sourceIssues.reason: The paper separates ⊗^L_A from ⊗_A, as in §2.6.1 ('p_2^⋆(𝓕) ⊗^L_A M = p_2^⋆(𝓕 ⊗_A M)') and Proposition 2.6.2. All schemes are of finite type over ℤ and M is a finite-type A-module. So the underived 𝓕 ⊗_A M = 𝓕 ⊗_{𝒪_X} p^⋆M is a coherent sheaf whether or not 𝓕 is flat, and 'bounded below' only makes sense for a complex. What A-flatness gives is Tor_i^A(𝓕, M) = 0 for i > 0, i.e. 𝓕 ⊗^L_A M = 𝓕 ⊗_A M is a sheaf concentrated in degree 0. Without flatness, 𝓕 ⊗^L_A M can have cohomology in infinitely many negative degrees. This identification is exactly what §2.6.1 uses to build T ⊗ 1 and what the proof of Proposition 2.6.2 uses. The remark only makes sense with ⊗^L, and the intended meaning is clear.

sourceIssues.locator: §2.6.12 (Second base change formula), pp. 22–23: the sentence that defines T′, just before Proposition 2.6.13 on p. 23, together with the proof of Proposition 2.6.13. The 2024 preprint has the same text word for word.
sourceIssues.printed: (p. 22–23, §2.6.12) "Let 𝓕 be a coherent sheaf over X, and T : p₂^⋆𝓕 → p₁^!𝓕 be a cohomological correspondence. We assume that X and S′ are tor independent and that 𝓕 is A-flat. We have a cohomological correspondence: T′ : (p′₂)^⋆𝓕′ → (p′₁)^!𝓕′ deduced by base change (we use here [CSb], prop. 11.4 and the tor-independence of X and S′)." Proof of Proposition 2.6.13 (p. 23): "... The proposition follows by applying ordinary projectors."
sourceIssues.correction: Replace the hypothesis "X and S′ are tor independent" with "X and C are both tor independent from S′ over S" (for example, X and C flat over S). Because O_{X′} = O_X ⊗^L_A A′, the new condition on C is equivalent to the square formed by p₁ : C → X and g : X′ → X (with g′ : C′ → C) being Tor-independent. Proper base change for that square gives p₁^! g⋆ ≃ g′⋆ (p′₁)^!. From this one gets a base-change map g′⋆ p₁^!𝓕 → (p′₁)^!𝓕′, and T′ is the composite (p′₂)⋆𝓕′ = g′⋆p₂⋆𝓕 → g′⋆p₁^!𝓕 → (p′₁)^!𝓕′. The justification should cite this Tor-independent proper base change, not the flat base change of [CSb], Prop. 11.4. If p₁ also has finite Tor-dimension, the base-change map is an isomorphism. That is not needed to construct T′, so the extra finite-Tor-dimension condition in the reported fix is sufficient but not minimal.
sourceIssues.reason:
The printed text on pp. 22–23 was checked against the rendered pages. In [CSb], Prop. 11.4 (Scholze, Lectures on condensed mathematics, Lecture XI) proves two things: that f^! ≅ f^!R ⊗^L f^* when f has finite Tor-dimension, and that g′^*f^! ≅ f′^!g^* when the base change g is flat. On p. 25 the paper itself cites this proposition as "flat base change", in a setting where p₁ and p₂ are assumed flat.

In §2.6.12 neither hypothesis is available. The relevant base change is along X′ → X, the pullback of the finite map S′ → S, which is not flat in general; in the application on p. 51 it is Spec Z/p^s → Spec Z/p^{s+1}. Nor is p₁ assumed to have finite Tor-dimension. Here C′ = C ×_X X′. Since O_{X′} = O_X ⊗^L_A A′, one gets O_C ⊗^L_{O_X} O_{X′} = O_C ⊗^L_A A′. So the square C′/C over X′/X is tor-independent exactly when C and S′ are tor-independent, and the hypothesis on X alone does not imply this.

Counterexample to the identification, under all the stated hypotheses:
- Take A = F_p[x], A′ = A/(x²), X = S = Spec A, C = Spec A/(x), and p₁ = p₂ the closed immersion.
- This is a correspondence with the strict dynamic compactification X̄ = X, C̄ = C, D₊ = D₋ = ∅.
- X and S′ are tor-independent, and 𝓕 = O_X is A-flat. Also C′ = Spec F_p = C.
- p₁^!O_X = RHom_A(A/x, A) = F_p[−1] by the Koszul complex, so g_C^*p₁^!O_X = F_p[−1].
- (p′₁)^!O_{X′} = RHom_{A′}(F_p, A′) = xA′ ≅ F_p in degree 0, since A′ = F_p[x]/(x²) is self-injective.
- Checked by direct computation: these differ, and every map F_p[−1] → F_p is zero. So no base-change isomorphism g_C^*p₁^!𝓕 ≅ (p′₁)^!𝓕′ exists under the stated hypotheses.

The proof of Proposition 2.6.13 only identifies the two complexes. It then "applies ordinary projectors" without checking that T ⊗ 1 corresponds to T′, which depends on how T′ is defined.

Limits of this finding:
- In the example T = 0 (Hom(O_C, O_C[−1]) = 0), so the example refutes the construction, not the formula.
- When p₁ is finite, T factors through H⁰, and a compatible T′ can still be defined from the map p₁*p₂^*𝓕 → 𝓕.
- In the uses on p. 51 and p. 54 the correspondences have finite flat projections and are flat over the base (Prop. 3.4.9), so the corrected hypotheses hold there.

What remains is a gap in Proposition 2.6.13 at the generality stated. No downstream result fails. To construct T′ one needs a map g′⋆p₁^!𝓕 → (p′₁)^!g⋆𝓕 for the cartesian square C′ = C ×_X X′ over g : X′ → X. The cited [CSb], Prop. 11.4 (Scholze, Lectures on condensed mathematics, Lecture XI) proves g′⋆f^! ≃ f′^! g⋆ only when g is flat and f has finite Tor-dimension. There the map is built from f^! g⋆ ≃ g′⋆ f′^!, which is adjoint to proper base change, and [CSb] notes (in the footnote to its proper base change statement) that in the coherent setting a square that is not Tor-independent needs derived schemes. Here g is the base change of the finite map S′ → S, which is in general not flat; in the applications S′ → S is Spec Z/p^{s−1} → Spec Z/p^s. Under the stated hypothesis O_{X′} = O_X ⊗^L_A A′, so O_C ⊗^L_{O_X} O_{X′} = O_C ⊗^L_A A′. The relevant square is therefore Tor-independent exactly when C and S′ are Tor-independent over S, and the Tor-independence of X and S′ does not give this. In the analogous place, Lemma 2.2.2(2) on p. 12, the paper does record the needed condition: "note that C̄ and X are tor-independent".

Example (checked by direct computation). Take A = F_p[x], A′ = A/(x²), X = S, C = Spec A/(x), and p₁ = p₂ the closed immersion. Then (C, X, ∅, ∅) is a strict dynamic compactification, X and S′ are Tor-independent, 𝓕 = O_X is A-flat, and C′ = Spec F_p. Now p₁^!O_X = RHom_A(A/(x), A) = F_p[−1], and its pullback to C′ is F_p[−1]. But (p′₁)^!O_{X′} = RHom_{A′}(F_p, A′) = xA′ ≅ F_p in degree 0, because A′ is self-injective. So the base-change identification the text relies on fails under the stated hypotheses; indeed Tor₁^A(A/(x), A′) ≅ F_p ≠ 0. In this example Hom(O_C, O_C[−1]) = 0, so T = 0 and the formula holds trivially. The example shows that the construction of T′ is unjustified, not that the displayed formula is false.

Defence examined. The proof of Proposition 2.6.13 uses the stated Tor-independence correctly, but only to get 𝓕 ⊗^L_A A′ = 𝓕′. Its final step ("follows by applying ordinary projectors") needs the operator induced by T on RΓ_{D₊,D₋}(X̄, 𝓕 ⊗_A A′) to agree with the one defined by T′ on X̄′. That requires T′ to be the base change of T, which is exactly the missing hypothesis. Reading "X" to cover every space ("similarly for all spaces") would repair this, but the text names only X.

Consequences. Proposition 2.6.13 is used on p. 51, in defining RΓ_w(K^pK_{w,p,P}, κ) and its variants as limits over s (these are then used in Proposition 4.4.5), and on p. 54, for the transition maps defining RΓ_w(K^pK_{p,P}). review.reason: Confirmed as a gap. §2.6.12 assumes only that `$X$ and $S'$ are tor independent' and then asserts a cohomological correspondence $T':(p'_2)^\star\mathcal F'\to(p'_1)^!\mathcal F'$ `deduced by base change'. Proposition 2.6.13's own proof needs only the printed hypothesis, so the gap is in the construction of $T'$ that precedes it.
