sourceIssues.printed: D_X̄(j⋆F) = RHom(j⋆F, p̄^!O_S) = lim_n I^n RHom(F̄, p̄^!O_S) = lim_m lim_n I^n RHom(F̄, (p̄^!O_S)_{σ≤m}). In the last equation, (p̄^!O_S)_{σ≤m} is the stupid truncation ([Sta22], Tag 0118). Since RHom(F̄, (p̄^!O_S)_{σ≤m}) is pseudo-coherent (it is represented by a bounded above complex of coherent sheaves as (p̄^!O_S)_{σ≤m} is and F̄ is locally free), by proposition 2.3.2, we have lim_n I^n RHom(F̄, (p̄^!O_S)_{σ≤m}) = j_! RHom(F, (p^!O_S)_{σ≤m}). Since p is smooth, (p^!O_S)_{σ≤m} = p^!O_S for m large enough.
sourceIssues.correction:
Keep the display. As the proof tacitly does, let K be a bounded below complex of coherent sheaves representing p̄^!O_S. Replace the last sentence with a limit argument, which works for every such K.

Step 1. The complex K|_X represents p^!O_S = Ω^d_{X/S}[d], so its cohomology is concentrated in degree −d ≤ 0.

Step 2. For m ≥ 0, the complex K|_X is acyclic in degrees ≥ m+1. So σ≥m+1(K|_X) ≃ Z^{m+1}[−m−1], where Z^{m+1} = ker(d^{m+1}) is a coherent sheaf on X.

Step 3. So the cone of j_!D_X(F) → j_!RHom(F, σ≤m(K|_X)) is j_!(F^∨ ⊗ Z^{m+1})[−m].

Step 4. By Proposition 2.3.2, j_! of a coherent sheaf is the derived limit of an inverse system of coherent sheaves. Products are exact, so it lies in degrees 0 and 1. Hence the cone lies in degrees m and m+1.

Step 5. By the Milnor sequence, the derived limit over m of these cones is 0. Hence lim_m j_!RHom(F, (p^!O_S)_{σ≤m}) = j_!D_X(F), and with the display this gives D_X̄(j⋆F) = j_!D_X(F).

Alternative route. Canonical truncations avoid choosing K at all. For each m, τ≤m p̄^!O_S lies in D^b_coh and is pseudo-coherent. Proposition 2.3.2 then gives lim_n I^n RHom(F̄, τ≤m p̄^!O_S) = j_!D_X(F) for m ≥ 0. The cone of τ≤m p̄^!O_S → p̄^!O_S lies in degrees ≥ m+1, and it stays there after tensoring with I^n F̄^∨ and taking lim_n. So the induced map j_!D_X(F) → D_X̄(j⋆F) is an isomorphism in degrees ≤ m, for every m. Note that canonical truncations form a direct system, so they cannot simply be put in place of σ≤m inside lim_m.

When the printed sentence is true. It holds for a representative whose terms K^i vanish on X for all large i, and trivially for a bounded representative. If p̄^!O_S is bounded, a bounded representative exists and the truncation is not needed. This happens, for example, when A is Gorenstein (such as Z/p^s) or when X̄ is flat over S.
sourceIssues.reason:
The printed text was checked on the page image of p. 23.

The stupid truncation is not an operation on the derived category: it depends on the complex K chosen to represent p̄^!O_S, and the proof never specifies that complex. The final sentence is about σ≤m(K|_X), because (p^!O_S)_{σ≤m} is what Proposition 2.3.2 produces from j⋆((p̄^!O_S)_{σ≤m}). Smoothness of p only says that K|_X has cohomology in the single degree −d.

Take m > −d. Then K|_X is exact in degree m, so H^m(σ≤m K|_X) = K^m/d(K^{m−1}) = K^m/ker d^m ≅ d^m(K^m). Hence σ≤m(K|_X) ≃ p^!O_S holds if and only if d^m vanishes on X. For example, this fails for any representative whose restriction to X is a complex of injectives that is unbounded above. Nothing in the proof arranges d^m|_X = 0, and "since p is smooth" does not give it.

The truncation is used exactly when p̄^!O_S is unbounded above; otherwise a bounded representative makes σ≤m harmless. That case does occur under the hypotheses of Proposition 2.7.2, which allow any A and do not require X̄ to be flat over S. Checked by direct computation:
- Take A = F_p[x,y]/(x,y)^2, which is not Gorenstein, and m_A its maximal ideal.
- Replace the chart A[t] of P^1_A by Spec B, with B = A[t] + m_A t^{-1} ⊂ A[t, t^{-1}]. The result X̄ is finite over P^1_A, hence proper.
- X = X̄ \ V(t) ≅ A^1_A is smooth over S, and V(t) is Cartier because t is a non-zero-divisor on B.
- B contains m_A t^{-1} ≅ k^2 as an A-module summand. So Tor_i^A(B, E) ≠ 0 for all i, where E is the injective hull of k: indeed Tor_i^A(k, E) ≅ Hom(Ext^i_A(k, A), E) and A has infinite injective dimension.
- Hence p̄^!O_S = RHom(Lp̄^*E, p̄^!E) is unbounded above.
So the step can fail precisely in the case the truncation was introduced for.

The first three equalities in the display are fine: K = lim_m σ≤m K, since the system is termwise surjective and termwise eventually constant. The repair above yields the stated isomorphism D_X̄(j⋆F) = j_! D_X(F).

Theorem 2.7.4 (p. 24) uses Proposition 2.7.2, and Theorem 5.5.1 (p. 57) uses Theorem 2.7.4. Because the statement of Proposition 2.7.2 remains true, only the proof is affected. This was checked on the page image of p. 23.

The defence fails for the following reasons.

1. A stupid truncation is not an operation on the derived category. It depends on the complex K chosen to represent p̄^!O_S, and the proof never names one.

2. For Proposition 2.3.2 to give the printed equality, one needs j⋆(F̄^∨ ⊗ σ≤m K) = F^∨ ⊗ σ≤m(K|_X). So the object written (p^!O_S)_{σ≤m} must be σ≤m(K|_X), the stupid truncation of the restricted complex, not a truncation of the one-term complex Ω^d_{X/S}[d]. Smoothness of p says only that K|_X has cohomology in the single degree −d.

3. For m ≥ 0, exactness of K|_X at m gives H^m(σ≤m(K|_X)) = K^m/d(K^{m−1}) = K^m/ker d^m ≅ d^m(K^m) on X. So σ≤m(K|_X) ≃ p^!O_S exactly when d^m vanishes on X. This holds for all large m exactly when the terms K^i vanish on X for all large i. Nothing in the proof arranges this.

4. The claim fails for some legitimate representatives. Take any coherent sheaf Ḡ with G = Ḡ|_X ≠ 0. Adding to K the acyclic complex ⊕_{m≥0}(Ḡ →id Ḡ), placed in degrees m and m+1, gives another bounded below complex of coherent sheaves representing p̄^!O_S. For it, σ≤m(K|_X) ≃ p^!O_S ⊕ G[−m] for every m ≥ 0.

5. Choosing a bounded representative rescues the sentence only when p̄^!O_S is bounded, and then the truncation is superfluous. The truncation matters exactly when p̄^!O_S is unbounded above. That case does occur under the hypotheses of Proposition 2.7.2, which allow any A and do not require X̄ to be flat over S. The following example was checked by direct computation.
- Let A = F_p[x,y]/(x,y)^2, which is not Gorenstein.
- Let X̄ be P^1_A with the chart Spec A[t] replaced by Spec B, where B = A[t] + m_A t^{−1} ⊂ A[t,t^{−1}].
- X̄ is finite over P^1_A, hence proper. D = V(t) is Cartier, because t is a non-zero-divisor on B. X = X̄ \ D ≅ A^1_A is smooth. F = O_X extends to O_X̄.
- The A-module B has m_A t^{−1} ≅ k^2 as a direct summand. Let E be the injective hull of k. Then Hom(Tor_i^A(k,E), E) ≅ Ext^i_A(k,A), so Tor_i^A(B,E) ≠ 0 for infinitely many i.
- Hence p̄^!O_S = RHom(Lp̄^⋆E, p̄^!E) is the dual, with respect to the dualizing complex p̄^!E, of a complex that is unbounded below. So it is unbounded above.
There, every representative has infinitely many nonzero terms. The printed step would need one whose high-degree terms are supported on D. The proof neither chooses such a representative nor shows that one exists.

The rest of the argument is sound.
- K = lim_m σ≤m K, since the system is termwise surjective and termwise eventually constant.
- σ≤m K is a bounded complex of coherent sheaves, so Proposition 2.3.2 applies.
- The limit argument in the correction closes the gap for every representative. So the statement of Proposition 2.7.2 is true as printed.

Consequences. Proposition 2.7.2 is used in the proof of Theorem 2.7.4 (p. 24). Theorem 2.7.4 is used in the proof of Theorem 5.5.1 (p. 57; stated in the introduction as Theorem 1.4.8). These results are unaffected because the statement of Proposition 2.7.2 stands. In addition, the artinian coefficient rings relevant to Theorem 5.5.1 are quotients of Z_p[ζ_{p^n}] by powers of p. These are Gorenstein, so there p̄^!O_S is a dualizing complex, hence bounded, and the printed argument works with a bounded representative.

The 2024 preprint has the same final sentence.

review.reason: Confirmed as a gap. The proof of Proposition 2.7.2 replaces $\bar p^!\mathcal O_S$ by its stupid truncations $(\bar p^!\mathcal O_S)_{\sigma\leq m}$ and ends `Since $p$ is smooth, $(p^!\mathcal O_S)_{\sigma\leq m}=p^!\mathcal O_S$ for $m$ large enough'. Stupid truncation is not an operation on the derived category — it depends on the representing complex, which the proof never fixes — and even for a fixed representative the terms need not vanish in large degrees on $X$, so the stabilisation asserted does not follow from smoothness of $p$. The conclusion is right, and the finding gives two correct routes to it, a Milnor-sequence limit over $m$ or canonical truncations; both need the observation that $p^!\mathcal O_S$ is concentrated in a single negative degree because $p$ is smooth, which is the content the printed sentence is reaching for.

sourceIssues.reason: Theorem 2.5.1 is proved under the standing assumption of §2.5 (p. 19): "We assume that there exists a strict dynamic compactification". The notation RΓ(X, F)^{C−ord} is defined only under that assumption. Later results that use it restate the hypothesis explicitly: the base change results of §2.6 ("a correspondence admitting a strict dynamical compactification") and Theorem 2.7.4 ("We assume that it admits a strict dynamical compactification"). By contrast, §2.8 starts afresh with "We let (C, X, p_1, p_2) be a correspondence" and adds only that p_1 and p_2 are flat. Lemma 2.8.1 is conditional ("Assume that (C, X, p_1, p_2) admits a dynamic (resp. strict dynamic ...) compactification"), and nothing in §2.8 asserts that hypothesis. Still, the appeal to Theorem 2.5.1 on p. 25 and the proof of Proposition 2.8.2 need it: the proof works with C̄^{(n)} and D_±^{(n)}, which are the compactification built in Lemma 2.8.1. So the omission is real. Because Lemma 2.8.1 was set up for exactly this use, and the objects in the statement are undefined without the hypothesis, the intended hypothesis is clear. It is an omitted hypothesis, not a mathematical error.

The operator in the sentence starts at RΓ′_n, goes up to RΓ′_{n+1} along (p_2^{(n+1)})^⋆ and comes back along (p_1^{(n+1)})_!. It comes from the correspondence C^{(n+1)} over C^{(n)}, so it is the operator of T_{n+1}. It is also the operator that defines RΓ_n = RΓ(C^{(n)}, O_{C^{(n)}})^{C^{(n+1)}−ord} on p. 25 via Theorem 2.5.1. The paper's later text agrees. On p. 26 comes the square introduced by "By construction, the following square commutes". In its top row, the first arrow (p_1^{(n+1)})_!(p_2^{(n+1)})^⋆O_{C^{(n)}} → (p_1^{(n+1)})_!(p_1^{(n+1)})^!O_{C^{(n)}} is labelled T_{n+1}. The arrow labelled T_n in its bottom row is induced by T_n : (p_2^{(n)})^⋆O_{C^{(n−1)}} → (p_1^{(n)})^!O_{C^{(n−1)}}, as in the definition. The final diagram on p. 27 computes the endomorphism of RΓ′_n through (p_1^{(n+1)})_!(p_2^{(n+1)})^⋆O_{C^{(n)}}. So "T_n" is an off-by-one index slip, not a different convention.

Neither slip affects the argument. The proof shows that the square (2.8.A) commutes, using the proper base change identity (p_1^{(n+1)})_!(p_2^{(n+1)})^⋆ = (p_2^{(n)})^⋆(p_1^{(n)})_!. By (2.8.A), for n ≥ 1 the two composites RΓ′_n → RΓ′_{n+1} → RΓ′_n and RΓ′_n → RΓ′_{n−1} → RΓ′_n both equal the operator of T_{n+1}, which is invertible on the ordinary part RΓ_n. That is what "if we can prove the commutativity, we conclude" relies on. With the vertex read as RΓ′_0 and the index as n+1, the argument reads as intended. The statement of Proposition 2.8.2 is correctly printed. Its only later citation is on p. 54: there the maps in a diagram of the cohomologies RΓ_w(K_{i,j}) are quasi-isomorphisms "by proposition 2.8.2". That use relies on the statement alone.

p. 28: "2.9.8. Action of a correspondence on the spectral sequence. Let (C, X, p_1, p_2) be a correspondence. Let T : p_2^⋆𝓕 → p_1^!𝓕 be a cohomological correspondence. Then we have an action of T on RΓ(Ẑ_l, 𝓕), RΓ_c(U_l, 𝓕)and RΓ_c(Ẑ_l \ Ẑ_{l−1}, 𝓕) for all i, compatible with the natural morphisms. The spectral sequence of theorem 2.9.7 is T-equivariant."
p. 29: "Proof. We need to explain how we can attach to T a map of triangles:" [a diagram from p_2^⋆(j_l)_!j_l^⋆𝓕 → p_2^⋆𝓕 → p_2^⋆(î_l)_⋆(î_l)^⋆𝓕 → to p_1^!(j_l)_!j_l^⋆𝓕 → p_1^!𝓕 → (p_1)^!(î_l)_⋆(î_l)^⋆𝓕 →, with middle vertical arrow T]. The proof then builds the left vertical arrow and ends: "... this map is just given by the co-unit of the adjunction (p′_1)_!(p′_1)^! → Id."
Definition 2.1.8 (p. 7): "A correspondence is a quadruple (C, X, p_1, p_2), where X and C are separated, finite type schemes over S, coming with two projections p_1, p_2 : C ⇒ X and such that p_1 × p_2 : C → X × X is a proper map."
§2.9.5 (p. 28): "We now let X be a scheme ..."
sourceIssues.correction:
Add to §2.9.8 (or to Proposition 2.9.9) the hypothesis that p_1 is proper, as Definition 2.1.24(1) (p. 9) requires for dynamic correspondences. For example, this holds when X is proper over S. Then the first projection pr_1 : X ×_S X → X is proper, and so is p_1 = pr_1 ∘ (p_1 × p_2). In particular it holds for a compactification (C̄, X̄, p̄_1, p̄_2) (Remark 2.1.10).

With this hypothesis, let G be (j_l)_!j_l^⋆𝓕, 𝓕 or (î_l)_⋆(î_l)^⋆𝓕. The action of T on RΓ(X, G) is the composite
RΓ(X, G) → RΓ(C, p_2^⋆G) → RΓ(C, p_1^!G) = RΓ(X, (p_1)_!p_1^!G) → RΓ(X, G).
- The first arrow is pullback along p_2.
- The middle arrow is the matching vertical arrow of the map of triangles built in the proof.
- The equality uses (p_1)_⋆ = (p_1)_!, which holds because p_1 is proper. The last arrow comes from the counit (p_1)_!p_1^! → Id. It is the trace map of Lemma 2.2.7 (p. 13) with D_+ = D_− = ∅.

The three middle arrows form a map of triangles, and the outer arrows are natural. So the three endomorphisms are compatible with the triangle RΓ_c(U_l, 𝓕) → RΓ(X, 𝓕) → RΓ(Ẑ_l, 𝓕) →. The action on RΓ_c(Ẑ_l \ Ẑ_{l−1}, 𝓕) then comes from the triangles of Lemma 2.9.6, as the paper intends.
sourceIssues.reason:
Proposition 2.9.9 is stated for any correspondence (C, X, p_1, p_2) in the sense of Definition 2.1.8, and §2.9 puts no properness condition on X (§2.9.5: "We now let X be a scheme"). Definition 2.1.8 asks only that p_1 × p_2 be proper. That does not make p_1 proper.

By §2.9.5 and Lemma 2.9.6 (p. 28), each complex in the proposition has the form RΓ(X, G) for a complex G on X:
- RΓ(Ẑ_l, 𝓕) = RΓ(X, (î_l)_⋆(î_l)^⋆𝓕);
- RΓ_c(U_l, 𝓕) = RΓ(X, (j_l)_!j_l^⋆𝓕), implicit in the triangle RΓ_c(U_l, 𝓕) → RΓ(X, 𝓕) → RΓ(Ẑ_l, 𝓕) → of §2.9.5;
- RΓ_c(Ẑ_l \ Ẑ_{l−1}, 𝓕) = RΓ(X, (î_l)_⋆(î_l)^⋆(j_{l−1})_!(j_{l−1})^⋆𝓕).

The proof builds only a map of triangles on C. It goes from p_2^⋆ of the triangle (j_l)_!j_l^⋆𝓕 → 𝓕 → (î_l)_⋆(î_l)^⋆𝓕 → to p_1^! of the same triangle. Apart from some notational slips, this part is correct and needs no properness: it uses only the adjunction between (p_1)_! and p_1^! and the counit for p′_1.

Turning this into an endomorphism of RΓ(X, G) takes two further steps. The first is to pull back along p_2, which is always possible. The second needs a map RΓ(C, p_1^!G) = RΓ(X, (p_1)_⋆p_1^!G) → RΓ(X, G), and the proof does not supply one. The formalism provides only the counit (p_1)_!p_1^! → Id. That counit gives the required map when (p_1)_⋆ = (p_1)_!, which holds when p_1 is proper.

Elsewhere in §2 the paper imposes exactly this condition. Lemma 2.2.7 (p. 13) says "If p̄ is proper, we also have canonical trace maps". The action of T on cohomology is otherwise built from a dynamic correspondence (Proposition 2.2.10, p. 14; Proposition 2.10.3, p. 30). Definition 2.1.24(1) (p. 9) requires of a dynamic correspondence that "p̄_1 and p̄_2 are proper maps". The support hypothesis of Proposition 2.9.9 says that each Z_l is contracted in the sense of Definition 2.1.19(4) (p. 9), as D_− is in a dynamic correspondence. But §2.9.8 does not carry over the properness of p_1.

Without this hypothesis the missing step fails. Here is an example.
- Setup: S = Spec k for a field k, X = C = A¹_k with coordinate t, p_2 = id, and p_1 the constant map with value 0. Then p_1 × p_2 is the closed immersion x ↦ (0, x), so (C, X, p_1, p_2) is a correspondence, but p_1 is not proper.
- The claim: take 𝓕 = O_X, d = 0 and Z_0 = X. The support hypothesis holds trivially and Ẑ_0 = X, so the proposition claims an action of T on RΓ(X, O_X) = k[t].
- T can be nonzero: write p_1 = i ∘ q, with q : A¹_k → Spec k and i the inclusion of the origin. Then i^!O_X = k[−1] and q^!k = Ω¹[1], so p_1^!O_X ≅ Ω¹_C. Hence T = dt : O_C = p_2^⋆O_X → Ω¹_C = p_1^!O_X is a nonzero cohomological correspondence.
- There is no nonzero trace: (p_1)_⋆p_1^!O_X = i_⋆V with V = k[t]dt in degree 0, and Hom(i_⋆V, O_X) = Hom(V, i^!O_X) = Hom(V, k[−1]) = 0. So every map (p_1)_⋆p_1^!O_X → O_X is zero. For every T, completing the construction of the proof with such a map gives only the zero endomorphism of k[t].

Read literally, the zero endomorphism is "an action" compatible with all the natural maps, so the wording of the proposition is not strictly contradicted. But in this generality T induces no nonzero action in this way. A genuine action induced by T is what the proposition is meant to provide and what §4.5.6 uses. So Proposition 2.9.9 needs the extra hypothesis that p_1 is proper.

Proposition 2.9.9 is used once, in §4.5.6 (p. 52): "We have an action of t ∈ T^{++}(Q_p) on the spectral sequence by proposition 2.9.9 and corollary 4.2.10." There X = S^tor, which is proper over Z_p. By §4.2.1 (p. 43), C_t^tor is the normalization of S^tor × S^tor in C^tor_{t,Q_p}, so it is finite over S^tor × S^tor. Hence p_1 is proper and the argument works. Theorem 4.5.2 and Corollaries 4.5.4 and 4.5.5 are unaffected.

sourceIssues.locator: §2.10, Lemma 2.10.1(3) and its proof, p. 29; applied in Lemma 2.10.2 (pp. 29–30) and Proposition 2.10.3 (p. 30)
sourceIssues.printed: Lemma 2.10.1 (3): "Let j_U : U ↪ Y and j_{U′} : U′ ↪ Y be open subsets. We assume that U ⊆ Z ⊆ U′ ⊆ Y. Then we have natural maps: RΓ(Y, (j_U)_! j_U^⋆ F) → RΓ_Z(Y, F) → RΓ_Ẑ(Y, F) → RΓ(Y, (j_{U′})_! j_{U′}^⋆ F)." Proof: "For the third point, we just use the standard adjunctions." Context (p. 29): Z is a closed subscheme with i : Z ↪ Y, "RΓ_Z(Y, F) = RΓ(Z, i^! F)", and î : Ẑ → Y is "the closed subset of the locale".
sourceIssues.correction:
In (3), the inclusion U ⊆ Z has to hold scheme-theoretically: j_U must factor through i. Equivalently, the ideal of Z must vanish on U, so that Z ∩ U = U as open subschemes. Then j_U^⋆ i_⋆ i^! F = F|_U. The first arrow is the map adjoint to the identity of F|_U, and the three maps compose to the change-of-support map (j_U)_! j_U^⋆ F → (j_{U′})_! j_{U′}^⋆ F.

In Lemma 2.10.2, the closed set X̄ ∖ (D′_+° ∪ D_−°) inside Y = X̄ ∖ D′_+° must be given a closed-subscheme structure that contains U = Y ∖ D_− scheme-theoretically. The same applies to C̄ ∖ (p̄_2^⋆D_−° ∪ p̄_1^⋆D_+°) in Proposition 2.10.3. Either of two choices works:
- V(J^n) for any ideal J defining the set and n large. J|_U lies in the nilradical of the noetherian, quasi-compact scheme U, so J^n|_U = 0.
- The scheme-theoretic union of the reduced structure with the scheme-theoretic closure of U.

The underlying set does not change, so the set stays proper and Lemma 2.10.1(4) still gives finiteness in Proposition 2.10.3. Where finiteness is not needed (Proposition 2.10.4(5), Theorem 6.2.9), one can instead map directly to RΓ_Ẑ, which needs only set-theoretic containment.
sourceIssues.reason:
On p. 29, in Lemma 2.10.2, the middle term is printed without a hat: RΓ_{X̄\(D′_+° ∪ D_−°)}(X̄ \ D′_+°, F).

Where the proof fails: by Definition 2.1.15(1) (p. 8), "D ⊆ D′" means that D is a subset of D′. In Lemma 2.10.2 the set Z = X̄ \ (D′_+° ∪ D_−°) is the complement of interiors, a purely topological set. It is given no scheme structure, and U = (X̄ \ D′_+°) \ D_− is contained in it only as a set. The "standard adjunction" gives Hom((j_U)_! j_U^⋆F, i_⋆ i^!F) = Hom(F|_U, (i_U)_⋆ (i_U)^! F|_U), where i_U : Z ∩ U → U. When i_U is a proper nilpotent thickening, this has no canonical map compatible with the counit to F.

Counterexample, checked by direct computation: A = k[ε]/(ε²) with k = F_p (A = Z/p² works the same way), Y = Spec A, Z = V(ε), U = U′ = Y. Then U ⊆ Z ⊆ U′ as sets. RΓ(Y, (j_U)_! j_U^⋆ O) = A has length 2. A is self-injective, so RΓ_Z(Y, O) = RHom_A(k, A) = εA ≅ k in degree 0, of length 1. Also RΓ_Ẑ(Y, O) = A, since Y \ Z = ∅. The map RΓ_Z → RΓ_Ẑ of (1) is the inclusion εA ⊆ A. For the factorization in Proposition 2.10.3 the composite must be the change-of-support map, here the identity of A. The identity of a module of length 2 cannot factor through a module of length 1. The literal statement (3) survives only through trivial "natural maps" such as zero, which are useless for Lemma 2.10.2 and Proposition 2.10.3.

The non-reduced case is in scope. §2 allows any scheme of finite type over Z and artinian bases (Proposition 2.3.5, Lemma 2.4.6 on finite rank over an artinian local ring, Theorem 2.6.8), and §6 works over Z/p^s.

The scheme-theoretic RΓ_Z cannot simply be swapped for RΓ_Ẑ in Proposition 2.10.3. Finiteness (4) is stated for RΓ_Z, and RΓ_Ẑ need not be finite: for Y = A^1_k and Ẑ = {0}, H^1 = k[x, x^{-1}]/k[x]. So the thickening is needed.

The corrected map is right: when Z ∩ U = U, j_U^⋆ i_⋆ i^! F = F|_U. A reduced Y needs no change, because a nil ideal on reduced U is zero.

Downstream: Proposition 2.10.3 is not cited anywhere else. Proposition 2.10.4 (p. 31) and Theorem 6.2.9 (p. 62, which writes RΓ_Ẑ explicitly) need only the maps, and these exist through RΓ_Ẑ with set-theoretic containment. All stated results remain true once the scheme structure is chosen as above.

This is a gap rather than an error: the lemma asserts only "natural maps", and the defect is an unstated scheme-theoretic hypothesis plus an unspecified choice of scheme structure where the lemma is applied. Attempted defences.

(a) Read "U ⊆ Z" scheme-theoretically, as saying that the open U is a subscheme of Z. Then (3) is correct as stated. But this is not the paper's convention: Definition 2.1.15(1) (p. 8) reads "We write D ⊆ D′ when D is a subset of D′". More importantly, the lemma is applied in Lemma 2.10.2 to Z = X̄ ∖ (D′_+° ∪ D_−°), which is defined only as a set and given no scheme structure. There U = (X̄ ∖ D′_+°) ∖ D_− lies inside Z only as a set. The middle term in Lemma 2.10.2 carries no hat, so it is the scheme-theoretic RΓ_Z. On p. 27 the authors note that a closed subset becomes a subscheme only "for the choice of some ideal J". Here the choice matters and is never made. The only canonical choice, the reduced structure, fails whenever X̄ is non-reduced along U.

(b) Route everything through the locale. With set-theoretic containment the maps RΓ(Y, (j_U)_! j_U^⋆F) → RΓ_Ẑ(Y, F) → RΓ(Y, (j_{U′})_! j_{U′}^⋆F) do exist and compose correctly. By the triangle î_⋆î^!F → F → j_⋆j^⋆F on p. 27, j_U^⋆ î_⋆ î^! F = j_U^⋆F whenever U does not meet Y ∖ Z. This does not rescue Proposition 2.10.3, which needs a middle term with finite cohomology. Lemma 2.10.1(4) supplies that only for the scheme-theoretic RΓ_Z. RΓ_Ẑ is not finite in general: for Y = P^1_k and Z = {0}, H^1 = k[y]/k.

Why the first arrow fails. Adjunction gives Hom((j_U)_! j_U^⋆F, i_⋆i^!F) = Hom(F|_U, (i_U)_⋆ i_U^! F|_U), where i_U : Z ∩ U → U. When i_U is a proper nilpotent thickening, this has no canonical element compatible with the counit to F.

Counterexample (checked by direct computation). Take A = k[ε]/(ε²), Y = Spec A, Z = V(ε) = Spec k and U = U′ = Y, so that U ⊆ Z ⊆ U′ as sets.
- RΓ(Y, (j_U)_! j_U^⋆ O_Y) = A, of length 2.
- The resolution … → A → A → A → k, with every map multiplication by ε, gives RΓ_Z(Y, O_Y) = RHom_A(k, A) = εA ≅ k in degree 0, of length 1.
- RΓ_Ẑ(Y, O_Y) = A because Y ∖ Z = ∅, and the map of (1) is the inclusion εA ⊂ A.
- The change-of-support map is the identity of A, which cannot factor through a module of length 1.
Natural maps A → εA do exist, such as multiplication by ε, but their composite is multiplication by ε, not the identity. More generally, taking F = O_Y shows that a factorization compatible with the counit forces the ideal of Z to vanish on U.

Non-reduced schemes are within the scope of §2 (finite type over Z, artinian bases in Lemma 2.4.6 and Theorem 2.5.1(2)), and §6 works over Z/p^s.

Consequences.
- Lemma 2.10.2 builds both lines by "applying lemma 2.10.1" twice.
- Proposition 2.10.3 uses "By lemma 2.10.2 … the following factorization". A factorization requires the composite to equal the original map, and finiteness then comes from 2.10.1(4) for the scheme-theoretic RΓ_Z.
- Proposition 2.10.4(5) uses "By lemma 2.10.2, we have a commutative diagram" whose horizontal arrows are change-of-support maps.
- Theorem 6.2.9 (p. 62) cites Lemma 2.10.1 but factors only through RΓ_Ẑ, so it is covered by (b).
- Theorem 2.11.4 (p. 33) uses an RΓ_c middle term, not this lemma.
- Proposition 2.10.3 and Lemma 2.4.6 are not cited later.

With the scheme structure chosen as in the correction, every stated result survives. The defect is an unstated hypothesis, together with a missing choice where the lemma is applied. It is a gap affecting the proofs, not the statements.

sourceIssues.printed: Setup (p. 29): "If Y → Spec A is a scheme, i : Z ↪ Y is a closed subscheme of Y, and if F ∈ D(O_{Y,■}), we let RΓ_Z(Y, F) = RΓ(Z, i^!F)." Lemma 2.10.1: "(4) If Z is proper and if F has coherent cohomology groups, RΓ_Z(Y, F) has finite cohomology groups." Proof: "For the last point, we observe that if F has coherent cohomology groups, the same holds for i^!F and one uses the finiteness of the cohomology of proper schemes."
sourceIssues.correction:
Add a bounded-below hypothesis. The corrected statement: (4) If Z is proper and 𝓕 is bounded below with coherent cohomology sheaves, then RΓ_Z(Y, 𝓕) has finite cohomology groups. Proof: Y is noetherian, so i^!𝓕 = RHom_{𝒪_Y}(𝒪_Z, 𝓕) is again bounded below with coherent cohomology. Locally, resolve 𝒪_Z by finite free modules. Because 𝓕 is bounded below, each cohomology sheaf of i^!𝓕 involves only finitely many terms of that resolution. Then use the finiteness of coherent cohomology of the proper scheme Z. Another fix is to keep 𝓕 unbounded but assume that 𝒪_Z has finite Tor-dimension over 𝒪_Y near Z, for example Y regular. Then i^! has bounded amplitude and Z has finite cohomological dimension.

Proposition 2.10.3 needs a matching repair. Its statement can stay as it is for 𝓕 bounded below with coherent cohomology, in particular for a coherent sheaf. Only the proof needs one more step. Near the closed set Z = C̄ \ (p̄₁⋆D̊₊ ∪ p̄₂⋆D̊₋), the target p₁^!𝓕 is bounded below, say in D^{≥a}. So T factors through τ^{≥a} p₂⋆𝓕. The bottom arrow of the diagram on p. 30 then factors through RΓ_Z(C̄ \ p̄₁⋆D̊₊, τ^{≥a} p₂⋆𝓕), and this complex has finite cohomology by the corrected (4). No flatness of p̄₂ is needed. Requiring p₂⋆𝓕 itself to be bounded below near Z (for example 𝓕 bounded and p̄₂ flat there, or 𝓕 perfect) also works, but it is stronger than necessary.
sourceIssues.reason:
Nothing in the statement or its setup requires F to be bounded: F is any object of D(O_{Y,■}) with coherent cohomology. Without boundedness, both the statement and the step "the same holds for i^!F" fail.

Counterexample, checked by direct computation. Let A = k be a field (e.g. F_p), R = k[x]/(x²), Y = Spec R, and Z = V(x) = Spec k, which is proper over Spec k. Let F = ⊕_{m≥0} k[m], where k = R/(x). Then H^{-m}(F) = k for every m ≥ 0, so every cohomology sheaf is coherent, but F is unbounded below.

To compute i^!F = RHom_R(k, F), resolve k by the free complex P: ⋯ → R → R → R → k, with every differential multiplication by x. P is a bounded-above complex of free modules, so the Hom complex Hom_R(P, F) computes RHom_R(k, F) for any F, bounded or not. Its degree-0 term is ∏_{n≥0} Hom_R(P^{-n}, F^{-n}) = ∏_{n≥0} k. All its differentials vanish, because x acts by 0 on F and F has zero differential. Hence H^0(i^!F) = ∏_{n≥0} k.

Another way to see it: in each degree F has only one nonzero summand, so F ≅ ∏_m k[m]. Products are exact, so RHom(k, ∏_m k[m]) = ∏_m RHom(k, k)[m], and its H^0 is ∏_m Ext^m_R(k, k) = ∏_{m≥0} k.

Since Z is a point, RΓ_Z(Y, F) = i^!F, and its H^0 is infinite-dimensional, so not a finite A-module. The same computation goes through in solid modules: products are exact there, and internal Hom out of R is the identity. The resulting H^0 is the product ∏_N k, which is still not finite.

The step that fails is "the same holds for i^!F". O_Z = R/(x) is pseudo-coherent but not perfect over R, so RHom(O_Z, −) keeps cohomology coherent only on bounded-below complexes. The second step, finiteness of cohomology on a proper scheme, is fine once i^!F is bounded below with coherent cohomology.

The paper watches for this elsewhere. Remark 2.6.3 (p. 21) notes that its hypothesis ensures the relevant object "is again a coherent sheaf (and in particular is bounded below)". Lemma 2.10.1(4) has no such hypothesis.

Consequences. Proposition 2.10.3 applies (4) to the derived pullback p_2^⋆F. For non-flat p_2 this can be unbounded below even when F is a coherent sheaf: for the closed point Spec k → Spec k[x]/(x²), the pullback of k is k ⊗^L_R k, which has nonzero Tor_n for every n. So the proof of Proposition 2.10.3 has a gap unless boundedness is added. Proposition 2.10.3 is not cited later in the paper, and part (4) of the lemma is not used anywhere else. The later uses of Lemma 2.10.1 (Lemma 2.10.2, and the proof of Theorem 6.2.9, p. 64) use only parts (1)–(3). So the fix is a missing hypothesis and does not affect the main theorems. 1. The statement is false as printed. Counterexample, checked by direct computation:
- Take A = k = F_p (finite type over Z, as §2.2 requires), Y = Spec k[x]/(x²), and Z = Spec k, which is proper over Spec k.
- Take 𝓕 = ⊕_{m≥0} k[m], a discrete object of D(𝒪_{Y,■}). Its cohomology sheaves are H^{-m}(𝓕) = k for m ≥ 0, all coherent. Its global cohomology groups H^{-m}(Y, 𝓕) = k are also finite, so the example works under either reading of "coherent cohomology groups".
- Each degree of this complex has only one nonzero term, and sums and products are exact and computed termwise. So 𝓕 ≅ ∏_{m≥0} k[m].
- Hence i^!𝓕 = RHom_{k[x]/(x²)}(k, 𝓕) = ∏_m RHom(k, k)[m].
- The periodic resolution ⋯ → R →x R →x R → k gives Ext^m(k, k) = k for every m ≥ 0.
- So H⁰(RΓ_Z(Y, 𝓕)) = H⁰(i^!𝓕) = ∏_{m≥0} k. This is not a finite k-module, which contradicts (4).
- The failing step is "the same holds for i^!𝓕": H⁰(i^!𝓕) = ∏ k is not coherent. The second step, finiteness of cohomology on proper Z, is not what breaks.

2. The defence does not work.
- The lemma allows any 𝓕 ∈ D(𝒪_{Y,■}), the unbounded solid derived category. The paper states boundedness explicitly where it wants it, for example "𝓕 ∈ D⁻(𝒪_{X,■})" in Theorem 2.9.7 on p. 28.
- One could charitably read 𝓕 as bounded. That reading does not cover the only application. In the proof of Proposition 2.10.3 the lemma is applied to the derived pullback p₂⋆𝓕.
- The paper itself describes p̄₂⋆𝓕 only as "pseudo coherent" (proof of Proposition 2.3.13, p. 18), that is, bounded above.
- When p̄₂ is not of finite Tor-dimension near Z, p₂⋆𝓕 is unbounded below even for a coherent sheaf 𝓕. For instance, pulling k back along Spec k → Spec k[x]/(x²) gives exactly the complex ⊕_m k[m] above.
- So as written, the proof of Proposition 2.10.3 rests on a false lemma.

3. Consequences.
- Part (4) is used only in Proposition 2.10.3.
- The later citations of Lemma 2.10.1 use only parts (1)–(3), the change-of-support maps. These are the proof of Lemma 2.10.2 (pp. 29–30) and the proof of Theorem 6.2.9.
- Proposition 2.10.3 is not cited anywhere else in the paper.
- For 𝓕 bounded below with coherent cohomology (the case of interest), the conclusion of Proposition 2.10.3 is recovered by the truncation argument in the correction. That argument uses the standard fact that the twisted inverse image p₁^! of a bounded-below complex with coherent cohomology is bounded below.
- No main result of the paper is affected. The stated result that is false as printed is Lemma 2.10.1(4) itself, together with the proof of Proposition 2.10.3 as written.

sourceIssues.correction:
Let Y = X̄∖D̊′_+ and give it a closed-subscheme structure in which X̄∖D′_+ is an open subscheme. The scheme-theoretic closure of X̄∖D′_+ in X̄ works. Its ideal vanishes on X̄∖D′_+, and its underlying set is the closure of X̄∖D′_+, which is X̄∖D̊′_+. The reduced structure does not work when X̄∖D′_+ is non-reduced. Let ι : Y → X̄ be the inclusion. On Y, write ℱ also for ι^⋆ℱ, and D_±, D′_± also for their intersections with Y. The last step of each chain should read

RΓ_{∅,D′_−}(Y, ℱ) → RΓ_{D′_+,D′_−}(Y, ℱ) = RΓ_{D′_+,D′_−}(X̄, ℱ),
RΓ_{D′_−,∅}(Y, ℱ) → RΓ_{D′_−,D′_+}(Y, ℱ) = RΓ_{D′_−,D′_+}(X̄, ℱ).

Each arrow is Lemma 2.2.6 on Y, using ∅ ⊆ D′_+. So the identification with X̄ belongs on the target, not on the source. "RΓ_{D′_−,}" means RΓ_{D′_−,∅}.

The first step of each chain is Lemma 2.2.7 for ι. Its target is RΓ_{∅,D_−}(Y, ℱ), resp. RΓ_{D_−,∅}(Y, ℱ), because D_+ ⊆ D̊′_+ does not meet Y. The two middle steps are Lemma 2.10.1(3) on Y, with U = Y∖D_− ⊆ Z = Y∖D̊_− ⊆ U′ = Y∖D′_−. For this, Z needs a closed-subscheme structure in which U is an open subscheme. One choice is the ideal ker(𝒪_Y → (j_U)_⋆𝒪_U) ∩ (the ideal of the reduced structure on Y∖D̊_−). These structures also give a meaning to the middle term in the statement. With them, Lemma 2.10.2 holds as printed.
sourceIssues.reason:
By footnote 1 (p. 9), D̊′_+ is the interior of D′_+. So Y = X̄∖D̊′_+ is a closed subset of X̄, namely the closure of X̄∖D′_+. The proof applies Lemmas 2.2.7, 2.10.1 and 2.2.6 to Y, and it uses RΓ_{∅,D_−}(Y, ℱ) in the sense of Definition 2.2.4 on Y. All of these are stated for schemes, but the paper never fixes a scheme structure on Y. §2.9.1 (p. 27) only says that a closed subset can be viewed as a closed subscheme "for the choice of some ideal J".

The printed equalities are false. Take X̄ = Spec(k×k) = {a} ⊔ {b} over a finite field k, with D′_+ = {a}, D_+ = D_− = D′_− = ∅ and ℱ = 𝒪. Hypotheses (1) and (2) hold, since D̊′_+ = {a}, and Y = {b}. Then RΓ_{∅,∅}(Y, 𝒪) = k, while RΓ_{∅,∅}(X̄, 𝒪) = k². The same failure occurs in the second chain. Here Y is open and closed, so reading Y as a closed subset of the locale, as in §2.10, gives the same values. Reading "=" as a map does not help either. The restriction map goes from RΓ_{∅,D′_−}(X̄, ℱ) to RΓ_{∅,D′_−}(Y, ℱ), which is the wrong direction for the chain. The trace map of Lemma 2.2.7 for the closed immersion ι : Y → X̄ starts from the cohomology of ι^!ℱ, not from the restriction of ℱ.

The corrected identities hold whenever Y∖D′_+ = X̄∖D′_+ as schemes. Use the maps j_±, i_± of §2.2.3 for (X̄, D′_+, D′_−), and write j′_±, i′_± for the same maps for (Y, D′_+, D′_−). Then Y∖(D′_+ ∪ D′_−) = X̄∖(D′_+ ∪ D′_−), j′_− = j_− and ι∘j′_+ = j_+. So ι_⋆(j′_+)_⋆(j′_−)_!ℱ = (j_+)_⋆(j_−)_!ℱ. Since RΓ(Y, –) = RΓ(X̄, ι_⋆ –), this gives the first identity. For the second, let ι′ : Y∖D′_− → X̄∖D′_− be the base change of ι, again a closed immersion. Then ι_⋆ = ι_!, ι′_⋆ = ι′_!, ι_!(i′_−)_! = (i_−)_!ι′_! and ι′_⋆(i′_+)_⋆ = (i_+)_⋆. Hence ι_⋆(i′_−)_!(i′_+)_⋆ℱ = (i_−)_!(i_+)_⋆ℱ.

The choice of structure matters. Take X̄ = Spec k[ε] ⊔ Spec k[ε], with D′_+ the first component and D_± = D′_− = ∅. With the reduced structure, Y = Spec k and RΓ_{D′_+,∅}(Y, 𝒪) = k, whereas RΓ_{D′_+,∅}(X̄, 𝒪) = k[ε]. The paper does work with non-reduced schemes, for example the toroidal compactifications over ℤ/p^sℤ in §6.2.

This is an error, not a misprint. As written, the last step of each chain rests on a false identity, so the proof fails there. The repair moves the identification to the other end of the arrow. It also needs a scheme structure on Y that the paper leaves unspecified, and the obvious choice, the reduced structure, can fail. Once a structure as in the correction is fixed, each cited lemma applies literally: Lemma 2.2.7 to ι, and Lemmas 2.10.1 and 2.2.6 on Y. The statement of Lemma 2.10.2 is correct.

Consequences. The lemma is used in the proofs of Proposition 2.10.3 (p. 30) and Proposition 2.10.4(5) (p. 31), and both stand. In Proposition 2.10.3, p̄⋆_1D̊^+ denotes the interior of p̄⋆_1D_+. This is the reading of Definition 2.1.19(3) and Remark 2.1.22 (p. 9), and it is the one the proof of Proposition 2.10.4(1) (p. 31) needs. So the vertical maps of the factorization there come from Lemma 2.10.2 on C̄, with (D_+, D_−, D′_+, D′_−) replaced by (p̄⋆_2D_+, p̄⋆_2D_−, p̄⋆_1D_+, p̄⋆_1D_−). The lemma's hypotheses then say that D_+ is compactly expanded and D_− is compactly contracted. The proof of Theorem 2.11.4 (pp. 32–33) asserts a diagram of the same kind through RΓ_c(X̄∖{D̊′_+ ∪ D_−}, ℱ″), saying only that the proof is similar to that of Proposition 2.10.4. The set X̄∖{D̊′_+ ∪ D_−} = Y∖D_− is locally closed but in general not open, so this term needs the same choice of structure on Y. With that choice, the maps in the diagram come from Lemma 2.2.7 for ι, Lemma 2.2.6 on Y and the corrected identities above. The later citations of Proposition 2.10.4 (Remark 2.11.2, p. 31; the proof of Theorem 6.2.9, p. 62) are unaffected.

sourceIssues.reason:
Conventions (Definitions 2.1.19 and 2.1.24, p. 9). D is expanded if p̄⋆2D ⊆ p̄⋆1D and compactly expanded if p̄⋆2D lies in the interior of p̄⋆1D. D is contracted if p̄⋆1D ⊆ p̄⋆2D. In a dynamic correspondence D+ is expanded and D− is contracted. The setting of §2.11 (p. 31) has D′′± ⊆ D̊′± ⊆ D′± ⊆ D̊± ⊆ D±.

(1) Proposition 2.10.4 (p. 30) takes pairs with D± ⊆ D̊′± ⊆ D′± and assumes "p̄⋆1D+ ⊇ p̄⋆2D′+ and that p̄⋆2D− ⊇ p̄⋆1D′−". The smaller divisor goes with p̄1 on the + side and with p̄2 on the − side. Remark 2.11.2 (p. 31) says the (D′+, D′−) and (D′′+, D′′−) compactifications are compact dynamic "by proposition 2.10.4". This needs the proposition for the pair D′′ ⊆ D̊′, and so needs p̄⋆2D′+ ⊆ p̄⋆1D′′+ and p̄⋆1D′− ⊆ p̄⋆2D′′−. Nothing is assumed that would let one use the pair (D′, D) instead.

(2) The proof of Theorem 2.11.4(3) (p. 33) uses maps "T : RΓ_{D′+,D−}(X̄,F′′) → RΓ_{D′′+,D−}(X̄,F′′)" and "T : RΓ_{D−,D′+}(X̄,F′′) → RΓ_{D−,D′′+}(X̄,F′′)". These are built as in the proof of Proposition 2.10.4 (p. 31): pull back along p̄2, change support by Lemma 2.2.6, apply T, then trace along p̄1. Lemma 2.2.6 (p. 12) gives RΓ_{A+,A−} → RΓ_{A′+,A′−} only when A+ ⊆ A′+ and A′− ⊆ A−. The change-of-support step goes from RΓ_{p̄⋆2D′+,·} to RΓ_{p̄⋆1D′′+,·}, so it needs p̄⋆2D′+ ⊆ p̄⋆1D′′+.

(3) §6.2 is where the theory is applied. Proposition 6.2.3 (p. 61) has (1) "D+ ≥ D+,ϵ′ ≥ D+,ϵ and D− ≥ D−,ϵ′ ≥ D−,ϵ", so D′ = D±,ϵ′ and D′′ = D±,ϵ. It also has (2) "p⋆1D+,ϵ ≥ p⋆2D+,ϵ′" and (3) "p⋆2D−,ϵ ≥ p⋆1D−,ϵ′". These are exactly the corrected inclusions. Item (4) is stated "over C_t^tor \ p⋆1D+,ϵ ∪ p⋆2D−,ϵ", which is C′′. The proof of Theorem 6.2.9 (p. 62) then applies Proposition 2.10.4 and Theorem 2.11.4. Nothing in §6 checks the printed inclusions.

(4) The printed form is degenerate. Checked by direct computation: p̄⋆1D′′+ ⊆ p̄⋆1D′+ ⊆ p̄⋆2D′′+ ⊆ p̄⋆1D′′+, using D′′+ ⊆ D′+, then the printed inclusion, then the fact that D′′+ is expanded. Also p̄⋆2D′′+ ⊆ p̄⋆2D′+ ⊆ p̄⋆1D′+, since D′+ is expanded. So all four sets p̄⋆1D′+, p̄⋆2D′+, p̄⋆1D′′+ and p̄⋆2D′′+ coincide. D′′+ can then be compactly expanded only if this common closed set is also open. The − side behaves the same way. Such a hypothesis cannot hold for the Hecke correspondences of §6.

Scope. Because D′± and D′′± are expanded or contracted, the printed inclusions imply the corrected ones: p̄⋆2D′+ ⊆ p̄⋆1D′+ ⊆ p̄⋆2D′′+ ⊆ p̄⋆1D′′+, and likewise p̄⋆1D′− ⊆ p̄⋆2D′− ⊆ p̄⋆1D′′− ⊆ p̄⋆2D′′−. So Remark 2.11.2 and Theorem 2.11.4 are not false as printed. They are stated under a stronger hypothesis that holds only in degenerate cases. The proofs use only the corrected inclusions, and the application in Theorem 6.2.9 supplies only those. As printed, Theorem 2.11.4 therefore does not cover its one use. The correction weakens the standing hypothesis of a stated theorem to the form that is proved and used.

(2) The printed condition cuts out W_M, not ᴹW. M normalises U_P, so W_M preserves Φ^{+,M} and every element of W_M satisfies it. Conversely, write w = uv with u ∈ W_M and v ∈ ᴹW. Then w⁻¹Φ^{+,M} = v⁻¹Φ^{+,M}. If this lies in Φ⁺, then together with v⁻¹Φ⁺_M ⊆ Φ⁺ (from (1)) we get v⁻¹Φ⁺ ⊆ Φ⁺. So v = 1 and w ∈ W_M.

For g = 1: G = GL₂, M = T, W_M = 1, so ᴹW = W = {1, s}. But s⁻¹Φ^{+,M} = {−β}, where β is the positive root, and this is not in Φ⁺. So the printed condition keeps only the identity.

(3) Checked by direct computation in the paper's own conventions for g = 1, 2, 3, 4. The conventions are: B consists of the root spaces E_{xy} with x before y in the order g+1, …, 2g, 1, …, g; the Weyl group acts by w·e_i = e_{w(i)}, from w(diag(t_i)) = diag(t_{w⁻¹(i)}); and the dominant cone reproduces the paper's 0 ≥ k₁ ≥ … ≥ k_g. Three sets coincide: the minimal-length coset representatives, the set cut out by wX⋆(T)⁺ ⊆ X⋆(T)^{+,M}, and the set cut out by w⁻¹Φ⁺_M ⊆ Φ⁺. They have 2, 4, 8 and 16 elements. The printed condition gives exactly W_M, with 1, 2, 6 and 24 elements.

(4) Nothing later depends on the slip. The paper consistently uses the correct set:
- Definition 1.3.1 (p. 3) defines ᴹW as minimal-length representatives.
- §1.3.3 (p. 3) states X⋆(T)^{M,+} = ∪_{w∈ᴹW} wX⋆(T)⁺.
- p. 34 gives the length function ℓ: ᴹW → [0, g(g+1)/2] and FL = ∐_{w∈ᴹW} C_w.
- The proof of Lemma 4.3.8 (p. 48) uses w⁻¹w_{0,M}ρ + ρ = Σ_{α∈(w⁻¹Φ^{+,M})∩Φ⁺} α. Writing A = w⁻¹Φ^{+,M} ∩ Φ⁺ and B = w⁻¹Φ^{+,M} ∩ Φ⁻, the condition w⁻¹Φ⁺_M ⊆ Φ⁺ gives Φ⁺ = w⁻¹Φ⁺_M ⊔ A ⊔ (−B). Hence 2ρ = 2w⁻¹ρ_M + ΣA − ΣB and 2w⁻¹ρ_nc = ΣA + ΣB. Since w_{0,M}ρ = ρ_nc − ρ_M, the identity follows. Under the printed condition the intersection with Φ⁺ would be redundant; for g = 1 and w = s both sides are 0, which needs s ∈ ᴹW.

So this is an isolated notational slip, Φ^{+,M} written for Φ⁺_M, in a parenthetical reformulation.

sourceIssues.printed: Finally, ᴹW is the subset of w such that w⁻¹(g + 1) < w⁻¹(g + 2) · · · < w⁻¹(2g).
sourceIssues.correction: ^MW is the set of w ∈ W such that w^{−1}(g+1) ≺ w^{−1}(g+2) ≺ ··· ≺ w^{−1}(2g). Here ≺ is the total order g+1 ≺ g+2 ≺ ··· ≺ 2g ≺ 1 ≺ 2 ≺ ··· ≺ g. sourceIssues.reason:
The page image of p. 34 confirms the printed sentence. It follows the definition of ᴹW as the minimal-length representatives of W_M\W.

**Conventions.** On p. 34, B ⊆ P is block lower triangular with upper-triangular diagonal blocks. So the root t_a/t_b, whose root space is E_{ab}, is B-positive exactly when a ≺ b. This agrees with the dominance condition for T⁺(Q_p) printed on the same page, and with the cone 0 ≥ k₁ ≥ ··· ≥ k_g. The stated action is w·diag(t_i) = diag(t_{w⁻¹(i)}), which is conjugation by the permutation matrix e_i ↦ e_{w(i)}. It gives w(t_a/t_b) = t_{w(a)}/t_{w(b)}.

**The correct condition.** An element w is minimal in W_M w if and only if w⁻¹ sends the simple roots t_{g+i}/t_{g+i+1} of M to positive roots. That is, w⁻¹(g+i) ≺ w⁻¹(g+i+1) for 1 ≤ i ≤ g−1. The printed condition uses the usual order 1 < ··· < 2g. That would be Kostant's condition for the upper-triangular Borel, which lies in P^std, not for B ⊆ P.

**Why the printed set is wrong.** Both conditions pick exactly one element from each coset, because a coset is determined by w⁻¹{g+1,…,2g}. They disagree on every coset where this set meets both halves of {1,…,2g}. That is 2^g − 2 of the 2^g cosets.

**Counterexample for g = 2.** Take w = (2 3). Then w⁻¹(3) = 2 < 4 = w⁻¹(4), so w satisfies the printed condition.
- In coordinates (k₁,k₂;k), w changes the sign of k₂.
- It makes three of the four positive roots (1,−1), (−1,−1), (0,−2), (−2,0) negative, so ℓ(w) = 3.
- The other element of its coset is w′ = s_α w, where α = (1,−1); w′⁻¹ is (3,1,4,2) in one-line notation. w′ has ℓ(w′) = 2 and satisfies the ≺ condition, but not the printed one.
- dim C_w = #{α > 0 : wα ∈ −Φ^{+,M}} = 2 ≠ ℓ(w).
- The identity in the proof of Lemma 4.3.8 (p. 48), w⁻¹w_{0,M}ρ + ρ = Σ_{α∈(w⁻¹Φ^{+,M})∩Φ⁺} α with ρ = (−1,−2;0), gives (−3,−1;0) on the left and (−2,0;0) on the right. For w′ both sides are (−2,0;0).
- In general, w⁻¹w_{0,M}ρ + ρ is the sum of the positive roots in w⁻¹(Φ^{+,M} ∪ Φ⁻_M). So the identity holds exactly for Kostant representatives.

**Further checks by direct computation.** For g = 2, 3, 4 the ≺-increasing element is the unique minimal-length element of each coset. The lengths in the printed set are {0,2,3,3} for g = 2, and include 7 > g(g+1)/2 = 6 for g = 3. So the printed set is incompatible with ℓ: ᴹW → [0, g(g+1)/2] and ℓ(w) = dim C_w, both on p. 34. It is also incompatible with "the length one element" of §5.6 on p. 58: the printed set has no element of length 1.

**Scope.** Every later use goes through the definition (minimal length, Kostant's condition) or through coset invariants, which are unaffected: the set w⁻¹{g+1,…,2g}, the sequence (w_i), C_w and the strata. So later results stand. The false statement is the concrete description itself.

**Related slip.** The equivalent condition two lines earlier, "w⁻¹Φ^{+,M} ⊆ Φ⁺", should read w⁻¹Φ⁺_M ⊆ Φ⁺. As printed it fails for w_{0,M}w₀ ∈ ᴹW, and it holds for all of W_M. **The paper's conventions (p. 34).** P is the stabiliser of ⟨e_{g+1},…,e_{2g}⟩, so it is block lower triangular. B ⊆ P is upper triangular on the diagonal g×g blocks.
- The root t ↦ t_a/t_b has root space spanned by E_{ab}. So it is B-positive exactly when a ≺ b, for the order g+1 ≺ ··· ≺ 2g ≺ 1 ≺ ··· ≺ g.
- The paper confirms this order three times:
  - the dominant cone 0 ≥ k_1 ≥ ··· ≥ k_g, whose simple roots are t_j/t_{j+1} and t_{2g}/t_1 (= t_1^{−2} in the (k;k) coordinates);
  - the condition v(t_{g+1}) ≥ ··· ≥ v(t_{2g}) ≥ v(t_1) ≥ ··· ≥ v(t_g) for T^+(Q_p);
  - the Iwahori flag on p. 41, with H_{g+i} corresponding to ⟨e_{g+1},…,e_{g+i}⟩.
- The natural order < is the positivity order of the upper triangular Borel. That Borel lies in P^std, not in P. For it the dominant cone would be k_1 ≥ ··· ≥ k_g ≥ 0, which contradicts the paper.
- Switching between a left and a right action of W on characters only exchanges w and w^{−1}. It never turns ≺ into <. So no faithful reading of the conventions makes the sentence true.

**The correct condition.** Since w·diag(t_i) = diag(t_{w^{−1}(i)}), w sends t_a/t_b to t_{w(a)}/t_{w(b)}.
- The simple roots of M are t_{g+i}/t_{g+i+1} for 1 ≤ i ≤ g−1.
- So w is minimal in W_M w (w^{−1}Φ^+_M ⊆ Φ^+, equivalently wX*(T)^+ ⊆ X*(T)^{+,M}) if and only if w^{−1}(g+i) ≺ w^{−1}(g+i+1) for all i.
- A coset W_M w is determined by S = w^{−1}{g+1,…,2g}. Its g! elements correspond to the orderings of S as w^{−1}(g+1),…,w^{−1}(2g).
- Both rules pick one element from each coset. They disagree exactly when S meets both halves of {1,…,2g}, which happens for 2^g − 2 of the 2^g cosets.

**Counterexample, g = 2.** Take w = (2 3), so w(1)=1, w(2)=3, w(3)=2, w(4)=4. It satisfies the printed condition, because w^{−1}(3) = 2 < 4 = w^{−1}(4).
- In coordinates (k_1,k_2;k), w changes the sign of k_2. It makes t_1/t_2, (t_1t_2)^{−1} and t_2^{−2} negative, so ℓ(w) = 3.
- The other element w′ of W_M w has w′^{−1} = (3,1,4,2) in one-line notation. It has ℓ(w′) = 2 and satisfies the ≺ condition.
- This contradicts three statements on p. 34:
  - ℓ(w) = dim C_w fails, since dim C_w = dim C_{w′} = 2;
  - w sends the dominant weight (−1,−3;0) to (−1,3;0), which is not M-dominant, so w violates the defining condition wX*(T)^+ ⊆ X*(T)^{+,M};
  - for g = 2 the printed set has lengths {0,2,3,3}. It has no element of length 1, but §5.6 on p. 58 argues with "the length one element".

**Checked by direct computation for g = 2, 3, 4:**
- The ≺-increasing element is the unique minimal-length element of each coset. It also equals the "entries > g first" description in the correction.
- The printed set has lengths up to 7 for g = 3 and 12 for g = 4. This exceeds the range [0, g(g+1)/2] asserted for ℓ on p. 34.
- The literal condition w^{−1}Φ^{+,M} ⊆ Φ^+ cuts out exactly W_M, since it says w^{−1}Pw ⊇ B. This confirms the related slip.

**Defence attempted.**
- The sentence is not a paraphrase of the definition. It is an independent concrete claim, and it is false.
- Its intended content cannot be recovered by fixing an index or a sign: a different order is needed.
- So it is an error rather than a misprint.

**What later uses the passage.** Later arguments use ^MW either through its definition (minimal length, Kostant) or through quantities that are the same for every element of a coset. So no later result depends on the false description.
- **Quantities that do not depend on the representative:**
  - the set w^{−1}{g+1,…,2g}, the sequence (w_i), and C_w;
  - the strata in 4.1.3 and Lemmas 4.1.6 and 4.1.9;
  - the filtration and Z_{>w−1} in 4.1.16 and 4.5;
  - the sets w^{−1}Φ^{±,M} in Proposition 4.2.4.
- **Places that need the Kostant representative:**
  - Lemma 4.3.4, which needs w(v(t)) to be M-dominant;
  - the identity w^{−1}w_{0,M}ρ + ρ = Σ_{α∈(w^{−1}Φ^{+,M})∩Φ^+} α in Lemma 4.3.8 (p. 48). In general the left side is the sum of the positive roots in w^{−1}(Φ^−_M ∪ Φ^{+,M}), so the identity holds exactly for Kostant w. For w = (2 3), with ρ = (−1,−2;0), the two sides are (−3,−1;0) and (−2,0;0);
  - Proposition 4.3.9, C(κ), and ν = −w^{−1}w_{0,M}(κ+ρ) − ρ;
  - X*(T)^{M,+} = ∪ wX*(T)^+ on p. 3;
  - the use of ℓ(w) in Theorem 4.5.2, Conjecture 5.6.1 and Proposition 5.6.3.
- All of these hold with the definition. They would fail if the printed description were used instead.
- The duality involution w ↦ w_{0,M}ww_0 preserves both sets.

**Scope.** The proposed correction is right and minimal. The false statement is the concrete description of ^MW itself. No numbered lemma, proposition or theorem is affected.

sourceIssues.locator: §3.2 (Shimura varieties), moduli description of S_{K,ℚ}, definition of isomorphisms of triples (A, λ, η), p. 34
sourceIssues.printed: An isomorphism ξ : (A, λ, η) → (A′, λ′, η′) is a quasi-isogeny ξ : A → A′ for which η′ = H₁(ξ) ∘ η and ξ^D λξ = rλ for some r ∈ ℚ_{>0}.
sourceIssues.correction: ξ^D λ′ ξ = rλ for some r ∈ ℚ_{>0}. Here λ′ is the quasi-polarization of the target, and the composite A → A′ → A′^D → A^D is compared with rλ : A → A^D. This is the usual condition that the quasi-isogeny respects the quasi-polarizations up to a positive rational scalar.
sourceIssues.reason: The page image at high resolution shows "ξ^D λξ = rλ" with no prime on the first λ. The line just above prints the target triple as (A′, λ′, η′) with a clearly visible prime, so the missing prime is in the source and not an artefact of the text layer. The paper's own conventions make the printed formula ill-typed. By item (2), λ : A → A^D. Since ξ : A → A′, its dual is ξ^D : A′^D → A^D. For ξ^D ∘ λ ∘ ξ to make sense, the middle map has to go from A′ to A′^D, which λ does not do unless A′ = A. Reading the composition left to right does not help either: then ξ is followed by λ, but ξ lands in A′ and λ starts from A. So the only sensible reading is ξ^D λ′ ξ = rλ, which has the correct type A → A^D on both sides. This is the standard condition for an isomorphism of polarized abelian schemes up to isogeny with level structure. The paper states the analogous conditions for the Igusa tower in words on p. 35 ("matching λ and λ′ up to an element in ℤ^×_{(p),>0}", and in the quasi-isogeny formulation "up to an element in ℚ_{>0}"), and there the target polarization λ′ is used. The formula is only a recollection of the standard moduli interpretation of the Siegel Shimura variety. Nothing later in the paper uses it: the Hecke correspondences (§4.2) are defined through the universal quasi-isogeny p₁^⋆A → p₂^⋆A over the Shimura variety of level tK_{p,n}t^{-1} ∩ K_{p,n}, with no reference to this formula. So no proof or stated result depends on the misprint.

sourceIssues.reason:
The page images confirm the wording, so this is not a text-layer artefact. The paper does not use one fixed order for the two summands of X_ord.

Multiplicative part first:
- §1.3.9 (p. 4): "A[p^∞] ≃ µ^g_{p^∞} ⊕ (Q_p/Z_p)^g".
- §3.4.1 (p. 35), including the displayed λ_can.
- The matrix in the proof of Lemma 3.4.3 (p. 36).
- The proof of Proposition 3.4.9 (p. 38): "x : µ^g_{p^∞} → A[p^∞]^m, y : (Q_p/Z_p)^g → A[p^∞]^e … (x^D, y^D) ∘ λ ∘ (x, y) = cλ_can".
- Remark 3.4.18 (p. 39).

Étale part first: §3.4.17 (p. 39), which sits between these passages. It calls j "the isomorphism (Q_p/Z_p)^g ⊕ µ^g_{p^∞} → A[p^∞]", although j has source X_ord, and sends it to "Z_p^g ⊕ Z_p^g(1) = Z_p^{2g} → T_p(A)".

Only the étale-first order fits the paper's group-theoretic conventions:
- On p. 33, P = P_µ is the stabiliser of ⟨e_{g+1},…,e_{2g}⟩ and P^std is the stabiliser of ⟨e_1,…,e_g⟩.
- On p. 35, π_HT(A, Ψ) = P g(Ψ)^{-1}, where Ψ(⟨g(Ψ)(e_{g+1}),…,g(Ψ)(e_{2g})⟩) = Lie_A(1).
- For ordinary A, the Hodge–Tate map kills the Tate module of the multiplicative part, since the ω of its Cartier dual (Q_p/Z_p)^g is 0. Hence T_p(A[p^∞]^m) ⊗ C = Lie_A(1).
- So a map that is P(Q_p)-equivariant and lands over the base point P of FL, as §3.4.17 states, must send e_{g+1},…,e_{2g} to the multiplicative part.
- The proof of Lemma 4.1.6 (p. 41) uses the same normalisation: "e_{w^{-1}(i)}, g+1 ≤ i ≤ 2g span the multiplicative part of the Tate module".

In the printed multiplicative-first coordinates, the displayed Aut(X̃_ord) is block upper triangular, so it lies in P^std, and Hom(X̃_et, X̃_m) is the upper-right block U_{P^std}. Lemma 3.4.3 instead says that M(Q_p) acts on U_{J_ord} as on U_P(Q_p), and Remark 3.4.6 describes J^int_ord as M(Z_p) ⋉ U_P(Z_p)(1). These two do not match, checked by direct computation:
- For m = diag(A, D) ∈ M, conjugation sends the lower-left block C of U_P to DCA^{-1} and the upper-right block B of U_{P^std} to ABD^{-1}.
- The element z = diag(1_g, p·1_g) is in G with similitude p and is central in M.
- So z acts by p on U_P and by p^{-1} on U_{P^std}. Directly on Hom(X̃_et, X̃_m) it is f ↦ 1∘f∘p^{-1} = p^{-1}f.

Hence, with M embedded block-diagonally in the printed coordinates, the M-module in Lemma 3.4.3 is U_{P^std}, not U_P. Lemma 3.4.3 holds only if the Levi is identified through the étale-first coordinates. Equivalently, one conjugates by the Weyl element swapping the two blocks, which normalises M and exchanges U_P and U_{P^std}. §3.4.17 makes this swap without saying so.

The proposed correction is consistent. Suppose the isocrystal is normalised through the rational Tate module, so that µ_{p^∞} (Tate module Z_p(1)) gets Frobenius p^{-1}, as for D_cris(Q_p(1)), with similitude p^{-1} matching the Weil pairing. Then the printed b_ord = diag(p^{-1}Id_g, Id_g) is written in the multiplicative-first order. In the étale-first order it becomes diag(Id_g, p^{-1}Id_g) = µ(p)^{-1}. The automorphism matrix then becomes block lower triangular, inside P.

No stated result is affected. Every later use is phrased with P and the étale-first normalisation of §3.4.17, namely:
- K_{p,P} = P(Q_p) ∩ xK_px^{-1};
- Lemmas 3.4.20 and 4.1.7;
- Proposition 4.2.4;
- the map T(Q_p) → P′(Q_p).

The fix is a consistent relabelling of coordinates.

sourceIssues.correction:
In the sentence before Proposition 3.4.9 and in Proposition 3.4.9(5), replace M_{K_{p,P}} by the image of K_{p,P} in M(Q_p), which is K_{p,P}/U_{K_{p,P}}. Galois acts trivially on M, so this image is a constant profinite group and its closure is profinite étale. The sequence 1 → U_{K_{p,P}} → K_{p,P} → K_{p,P}/U_{K_{p,P}} → 1 is exact. The image equals M_{K_{p,P}} = K_{p,P} ∩ M(Q_p) whenever K_{p,P} = M_{K_{p,P}} ⋉ U_{K_{p,P}}, which by the argument on p. 37 holds for every K_{p,P} when p > 2.

An equally good fix is to keep the text and add, for p = 2, the hypothesis K_{p,P} = M_{K_{p,P}} ⋉ U_{K_{p,P}}. This is condition (1) of "decomposable" in §5.1 (p. 53).

The local replacement is the minimal fix. Redefining M_{K_{p,P}} everywhere as the image would make condition (1) of §5.1 and Remark 3.4.7 need rewording.
sourceIssues.reason:
Page 37 was checked on the rendered image. The paper allows any prime p ("We now fix a prime p", §3.3, p. 34). It also allows every compact open subgroup of P'(Q_p). By p. 36 these are the compact open subgroups of P(Q_p) that are stable under the Galois action, where Galois acts trivially on M and by χ_cycl on the unipotent radical. The splitting K = M_K ⋉ U_K is proved only for p > 2: the argument needs σ with χ_cycl(σ) − 1 ∈ Z_p^×, and no such σ exists when p = 2. Even so, the next paragraph uses the "exact sequence" 1 → U_K → K → M_K → 1 with no condition on p, and Proposition 3.4.9(5) relies on it.

The counterexample was checked by hand and by direct computation modulo 16. Since K below contains the kernel of reduction mod 4, a check modulo 16 decides the question over Z_2. Take p = 2 and g = 1, so G = GSp_2 = GL_2. Here P, the stabiliser of ⟨e_2⟩ (p. 33), is the lower triangular Borel and M = T is the diagonal torus. Galois acts by σ(a 0; c d) = (a 0; χ(σ)c d).
- Let K₀ = {(a 0; c d) : a ≡ d ≡ 1 mod 4, c ≡ 0 mod 2}. This is the preimage of a normal subgroup of B(Z/4), so it is normal in B(Z_2). It is Galois-stable.
- Let g₀ = (1 0; −1 −1). Then g₀ ∈ B(Z_2) and g₀² = 1, so g₀ normalises K₀ and K = K₀ ∪ g₀K₀ is a compact open subgroup.
- K is Galois-stable, because g₀^{-1}σ(g₀) = (1 0; χ(σ)−1 1) ∈ K₀.
- Every element g₀(a 0; c d) = (a 0; −a−c −d) of g₀K₀ has an odd lower-left entry. So K ∩ T = K₀ ∩ T ≅ (1+4Z_2)², which is torsion-free.
- The image of K in T contains diag(1,−1), an element of order 2.

So K/U_K is not K ∩ M(Q_p), not even as an abstract group, and the printed sequence is not exact. The fibres of 𝔍𝔊_{K^pU_K} → 𝔍𝔊_{K^pK} are torsors under K/U_K. The subgroup M_K = K ∩ M(Q_p) has index 2 in K/U_K here, so it acts freely but not transitively on those fibres. Hence Proposition 3.4.9(5) is false as printed for this K.

The authors appear aware of the issue elsewhere:
- Remark 3.4.7 states the bijection only for p > 2.
- Condition (1) of §5.1 (p. 53) imposes K_{p,P} = M_{K_{p,P}} ⋉ U_{K_{p,P}}, "automatic if p > 2".
- The proof of Lemma 3.4.8 uses the "Levi quotient K_{p,M}", which is the image.

No later result is affected:
- Where Proposition 3.4.9 is used later (§3.4.13 on p. 39, the proof on p. 48, Remark 3.4.10), only finite flatness or the profinite étaleness of the map is needed, not the name of its group.
- §4 uses K_{p,P,w} = wK_{p,n}w^{-1} ∩ P(Q_p) (Lemma 4.1.7, p. 41), with K_{p,n} of Iwahori type. §6 (p. 63) uses subgroups of the same kind. All of these are semidirect products.
- §5 works only with decomposable subgroups, and §5.3.2 (p. 55) restates the exact sequence for those.

The defect is therefore confined to Proposition 3.4.9(5) and the sentence before it, for p = 2. No defence works:
- The paper allows p = 2. It fixes an arbitrary prime in §3.3 (p. 34). The paper itself says p > 2 is needed for the splitting (p. 37, Remark 3.4.7, and §5.1(1) "automatic if p > 2").
- The paper allows every compact open subgroup of P'(Q_p). Remark 3.4.6 explicitly includes every finite-index subgroup of P'(Z_p). By p. 36 these are the compact open subgroups of P(Q_p) stable under Galois, where Galois acts trivially on M and by χ_cycl on U_P.
- M_{K_{p,P}} cannot be read as the quotient K/U_K. Two lines earlier it is defined as K ∩ M(Q_p) = K^{Gal}, which is the group of Q_p-points of the twisted group K. The map from K^{Gal} to the Galois-fixed points of K/U_K can fail to be surjective, because of H^1(Gal, U_K), and it does fail for p = 2. The proof of Lemma 3.4.8 uses a separate symbol K_{p,M} ("Levi quotient") for the image.
- The splitting argument needs some σ with χ_cycl(σ) − 1 ∈ Z_p^×. For p = 2 there is no such σ.

Counterexample, checked by hand and by direct computation modulo 16. The group below contains the level-4 congruence subgroup of B(Z_2), so this computation decides the question.
- Take p = 2 and g = 1, so G = GL_2. P is the stabiliser of ⟨e_2⟩, the lower triangular Borel, and M = T. The Galois action is (a 0; c d) ↦ (a 0; χ(σ)c d).
- Let K = {(a 0; c d) ∈ GL_2(Z_2) : c ≡ (a−1)/2 mod 2}.
- K is a subgroup. The product has lower-left entry ca' + dc' ≡ c + c' mod 2, and (aa'−1)/2 ≡ (a−1)/2 + (a'−1)/2 mod 2.
- K is open and Galois-stable, since χ(σ) is odd.
- The image of K in T is all of T(Z_2).
- K ∩ T = {diag(a,d) : a ≡ 1 mod 4} has index 2 in that image. For example, (−1 0; 1 1) ∈ K, but its Levi component diag(−1,1) is not in K.

So K → M(Q_p) does not land in M_K, and the displayed sequence is not exact. The construction g_0 = (1 0; −1 −1), K = K_0 ∪ g_0K_0 with K_0 = {a ≡ d ≡ 1 mod 4, c even} gives another counterexample, checked in the same way.

Why (5) fails for this K:
- By (2), 𝔍𝔊_{K^p} → 𝔍𝔊_{K^pK} is a \overline{K}-torsor.
- So 𝔍𝔊_{K^pU_K} → 𝔍𝔊_{K^pK} is a torsor under \overline{K}/\overline{U_K}, whose group is the image T(Z_2).
- M_K acts freely on the fibres but not transitively, since it has index 2. The two groups are not even abstractly isomorphic: their 2-torsion subgroups have orders 2 and 4.

The proof on p. 38 only says "We deduce point (5)."

Later uses are unaffected:
- Remark 3.4.10 uses only étaleness.
- The Hecke correspondences on p. 39 use (7), and Lemma 3.4.24 uses (3).
- Lemma 4.3.8 goes through Remark 3.4.11.
- §5.3.2 (p. 55) restates the sequence and the M_K-torsor only for decomposable K.
- Lemma 4.1.7 and §6.2.11 (p. 63) use K = wK_{p,n}w^{-1} ∩ P(Q_p). This group is a semidirect product, because B_w ∩ P = (B_w ∩ M) ⋉ (B_w ∩ U_P).

The false statement is therefore Proposition 3.4.9(5), with the sentence before it, for p = 2 and non-split K only. The main results are untouched.

review.reason: Confirmed as a gap. Page 37 proves $K_{p,P}=M_{K_{p,P}}\ltimes U_{K_{p,P}}$ only `When $p>2$', the argument needing $\chi_{\mathrm{cycl}}(\sigma)-1\in\Z_p^\times$, yet the exact sequence stated just before Proposition 3.4.9 and point (5) of that proposition both use $M_{K_{p,P}}=K_{p,P}\cap M(\Q_p)$ as the quotient of $K_{p,P}$ by $U_{K_{p,P}}$, with no hypothesis on $p$; §3.3 fixes an arbitrary prime. sourceIssues.correction: The missing statement is a Z_p^cycl version of Proposition 3.4.9(1)–(3) for every compact open subgroup K of P(Q_p), not only the Galois-stable ones: the quotient IG_{K^pK,Z_p^cycl} exists and is smooth over Z_p^cycl, and hence normal. It follows from Proposition 3.4.9 as follows. Let U_K = K ∩ U_P(Q_p), and let M_1 be an open subgroup of K ∩ M(Q_p) that is normal in the image of K in M(Q_p). Then K_1 = M_1 ⋉ U_K is open and normal in K and comes from P′(Q_p), and \overline{K}/\overline{K_1} is the constant group K/K_1. So IG_{K^pK,Z_p^cycl} is the quotient of the smooth IG_{K^pK_1} ×_{Spf Z_p} Spf Z_p^cycl by a free action of a finite group. With this added, the proof of Lemma 3.4.24 works for all x and K_p. In the analogue of 3.4.9(5), the group must be the image of K in M(Q_p), not K ∩ M(Q_p). The other possible repair, restricting §3.4.17 and Lemma 3.4.24 to levels that are semi-direct products of their M- and U_P-parts, covers every formal-level use in §4. It does not cover everything §3.4.12 is used for.
sourceIssues.reason:
Proposition 3.4.9 is stated over Z_p, where the only compact open subgroups available are those of P′(Q_p). By §3.4.5 (p. 36) and Remark 3.4.7 (p. 37), these are exactly the Galois-stable compact open subgroups of P(Q_p). For p > 2 they are also exactly the ones that split as (K ∩ M) ⋉ (K ∩ U_P).

Section 3.4.12 defines IG_{K^pK_{p,P},Z_p^cycl} for every compact open K_{p,P} of P(Q_p). It identifies this with a base change only when K_{p,P} comes from P′(Q_p). For other K_{p,P}, neither the existence of the quotient nor any property of it is stated or proved. Yet Lemma 3.4.24 is asserted for K_{p,P} = P(Q_p) ∩ xK_px^{−1} with arbitrary x and K_p, and its proof gets normality of the source only by citing Proposition 3.4.9.

Such K_{p,P} need not be Galois-stable. Take g = 1, so G = GL_2. Here P is the stabiliser of ⟨e_2⟩ (p. 33), i.e. the lower triangular group, and Galois acts on (a 0; c b) by c ↦ χ_cycl(σ)c. Let p be odd, x = 1, and
K_p = {γ ∈ GL_2(Z_p) : γ11, γ22 ∈ 1+pZ_p, γ12 ∈ p²Z_p, γ21 ≡ (γ11−1)/p mod p}.
- K_p contains 1+p²M_2(Z_p).
- K_p is closed under products, because (γδ)11 ≡ γ11δ11 mod p² and (γδ)21 ≡ γ21+δ21 mod p.
- Hence K_p is a compact open subgroup.
- K_p ∩ P(Q_p) = {(a 0; c b) : a, b ∈ 1+pZ_p, c ≡ (a−1)/p mod p}.
- Its intersection with M(Q_p) is {a ≡ 1 mod p², b ≡ 1 mod p}, but its image in M(Q_p) is all of (1+pZ_p)², so it is not a semidirect product.
- A σ with χ_cycl(σ) ≢ 1 mod p does not preserve the congruence on c, so K_p ∩ P(Q_p) is not Galois-stable.
These facts were checked by direct computation modulo p² for p = 3 and 5. For p = 3 the group K_p ∩ P(Q_p) has 27 elements mod p², while (K ∩ M)(K ∩ U_P) has only 9.

So the cited proposition does not give the quotient or its normality for this group. The step has no adequate proof as written.

The statement itself is true. The argument of Proposition 3.4.9 adapts as described in the correction. In this example, the extra generator (1+p 0; 1 1) acts through the diamond operator on the Igusa cover, so the quotient is even étale over the Galois-stable level {a ≡ 1 mod p², b ≡ 1 mod p, c ∈ pZ_p}.

Nothing downstream depends on the missing generality:
- Lemma 4.1.7 and the formal-scheme identifications in Proposition 4.2.4 use K_{p,P,w} = wK_{p,n}w^{−1} ∩ P(Q_p) and w(t)K_{p,P,w}w(t)^{−1} ∩ K_{p,P,w}.
- Both groups are cut out by congruence conditions on root subgroups, so they are Galois-stable. What the paper states. Proposition 3.4.9 (p. 37) is about IG_{K^p} over Z_p and about compact open subgroups of P′(Q_p). By p. 36 these are the compact open subgroups of P(Q_p) that are stable under the Galois action, which acts on U_P through χ_cycl. §3.4.12 (p. 38) defines IG_{K^pK_{p,P},Z_p^cycl} for every compact open K_{p,P} ⊆ P(Q_p), but proves nothing about it. The only thing it adds is the identification with a base change when K_{p,P} comes from P′(Q_p). The level K_{p,P} = P(Q_p) ∩ xK_px^{−1} of §3.4.17 need not be of that kind.

Example. Take g = 1, so G = GL_2, and P, the stabiliser of ⟨e_2⟩, is the lower triangular Borel. Take p odd and x = 1. Let K_p = {γ ∈ GL_2(Z_p) : γ_11, γ_22 ∈ 1+pZ_p, γ_12 ∈ p²Z_p, γ_21 ≡ (γ_11−1)/p mod p}. This is a compact open subgroup:
- (γδ)_11 ≡ γ_11δ_11 mod p² and (γδ)_21 ≡ γ_21+δ_21 mod p;
- it contains 1+p²M_2(Z_p);
- closure under products was also checked by direct computation mod p² for p = 3, 5.
Then K_p ∩ P(Q_p) = {(a 0; c d) : a, d ∈ 1+pZ_p, c ≡ (a−1)/p mod p}. Its intersection with M(Q_p) is {a ≡ 1 mod p²}, which has index p in its image (1+pZ_p)² in M(Q_p). So it is not the semi-direct product of its M- and U_P-parts. It is not Galois-stable either: c ↦ χ_cycl(σ)c does not preserve it when χ_cycl(σ) ≢ 1 mod p. So Proposition 3.4.9, as cited for normality in the proof of Lemma 3.4.24, does not cover this level. Copying 3.4.9(5) over word for word would also be wrong here: the group of IG_{K^pU_K} → IG_{K^pK} is the image of K in M(Q_p), not M_{K_{p,P}} = K_{p,P} ∩ M(Q_p).

Defence: the claim is true. Over Z_p^cycl, with Z_p(1) = Z_p fixed, each element of P(Q_p) gives a Z_p^cycl-point of J_ord. Let K ⊆ P(Q_p) be compact open.
1. U_K = K ∩ U_P(Q_p) is a Z_p-lattice, so it is Galois-stable.
2. K ∩ M(Q_p) is open in the image K̄ of K, so it contains an open subgroup M_1 that is normal in K̄.
3. K_1 = M_1 ⋉ U_K is open and normal in K, comes from P′(Q_p), and satisfies K/K_1 ≅ K̄/M_1.
4. The closure of a coset kK_1 is the translate k·\overline{K_1}. These translates are disjoint, since they have different images in M(Q_p)/M_1. Hence \overline{K}/\overline{K_1} is the constant group K/K_1.
5. So IG_{K^pK,Z_p^cycl} is the quotient of IG_{K^pK_1} ×_{Spf Z_p} Spf Z_p^cycl, which is smooth by 3.4.9(3), by a free action of a finite constant group. It is therefore smooth over Z_p^cycl, in particular normal.
The argument is short, but the paper states none of it. Its only hints are §3.4.12 and Remark 3.4.14 (p. 39), which also uses the Z_p^cycl variant for g ∈ P(Q_p) without comment. So this is a gap in the proof, not an error, and Lemma 3.4.24 holds as stated.

Consequences. Lemma 3.4.24 is used at the formal level in two places:
- Lemma 4.1.7 (p. 41), at K_{p,P,w} = wK_{p,n}w^{−1} ∩ P(Q_p);
- the proof of Proposition 4.2.4 (p. 43), at K_{p,P,w} ∩ w(t)K_{p,P,w}w(t)^{−1}.
Both groups have Iwahori factorisations: they are semi-direct products whose U_P-part is a Z_p-lattice, so they come from P′(Q_p) and Proposition 3.4.9 applies directly. Levels that are not semi-direct products do occur in the proof of Proposition 4.2.4, for the components x ≢ 1. For example, take g = 1, n = 1, t = diag(1, p⁴) ∈ T^{++}, w the non-trivial Weyl element and x = (1 0; p 1). Then P(Q_p) ∩ wx(K_{p,1} ∩ tK_{p,1}t^{−1})(wx)^{−1} = {(a 0; c d) : a, d ∈ Z_p^×, c ∈ pZ_p, a−d ≡ −pc mod p³} (checked by direct computation). Its M-part {a ≡ d mod p³} has index p in its image {a ≡ d mod p²}. These components enter only through their generic fibres, and they are discarded. So no stated result is affected.

review.reason: Confirmed as a gap. §3.4.12 forms $\mathfrak{IG}_{K^pK_{p,P},\Z_p^{\mathrm{cycl}}}$ as a quotient `For any compact open subgroup $K_{p,P}$ of $P(\Q_p)$', while Proposition 3.4.9, which produces those quotients and their smoothness, is stated over $\Z_p$ for compact opens of $P'(\Q_p)$ — that is, by §3.4.5, for the Galois-stable ones. §3.4.17 then takes $K_{p,P}=P(\Q_p)\cap xK_px^{-1}$, which need not be Galois stable, and the proof of Lemma 3.4.24 cites Proposition 3.4.9 for the normality of that source. So a $\Z_p^{\mathrm{cycl}}$ statement for all compact opens of $P(\Q_p)$ is being used and is not proved. The finding's repair is correct and short, descending from a Galois-stable open normal subgroup by a free finite group action.

sourceIssues.printed: We finally deduce point (6) by passing to the quotient by \overline{U_{K_{p,P}}}/\overline{U_P(\mathbb{Z}_p)(1)_n} for n large enough. This implies (3). Indeed, by (4) the formal schemes \mathfrak{IG}_{K^pK_{p,P}} are formally smooth, and they are also of finite type (as we noticed earlier during the proof of (1) and (2)). The remaining points follow easily.
sourceIssues.correction: "This implies (3). Indeed, by (6) (together with (5), cf. Remark 3.4.10) the formal schemes \mathfrak{IG}_{K^pK_{p,P}} are formally smooth, and they are also of finite type …"
sourceIssues.reason: On p. 38 the printed text reads "by (4)". Point (4) of Proposition 3.4.9 (p. 37) says only that "the fpqc quotient of \mathfrak{IG}_{K^p} by \overline{U_{K_{p,P}}} exists as a p-adic formal scheme and is denoted by \mathfrak{IG}_{K^pU_{K_{p,P}}}". It says nothing about smoothness. It also concerns the U-level space, not the space \mathfrak{IG}_{K^pK_{p,P}} of item (3). The page has no displayed equation numbered (4) that "(4)" could refer to instead. The proof itself explains where formal smoothness comes from. The sentence just before it establishes (6): "We finally deduce point (6) … This implies (3)". Point (6) says the formal completions of \mathfrak{IG}_{K^pU_{K_{p,P}}} at closed points are homogeneous spaces under the formal torus \hat T_{K_{p,P}}. Remark 3.4.10 (p. 37) then spells out the argument: "The point (6), implies that the completed local rings at a closed point x … is isomorphic to \mathscr{O}_{\hat T_{K_{p,P}}}\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}_p} W(k(x)). By (5), for any closed point x ∈ \mathfrak{IG}_{K^pK_{p,P}} and any x′ above x", the completed local ring at x, after completed base change to W(k(x′)), is the completed local ring at x′. That completed local ring is a power-series ring over W(k(x′)). Regularity descends along the faithfully flat map W(k(x)) → W(k(x′)), for both the ring and its reduction mod p. So the completed local ring of \mathfrak{IG}_{K^pK_{p,P}} at x is a power-series ring over W(k(x)). Together with finite type, this gives smoothness, which is (3). The step therefore uses (6) and (5), not (4). The paper's own wording ("This implies (3)", with "This" referring to (6)) and Remark 3.4.10 show that the intended reference is (6). Point (4) only enters indirectly, because it defines the space that appears in (6). No quotient argument of the kind used for (4) could supply smoothness: a quotient by a finite flat group scheme need not preserve smoothness. The error is a wrong item number. The statement (3) and its proof stand once the reference is corrected. Later uses of Proposition 3.4.9 rely on (7) and on Remark 3.4.11: the Hecke projections in 3.4.13 on p. 39 and the proof on p. 48. None of these depends on the mis-cited item.
