sourceIssues.printed: "We let A_{g,δ} → A_{g,d} be the locally closed substack where the kernel of the polarization is isomorphic, locally in the étale topology, to ∏_{i=1}^g Z/δ_iZ × μ_{δ_i}. By definition, we have A_{g,δ,Q} = S_{K_δ,Q}. [...] We let 𝔄_{g,δ} be the p-adic formal completion of A_{g,δ} and we let 𝔄^{ord}_{g,δ} be the ordinary locus. We have 𝔄^{ord}_{g,d} = ∐_δ 𝔄^{ord}_{g,δ}. Lemma 3.4.20. We have 𝔄^{ord}_{g,δ} = 𝔍𝔊_{K_{δ,P}} where K_{δ,P} = K^p_δ(K_{δ,p} ∩ P(Q_p)). Proof. Clear from the definition."
sourceIssues.correction: Replace "locally in the étale topology" with "locally in the fppf topology". The two conditions agree over Z[1/d], so A_{g,δ,Q} = S_{K_δ,Q} is unaffected. With this definition, a point of 𝔄^ord_{g,d} lies in 𝔄^ord_{g,δ} exactly when the étale quotient of the p-primary part of the kernel has type (p^{v_p(δ_i)})_i, and Lemma 3.4.20 becomes the intended statement. The displayed equality 𝔄^ord_{g,d} = ∐_δ 𝔄^ord_{g,δ} must then be read as an equality of underlying topological spaces: for g ≥ 2 it is not an equality of formal schemes (see the reason). Defining A_{g,δ} instead as the schematic closure of A_{g,δ,Q} in A_{g,d} does not work.
sourceIssues.reason:
The failure already shows for g = 1 and d = p. The case p | d is the one the paper needs: in 4.1.1 the degrees are d_i = p^{2ng−2in}. Every polarization of degree p² on an elliptic curve is p times the principal one. So δ = (p) is the only type, the kernel is E[p], and A_{1,(p)} should be all of A_{1,p}.

(1) The printed locus is not locally closed. Let E be ordinary over a separably closed field L of characteristic p. Then E[p] ≅ Z/p × μ_p exactly when the connected–étale sequence splits, that is, when E has an étale subgroup C of order p. In that case the dual of E → E/C is purely inseparable of degree p, hence a Frobenius, so E ≅ (E/C)^{(p)} and j(E) ∈ L^p. Conversely, if j(E) = a^p, then E ≅ E'^{(p)} for some E' with j(E') = a, and E'^{(p)} contains the étale group ker V_{E'}.

Now take the generic point of the ordinary locus of the special fibre (on an étale atlas, for example level N ≥ 3 prime to p). Its function field K is separable over F_p(j). A p-th root of j in K^sep would be both separable and purely inseparable over F_p(j), so it would lie in F_p(j). That is impossible, since j ∉ F_p(j^p). So the condition fails at this generic point. It holds at every ordinary closed point, because the residue field is finite and its separable closure is perfect. The locus therefore meets the special fibre in infinitely many closed points but not in the generic point. Such a set is not constructible, so the locus is not a locally closed substack.

(2) The same happens formally. Over the Serre–Tate deformation ring W(k̄)[[t]] of an ordinary point, E[p] is the extension of Z/p by μ_p whose Kummer class is q = 1 + t. This class is not a p-th power even modulo p, since p-th powers in k̄[[t]] are series in t^p. The ring is strictly henselian, so E[p] does not split étale-locally either. As defined, then, 𝔄^{ord}_{1,(p)} contains no formal neighbourhood of any ordinary point. So 𝔄^{ord}_{1,p} = ∐_δ 𝔄^{ord}_{1,δ} fails.

(3) Lemma 3.4.20 fails too. Its right-hand side 𝔍𝔊_{K_{δ,P}} is a smooth formal scheme. Here K_{δ,p} ∩ P(Q_p) = diag(p,1)P(Z_p)diag(p,1)^{-1} is T(Q_p)-conjugate to P(Z_p), so 𝔍𝔊_{K_{δ,P}} is the whole ordinary locus.

(4) With the fppf condition everything works. On the ordinary locus, the p-primary part of the kernel is an extension of an étale group by a multiplicative group, and such an extension splits fppf-locally (extract p-power roots of the Kummer class). The type δ is determined by the étale quotient, which is locally constant. So the loci are open and closed in the ordinary locus, and the decomposition and Lemma 3.4.20 hold.

A_{g,δ} is used later only through these ordinary loci, in the proof of Lemma 3.4.24. The integral models in 3.4.19–3.4.23 and 4.1.1 are normalizations of A_{g,d_i}, not of A_{g,δ}. So correcting the definition changes nothing further. (1) The printed condition fails. Take g = 1 and d = p. A polarization of degree p² on an elliptic curve is p times the principal one, so its kernel is E[p]. Then δ = (p) is the only type, and K_{δ,p} is GL_2(Z_p) conjugated by diag(p,1), so A_{1,(p),Q} = A_{1,p,Q}. On the ordinary locus, E[p] is (étale-locally) an extension of Z/p by μ_p. Since E[p] is killed by p, its class lies in H^1_fppf(R, μ_p), which is R^×/R^{×p} for local R. Over the Serre–Tate deformation ring W(k)[[t]] of an ordinary curve (k = F̄_p), the class is that of q = 1 + t, which is not a p-th power even modulo p. That ring is strictly henselian, so E[p] is not étale-locally ≅ Z/p × μ_p on the formal neighbourhood of any ordinary point.

Over a field k of characteristic p, E[p] splits iff E has an étale subgroup of order p, iff E is a Frobenius twist, iff j(E) ∈ k^p. Separable extensions do not help, because k ∩ (k^sep)^p = k^p. So the condition holds at every closed point of the ordinary locus of A_{1,p} ⊗ F_p (their residue fields are perfect) but fails at its generic point (j is not a p-th power there). The set of points satisfying the printed condition is therefore not constructible, so there is no locally closed substack "where" the condition holds.

Lemma 3.4.20 also fails with the printed definition. Here P is the stabilizer of ⟨e_{g+1},…,e_{2g}⟩ (p. 33), so K_{δ,p} ∩ P(Q_p) = {(a 0; c d) : a, d ∈ Z_p^×, c ∈ p^{-1}Z_p}. This group is conjugate by diag(1,p) ∈ T(Q_p) to P(Z_p). Hence 𝔍𝔊_{K_{δ,P}} is the whole ordinary locus of 𝔄_{1,1} ≅ 𝔄_{1,p}, which the étale-local locus is not.

(2) Defence. The words work only if the condition is tested at geometric points, where "étale-locally" says nothing, and the locus is given its reduced structure. The text does not say this, and "locally in the étale topology" is a condition on families. The scheme structure matters, because Lemma 3.4.20 compares 𝔄^ord_{g,δ} with a formal scheme. The reference [dJ93] is cited only for A_{g,d}, not for A_{g,δ}.

(3) The fppf repair and what it gives. For g = 1 the class of E[p] dies fppf-locally, so A_{1,(p)} = A_{1,p} minus the supersingular points and Lemma 3.4.20 holds. In general, on 𝔄^ord_{g,d} the p-part K of ker λ is an extension of an étale group K^et by a multiplicative group K^m, and the Weil pairing gives K^m ≅ D(K^et). So each point has a type that can be read from K^et, and the fppf locus is the intended one.

However, such extensions need not split fppf-locally over non-reduced bases: Ext^1(Z/p, μ_p) contains μ_p(R). Also, 𝔄_{g,d} can be non-reduced at ordinary points. Example: g = 2, d = p², and x = (A_0, pλ_0) with A_0 ordinary and λ_0 principal. Put Q(α,β) = q(α, λ_0β), where q is the Serre–Tate parameter. By Katz's lifting criterion, pλ_0 lifts iff Q(e_1,e_2)^p = Q(e_2,e_1)^p. So the complete local ring at x is W[[x_11, x_22, x_12, x_21]]/((1+x_12)^p − (1+x_21)^p). Its reduction mod p is k[[…]]/((x_12 − x_21)^p) (checked by direct computation), which is not reduced. Near x:
- The type-(p,p) locus is x_12 = x_21, the locus where λ_0 itself lifts.
- The fppf type-(1,p²) locus lies in the generic fibre, so it does not meet the p-adic completion.
- Hence ∐_δ 𝔄^ord_{2,δ} ⊊ 𝔄^ord_{2,p²}: the two have the same underlying space but are different formal schemes.

The branches 1+x_12 = ζ(1+x_21) with ζ ≠ 1 carry characteristic-0 polarizations of type (1,p²). So x lies in the closures of both A_{2,(p,p),Q} and A_{2,(1,p²),Q}. With the schematic-closure definition, the ordinary loci would therefore overlap. For p odd, the closure of the type-(1,p²) locus at x is Spf W[[…]]/(((1+x_12)^p − (1+x_21)^p)/(x_12 − x_21)), whose special fibre is k[[…]]/((x_12 − x_21)^{p−1}). So it is not smooth over Z_p there, whereas 𝔍𝔊 is smooth by Prop. 3.4.9(3).

(4) Later use. The decomposition itself is not used later. Lemma 3.4.20 enters only in the proof of Lemma 3.4.24 (p. 40), through the finite maps 𝔍𝔊_{K^pK_{p,P}} → ∏ 𝔄^ord_{g,δ_i} with normal source. The fppf version of Lemma 3.4.20 supplies these maps, and normalization ignores nilpotents. So Lemma 3.4.24, Lemma 4.1.7 (p. 41) and Proposition 4.2.4 (p. 43) stand once the definition is corrected. The integral models (normalizations of ∏ A_{g,d_i}) do not involve A_{g,δ}.

review.reason: Confirmed as an error, and the smallest case settles it. §3.4.19 defines $\mathcal A_{g,\delta}\to\mathcal A_{g,d}$ as the locally closed substack `where the kernel of the polarization is isomorphic, locally in the étale topology, to $\prod_i\Z/\delta_i\Z\times\mu_{\delta_i}$'. Reading it fppf-locally, as the finding proposes, leaves $\mathcal A_{g,\delta,\Q}=S_{K_\delta,\Q}$ untouched and makes the decomposition of the ordinary locus correct.

sourceIssues.locator: §4.1, first line, p. 40
sourceIssues.printed: 4.1. The Siegel variety of Iwahori level. Let n ∈ ℤ_{≥0}. Let K_{p,n} ⊆ G(ℚ_p) be the Iwahori subgroup of matrices in G(ℤ_p), reducing modulo p^n to B(ℤ/p^nℤ).
sourceIssues.correction: Replace "Let n ∈ ℤ_{≥0}" with "Let n ∈ ℤ_{≥1}", i.e. n ≥ 1. No other text needs to change.
sourceIssues.reason:
The page image shows "Let n ∈ ℤ_{≥0}" (subscript ≥0), so this is not a text-layer artefact. For n = 0 the definition gives the reduction modulo p^0 = 1 to B(ℤ/ℤ), which is the trivial group. So K_{p,0} = G(ℤ_p), the hyperspecial maximal compact subgroup, not an Iwahori subgroup. Several statements of §4.1 then fail, as checked by direct computation.

(i) Flag and filtration. In §4.1.1 (p. 41), Ker(A_g → A_{g+i}) is a subgroup of A[p^0] = 0. Every H_i and every Gr_i = H_i/H_{i−1} is therefore the trivial group scheme, which is both étale and multiplicative.

(ii) Strata and Remark 4.1.4. For each w ∈ ^MW, the stratum S^tor_{K^pK_{p,n},F_p,w} of §4.1.3 is the locus where Gr_{w^{-1}(i)} is multiplicative for i = g+1, …, 2g. For n = 0 this is the whole special fibre. Remark 4.1.4 (p. 41) says: "Clearly, S^tor_{K^pK_{p,n},F_p,w} is included in the ordinary locus". That is false at n = 0, because the special fibre of the Siegel variety at hyperspecial level has non-ordinary points (for example supersingular ones).

(iii) Lemmas 4.1.6, 4.1.7 and 4.1.9. G(ℤ_p) acts transitively on FL(ℚ_p) = G(ℤ_p)/P(ℤ_p). So for n = 0 every w·K_{p,0} equals FL(ℚ_p). The proof of Lemma 4.1.6 says π_HT^{-1}(FL(ℚ_p)) is the closure of the ordinary locus, but the lemma would make it the closure of S^tor_w, which is the whole space. Lemma 4.1.7 (S^tor_w equals an ordinary Igusa variety) fails for the same reason. The divisors D_i of §4.1.8 are all zero (D_i + D_{2g+1−i} = V(p^0)), so Lemma 4.1.9 gives the whole special fibre for every w. That contradicts Remark 4.1.4 again.

(iv) The rest of the paper also needs n ≥ 1:
- The Casselman algebra map t ↦ [K_{p,n} t K_{p,n}] of §4.2 (p. 43) needs a subgroup with an Iwahori decomposition.
- Remark 4.1.2 takes n = 1 as the usual Iwahori level.
- The support conditions deg H_{g+i} ≥ n(w_i − ε) of §6.1.8 (p. 60) are empty conditions when n = 0.

So the authors clearly mean n ≥ 1, and ℤ_{≥0} is a slip in the range. No later result needs K_{p,0}. The other statements that allow n ∈ ℤ_{≥0} (Theorem 1.4.3 (4),(5) on p. 5, Theorem 5.1.4 on p. 53) use a different parameter: a congruence level for T_{K_p}, or reduction modulo p^n. They do not use the group K_{p,n} of §4.1. Correcting the range therefore changes nothing downstream. The published Springer text could not be compared. The page image shows "ℤ_{≥0}", so this is not an extraction artefact.

Defence tried. Could n = 0 be a harmless degenerate case, or be excluded by the words "the Iwahori subgroup"? At n = 0 the condition is reduction modulo p^0 = 1 into B(ℤ/ℤ), which is trivial, so K_{p,0} = G(ℤ_p). This is the hyperspecial maximal compact subgroup, not an Iwahori subgroup. The phrase "the Iwahori subgroup", the title of §4.1 and Remark 4.1.2 ("When n = 1, S^tor_{K^pK_{p,1}} is the usual integral model of Iwahori level") all show that the authors mean n ≥ 1. So the range ℤ_{≥0} is a slip, not a deliberate inclusion. At n = 0 the statements of §4 are not vacuous; they are false:
- p. 41: Ker(A_g → A_{g+i}) ⊆ A[p^0] = 0. So every H_i and every Gr_i is the trivial group scheme, which is both étale and multiplicative. By §4.1.3, the stratum S^tor_{K^pK_{p,0},F_p,w} is then the whole special fibre for every w. This contradicts Remark 4.1.4 ("Clearly, S^tor_{K^pK_{p,n},F_p,w} is included in the ordinary locus"), because the special fibre at hyperspecial level has non-ordinary (e.g. supersingular) points.
- G(ℤ_p) acts transitively on FL(ℚ_p). So w·K_{p,0} = FL(ℚ_p) for every w, and Lemmas 4.1.6 and 4.1.7 fail for the same reason.
- By §4.1.8, "D_i + D_{2g+1−i} = V(p^n)" becomes the zero divisor, so every D_i = 0. In Proposition 4.1.13 (2), every Z_i and V(p^{nj}) is then 0. So S̃_{=j_1,…,=j_k} is the whole space even when some j_i − j_{i−1} ∉ {0,1}, although (2) says it is then empty.
- §4.2, p. 43: the map t ↦ [K_{p,n} t K_{p,n}] from [Cas] lem. 4.1.5 is an algebra map only for groups with an Iwahori decomposition. For g = 1 at level GL_2(ℤ_p), with t = diag(1,p), one has [KtK]^2 = [Kt^2K] + (p+1)[K pI K] (degrees (p+1)^2 = (p^2+p) + (p+1), checked by direct computation). So the map is not multiplicative.
- Proof of Proposition 6.1.11, p. 61: it uses "the Iwahori decomposition K_{p,n} = B_{K_{p,n}} × U^{op}_{K_{p,n}}". G(ℤ_p) has no such decomposition: U(ℤ_p)T(ℤ_p)Ū(ℤ_p) misses the Weyl element. The same proof also pulls back ]X_{w,F_p}[, which is K_{p,n}-stable for n ≥ 1 but not G(ℤ_p)-stable.

Nothing later uses n = 0. Every later use of K_{p,n} relies on the flag H_i, the divisors D_i or the Iwahori decomposition:
- §4.2–4.5;
- the Nebentypus of §4.3.5;
- §6.1.8–6.1.11 (whose conditions deg H_{g+i} ≥ n(w_i − ε) are empty at n = 0);
- §6.2.

The other places where the paper writes "n ∈ ℤ_{≥0}" use a different parameter:
- Theorem 1.4.3 (4),(5), p. 5: the conductor of T_{K_p}, where K_p must admit an Iwahori decomposition, which G(ℤ_p) does not;
- Theorem 5.1.4, p. 53: reduction modulo p^n.

So these statements never involve K_{p,0}. The corrected range n ≥ 1 is right and minimal, and no stated result or proof changes.

sourceIssues.reason:
On p. 40 (§3.4.19) the paper says: "We let A_{g,d} → Spec Z be the moduli stack of abelian varieties of dimension g, with a degree d² polarization (see [dJ93]). For any δ = (δ_1, …, δ_g) ∈ Z^g_{≥0} with (δ_1 | δ_2 | ⋯ | δ_g) and ∏_{i=1}^g δ_i = d …". The kernel is then locally ∏ Z/δ_iZ × μ_{δ_i}, of order d². So in the paper, "degree" means the order of the kernel, and the index d of A_{g,d} is its square root.

Recomputed directly: H_{g+i} = Ker(A_g → A_{g+i}) is a totally isotropic subgroup of A[p^n], locally isomorphic to (Z/p^nZ)^i, so it has order p^{ni}. The polarization λ_{g+i} on A_{g+i} = A/H_{g+i} comes from descending p^nλ, so π^∨ ∘ λ_{g+i} ∘ π = p^nλ. Taking degrees gives p^{ni} · deg λ_{g+i} · p^{ni} = p^{2ng}, so deg λ_{g+i} = p^{2n(g−i)}. Equivalently, its kernel H_{g+i}^⊥/H_{g+i} has order p^{2ng−ni}/p^{ni}. The kernel is locally (Z/p^nZ)^{g−i} × μ_{p^n}^{g−i}, so the type is δ = (1, …, 1, p^n, …, p^n), with i ones and g−i entries equal to p^n, and ∏δ_j = p^{n(g−i)}.

So the printed degree p^{2ng−2in} is right, but it equals d_i², not d_i. The point (A_{g+i}, λ_{g+i}) lies in A_{g,p^{n(g−i)}}. Read literally, d_i = p^{2n(g−i)} would require a polarization with ∏δ_j = p^{2n(g−i)}, and there is no natural one. An integer multiple mλ_{g+i} has ∏δ_j = m^g p^{n(g−i)}, which fails already for g = 2, i = 1, n = 1, since m² = p has no integer solution. The two readings agree only for i = g, where d_g = 1, and for i = 0, where d_0 = 1 is set separately. The text layer is not the cause: the page image shows the same "p^{2ng−2in} = d_i" and "A_{g,d_i}".

No later result depends on this. The d_i only name the auxiliary spaces A_{g,d_i} used in the normalization that defines the integral model. Remark 3.4.21 already says the model depends on these auxiliary choices. The later statements (Remark 4.1.2, Lemma 4.1.7 via Lemma 3.4.24, Proposition 4.1.13) use only the chain of isogenies, the flag H_i, and the independence of the ordinary locus from the choices. None of them uses the numerical value of d_i.

sourceIssues.reason:
I checked the text against the rendered page. The flag is indexed g+1, …, 2g, 1, …, g, and the same sentence states explicitly that A[p^n] = H_g. Read literally, "Gr_i = H_i/H_{i−1}" fails at two indices. (a) At i = g+1 it gives H_{g+1}/H_g = H_{g+1}/A[p^n]. That is not a quotient, because A[p^n] is not contained in H_{g+1}. (b) At i = 1 it gives H_1/H_0, and H_0 is never defined in the paper.

The intended meaning is clear from the next sentence, which says every Gr_i has order p^n and Gr_{2g−i+1} = Gr_i^D. I checked both claims by direct computation with the corrected convention. H_{g+j} has order p^{nj} and H_j has order p^{n(g+j)}, so every step of the flag has order p^n. The flag is self-dual: H_{g+j}^⊥ = H_{g−j}, and H_{2g−i+1}^⊥ = H_{i−1}. The Weil pairing then gives H_i/H_{i−1} = H_{2g−i}^⊥/H_{2g−i+1}^⊥ ≅ (H_{2g−i+1}/H_{2g−i})^D. The endpoint cases also check out. For i = 1: Gr_1 = H_1/H_{2g} = H_{2g−1}^⊥/H_{2g}^⊥ ≅ Gr_{2g}^D. For i = g: Gr_g = A[p^n]/H_{g−1} = A[p^n]/H_{g+1}^⊥ ≅ H_{g+1}^D = Gr_{g+1}^D.

- Proof of Lemma 4.1.6 (p. 41): with H_{g+i} corresponding to ⟨e_{g+1}, …, e_{g+i}⟩ mod p^n, Gr_{g+i} is multiplicative exactly when g+i ∈ w^{-1}{g+1, …, 2g}. For i = 1 this needs Gr_{g+1} = H_{g+1}.

- §4.2.5 (p. 44): H_{g+i} has rank p^{in} for 1 ≤ i ≤ 2g, so the index is read mod 2g, and H″_{g+i}/(H″_{g+i} ∩ H_{g+i−1}) ≅ Gr_{g+i} is used with i = 1, where H_{g+i−1} = H_g must be 0.

sourceIssues.correction:
Over the whole of S^tor, let Gr_i be the kernel of the i-th isogeny f_i: A_{i−1} → A_i in the chain of semi-abelian schemes from p. 41, which comes from [FC90], I, 2.7. This kernel is quasi-finite and flat but in general not finite, and over the interior it equals H_i/H_{i−1}. Define D_i as the divisor of the determinant of its co-Lie complex [ω_{A_i} → ω_{A_{i−1}}], that is, the zero locus of det Lie(f_i). This is essentially the preprint's formulation.

- D_i is an effective Cartier divisor, because S^tor is normal and Z_p-flat and det Lie(f_i) becomes invertible once p is inverted.
- On the interior it is Fargues' divisor.
- Its complement is the locus where f_i, equivalently Gr_i, is étale.

The identity D_i + D_{2g+1−i} = V(p^n) needs its own argument at the boundary. It holds on the interior by [Far10], and both sides are trivial on the generic fibre. Since S^tor is normal, it follows on all of S^tor once one knows that no irreducible component of the special fibre lies in the boundary. Alternatively, it follows from a local computation with the Raynaud extension, splitting into torus, abelian and étale parts. This density statement, or the local computation, should be stated and justified. Taking the schematic closure of the divisor on the interior would not be enough on its own, because one would still have to show that the closure is Cartier.

- Since Z_{1,>0} = D_4 and Z_{1,<0} = 0, the set S̃_{=0} is the preimage in S̃ = S̃_3 of U = S^tor \ D_4, the locus where Gr_4 is étale.
- On U we have Z_2 = D_5 and Z_3 = D_5 + D_6. Locally write D_5 = V(x_5), D_6 = V(x_6) and D_2 = V(y_5). Then x_5·y_5 = p·(unit), because D_5 + D_2 = V(p).
- The ideals (x_5, p^j) are principal, so S̃_2 → S is an isomorphism over U.
- At the third stage, for j = 1, the ideal is (x_5x_6, p) = x_5·(x_6, y_5).

Now take the point P given by A = E × E_1 × E_2 with the product principal polarization. Here E is ordinary, E_1 and E_2 are supersingular, and K_i ⊂ E_i[p] is the subgroup of order p. The flag is:
- H_4 = E[p]^ét,
- H_5 = H_4 × K_1,
- H_6 = H_4 × K_1 × K_2, which is Lagrangian,
- H_1 = H_4 × K_1 × E_2[p],
- H_2 = H_4 × E_1[p] × E_2[p].

Gr_4 is étale, so P ∈ U. Move (E_1,K_1) and (E_2,K_2) along the two components of the special fibre of Y_0(p), which meet at supersingular points. This gives two points that specialize to P:
- Q, with (Gr_4, Gr_5, Gr_6) = (étale, multiplicative, multiplicative);
- Q', with (étale, étale, étale).

Q lies on D_6 but not on D_2, because Gr_2 = Gr_5^D is étale there. Q' lies on D_2 but not on D_6. So in the local ring at P neither x_6 nor y_5 divides the other.

In a local ring, if (a,b) is invertible then it equals (a) or (b). Hence (x_6, y_5) is not invertible at P, and neither is x_5·(x_6, y_5). So S̃_3 → S̃_2 ≅ S is not an isomorphism over any neighbourhood of P in U. This map is proper and is an isomorphism on the dense generic fibre, so it is surjective onto U. A surjective open immersion would be an isomorphism, so S̃_{=0} → S^tor is not an open immersion. This contradicts (2) for k = 1.

For k ≥ g−1 the argument in the proof is valid. Later arguments use only the case k = g (Corollary 4.1.14). So the false case of the stated proposition does not propagate. Notation: S = S^tor_{K^pK_{p,n}}, S̃_k is the k-th stage of the tower in the proof, and S̃ = S̃_g. For a sequence (j_1,…,j_k), U(j) ⊂ S is the open set where Z_i = V(p^{nj_i}) for i ≤ k. This is the same as saying that Gr_{g+i} is multiplicative or étale, as prescribed in (2).

1. What the proof proves. In the step from k to k+1 (p. 42), U(j_1,…,j_k) is identified with S̃_{k,=j_1,…,=j_k}. On this set Z_k = V(p^{nj_k}). So Z_{k+1} − V(p^{nj}) equals D_{g+k+1} + V(p^{n(j_k−j)}) when j ≤ j_k, and −D_{g−k} − V(p^{n(j−j_k−1)}) when j > j_k. Hence every ideal blown up at stage k+1 is invertible there, and S̃_{k+1} → S̃_k is an isomorphism over this set. This gives (2) for sequences of length k on S̃_k, and on S̃_{k+1}. In particular it gives (2) on S̃ for k = g − 1 and k = g.
The proof does not show that the later maps S̃_{k'+1} → S̃_{k'} with k' ≥ k + 1 are isomorphisms over U(j_1,…,j_k). Over that set, Z_{k'+1} = V(p^{nj_k}) + D_{g+k+1} + … + D_{g+k'+1}, which has at least two unconstrained summands. So the induction hypothesis "S̃_k satisfies the properties for all indices i ≤ k" is not carried over to S̃_{k+1} for sequences shorter than k.

2. Counterexample: g = 3, n = 1, k = 1, j_1 = 0.
- Here Z_{1,>0} = D_4 and Z_{1,<0} = 0. So S̃_{=0} is the full preimage of U = S \ D_4, the locus where Gr_4 is étale. Since a blow-up is surjective, (2) would say that S̃ → S is an isomorphism over U.
- Over U, the map S̃_2 → S̃_1 = S is an isomorphism, by step 1 with k = 1.
- The map S̃_3 → S̃_2 blows up, among other ideals, (O(−Z_3), p). On U, Z_3 = D_5 + D_6. Since D_5 + D_2 = V(p), we have p = x_5·y_5 up to a unit, where x_i is a local equation of D_i and y_5 is a local equation of D_2. So (O(−Z_3), p) = x_5·(x_6, y_5).
- If S̃ → S were an isomorphism over U, this ideal would be invertible on U. Then (x_6, y_5) would be invertible too, because x_5 is a nonzerodivisor. By Nakayama, in each local ring it would then be generated by x_6 or by y_5. Since S is normal, this would mean that D_6 ≤ D_2 or D_2 ≤ D_6 at every height-one prime through the point.

3. A point where this fails.
- Let E_1 be ordinary, with C_1 ⊂ E_1[p] its étale subgroup. Let E_2, E_3 be supersingular, with C_i = ker F for i = 2, 3.
- Let x be the point given by A = E_1 × E_2 × E_3 with the product polarization, H_4 = C_1, H_5 = C_1 × C_2, H_6 = C_1 × C_2 × C_3, and the dual chain. Then Gr_4 = C_1 is étale, so x ∈ U.
- The product of three Deligne–Rapoport models of X_0(p) is normal and flat, so it maps to the normalization S, and the product point goes to x. Both components of the special fibre of X_0(p) pass through every supersingular point. So x is a limit of ordinary points of type (Gr_4, Gr_5, Gr_6) = (étale, multiplicative, multiplicative). It is also a limit of ordinary points where all three are étale.
- The points of each type form an open subset of the special fibre: the complement of D_4 ∪ D_2 ∪ D_1, and the complement of D_4 ∪ D_5 ∪ D_6. So x lies on special-fibre components C and C' whose generic points have these two types.
- Along C: Gr_1 = Gr_6^D is étale, so D_6 = V(p) − D_1 has positive multiplicity. Gr_2 = Gr_5^D is étale, so D_2 has multiplicity 0.
- Along C': D_6 has multiplicity 0, and D_2 = V(p) − D_5 has positive multiplicity.
- So neither x_6 nor y_5 divides the other in O_{S,x}. Hence (x_6, y_5) is not principal, S̃ → S is not an isomorphism over x ∈ U, and S̃_{=0} → S is not an open immersion.

4. Second check, by direct computation. The complete local ring of the product of modular curves at this point is W[[u, s_2, t_2, s_3, t_3]]/(s_2t_2 − p, s_3t_3 − p). Here s_3 cuts out the branch where C_3 is multiplicative, and t_2 the branch where C_2 is étale. The pullbacks of D_6 (the divisor of C_3) and of D_2 (the divisor of C_2^D) are cut out, up to units, by s_3 and t_2. These two elements are independent in m/m², so the pulled-back ideal (s_3, t_2) needs two generators.

5. Consequences. The inductive construction itself uses (2) only for sequences of length k on S̃_k. Part (1), which Lemma 4.2.11 uses, is unaffected. Part (3) holds on S̃ with pulled-back divisors. Corollary 4.1.14 and Proposition 6.2.2(3) use only complete sequences (k = g), where the claim holds. So only the printed statement of (2) for g ≥ 3 and k ≤ g − 2 is false. The correction above is the minimal one.

The printed text was checked against the rendered page (p. 43). The letter i is the free filtration index in F_i, F_{i−1} and ℓ(w)=i. The same letter is also the bound variable of ∩_{i=1}^g, and it appears inside the intersection as Z_{i,>w_i−1}, Z^c_{i,>w_i}. The formula was evidently copied from the definition Z_{>w−1} = ∩_{i=1}^g Z_{i,>w_i−1} in 4.1.16, where i is not free. Read with standard scoping the formula still has the intended meaning, so this is a harmless index clash, not a wrong statement. A similar clash occurs in 4.1.12, 'Z_i = Σ_{i=1}^k D_{g+i}', p. 42. The only later use is Lemma 4.5.7, p. 52, which states it as F_i \ F_{i−1} = ∐_{w,ℓ(w)=i}(Z_{>w−1} \ D_{−,w}) with D_{−,w} = Σ_{i=1}^g Z_{i,>w_i}. There is no clash there, and it matches the correction.

The corrected statement is true under the paper's definitions.

(a) Each point has a sequence a_j with differences 0 or 1. Take a point x of the special fibre of the blow-up. In its local ring, let f_j be the local equation of Z_j = Σ_{k≤j} D_{g+k}. By Prop. 4.1.13(1), the ideal (f_j, p^{nm}) is invertible, so in the local ring one of f_j, p^{nm} divides the other. Hence x ∈ Z_{j,>m} if and only if f_j ∈ p^{nm}·m_x. Put a_j(x) = max{m : x ∈ Z_{j,>m−1}}, with a_0 = 0. Since f_{j−1} divides f_j, we get a_j ≥ a_{j−1}. Now write f_j = f_{j−1}d_j. Because D_{g+j} + D_{g+1−j} = V(p^n), we have d_j e_j = p^n. Suppose f_j ∈ p^{n(m+1)}m_x with m = a_{j−1}. Cancelling d_j gives f_{j−1} ∈ p^{nm}e_j·m_x ⊆ p^{nm}m_x, a contradiction. So a_j − a_{j−1} ∈ {0,1}, and a(x) is the sequence of a unique w ∈ ^MW. There are 2^g such sequences, and each one occurs.

(b) Z_{>w−1} is an up-set. By Lemma 4.1.17(1), x ∈ Z_{>w−1} if and only if a(x) ≥ w componentwise.

(c) The length formula. ℓ(w) = g(g+1)/2 − Σ_j w_j. This was checked by direct computation of the Coxeter lengths of the minimal coset representatives in W_M\W for g ≤ 4, using the positive system fixed by T^+ on p. 30. It also agrees with ℓ(w) = dim C_w and w_j = dim(L ∩ ⟨e_{g+1},…,e_{g+j}⟩), since Σ_j w_j is the codimension of the Schubert cell in the Lagrangian Grassmannian. So ℓ is decreasing for the componentwise order.

Hence x ∈ F_i if and only if ℓ(a(x)) ≤ i, and F_i \ F_{i−1} = {x : ℓ(a(x)) = i}, which is the corrected formula. Only the name of a bound variable changes, so nothing downstream is affected.

Conventions of the paper. P = P_μ is the stabilizer of ⟨e_{g+1},…,e_{2g}⟩ (§3.1, p. 33), so it is block lower triangular. B ⊆ P is upper triangular on the diagonal g×g blocks, and Φ^+ is the set of roots of B (p. 34). So Φ^+ contains the roots of the lower-left block, and Φ^{-,M} (not defined explicitly, but necessarily the roots opposite to Φ^{+,M}) consists of the upper-right block roots. K_{p,n} is the group of matrices in G(Z_p) that reduce mod p^n into B(Z/p^n) (§4.1). Hence K_{p,n} ∩ U_α = U_α(Z_p) = U_{α,0} for α ∈ Φ^+, and K_{p,n} ∩ U_α = U_α(p^nZ_p) = U_{α,n} for α ∈ Φ^-. For n ≥ 1, K_{p,n} has an Iwahori factorization with respect to the parabolic w^{-1}Pw: K_{p,n} = (K_{p,n} ∩ w^{-1}Pw)(K_{p,n} ∩ w^{-1}Ū_P w). The first factor is absorbed into P after conjugation by w. So P wK_{p,n} = P w ∏_{α∈w^{-1}Φ^{-,M}} (K_{p,n} ∩ U_α), and this is unique because P ∩ Ū_P = 1. That gives the corrected formula, not the printed one.

Direct check for g = 1, n = 1, w = 1. Here G = GL_2, P = B is the lower triangular group, Φ^+ = {β} with U_β = (1 0; c 1), and U_{-β} = (1 b; 0 1). The printed right-hand side is P·U_{-β}(Z_p), which contains u = (1 1; 0 1). Now K_{p,1} = {(a b; c d) ∈ GL_2(Z_p) : b ∈ pZ_p}. Suppose u = qk with q ∈ P, and write q^{-1} = (a' 0; c' d'). Then k = (a' a'; c' c'+d'). This forces a' ∈ pZ_p and d' ∈ Z_p, so det k = a'd' ∈ pZ_p, which is impossible. So u ∉ P K_{p,1} = P·U_{-β}(pZ_p). The printed identity is false. In fact it describes the orbits of the opposite Iwahori subgroup.

With the subscripts exchanged the argument works. For t ∈ T^+ (p. 34: v(t_{g+1}) ≥ … ≥ v(t_{2g}) ≥ v(t_1) ≥ … ≥ v(t_g)) we have v(α(t)) ≥ 0 for all α ∈ Φ^+. So t^{-1}U_{α,n}t ⊆ U_{α,n} for α ∈ Φ^-. For α ∈ Φ^+, t^{-1}u_α(a)t = u_α(α(t)^{-1}a) lies in U_{α,0} if and only if v(a) ≥ v(α(t)). Together these give "t^{-1}xt ∈ (product) ⇔ x ∈ tK_{p,n}t^{-1}", which is the equivalence the proof states next. With the printed sets that equivalence fails already for t = 1 and x = u above.

The error is consistent in all three places, so it is a systematic exchange of subscripts (or of ϕ^+ and ϕ^-). It is not an artefact of the text layer: the page images show exactly the printed formulas. Proposition 4.2.4 itself, and everything that uses it later, is unaffected, because the corrected argument proves the stated isomorphism.

sourceIssues.printed: p. 43: "4.1.16. A filtration. Let w ∈ ᴹW. We let Z_{>w−1} = ∩_{i=1}^g Z_{i,>w_i−1}" and "We construct a filtration by closed subsets: F_{−1} = ∅ ⊆ F_0 ⊆ ··· ⊆ F_{g(g+1)/2} = S^tor_{F_p}, by letting F_i = ∪_{w∈ᴹW, ℓ(w)≤i} Z_{>w−1}." sourceIssues.reason:
The symbol is undefined. At the end of §3.1 (p. 34), the sequence attached to w ∈ ᴹW satisfies w_0 = 0 and w_i − w_{i−1} ∈ {0,1}. So 0 ≤ w_i ≤ i, and w_i = 0 does occur. For example, w_1 = 0 exactly when g+1 ∉ w^{−1}{g+1,…,2g}. Whenever w_i = 0, the index w_i − 1 in Z_{i,>w_i−1} is −1. But Prop. 4.1.13(1) defines Z_{i,>j} only for 0 ≤ j ≤ i, and the paper gives no convention for j = −1.

This case matters. Let w_max be the longest element of ᴹW (the open cell). Then w_max^{−1}{g+1,…,2g} = {1,…,g}, so every w_i = 0 and every factor of Z_{>w_max−1} is undefined. Every w satisfies w ≤ w_max. Lemma 4.1.17(2) is stated for all w, so it gives F_{g(g+1)/2} = Z_{>w_max−1} = ∩_i Z_{i,>−1}. Hence, given Lemma 4.1.17(2), the stated equality F_{g(g+1)/2} = S^tor_{F_p} holds exactly when each Z_{i,>−1} contains the special fibre.

Example, g = 1. Here ᴹW = {1, s}, with ℓ(1) = 0 and ℓ(s) = 1. For the identity w_1 = 1, and for s, w_1 = 0. We have Z_1 = D_2, and D_1 + D_2 = V(p^n) by §4.1.8 (p. 41). The proof of Prop. 4.1.13 gives Z_{1,>0} = D_2. Also Z_{1,>1} = 0: we have Z_{1,>1} − Z_{1,<1} = Z_1 − V(p^n) = −D_1 ≤ 0, and the two divisors have disjoint supports. So F_0 = D_2 and F_1 = D_2 ∪ Z_{1,>−1}. Thus F_1 = S^tor_{F_p} requires Z_{1,>−1} to contain S^tor_{F_p} \ D_2. By Cor. 4.1.14, this set is the stratum S^tor_{F_p,s}.

The paper's own formula forces the value. Put j = −1 in Z_{i,>j} − Z_{i,<j} = Z_i − V(p^{nj}). This gives Z_{i,>−1} − Z_{i,<−1} = Z_i + V(p^n), which is effective. Now let A and B be effective Cartier divisors with disjoint supports such that A − B is effective. Near any point of the support of B, A is trivial, so −B ≥ 0 there. Hence B = 0. So Z_{i,<−1} = 0 and Z_{i,>−1} = Z_i + V(p^n). By §4.1.8 (p. 41), D_{g+k} + D_{g+1−k} = V(p^n), so each D_{g+k} ≤ V(p^n). Hence Z_i is supported in the special fibre, and Z_i + V(p^n) has support exactly S^tor_{F_p}.

The paper uses the same formula at negative indices elsewhere. Prop. 6.2.2(2), p. 61, asserts divisors with Z_{i,>w_j+η} − Z_{i,<w_j+η} = Z_i − V(p^{n(w_j+η)}) for η ∈ {±ε, ±ε′}, and w_j − ε < 0 when w_j = 0. The paper also identifies such a divisor with the whole special fibre around it. The proof of Prop. 4.1.13 (p. 42) writes "Z_{k+1,>j} = S̃^tor_{k,=j_1,…,=j_k} for j < j_k". On that open Z_k = V(p^{nj_k}), so Z_{k+1,>j} = V(p^{n(j_k−j)}) + D_{g+k+1}, whose support is the whole special fibre there.

With this convention, the surrounding statements hold:
- The formula at j = 0 gives Z_{i,>0} = Z_i and Z_{i,<0} = 0. So Lemma 4.1.17(1) extends to the index −1: for 0 ≤ j ≤ i we have Z_{i,>j} ≤ Z_{i,>0} = Z_i ≤ Z_i + V(p^n), and Z_{i,<−1} = 0. Hence Lemma 4.1.17(2) holds for all w and w′, and F_{g(g+1)/2} = ∩_i Z_{i,>−1} = S^tor_{F_p}.
- Consider the open S̃^tor_{=w_1,…,=w_g}, whose special fibre is S^tor_{F_p,w} (Cor. 4.1.14). On it, Z_{i,>w_i} and Z_{i,<w_i} are trivial, so Z_i = V(p^{nw_i}). For w_i ≥ 1 this gives Z_{i,>w_i−1} − Z_{i,<w_i−1} = V(p^n), so Z_{i,>w_i−1} = V(p^n) there by the disjoint-support argument. For w_i = 0 the convention gives Z_i + V(p^n) = V(p^n) as well. So on this open every Z_{i,>w_i−1} equals V(p^n). This proves the inclusion S^tor_{F_p,w} ⊆ ∩_i (Z_{i,>w_i−1} ∩ Z^c_{i,>w_i}) stated on p. 43.
- The same computation shows two more things over 𝔖^tor_w. First, the closed set Z_{>w−1} is the whole special fibre there. Second, the ideal of Z_{>w−1} obtained from these divisors is (p^n) there, with n the level, and this ideal has the same radical as (p). This is all that the last step of the proof of Prop. 4.5.8 (p. 53) needs: "the inclusion (p) ⊆ 𝓘_{Z,>w−1} is an equality over 𝔖^tor_w". The reason is that the completion lim_m 𝒪/𝓘^m of §2.9.1 depends on 𝓘 only up to radical, since on a noetherian scheme two ideals with the same radical have cofinal powers.
- Lemma 4.1.18 gives the expected strata. For g = 1 it gives F_1 \ F_0 = Z_{1,>−1} ∩ Z^c_{1,>0} = S^tor_{F_p} \ D_2 = S^tor_{F_p,s}. In general its top piece is S^tor_{F_p} \ Z_g, which is S^tor_{F_p,w_max} by Cor. 4.1.14.

So the text uses a symbol it never defines. The paper's own formula allows only one value for it, and that is the value the stated equality F_{g(g+1)/2} = S^tor_{F_p} needs. With that value filled in, the statements above follow from the paper's own arguments with no new step. Nothing false is stated and no argument is missing; the definition simply omits the case j = −1. The filtration and its top step feed the spectral sequence of Theorem 2.9.7 in §4.5.6 (p. 52). Lemma 4.5.7 and Prop. 4.5.8 involve Z_{>w−1} for every w, including those with w_1 = 0. The omission does not affect any of these results, nor Theorem 4.5.2.

sourceIssues.printed: Proof of Cor. 4.2.10 (p. 45): "We may therefore apply proposition 4.2.8 and deduce that deg(p⋆2 H_{g+i,x}) ≥ deg(p⋆1 H_{g+i,x}). Moreover, in case t ∈ T^{++}(Q_p) and we have equality, the groups p⋆1 H_{g+i,x} and p⋆1 H_{g+i,x} are BT_n's and their degree is a multiple of n."  Proof of Prop. 4.2.15 (p. 46): "We therefore assume that for all g+1 ≤ k′ ≤ k, deg(p⋆2 H_{k′,x}) = deg(p⋆1 H_{k′,x}). We deduce from proposition 4.2.8 that p⋆1 H_{k′,x} is a BT_n. sourceIssues.correction: Prove only the degree statement; it is all that is needed. Corollary 4.2.10: write the transports of H = p1*H_{g+i,x} along the factorization of §4.2.5 as H = H^(0), H^(1), …, H^(k) = p2*H_{g+i,x}. By Prop. 4.2.8, deg H^(0) ≤ … ≤ deg H^(k). If the two ends have equal degree, every step is an equality. Let j0 be the first step with kernel rank p^s where s = 2g − i; such a step exists by Remark 4.2.6. There Prop. 4.2.8(2) applies to H^(j0) and shows that H^(j0) is a BT_n. Every later step has i + s ≤ 2g, so it is a generic isomorphism, and it has equal degrees, so it is an isomorphism ([Far10], sect. 3, cor. 3, as in the proof of Prop. 4.2.8). Hence p2*H_{g+i,x} ≅ H^(j0) is a BT_n. Its degree is then n times its dimension, so deg p1*H_{g+i,x} = deg p2*H_{g+i,x} ∈ nZ. The claim that p1*H_{g+i,x} is a BT_n should be dropped or given a separate proof. Proposition 4.2.15: apply this for every 1 ≤ k′ ≤ k. By additivity of the degree, deg p1*Gr_{g+k′,x} = deg p2*Gr_{g+k′,x} lies in nZ ∩ [0, n] = {0, n}. So on both sides Gr_{g+k′,x} is étale (degree 0) or multiplicative (degree n), and of the same type. The same passage also contains three small misprints: the second "p⋆1H_{g+i,x}" on p. 45 should be p⋆2H_{g+i,x}; "section 4.2.1" should be 4.2.5; and "for all g+1 ≤ k′ ≤ k, deg(p⋆2H_{k′,x}) = deg(p⋆1H_{k′,x})" should read "for all 1 ≤ k′ ≤ k, deg(p⋆2H_{g+k′,x}) = deg(p⋆1H_{g+k′,x})".
sourceIssues.reason:
In §4.2.5 the isogeny p⋆1 A → p⋆2 A is factored as G_0 → G_1 → … → G_k, with kernels L[p^{j+1}]/L[p^j] of rank p^{s_j}. Multiplication by p embeds L[p^{j+2}]/L[p^{j+1}] into L[p^{j+1}]/L[p^j], so s_j does not increase with j. For t ∈ T^{++} the s_j take every value 1, …, 2g−1 (Remark 4.2.6).

The second assertion of Prop. 4.2.8 is about one step: if i + s = h and deg H = deg H′, then the source H of that step is a BT_n. For the flag member of rank p^{in}, this is the step with s = 2g − i.

For i = 1 the proof works. Every step before that one has s = 2g, where H′ = φ(p^{-1}H) is identified with H through G/G[p] ≅ G, so the source really is p⋆1 H.

For g ≥ 2 and 2 ≤ i ≤ g it does not work. The step with s = 2g − i comes after a step with s = 2g − 1, and there i + s > 2g. At that earlier step case (2) applies: the transported group is φ(p^{-1}H ∩ p^{-n}L), and §4.2.5 identifies only its graded piece Gr′ with Gr, not the group with H. At such a step Prop. 4.2.8 gives only deg H′ ≥ deg H. So Prop. 4.2.8 makes an intermediate group a BT_n, not p⋆1 H_{g+i,x}. The step "We deduce from proposition 4.2.8 that p⋆1 H_{k′,x} is a BT_n" (k′ ≥ g+2) is asserted without proof, and Cor. 4.2.10 makes the same claim for p⋆1 H_{g+i,x}.

The conclusions survive. The BT_n statement does transfer forward to p⋆2 H, and the degree argument in the correction gives everything the two results use. A direct computation at ordinary points, where degrees are read off the multiplicative part of the Tate module, found no failure of the p⋆1 claim itself. It used g = 2, t with elementary divisors (1, p^{-1}, p^{-2}, p^{-3}), p = 2, 3 and n = 2, 3, over randomly sampled flags and multiplicative parts. The degrees never decreased along the chain. In every sampled case with equality for i = 2, p⋆1 H_{g+2} was a BT_n, and a degree-preserving case-(2) step never changed the type of the multiplicative part. So what is missing is a proof, not a true statement. Section 4.2.5 factors p1*A → p2*A as G_0 → G_1 → … → G_k. The step G_j → G_{j+1} has kernel L[p^{j+1}]/L[p^j], of rank p^s with s non-increasing in j. The flag is carried step by step: H' = φ(H) if i + s ≤ 2g, and H' = φ(p^{-1}H ∩ p^{-n}L) if i + s > 2g. Proposition 4.2.8 gives deg H' ≥ deg H at every step. So deg p1*H ≤ deg p2*H, and when the two are equal, every step is an equality.

The second part of Prop. 4.2.8 (L is a BT_1 and H is a BT_n) needs i + s = h = 2g. So it applies only at a step whose kernel has rank p^{2g−i}, and only to the group carried to that G_j, not to p1*H_{g+i,x}. For t ∈ T^{++}, every rank p, …, p^{2g−1} occurs (Remark 4.2.6). Hence for i ≥ 2 (so g ≥ 2), a step with 2g − i < s < 2g, for example s = 2g − 1, comes before it. At such a step, φ gives only one relation between H' and H. Multiplication by p maps H' onto H'' = H ∩ p^{-(n-1)}L. That map has kernel G[p]/L, of order p^{2g−s}, and H'' has order p^{ni − (2g−s)} < p^{ni}. The construction of §4.2.5 identifies only the graded pieces Gr_{g+i} and Gr'_{g+i}. Example: g = 2, i = 2, s = 3 with p = 2, n = 2. There H' has order 16, but its image H'' in H has order 8, checked by direct computation. So no statement about H' being a BT_n carries back to H.

Defence attempts:
- The case i = 1 is fine. Every earlier step then has s = 2g and L = G[p], and H' is H under G/G[p] ≅ G.
- The p2 side is fine as well. After the first step with i + s = 2g, every step is a generic isomorphism, and equal degrees make it an isomorphism. So p2*H_{g+i,x} is a BT_n.
- Running the isogeny backwards does not help. At a step with i + s > 2g, H' contains φ(G[p]), which is the kernel of the reverse isogeny. So the hypotheses of Prop. 4.2.8 fail for the reverse step.
- No other statement in the paper supplies the p1 claim. In the setting of Prop. 4.2.15 the claim does hold, but only a posteriori. Once every Gr_{g+k′} is known to be étale or multiplicative, H_{g+k′} is an extension of étale by multiplicative groups of this type, killed by p^n, hence a BT_n. That knowledge comes from the degree argument. In Cor. 4.2.10, where equality is assumed for a single i, the paper does not settle the claim.

So the step "p1*H is a BT_n, by Prop. 4.2.8" is asserted without proof. The consequences it is used for still hold by the degree argument given in the correction.

Later uses need only the degree and support conclusions:
- Prop. 4.2.15(3) in the proof of Prop. 4.3.13 (p. 48);
- Cor. 4.2.10 in the proof of Lemma 4.4.2 (p. 50) and for the action of t on the spectral sequence (p. 52);
- Prop. 4.2.15 in the proof of Prop. 6.1.9 (p. 60), in the form "deg H_{g+i}(p1(x)) ≤ deg H_{g+i}(p2(x)) and if equality holds they are multiples of n".

No stated result changes.

review.reason: Confirmed as a gap. Both proofs jump from equality of degrees to the assertion that $p_1^\star H$ is a $\mathrm{BT}_n$: Corollary 4.2.10 says `the groups … are $\mathrm{BT}_n$'s and their degree is a multiple of $n$', and Proposition 4.2.15 says `We deduce from proposition 4.2.8 that $p_1^\star H_{k',x}$ is a $\mathrm{BT}_n$'. Proposition 4.2.8 concludes that only at a step with $i+s=h$, and in the factorisation of §4.2.5 that step is one particular one; the earlier and later steps give nothing directly about $p_1^\star H$. The finding's repair keeps what is used — the degree lies in $n\Z$, hence in $\{0,n\}$ for a graded piece, hence the piece is étale or multiplicative — and it is obtained exactly as it sets out, by locating the step with $i+s=2g$ and noting that every later step is a generic isomorphism of equal degrees, hence an isomorphism. Its three accompanying misprints are E79, E80 and E83, and I confirm them there.

Every other term in the inequality is integral: p^{−1}H, X and G[p^{n+1}]. The inequality comes from the displayed generic sequence. Embed X in p^{−1}H × p^{−n}L by x ↦ (x, −x), and map the product to G[p^{n+1}] by (a, b) ↦ a + b. Over K this is the displayed sequence. So the quotient (p^{−1}H × p^{−n}L)/X maps to G[p^{n+1}] by a generic isomorphism, and its degree is at most deg G[p^{n+1}] ([Far10], sect. 3, cor. 3). Additivity of the degree then bounds the degree of the integral product p^{−1}H × p^{−n}L by deg X + deg G[p^{n+1}]. The next sentence computes deg p^{−n}L = deg L + deg G[p^n] from 0 → G[p^n] → p^{−n}L → L → 0. So the term meant is the integral group p^{−n}L.

(2) Multiplication by p on G is finite flat and surjective with kernel G[p]. So p^{−1}H → H is surjective with kernel G[p], not H[p]. Ranks confirm this. Étale locally H_K ≃ (Z/p^n)^i, so the generic fibre of H[p] has rank p^i. The kernel G[p] has rank p^h, where h is the height of G. These differ unless i = h. The formula in the same sentence, deg p^{−1}H = deg H + deg G[p], uses the correct kernel G[p].

With both corrections the argument closes. Since v(p) = 1, deg G[p^m] = m·dim G. Hence deg p^{−1}H + deg p^{−n}L − deg G[p^{n+1}] = (deg H + dim G) + (deg L + n·dim G) − (n+1)·dim G = deg H + deg L. So deg X ≥ deg H + deg L.

The final equality deg H′ = deg X − deg L holds exactly, not only as an inequality. L ⊂ G[p] ⊂ p^{−1}H and L ⊂ p^{−n}L, so L_K ⊂ X_K. Since L is finite flat, it is the closure of L_K, so L ⊂ X. The quotient X/L is finite flat. The kernel of X → G′ is X ∩ L = L, so the induced map X/L → G/L = G′ has trivial kernel. It lands in G′[p^{n+1}], so it is a monomorphism of finite V-schemes and hence a closed immersion. Its generic fibre is φ(p^{−1}H_K ∩ p^{−n}L_K). A closed subscheme that is flat over V is the schematic closure of its generic fibre, so H′ = X/L. Additivity of the degree then gives deg H′ = deg X − deg L. Therefore deg H′ ≥ deg H, as the paper states, and the printed "=" does not need to be weakened to "≥". Only in the case i + s ≤ h is the map H → H′ merely a generic isomorphism, and there the proof correctly uses [Far10], sect. 3, cor. 3.

In each slip the intended meaning is fixed by the degree formulas that follow it in the proof, deg p^{−1}H = deg H + deg G[p] and deg p^{−n}L = deg L + deg G[p^n]. These formulas use the kernel G[p] and the integral group p^{−n}L. Neither slip affects the statement of Proposition 4.2.8, or the results that use it: Corollary 4.2.10 and Propositions 4.2.14 and 4.2.15.

sourceIssues.locator: §4.2.9, Corollary 4.2.10 and its proof, p. 45
sourceIssues.printed:
Corollary 4.2.10. Over C_t^{tor}, we have: p⋆₂Z_i ≥ p⋆₁Z_i for all 1 ≤ i ≤ g. Moreover, if t ∈ T^{++}(Q_p), the support of p⋆₂Z_i − p⋆₁Z_i contains p⋆₁ ∩_{j=0}^{i} (Z_{i<j} ∪ Z_{i>j}) and p⋆₂ ∩_{j=0}^{i} (Z_{i<j} ∪ Z_{i>j}).
Proof. By normality, it suffices to check this in codimension 1. Let V = 𝒪_{C_t^{tor},x} where x is a generic point of the special fiber (indeed, both divisors are supported on the special fiber). The isogeny p⋆₁A → p⋆₂A can be written as a composition of isogenies whose kernel is a finite flat group scheme killed by p (see section 4.2.1). We may therefore apply proposition 4.2.8 and deduce that deg(p⋆₂H_{g+i,x}) ≥ deg(p⋆₁H_{g+i,x}). Moreover, in case t ∈ T^{++}(Q_p) and we have equality, the groups p⋆₁H_{g+i,x} and p⋆₁H_{g+i,x} are BT_n's and their degree is a multiple of n. □
sourceIssues.correction:
The reduction to codimension 1 proves the inequality p⋆_2 Z_i ≥ p⋆_1 Z_i. On a normal scheme, a rational function is regular once it is regular at every codimension-one point. At a generic point x of the special fibre, 𝒪_{C_t^{tor},x} is a DVR to which Proposition 4.2.8 applies. The reduction does not prove the 'Moreover'. That is a containment of closed sets whose left-hand side need not be a union of codimension-one pieces, so it has to be proved at every point.

Repair, with the same tools. Let y ∈ C_t^{tor} with p_1(y) ∈ ∩_{j=0}^{i}(Z_{i,<j} ∪ Z_{i,>j}). Take a complete rank-one valuation ring V (normalised by v(p) = 1) and a map Spec V → C_t^{tor} sending the closed point to y and the generic point into the generic fibre, as in the proofs of Propositions 4.2.14–4.2.15.

For each 0 ≤ j ≤ i, the point p_1(y) lies in exactly one of Z_{i,>j} and Z_{i,<j}, because their supports are disjoint (Proposition 4.1.13(1)). Hence v(p⋆_1 Z_i) − nj = v(p⋆_1 Z_{i,>j}) − v(p⋆_1 Z_{i,<j}) ≠ 0. Since deg p⋆_1 H_{g+i} = v(p⋆_1 Z_i) lies in [0, ni], this degree is not a multiple of n.

Factor the isogeny p⋆_1 A → p⋆_2 A into isogenies with kernel killed by p, as in §4.2.5. By Proposition 4.2.8, the degrees of the successive images of H_{g+i} do not decrease. Since t ∈ T^{++}, Remark 4.2.6 gives a step whose kernel has rank p^{2g−i}, that is, a step with i + s = 2g. If deg p⋆_2 H_{g+i} = deg p⋆_1 H_{g+i}, all the degrees in the chain are equal. Proposition 4.2.8 then makes the group at that step a BT_n, so its degree deg p⋆_1 H_{g+i} is a multiple of n, which is a contradiction.

So the local equation f of the Cartier divisor p⋆_2 Z_i − p⋆_1 Z_i at y satisfies v(f) = deg p⋆_2 H_{g+i} − deg p⋆_1 H_{g+i} > 0. Hence f is not a unit at y, and y lies in the support. The same argument applied to p_2(y) gives the second containment.

The same proof also has two misprints: 'see section 4.2.1' should read 'see section 4.2.5', where the factorisation is constructed; and the second 'p⋆_1 H_{g+i,x}' should read 'p⋆_2 H_{g+i,x}'.

The proof takes V = 𝒪_{C_t^{tor},x} with x a generic point of the special fibre and argues only there. For the inequality that is enough. The 'Moreover' is a containment of closed sets. The support of an effective Cartier divisor on a normal scheme has pure codimension 1, so a point y lies in supp(p⋆₂Z_i − p⋆₁Z_i) exactly when some codimension-one point specialising to y does. The printed argument shows only that generic points x of the special fibre with p₁(x) (or p₂(x)) in ∩_j(Z_{i,<j} ∪ Z_{i,>j}) lie in the support. It says nothing about points of the preimage that are not specialisations of such x.

Such points occur. For g = 1, n = 1, i = 1, Proposition 4.1.13 and its proof give Z_{1,>0} = D_2, Z_{1,<0} = 0, Z_{1,>1} = 0 and Z_{1,<1} = D_1, so the set is D_1 ∩ D_2. By Lemma 4.1.9 and Remark 4.1.4 this is the non-ordinary (supersingular) locus of the Iwahori-level model, a finite set of closed points of the two-dimensional S^{tor}; no blow-up is needed when g = 1. The fibres of p₁ and p₂ over these points are finite: over F̄_p a supersingular elliptic curve has a unique subgroup scheme of each p-power order, namely ker F^j. So the preimage in C_t^{tor} has codimension 2, and no generic point of the special fibre maps into it.

The statement is still true. It follows from the valuation argument above, which was checked step by step. For g = 1 it was also checked by direct computation with the Katz–Lubin degrees. For a supersingular E with Hasse valuation h < p/(p+1), the canonical subgroup has degree 1−h and the other subgroups have degree h/p. For h ≥ p/(p+1), every subgroup has degree 1/(p+1). The new subgroup E[p]/L has degree 1 − deg L, which is strictly larger than deg H in every case with 0 < deg H < 1.

Dependence: the 'Moreover' is used in the proof of Lemma 4.4.2 (p. 50). There it shows that, on C_{t,F_p,(w−1,w+1)}, the support of p⋆₂(Z_{i,>w_i}−Z_{i,<w_i}) − p⋆₁(Z_{i,>w_i}−Z_{i,<w_i}) contains p⋆₁Z_{i,>w_i} and p⋆₂Z_{i,<w_i}. For g = 1 and w the identity (w_1 = 1), S_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)} is D_2 and D_{w,+} = Z_{1,<1} = D_1. So the needed containment is at points lying over D_1 ∩ D_2, exactly the codimension-two case. Lemma 4.4.2 feeds Proposition 4.4.4 (strict dynamic compactifications), on which the complexes RΓ_w and Theorem 4.5.2 rest.

The citation of Corollary 4.2.10 on p. 52, for the action of t on the spectral sequence, needs only the inclusion p₁^{-1}(F_l) ⊆ p₂^{-1}(F_l) that Proposition 2.9.9 requires. That inclusion follows from Lemma 4.2.11, which uses only the first (inequality) part. So the gap does not touch the p. 52 citation.

The statement is true and the repair is short, so only the proof is affected. The proof works only at the local rings 𝒪_{C_t^{tor},x} of generic points x of the special fibre. That shows only this: a generic point x with p_1(x) (or p_2(x)) in T := ∩_{j=0}^{i}(Z_{i,<j} ∪ Z_{i,>j}) lies in the support, and so do its specialisations. A point of p_1^{-1}(T) that is not a specialisation of such an x is not covered.

Such points exist. Take g = 1, n = 1, i = 1. By Proposition 4.1.13 and its proof (the blow-up is trivial for g = 1), Z_{1,>0} = D_2, Z_{1,<0} = 0, Z_{1,<1} = D_1 and Z_{1,>1} = 0. The quasi-isogeny extends over C_t^{tor} (Lemma 4.2.2). Over F̄_p a supersingular elliptic curve has only finitely many finite subgroup schemes of each order (one of each p-power order). So p_1 and p_2 have finite fibres over these points. The preimage therefore has codimension 2, and no generic point of the special fibre maps into it. So the codimension-one argument proves nothing about this set.

A charitable reading does not save the argument. One could read ∩ and ∪ as gcd and lcm of divisors, which would make the codimension-one reduction valid. But then the claim is empty in this example (gcd(D_1, D_2) = 0), and the paper itself uses ∩ of the Z's as intersections of closed sets (§4.1.16, Lemma 4.1.18, §4.4.1). Lemma 4.4.2 needs the set-theoretic claim. Proposition 4.2.15 concerns Σ_{l≤k} Z_l, not a single Z_i, so it does not supply the step. Only its technique does: a valuation ring through an arbitrary point.

The statement itself is true, by the repair above. In the example it was also checked by direct computation with the Katz–Lubin degrees. Let h be the valuation of the Hasse invariant.
- If 0 < h < p/(p+1), the canonical subgroup has degree 1 − h and the other subgroups have degree h/p.
- If h ≥ p/(p+1), every subgroup of order p has degree 1/(p+1).
For H ∩ L = 0 the new level subgroup E[p]/L has degree 1 − deg L. In every supersingular case this is strictly larger than deg H: 1 − h/p > 1 − h, h > h/p, 1 − h/p > h/p, and p/(p+1) > 1/(p+1).

Lemma 4.4.2 feeds Proposition 4.4.4, the complexes RΓ_w, Proposition 4.4.5 and Theorem 4.5.2, and it is also invoked in §6 (pp. 58, 61).

The citation on p. 52 (the action of t on the Cousin spectral sequence) needs only p_1^{-1}(F_l) ⊆ p_2^{-1}(F_l) for Proposition 2.9.9. That follows from Lemma 4.2.11, which uses only the inequality, so that citation is unaffected.

sourceIssues.printed: We consider a valuation ring V of mixed characteristic and a map x : Spec V → C_t^{tor} mapping to this open subscheme. We therefore assume that for all g+1 ≤ k′ ≤ k, deg(p⋆_2 H_{k′,x}) = deg(p⋆_1 H_{k′,x}). We deduce from proposition 4.2.8 that p⋆_1 H_{k′,x} is a BT_n.
sourceIssues.correction: "for all g+1 ≤ k′ ≤ g+k, deg(p⋆_2 H_{k′,x}) = deg(p⋆_1 H_{k′,x})". Equivalently: deg(p⋆_2 H_{g+k′,x}) = deg(p⋆_1 H_{g+k′,x}) for 1 ≤ k′ ≤ k.
sourceIssues.reason:
The page image confirms the printed range "g+1 ≤ k′ ≤ k". Proposition 4.2.15 begins "Let t ∈ T^{++}(Q_p) and let 1 ≤ k ≤ g", so k ≤ g < g+1 and the printed range is empty. Read literally, the sentence assumes nothing.

The range the argument needs follows from the paper's conventions. On p. 41 the Iwahori flag is 0 ⊆ H_{g+1} ⊆ H_{g+2} ⊆ … ⊆ H_{2g} ⊆ H_1 ⊆ … ⊆ H_g = A[p^n], with Gr_i = H_i/H_{i−1}. Also on p. 41 (§4.1.8), D_i is the Fargues divisor of Gr_i, and Z_i = Σ_{j=1}^{i} D_{g+j}. Fargues' degree is additive in short exact sequences. Pulling back along x therefore gives deg(x^* Σ_{i=1}^{k′} D_{g+i}) = Σ_{i=1}^{k′} deg Gr_{g+i,x} = deg H_{g+k′,x}.

The same proof, a few lines earlier, restricts to the open subscheme where p⋆_2 Σ_{i=1}^{k′} D_{g+i} = p⋆_1 Σ_{i=1}^{k′} D_{g+i} for all k′ ≤ k. This follows because Σ_{i=1}^{k} Z_i = Σ_{i=1}^{k}(k+1−i)D_{g+i} and p⋆_2 Z_i ≥ p⋆_1 Z_i by Corollary 4.2.10. That condition is exactly deg p⋆_2 H_{g+k′,x} = deg p⋆_1 H_{g+k′,x} for 1 ≤ k′ ≤ k, i.e. for the groups H_{g+1}, …, H_{g+k}. So the upper bound should be g+k, not k.

The rest of the proof agrees. It then concludes that p⋆_1 Gr_{k′,x} ≃ p⋆_2 Gr_{k′,x} is multiplicative or étale "for all k′", which is point (1) for the graded pieces Gr_{g+1}, …, Gr_{g+k}. This only works if k′ runs over g+1, …, g+k.

review.reason: Confirmed as printed: `$V_\kappa$ … equipped with the action $m'.f(m)=f(m^{-1}m')$'. The defining equivariance $f(mb)=w_{0,M}\kappa(b^{-1})f(m)$ is right-translation by $B\cap M$, so the $M$-action has to be by left translation, $(m'.f)(m)=f(m'^{-1}m)$; the printed formula is not even a left action, since $m\mapsto f(m^{-1}m')$ sends $f$ to a function whose composition rule reverses. These are the only sums in the paper with upper limit d. Nothing called d is defined in §4. The only other d in the paper is in §3.4 (p. 40), where A_{g,d} is the moduli of abelian varieties with a polarization of degree d^2. - Lemma 4.1.9 (p. 41) identifies S^{tor}_{F_p,w} with S^{tor}_{F_p} \ Σ_{i=1}^g D_{w^{-1}(i)}, and the union over w ∈ ^MW of these loci with S^{tor}_{F_p} \ Σ_{i=1}^g D_i ∩ D_{2g+1−i}.

With the pairs (i, 2g+1−i), 1 ≤ i ≤ g, every one of D_1, …, D_{2g} is used. The intended loci are clear from the surrounding statements, so no result or argument changes; later uses of O(χ), ω^κ(χ) and the correspondence t (Propositions 4.3.17 and 4.3.18) are stated over the correct loci.

sourceIssues.printed: Lemma 4.3.6. The restriction of the map π : S^tor_{K^pK_{p,1,n},Z_p(ζ_{p^n})} → S^tor_{Z_p(ζ_{p^n})} to S^tor_{Z_p(ζ_{p^n})} \ Σ_{i=1}^g D_i ∩ D_{2g+1−i} is a finite étale map with Galois group T(Z/p^nZ). Moreover, S^tor_{K^pK_{p,1,n},Z_p(ζ_{p^n})} ×_{S^tor_{Z_p(ζ_{p^n})}} 𝔍𝔊^tor_{K_{p,P,w}K^p,Z_p(ζ_{p^n})} = 𝔍𝔊^tor_{K_{p,P,1,w}K^p,Z_p(ζ_{p^n})} where K_{p,P,1,w} = wK_{p,1,n}w^{−1} ∩ P(Q_p). [The proof ends:] We take an étale map U → S^tor_{Z_p(ζ_{p^n})} \ Σ_{i=1}^d D_{w^{−1}(i)} such that Gr_{w^{−1}(l)}|_U is isomorphic to Z/p^nZ and Gr_{w^{−1}(g+l)} is isomorphic to μ_{p^n}. It is clear that S^tor_{K^pK_{p,1,n},Q_p(ζ_{p^n})} ×_{S^tor_{Z_p(ζ_{p^n})}} U_{Q_p} = T(Z/p^nZ) × U_{Q_p}. We deduce that S^tor_{K^pK_{p,1,n},Z_p(ζ_{p^n})} ×_{S^tor_{Z_p(ζ_{p^n})}} U = T(Z/p^nZ) ×_{Spec Z_p(ζ_{p^n})} U. □
sourceIssues.correction: Complete the proof of the second assertion. Over the w-stratum, which is 𝔍𝔊_{K_{p,P,w}K^p} by Lemma 4.1.7, Gr_{w^{-1}(l)} is étale and Gr_{w^{-1}(g+l)} is multiplicative for 1 ≤ l ≤ g. Let E be the T(Z/p^nZ)-torsor of trivialisations Z/p^nZ ≅ Gr_{w^{-1}(l)} and μ_{p^n} ≅ Gr_{w^{-1}(g+l)}, compatible with the pairings Gr_i × Gr_{2g+1−i} → μ_{p^n} up to a common similitude. On generic fibres, E is identified with the K_{p,1,n}-level structure (trivialisations Z/p^nZ ≅ Gr_i) by composing with μ_{p^n} ≅ Z/p^nZ, ζ_{p^n} ↦ 1. E is finite étale over a normal flat base, so it is normal. It is therefore the normalisation, which proves the first assertion over this stratum. On the Igusa side, K_{p,P,1,w} is normal in K_{p,P,w} with quotient w T(Z/p^nZ) w^{-1}. So 𝔍𝔊_{K_{p,P,1,w}K^p} → 𝔍𝔊_{K_{p,P,w}K^p} is the torsor of the same trivialisations of the graded pieces of X_ord[p^n] = μ_{p^n}^g ⊕ (Z/p^nZ)^g, transported by j, and the similitude c mod p^n corresponds to the Weil-pairing root of unity. Comparing the two torsors gives the equality over Z_p(ζ_{p^n}), with the T(Z/p^nZ)-actions matched through conjugation by w. Equivalently: apply Lemma 3.4.24 with K_p = K_{p,1,n} and x = w. The fixed isomorphism Z_p(1) ≅ Z_p enters only modulo p^n, so the open immersion descends from Z_p^cycl to Z_p(ζ_{p^n}). It is onto the full preimage of the w-stratum because both sides are T(Z/p^nZ)-torsors over 𝔍𝔊_{K_{p,P,w}K^p}. The statement itself needs no change.
sourceIssues.reason:
The printed proof establishes only the first assertion. It extends the Gr_i to finite flat group schemes off Σ D_i ∩ D_{2g+1−i}, chooses an étale U on which Gr_{w^{-1}(l)} ≅ Z/p^nZ and Gr_{w^{-1}(g+l)} ≅ μ_{p^n}, and concludes that the cover is T(Z/p^nZ) × U over U. That is local triviality of the cover. The Igusa variety 𝔍𝔊_{K_{p,P,1,w}K^p} never appears in the proof, and nothing identifies the cover over the w-locus with it. No earlier result covers this level:
- Lemma 4.1.7 (p. 41) treats only level K_{p,n}. Its proof says it follows from Lemma 3.4.24 and notes that "here the embedding is defined over Z_p, not only Z_p^cycl".
- Lemma 3.4.24 (p. 40) is stated over Z_p^cycl for models normalised over Z_p^cycl, and Remark 3.4.22 says these are in general not base changes.
- Remark 3.4.18 (p. 39) warns: "In general this map doesn't descend to a map IG_{K^pK_{p,P}} → S_{K^pK_p} because the level structure on both sides are formulated in a different way. One uses isomorphisms with μ_{p^∞}^g ⊕ (Q_p/Z_p)^g on the left, and isomorphisms with (Q_p/Z_p)^{2g} on the right." It then points to Section 4.1, which handles only K_{p,n}.
Level K_{p,1,n} over Z_p(ζ_{p^n}) is exactly a case where this descent must be argued: one has to match trivialisations by Z/p^nZ on the Shimura side with trivialisations by μ_{p^n} on the Igusa side.

The assertion itself is correct. Both sides are finite étale T(Z/p^nZ)-covers of a smooth formal scheme, hence normal, and they agree on the generic fibre once ζ_{p^n} is fixed. Checked directly for g = 1. There K_{p,1,n} = {(a b; c d) : a ≡ d ≡ 1, c ≡ 0 mod p^n}, so a K_{p,1,n}-level structure is a point P of exact order p^n (generating the flag subgroup H) together with a generator of A[p^n]/H. On the locus where H is multiplicative (resp. étale), it becomes a trivialisation μ_{p^n} ≅ H and Z/p^n ≅ A[p^n]/H (resp. Z/p^n ≅ H and μ_{p^n} ≅ A[p^n]/H) once ζ_{p^n} is fixed. That is the Igusa level structure for K_{p,P,1,w}.

So the lemma is true, but its second half is asserted without any argument. It is not idle: the nebentypus comparison RΓ_w(K^pK_{w,p,P},κ,χ) = RΓ_w(K^p,κ,χ) stated on p. 56 compares the sheaf ω^κ(χ), defined through this normalised cover, with the Igusa tower. That comparison needs this identification. The lemma makes two claims. The printed proof establishes only the first. After extending the Gr_i as finite flat groups, it shows étale-locally on U that the normalisation is T(Z/p^nZ) ×_{Spec Z_p(ζ_{p^n})} U, and it ends there. The Igusa variety 𝔍𝔊_{K_{p,P,1,w}K^p} does not appear anywhere in the proof, so the second claim ("Moreover, ...") is asserted without argument. Showing that a torsor is trivial étale-locally does not identify it with a particular global torsor.

Defence attempts:
(a) Lemma 3.4.24 (p. 40) gives an open immersion 𝔍𝔊_{K^pK_{p,P}} ↪ S_{K^pK_p} for K_{p,P} = P(Q_p) ∩ xK_p x^{-1}, but only over Z_p^cycl, after fixing Z_p(1) = Z_p. Remarks 3.4.18 and 3.4.25 say explicitly that in general this map does not descend, because the Igusa level structure uses μ_{p^∞}^g ⊕ (Q_p/Z_p)^g and the Shimura level structure uses (Q_p/Z_p)^{2g}. Remark 1.4.6 (p. 5) says scalars must be extended to Q_p(ζ_{p^n}) for exactly this reason.
(b) Lemma 4.1.7 (p. 41) is the analogue at level K_{p,n}, where the authors do give a justification ("follows from lemma 3.4.24 ... here the embedding is defined over Z_p"). Nothing comparable is given at level K_{p,1,n}, where the descent to Z_p(ζ_{p^n}) is the only non-formal point.
So no nearby statement supplies the step as written.

The claim is nevertheless true, and the missing argument is routine (see the correction). Checked directly: K_{p,1,n} = ker(K_{p,n} → T(Z/p^nZ)), so K_{p,P,1,w} is normal in K_{p,P,w}. The quotient is all of T(Z/p^nZ), because T ⊂ M ⊂ P. The pairing matches Gr_{w^{-1}(l)} (étale) with Gr_{w^{-1}(2g+1−l)} (multiplicative), so the similitude data agree once ζ_{p^n} is fixed.

Later use: the lemma is not cited by number elsewhere. Its second assertion is what underlies the identification on p. 56, "RΓ_w(K^pK_{w,p,P}, κ, χ) = RΓ_w(K^p, κ, χ)" (itself stated without proof). That identification compares the Shimura-side complexes with Nebentypus (built from O(χ) on p. 47) with the Igusa-side complexes. Through it the lemma supports Theorem 1.4.3(4),(5) and Proposition 1.4.7 for levels with torus part T(1+p^nZ_p) and nontrivial χ. Since the assertion holds, those results are unaffected, and only the proof is incomplete.

sourceIssues.reason:
I rendered pp. 48–49 at high resolution, and the subscript clearly reads "2g+i−1". The printed index cannot be right, for three reasons.

1. **Undefined divisors.** In §4.1.8 (p. 41), D_i is defined only for 1 ≤ i ≤ 2g ("For all 1 ≤ i ≤ 2g, we let D_i be the effective Cartier divisor … associated to … Gr_i"). For g ≥ 2 and 2 ≤ i ≤ g, the index 2g+i−1 is between 2g+1 and 3g−1, so D_{2g+i−1} is not defined. For i = 1 the two indices agree (both equal 2g), so for g = 1 the printed formula happens to be correct.

2. **Inconsistency with the rest of the paper.** Everywhere else the relevant locus pairs D_i with D_{2g+1−i}:
   - §4.1.8 states D_i + D_{2g+1−i} = V(p^n).
   - Lemma 4.1.9 (p. 41) gives ∪_{w∈^MW} S^{tor}_{K^pK_{p,n},𝔽_p,w} = S^{tor}_{K^pK_{p,n},𝔽_p} ∖ ∑_{i=1}^g D_i∩D_{2g+1−i}.
   - Proposition 4.2.14 (pp. 45–46) describes ∪_w C^{tor}_{t,w} as the complement of ∑ p_1^⋆D_i∩p_2^⋆D_{2g+1−i}.
   - On the same page, the source of p_1 in the proof of Proposition 4.3.11 is printed correctly as C_t^{tor}∖∑ p_1^⋆D_i∩p_2^⋆D_{2g+1−i}, while its target, written in the same line, has 2g+i−1.

   The slip is the transposition "+i−1" for "+1−i".

3. **The corrected set is the right target.** By Lemma 4.2.13, C^{tor}_{t,w} lies in the complement of ∑_{i=1}^g p_1^⋆D_{w^{-1}(i)}. So p_1 maps C^{tor}_{t,w} into the complement of ∑_i D_{w^{-1}(i)}, which by Lemma 4.1.9 is the w-stratum of the special fibre. Hence p_1 maps the stated source into S^{tor}∖∑ D_i∩D_{2g+1−i}.

**Consequences.** None of the later arguments uses the misprinted index. Proposition 4.3.13, Proposition 4.3.18 and Lemma 4.3.14 use the correspondence over C_t^{tor}∖∑ p_1^⋆D_i∩p_2^⋆D_{2g+1−i}, which is printed correctly, and they use Proposition 4.2.15(3). No stated result changes.

A separate slip nearby: Lemma 4.3.16 (p. 49) has ∑_{i=1}^d where ∑_{i=1}^g is meant.

The published text could not be checked because it is paywalled.

sourceIssues.locator: §4.3: Remark 4.3.12, p. 48, and Proposition 4.3.17 (§4.3.15, Nebentypus), p. 49. The 2024 preprint has the same text, with both passages on its p. 47.
sourceIssues.printed:
Remark 4.3.12 (p. 48): "More generally, for all w′ ∈ ^MW, it restricts to p^{n_{w′}} t_{w′}, where n_{w′} = ⟨(w′)^{−1}(w_{0,M}(κ + ρ) + ρ, t⟩ − ⟨w^{−1}(w_{0,M}(κ + ρ) + ρ, t⟩. If t ∈ T^{++}(Q_p), n_{w′} > 0 for w′ ∉ C(κ)."
Proposition 4.3.17 (p. 49): "Over ℭ^{tor}_{t,w,Z_p(ζ_{p^n})}, we have a natural cohomological correspondence t_w : p_2^⋆ω^κ(χ) → p_1^!ω^κ(χ) which is ⟨−w^{−1}(w_{0,M}(κ + ρ) − ρ, t⟩t_w^{naive} where t_w^{naive} is the rational map obtained as the tensor product of …"
In all three pairings, the parenthesis opened after (w′)^{−1} or w^{−1} is never closed.
sourceIssues.correction:
In all three pairings, delete the unmatched "(" after (w′)^{−1} or w^{−1}. Equivalently, close it right after (κ + ρ).
- Remark 4.3.12 should read n_{w′} = ⟨(w′)^{−1}w_{0,M}(κ + ρ) + ρ, t⟩ − ⟨w^{−1}w_{0,M}(κ + ρ) + ρ, t⟩. Here the pairing is used additively, as the pairing with v(t). The ρ terms cancel, so n_{w′} = ⟨(w′)^{−1}w_{0,M}(κ + ρ) − w^{−1}w_{0,M}(κ + ρ), v(t)⟩.
- Proposition 4.3.17 should read ⟨−w^{−1}w_{0,M}(κ + ρ) − ρ, t⟩t_w^{naive}. This is the normalisation of Proposition 4.3.9, and the one used to define t right after Proposition 4.3.17.
sourceIssues.reason:
The parentheses are unbalanced as printed on pp. 48–49, and the 2024 preprint has the same text. Each pairing can be balanced in two ways: close the parenthesis after (κ + ρ), or after the trailing ±ρ. The paper's own normalisations settle which is meant. The second reading makes the Remark's positivity claim false and gives the wrong normalisation in Proposition 4.3.17.

Notation. Write λ = w_{0,M}(κ + ρ). Characters are written (k_1, …, k_g; k) as on p. 33. In these coordinates W acts by signed permutations of (k_1, …, k_g) and fixes k. The conventions on p. 34 are:
- X^⋆(T)^+ is the cone 0 ≥ k_1 ≥ ⋯ ≥ k_g.
- T^+(Q_p) is the set of t with v(t) dominant; T^{++}(Q_p) is the set with v(t) dominant regular. So ⟨α, v(t)⟩ ≥ 0 for every α ∈ Φ^+, strictly for t ∈ T^{++}(Q_p).
- ^MW is defined by the condition wX^⋆(T)^+ ⊆ X^⋆(T)^{+,M}.
C(κ) is defined on p. 48: w ∈ ^MW lies in C(κ) exactly when w^{−1}λ ∈ X^⋆(T)^−_Q. This is the antidominant cone −X^⋆(T)^+_Q; compare the definition of C(κ) on p. 3.

Remark 4.3.12. The intended formula follows from the normalisations:
- By Proposition 4.3.9, t_{w′} = ⟨−(w′)^{−1}λ − ρ, t⟩t_{w′}^{naive}.
- By Proposition 4.3.11, t = ⟨−w^{−1}λ − ρ, t⟩t^{naive} for any w ∈ C(κ).
- On ℭ^{tor}_{t,w′}, the rational map t^{naive} restricts to t_{w′}^{naive}.
So t restricts there to ⟨(w′)^{−1}λ − w^{−1}λ, t⟩t_{w′}. The p-adic valuation of this factor is ⟨(w′)^{−1}λ + ρ, v(t)⟩ − ⟨w^{−1}λ + ρ, v(t)⟩ = ⟨(w′)^{−1}λ − w^{−1}λ, v(t)⟩. That is the printed formula with ")" inserted after (κ + ρ).

Closing the parenthesis after "+ ρ" instead gives ⟨(w′)^{−1}(λ + ρ) − w^{−1}(λ + ρ), v(t)⟩. This adds the term ⟨(w′)^{−1}ρ − w^{−1}ρ, v(t)⟩, which is nonzero in general, and with it the Remark's positivity claim fails.

Example: GSp_4 (g = 2) with κ = (2, −6; k), where k is even (the parity condition of p. 33). Then ρ = (−1, −2; 0) and λ = (−8, 1; k). C(κ) = {w}, where w^{−1}λ = (1, 8; k). Take the w′ ∈ ^MW with (w′)^{−1}λ = (−1, 8; k); it does not lie in C(κ). Then:
- (w′)^{−1}λ − w^{−1}λ = (−2, 0; 0). This is the positive root t ↦ t_4/t_1. The intended value is n_{w′} = v(t_4) − v(t_1), which is > 0 for every t = diag(t_1, …, t_4) ∈ T^{++}(Q_p).
- (w′)^{−1}ρ − w^{−1}ρ = (4, 0; 0), which is −2 times that root. So the other reading gives v(t_1) − v(t_4), which is < 0 for every such t.
For instance, take (v(t_1), …, v(t_4)) = (−1, −2, 2, 1). This t lies in T^{++}(Q_p), since v(t_3) > v(t_4) > v(t_1) > v(t_2). The intended value is 2 and the other reading gives −2.

The positivity claim holds with the intended formula. For w ∈ C(κ), μ = w^{−1}λ is the unique antidominant element of Wλ. Hence σμ − μ is a non-negative rational combination of positive roots for every σ ∈ W, and it is nonzero when σμ ≠ μ. Take σ = (w′)^{−1}w. Then n_{w′} = ⟨σμ − μ, v(t)⟩ ≥ 0 for t ∈ T^+(Q_p). If w′ ∉ C(κ), then (w′)^{−1}λ is not antidominant, so it differs from μ, and n_{w′} > 0 for t ∈ T^{++}(Q_p).

Proposition 4.3.17. The other balancing, ⟨−w^{−1}(w_{0,M}(κ + ρ) − ρ), t⟩, gives the weight −w^{−1}λ + w^{−1}ρ instead of −w^{−1}λ − ρ. This is a different normalisation: the valuations differ by ⟨w^{−1}ρ + ρ, v(t)⟩. In the GSp_4 example above, with (v(t_1), …, v(t_4)) = (−1, −2, 2, 1), the intended factor has valuation 12 and the other reading gives 17. The paper excludes that reading in four ways:
- The proof says only "This is analogue to proposition 4.3.9", and Proposition 4.3.9 (p. 48) has ⟨−w^{−1}w_{0,M}(κ + ρ) − ρ, t⟩t_w^{naive}.
- The Nebentypus adds no normalisation, since p_2^⋆O(χ) → p_1^⋆O(χ) is an isomorphism (Lemma 4.3.16).
- The definition of t immediately after the proposition (p. 49) uses the balanced factor ⟨−w^{−1}w_{0,M}(κ + ρ) − ρ, t⟩. So does Proposition 6.2.6 (p. 61), the correspondence with Nebentypus used in §6.
- Proposition 4.4.5 (p. 51) and Corollary 4.5.5 (p. 52) give the algebraic part of the resulting action as ν = −w^{−1}w_{0,M}(κ + ρ) − ρ. Remark 4.4.6 (p. 51) says that T(Z_p) acts on the Nebentypus complexes by νχ.

Consequences. Neither Remark 4.3.12 nor Proposition 4.3.17 is cited by number later in the paper. Proposition 4.3.17 supplies the correspondence t_w behind the Nebentypus complexes RΓ_w(K^pK_{w,p,P}, κ, χ) of p. 51, and their weight νχ matches the intended normalisation. The Remark's positivity statement is the fact that makes the summands with w′ ∉ C(κ) vanish in the Cousin spectral sequence of Theorem 4.5.2, and it holds for the intended formula. The intended meaning is clear in all three places, so this is a typographical slip that changes no result or argument.

sourceIssues.correction: We let S^{tor}_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)} = ∩_i (Z_{i,<w_i+1} ∩ Z_{i,>w_i−1}). The second index should be w_i − 1, not w_i + 1. p. 50 reads: "We let S^{tor}_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)} = ∩_i Z_{i,<w_i+1} ∩ Z_{i,>w_i+1}." Notation:

- For 0 ≤ j ≤ i, Z_{i,>j} and Z_{i,<j} are the Cartier divisors of Proposition 4.1.13 (p. 42). They have disjoint supports, and Z_{i,>j} − Z_{i,<j} = Z_i − V(p^{nj}).
- (w_1, …, w_g) is the sequence attached to w at the end of §3.1. The identity has w_i = i.
- All intersections are taken of supports, inside the special fibre.

1. The printed set cannot be what is meant.
- Lemma 4.1.17(1) gives Z_{i,>w_i+1} ⊆ Z_{i,>w_i}.
- By p. 43, S_{F_p,w} ⊆ ∩_i (Z_{i,>w_i−1} ∩ Z^c_{i,>w_i}).
- So the printed set never meets the non-empty stratum S_{F_p,w}.
- In fact the printed set is empty for every w, because each factor Z_{i,<w_i+1} ∩ Z_{i,>w_i+1} is empty. If w_i < i, then j = w_i + 1 ≤ i, and Z_{i,<j} and Z_{i,>j} have disjoint supports. If w_i = i, the extension in the correction gives Z_{i,>i+1} = 0, since Z_i − V(p^{n(i+1)}) = −V(p^n) − (D_{g+1−i} + … + D_g) is anti-effective.

Lemma 4.4.2, however, says that this set compactifies S_{F_p,w}. By Definitions 2.1.9 and 2.1.26 (pp. 7 and 10), S_{F_p,w} must be open in it, with complement D_{w,+} ∪ D_{w,−}. So Lemma 4.4.2 is false as printed.

Example, g = 1. The proof of Proposition 4.1.13 gives Z_{1,>0} = D_2 and Z_{1,<1} = D_1, and §4.1.8 gives D_1 + D_2 = V(p^n). Hence Z_{1,>1} − Z_{1,<1} = −D_1, so Z_{1,>1} = 0. For w ≠ Id, §3.1 gives w_1 = 0. The printed set is then Z_{1,<1} ∩ Z_{1,>1} = ∅. But S_{F_p,w} = S_{F_p} ∖ D_2 (Lemma 4.1.9) is not empty: it is the locus where H_2 is étale.

2. The corrected set works.
- Let S̃_{=w} = ∩_i (Z^c_{i,>w_i} ∩ Z^c_{i,<w_i}) be the open set of Proposition 4.1.13(2). It is the complement of D_{w,+} ∪ D_{w,−}.
- On S̃_{=w}, Z_i = V(p^{nw_i}) (proof of Proposition 4.1.13). So there Z_{i,<w_i+1} − Z_{i,>w_i+1} = V(p^n) and Z_{i,>w_i−1} − Z_{i,<w_i−1} = V(p^n).
- In each pair the two divisors have disjoint supports. So Z_{i,<w_i+1} and Z_{i,>w_i−1} both contain the whole special fibre of S̃_{=w}, which is S_{F_p,w} (Corollary 4.1.14).
- Hence the corrected set is closed in the proper S^{tor}_{F_p} and contains S_{F_p,w}. Removing D_{w,+} ∪ D_{w,−} from it leaves exactly S_{F_p,w}.
- For g = 1 and w ≠ Id: the corrected set is Z_{1,<1} = D_1, D_{w,+} = Z_{1,<0} = ∅ and D_{w,−} = Z_{1,>0} = D_2. So D_1 ∖ D_2 = S_{F_p} ∖ D_2 = S_{F_p,w}.

The proof of Lemma 4.4.2 uses exactly these two bounds. Inside the set, it needs Z_{i,>w_i} and Z_{i,<w_i} to lie in ∩_{j=0}^{i}(Z_{i,<j} ∪ Z_{i,>j}). This follows from Lemma 4.1.17(1):
- for j ≤ w_i, Z_{i,>w_i} ⊆ Z_{i,>j};
- for j ≥ w_i + 1, the set lies in Z_{i,<w_i+1} ⊆ Z_{i,<j};
- the case of Z_{i,<w_i} is symmetric, using Z_{i,>w_i−1}.

3. The paper itself uses the corrected set.
- The notation "(w−1, w+1)" and Z_{>w−1} = ∩_i Z_{i,>w_i−1} (§4.1.16, p. 43) both point to the lower bound w_i − 1.
- On p. 58 (proof of Proposition 5.6.3, g = 2, w of length one) the paper writes "Concretely, S^{tor}_{(w−1,w+1)} = Z_{2,<2} ∩ Z_{1,>0}". Here (w_1, w_2) = (1, 1), which matches D_{w,+} = Z_{1,<1} and D_{w,−} = Z_{2,>1} on the same page.
- The corrected definition gives Z_{1,<2} ∩ Z_{1,>0} ∩ Z_{2,<2} ∩ Z_{2,>0}. Here Z_{1,<2} is the whole special fibre and Z_{1,>0} = Z_1 ⊆ Z_2 = Z_{2,>0}. So it equals Z_{2,<2} ∩ Z_{1,>0}, exactly as on p. 58. The printed definition would give ∅, since it includes Z_{2,<2} ∩ Z_{2,>2}.
- The proof of Corollary 4.4.3 uses (∪_{w'} C^{tor}_{t,F_p,w'}) ∩ p_i^{-1}S^{tor}_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)} = C^{tor}_{t,F_p,w}. Here p_i maps C^{tor}_{t,F_p,w'} into S_{F_p,w'}. On S̃_{=w'} we have Z_i = V(p^{nw'_i}). So there Z_{i,<w_i+1} − Z_{i,>w_i+1} = V(p^{n(w_i+1−w'_i)}) and Z_{i,>w_i−1} − Z_{i,<w_i−1} = V(p^{n(w'_i−w_i+1)}). Hence the first factor misses S_{F_p,w'} when w'_i > w_i, and the second misses it when w'_i < w_i. So S_{F_p,w'} meets the corrected set only if w'_i = w_i for all i. Since the sequence determines w (§3.1), this means w' = w, so the equality holds for the corrected set. With the printed set the left-hand side is empty.

So the slip is a single index, and the notation and p. 58 fix the intended set. With that set, Lemma 4.4.2 holds as intended. The later uses of the set and of the lemma (Corollary 4.4.3, Proposition 4.4.4 and Proposition 5.6.3) all refer to the corrected set.
