sourceIssues.printed: "Proof. We first work on C_t. By lemma 4.2.11, we see that p_2^⋆Z_{i,>w_i} ≥ p_1^⋆Z_{i,>w_i} and p_1^⋆Z_{i,<w_i} ≥ p_1^⋆Z_{i,<w_i}. By corollary 4.2.10, we find that the support of p_2^⋆(Z_{i,>w_i} − Z_{i,<w_i}) − p_1^⋆(Z_{i,>w_i} − Z_{i,<w_i}) contains p_1^⋆ ∩_{j=0}^{i} (Z_{i<j} ∪ Z_{i>j}) and p_2^⋆ ∩_{j=0}^{i} (Z_{i<j} ∪ Z_{i>j}). We now consider this property in C^{tor}_{t,F_p,(w−1,w+1)}. We deduce that the support of p_2^⋆(Z_{i,>w_i} − Z_{i,<w_i}) − p_1^⋆(Z_{i,>w_i} − Z_{i,<w_i}) contains p_1^⋆Z_{i,>w_i} and p_2^⋆Z_{i,<w_i}. In particular, the support of p_1^⋆Z_{i,<w_i} − p_2^⋆Z_{i,<w_i} + p_2^⋆Z_{i,>w_i} contains p_1^⋆Z_{i,>w_i}. Taking local generators f_+ and f_− of Z_{i,<w_i} and Z_{i,>w_i}, we deduce that there exists an identity: p_1^⋆f_+p_2^⋆f_− = hp_2^⋆f_+ where h vanishes (at least) on p_1^⋆Z_{i,<w_i}."
sourceIssues.correction:
There are two changes, both in the first paragraph of the proof.
(1) The first sentence should end "and p_1^⋆Z_{i,<w_i} ≥ p_2^⋆Z_{i,<w_i}". This is the second inequality of Lemma 4.2.11 with j = w_i.
(2) The "In particular" sentence should end "contains p_1^⋆Z_{i,<w_i}", not "contains p_1^⋆Z_{i,>w_i}".
The sentence just before the "In particular" sentence ("We deduce that the support of … contains p_1^⋆Z_{i,>w_i} and p_2^⋆Z_{i,<w_i}") is correct as printed and should stay. Replacing its pair by p_1^⋆Z_{i,<w_i} and p_2^⋆Z_{i,>w_i} would also give a true statement, but that change is not needed: the printed pair already implies both containments the argument uses (see the reason).
sourceIssues.reason:
The 2024 preprint has the same paragraph, with both slips, on its p. 48.

Notation. Fix i and write Z_> = Z_{i,>w_i} and Z_< = Z_{i,<w_i}. As in the proof, f_+ and f_− are local generators of Z_< and Z_>. Lemma 4.2.11 (p. 45) states p_1^⋆Z_{i,>j} ≤ p_2^⋆Z_{i,>j} and p_2^⋆Z_{i,<j} ≤ p_1^⋆Z_{i,<j}. Take j = w_i. Put E = p_2^⋆(Z_> − Z_<) − p_1^⋆(Z_> − Z_<). By Lemma 4.2.11, E = (p_2^⋆Z_> − p_1^⋆Z_>) + (p_1^⋆Z_< − p_2^⋆Z_<) is a sum of two effective divisors. The proof of Lemma 4.2.11 uses Z_> − Z_< = Z_i − V(p^{nw_i}) (Proposition 4.1.13(1)) and p_1^⋆V(p^{nw_i}) = p_2^⋆V(p^{nw_i}). So E = p_2^⋆Z_i − p_1^⋆Z_i, which is why Corollary 4.2.10 applies. Put F = p_1^⋆Z_< − p_2^⋆Z_< + p_2^⋆Z_>. Then F = E + p_1^⋆Z_>. Also, F is the divisor of the function h = p_1^⋆f_+ p_2^⋆f_− / p_2^⋆f_+ that the proof's identity p_1^⋆f_+ p_2^⋆f_− = h p_2^⋆f_+ defines.

(1) The first sentence. As printed, the second inequality compares a divisor with itself, so it says nothing. The inequality that Lemma 4.2.11 gives, and that the proof uses, is p_1^⋆Z_< ≥ p_2^⋆Z_<. This inequality makes F effective, so h is regular. Without it, h is not known to be regular. The end of the proof states the same inequality in strict form: "there exists 0 < s < 1 such that s p_1^⋆Z_{i,<w_i} ≥ p_2^⋆Z_{i,<w_i}". So the subscript 1 on the right-hand side is a slip for 2.

(2) The "In particular" sentence. The printed claim is that the support of F contains p_1^⋆Z_>. This is trivially true, because F = E + p_1^⋆Z_> with E effective. It is also not what the argument uses. The next sentence says that h vanishes on p_1^⋆Z_<, and this is the property the argument needs. Since Z_> and Z_< have disjoint supports, there are local functions a and b with af_+ + bf_− = 1. Together with p_1^⋆f_+ p_2^⋆f_− = h p_2^⋆f_+, this gives p_1^⋆f_+ = (p_1^⋆f_+ p_2^⋆a + h p_2^⋆b) p_2^⋆f_+. Because h vanishes on p_1^⋆Z_<, so does the factor p_1^⋆f_+ p_2^⋆a + h p_2^⋆b. That gives s p_1^⋆Z_< ≥ p_2^⋆Z_< for some 0 < s < 1. This is the condition of Definition 2.1.19(2) (p. 9) for Z_{i,<w_i}. Summing over i, as the proof does at the end, gives the same condition for D_{w,+}. So the sentence should end with p_1^⋆Z_<.

(3) The sentence just before the "In particular" sentence is true, and it is enough. It says that, on C^{tor}_{t,F_p,(w−1,w+1)}, the support of E contains p_1^⋆Z_> and p_2^⋆Z_<. We have p_1^⋆Z_< − p_2^⋆Z_< ≤ E. So the support of p_1^⋆Z_< = (p_1^⋆Z_< − p_2^⋆Z_<) + p_2^⋆Z_< lies in supp E ∪ supp p_2^⋆Z_<. By that sentence, this union is supp E, and supp E ⊆ supp F. This proves the corrected sentence (2). In the same way, p_2^⋆Z_> ≤ E + p_1^⋆Z_>, and supp E ⊇ p_1^⋆Z_>, so supp E ⊇ p_2^⋆Z_>. This is the input needed for "One argues similarly with Z_{i,>w_i}". There, h' = p_2^⋆f_− p_1^⋆f_+ / p_1^⋆f_− has divisor E + p_2^⋆Z_<, and h' must vanish on p_2^⋆Z_>.

That sentence follows from Corollary 4.2.10 as follows. The definition just before the lemma on p. 50 prints S^{tor}_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)} = ∩_i Z_{i,<w_i+1} ∩ Z_{i,>w_i+1}. As printed, this set is empty, because Z_{i,<j} and Z_{i,>j} have disjoint supports. So the second term should read Z_{i,>w_i−1}. By Lemma 4.1.17(1) (p. 43), Z_{i,>j} decreases and Z_{i,<j} increases as j grows. Hence Z_{i,>w_i} ∩ Z_{i,<w_i+1} ⊆ ∩_{j=0}^{i} (Z_{i,<j} ∪ Z_{i,>j}) and Z_{i,<w_i} ∩ Z_{i,>w_i−1} ⊆ ∩_{j=0}^{i} (Z_{i,<j} ∪ Z_{i,>j}). So on C^{tor}_{t,F_p,(w−1,w+1)}, the support of E contains p_1^⋆ and p_2^⋆ of both Z_{i,<w_i} and Z_{i,>w_i}. In particular it contains the printed pair, and also the alternative pair.

Why this is a misprint that affects nothing. Each slip is a wrong subscript, and the intended form is clear. Lemma 4.2.11 and the proof's own final inequality fix the first slip. The sentence that follows fixes the second. With these two corrections, the paragraph's argument goes through. The statement of Lemma 4.4.2 is unaffected, and so is Proposition 4.4.4 (p. 51), which rests on it.

By Proposition 4.2.15(3) with k = g = 1, supp(p_2^⋆Z_1 − p_1^⋆Z_1) = p_1^⋆D_1 ∩ p_2^⋆D_2. This contains those supersingular points, for i = 1 and for i = 2. For i = 1 it also contains a component on which p_1^⋆H is étale and p_2^⋆H is multiplicative. That component comes from triples (E, H, L) with E ordinary, H ≠ L both non-canonical, and φ(H) = E[p]/L the canonical subgroup of E/L. So the two supports differ, and both 'have the same support' and 'the complement … is C_{t,F_p,w}' are false. The claims also fail for general w, since the complement of p_j^⋆D_{w,+} includes points over D_{w,−} \ D_{w,+}.

The corollary still holds. To get f_i^n ∈ (g_i) one only needs V(g_i) ⊆ V(f_i), that is, the inclusion of supports. This inclusion holds:
- The divisors in Propositions 4.2.14(1) and 4.2.15(3) coincide after reindexing: both are Σ_j p_1^⋆D_j ∩ p_2^⋆D_{2g+1−j}. So the complement of supp(p_2^⋆ΣZ_i − p_1^⋆ΣZ_i) in C_{t,F_p} is ∪_{w′} C_{t,F_p,w′}.
- At a point y ∈ S_{F_p,w′}, locally Z_k − V(p^{nj}) = V(p^{n(w′_k−j)}). Hence y ∈ Z_{k,<w_k+1} if and only if w′_k ≤ w_k, and y ∈ Z_{k,>w_k−1} if and only if w′_k ≥ w_k. So S_{F_p,w′} meets S_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)} only when w′ = w.
- S_{F_p,w} is disjoint from D_{w,+}.
So the paper's own third sentence already gives the inclusion. The corrected statement about complements was checked the same way, using S_{F_p} \ (D_{w,+} ∪ D_{w,−}) = S_{F_p,w} (Proposition 4.1.13(2)).

The two slips:
- Since Y_i^n ↦ f_i^n, the relation Y_i^n = a_{i,j}Y_j^n gives f_i^n = a_{i,j}f_j^n. The printed relation g_j(h_j − b_{i,j}a_{i,j}^{-1}h_i) = 0 follows from exactly this, via h_ig_i = f_i^n = a_{i,j}h_jg_j and g_i = b_{i,j}g_j. With f_i = a_{i,j}f_j it would read a_{i,j}^{-n}.
- Gluing Y_i^{2n} ↦ g_ih_i^2X_i requires g_j(a_{i,j}^2h_j^2 − b_{i,j}^2h_i^2) = 0, which is the printed identity. The composite sends Y_i^{2n} to g_i^2h_i^2 = f_i^{2n}, which is the canonical map. So the source is O(−m(…)) with m = 2n, and the printed −2m is inconsistent, though harmless because m is only asserted to exist.
All of this was checked by direct computation.

Downstream. Corollary 4.4.3 is used only through its statement, in the proof of Proposition 4.5.8 (p. 53). That statement is correct, so only the proof is affected. Setting (pp. 41–42, 50):
- Z_k = Σ_{l≤k} D_{g+l}.
- Z_{k,>j} and Z_{k,<j} are effective, have disjoint support, and satisfy Z_{k,>j} − Z_{k,<j} = Z_k − V(p^{nj}) (Prop. 4.1.13).
- D_{w,+} = ∪_k Z_{k,<w_k} and D_{w,−} = ∪_k Z_{k,>w_k}.
- S_{F_p,w} is the special fibre of S̃_{=w_1,…,w_g} = ∩_k Z^c_{k,>w_k} ∩ Z^c_{k,<w_k} (Prop. 4.1.13(2), Cor. 4.1.14). So S_{F_p,w} is disjoint from D_{w,+} ∪ D_{w,−}.
- Write E = p_2^⋆ΣZ_k − p_1^⋆ΣZ_k, which is effective by Cor. 4.2.10.

Counterexample. Take g = 1 and w = s, the non-trivial element of ^MW = W. By §3.1, w_1 = 0, since 2 ∉ s^{-1}{2}.
- Z_{1,>0} − Z_{1,<0} = Z_1 = D_2 is effective and the two parts have disjoint support, so Z_{1,<0} = 0. Hence D_{w,+} = ∅ and p_1^⋆D_{w,+} + p_2^⋆D_{w,+} = 0 has empty support.
- S_{F_p,w} = S_{F_p} \ D_2 is the locus where H = Gr_2 is étale. With the corrected definition, S_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)} = Z_{1,<1} = D_1 (p. 42 gives Z_{1,<1} = D_g).

(a) Supersingular points. Cor. 4.2.10 with i = 1 shows that supp E contains p_1^{-1}(D_1 ∩ D_2) and p_2^{-1}(D_1 ∩ D_2). This set is non-empty: over a supersingular curve A[p^n] is connected, so neither Gr_1 nor Gr_2 is étale. It lies in p_i^{-1}(D_1) for i = 1 and for i = 2.

(b) Points over S_{F_p,w} itself. These do not depend on the misprinted definition, because Lemma 4.4.2 requires S_{F_p,w} ⊆ S_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)}.
- In the correspondence of §4.2.5, L has order p and meets H trivially, and H′ = φ(H).
- Take E ordinary with H non-canonical, and L ≠ H non-canonical.
- Then φ(H) = E[p]/L is the kernel of the dual isogeny, which is the multiplicative (canonical) subgroup of E/L.
- At the resulting point y, p_1(y) ∈ S_{F_p,w} while p_2^⋆D_2 > 0 = p_1^⋆D_2. So y ∈ supp E.
So over p_1^{-1}S_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)} the support of E is non-empty, while that of p_1^⋆D_{w,+} + p_2^⋆D_{w,+} is empty. This refutes the first sentence. The point y lies in the complement of p_1^⋆D_{w,+} + p_2^⋆D_{w,+}, but not in C_{t,F_p,w} = p_1^{-1}S_{F_p,w} ∩ p_2^{-1}S_{F_p,w}. This refutes the second sentence.

The failure is general. For i = 1, any y with p_1(y) ∈ S_{F_p,w} and p_2(y) ∈ S_{F_p,w′}, where w′ ≠ w, gives a counterexample:
- y ∈ supp E by Props. 4.2.14(1) and 4.2.15(3).
- p_2^⋆Z_k ≥ p_1^⋆Z_k forces w′_k ≥ w_k, so p_2(y) ∉ D_{w,+}.
Equality holds only in special cases, such as w = Id, where D_{w,−} = ∅.

Defence. No faithful reading saves the equality. The claim uses D_{w,+} alone, and the point in (b) does not involve D_{w,−}. What is true is this: since S_{F_p} \ (D_{w,+} ∪ D_{w,−}) = S_{F_p,w}, the complement of p_1^⋆(D_{w,+}+D_{w,−}) + p_2^⋆(D_{w,+}+D_{w,−}) inside p_i^{-1}S_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)} is C_{t,F_p,w}.

Why the corollary survives. The step "f_i^n = h_ig_i" needs only V(g_i) ⊆ V(f_i), that is, the inclusion of supports. The paper's third sentence supplies it:
- The complement of supp E in C_{t,F_p} is ∪_{w′}C_{t,F_p,w′}. After reindexing, the divisors in Props. 4.2.14(1) and 4.2.15(3) agree.
- At a point of S_{F_p,w′}, locally Z_k − V(p^{nj}) = V(p^{n(w′_k−j)}). So the point lies in Z_{k,<w_k+1} if and only if w′_k ≤ w_k, and in Z_{k,>w_k−1} if and only if w′_k ≥ w_k. Hence S_{F_p,w′} meets S_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)} only when w′ = w.
- This needs the reading Z_{k,>w_k−1}. With the printed Z_{i,>w_i+1}, S_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)} would miss S_{F_p,w}. The GSp_4 case on p. 58 uses Z_{1,>0} for (w_1,w_2) = (1,1), which agrees with the corrected reading.
- C_{t,F_p,w} avoids p_1^{-1}D_{w,+} ∪ p_2^{-1}D_{w,+}.
Then f_i^n ∈ (g_i), because O(U_i) is Noetherian. The squares h_i^2 make g_ih_i^2 independent of the choice of h_i, so the gluing goes through.

The two slips:
- Only f_i^n = a_{i,j}f_j^n yields the printed g_j(h_j − b_{i,j}a_{i,j}^{-1}h_i) = 0. The printed f_i = a_{i,j}f_j would give a_{i,j}^{-n} instead.

The identities were checked by direct computation.

sourceIssues.printed: Proof. We let S̄^{tor}_{w,Z/p^sZ} be the the closure of S^{tor}_{w,Z/p^sZ} in S^{tor}_{Z/p^sZ} and C̄^{tor}_{t,w,Z/p^sZ} be p_1^⋆ S̄^{tor}_{w,Z/p^sZ} ∩ p_2^⋆ S̄^{tor}_{w,Z/p^sZ}. sourceIssues.correction: For s = 1, cite Lemma 4.4.2 together with Lemma 2.1.29 (p. 10). S̄^tor_{w,F_p} is closed in S^tor_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)} and contains S^tor_{F_p,w} as an open subscheme. So the closed immersions S̄^tor_{w,F_p} ⊂ S^tor_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)} and C̄^tor_{t,w,F_p} ⊂ C^tor_{t,F_p,(w−1,w+1)} form a strict map of compactifications of (C^tor_{t,w,F_p}, S^tor_{w,F_p}). Lemma 2.1.29 then makes (C̄^tor_{t,w,F_p}, S̄^tor_{w,F_p}), with the pull-backs of D_{w,+} and D_{w,−}, a strict dynamic compactification. For general s, add one more step before citing Lemma 2.1.35. The reductions of C̄^tor_{t,w,Z/p^sZ} and S̄^tor_{w,Z/p^sZ} are the reductions of C̄^tor_{t,w,F_p} and S̄^tor_{w,F_p}. They inherit the strict dynamic structure because inclusions of powers of ideals are preserved under pull-back, which is the same argument as in the proof of Lemma 2.1.34. The proposed correction is right. Its minimal form is to add these two citations or remarks.
sourceIssues.reason:
The two compactifications differ. Lemma 4.4.2 (p. 50) is about X̄ = S^tor_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)} with C̄ = p_1^{-1}X̄ ∩ p_2^{-1}X̄. The proof of Proposition 4.4.4 uses a different space: the closure S̄^tor_{w,F_p} of S^tor_{F_p,w}, with C̄^tor_{t,w,F_p} = p_1^⋆S̄ ∩ p_2^⋆S̄.

A side remark on the definition on p. 50. It is printed as ∩_i Z_{i,<w_i+1} ∩ Z_{i,>w_i+1}, and must be read with Z_{i,>w_i−1}. The worked case on p. 58, "S^tor_{(w−1,w+1)} = Z_{2,<2} ∩ Z_{1,>0}", uses that reading, and Z_{i,>w_i+1} does not meet S^tor_{F_p,w}. With the intended definition, S^tor_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)} is closed and contains S^tor_{F_p,w}, so it contains the closure.

In general the closure is strictly smaller. Example: g = 1, n ≥ 2, where no blow-up is made and Z_{1,<1} = D_1. For w with w_1 = 0, S^tor_{F_p,w} is the ordinary part of the component on which H_2 is étale. S^tor_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)} = D_1 ∩ S_{F_p} contains every component on which A[p^n]/H_2 is not étale. That includes the components on whose ordinary locus H_2 is an extension of Z/p^b by μ_{p^a} with a, b ≥ 1 (compare Remark 4.1.4), and these are not in the closure. So the sentence "lemma 4.4.2 proves that this is a strict dynamical compactification" leaves out a step: restricting to a closed subscheme.

Defence: the missing step is routine, and the paper itself supplies it in Lemma 2.1.29 (p. 10; Lemma 2.1.28 in the preprint). The pair (C̄^tor_{t,w,F_p}, S̄^tor_{w,F_p}) is a compactification in the sense of Definition 2.1.9. Both spaces are proper, being closed in proper schemes. Also C̄ ×_{S̄×S̄} (S_w × S_w) = p_1^{-1}S^tor_{F_p,w} ∩ p_2^{-1}S^tor_{F_p,w} = C^tor_{t,w,F_p}. sourceIssues.correction:
The sentence "We deduce that T^+(Q_p) acts on RΓ_{D_+,D_−}(S̄^{tor}_{w,Z/p^sZ}, ω^κ)" needs two ingredients that the paper does not supply.
(a) For each t ∈ T^+(Q_p), the operator T_t is defined on that complex. This part is easy. By Lemma 4.2.11, the tuple (C̄_{t,w}, S̄_w, D_+, D_−) is a dynamic compactification for every t ∈ T^+(Q_p), not only for t ∈ T^{++}(Q_p). Proposition 2.2.10 applied to t_w of Proposition 4.3.9 then gives T_t.
(b) A composition law: T_t T_{t′} ≃ T_{tt′} ≃ T_{t′} T_t for all t, t′ ∈ T^+(Q_p). This is the missing step. Proving it requires:
- an identification C_{t,w} ×_{S_w} C_{t′,w} ≅ C_{tt′,w}, which is the integral, Igusa-level analogue, via Proposition 4.2.4, of the double-coset identity [K t K][K t′ K] = [K tt′ K] from [Cas], lem. 4.1.5, cited on p. 43;
- multiplicativity of the normalizing factors ⟨−w^{-1}w_{0,M}(κ+ρ)−ρ, t⟩;
- a proper-base-change argument, as in the proof of Proposition 2.8.2, showing that composing the operators on cohomology with partial support gives the operator of the composite correspondence.
Once (b) is available, the deduction is indeed easy.
sourceIssues.reason:
Checked against the paper's constructions. The operators on RΓ_{D_+,D_−} come from these results:
- Proposition 4.3.9 (p. 48): for each t separately, the normalized cohomological correspondence t_w = ⟨−w^{-1}w_{0,M}(κ+ρ)−ρ, t⟩ t_w^{naive} on C^{tor}_{t,w}.
- §§2.2–2.3 (Proposition 2.3.13, p. 17): its extension to a dynamic compactification.
- Proposition 4.4.4: the compactification p_1^⋆S̄ ∩ p_2^⋆S̄.

The only justification offered for "T^+(Q_p) acts" is that the compactification S̄^{tor}_{w,Z/p^sZ} does not depend on t. That gives one endomorphism T_x for each x on a common complex. It says nothing about how these endomorphisms relate to one another.

The relations t^n = t′u′ and (t′)^n = tu hold in the group. They carry information about the operators only through T_{t^n} = T_t^n = T_{t′}T_{u′} (and symmetrically) with commuting operators. Without this, the t- and t′-ordinary projectors on RΓ_{D_+,D_−} are unrelated.

The paper proves no such composition law in this setting:
- §2.8 (Proposition 2.8.2, pp. 25–27) handles only the iterates C^{(n)} of a single correspondence. It does not compare C_t ×_S C_{t′} (or C_t^{(n)}) with C_{tt′} (or C_{t^n}), and it says nothing about the normalizations.
- Casselman's lemma, cited on p. 48, gives the algebra map Z[T^+(Q_p)/T(Z_p)] → C_c(K_{p,n}\G(Q_p)/K_{p,n}, Z). That is multiplicativity in the abstract Hecke algebra, i.e. on cohomology of the generic fibre. It does not cover the mod p^s cohomology with partial support over the strata S^{tor}_w, defined via integral models and integrally normalized maps.

That §2.8 is needed even for iterates of one correspondence shows that such compatibilities are not formal in this framework. The step is therefore asserted without adequate proof.

The result itself is not in doubt, and the gap looks fillable:
- For t, t′ ∈ T^+ the double cosets multiply at level K_{p,n}, so the composite correspondence is C_{tt′} on the generic fibre.
- The normalizing factors are multiplicative in t.
- Maps p_2^⋆ω^κ → p_1^!ω^κ on the normal Z_p-flat integral models are determined by their generic fibre.
- The remaining bookkeeping is of the kind done in Proposition 2.8.2.

As printed, however, "it is easy to deduce" rests on the unproved sentence "We deduce that T^+(Q_p) acts". The multiplicativity is also needed for the asserted T(Q_p)-action, since T(Q_p) is generated by T^{++}(Q_p) acting invertibly on the ordinary part. 1. What the paper actually shows. Independence of the compactification from t gives, for each t, an endomorphism T_t of the one complex M = RΓ_{D_+,D_−}(S̄^{tor}_{w,Z/p^sZ}, ω^κ). It does not give a monoid action, meaning T_{tt′} = T_t T_{t′} with the operators commuting.

2. Why the argument needs such an action. The relation t^n = t′u′ is useful only if T_t^n = T_{t′}T_{u′} and T_t commutes with T_{t′}.

3. Nothing nearby supplies the composition law. I searched the paper for it and found the following.
- Section 2 constructs the operator of a single dynamic correspondence (Proposition 2.2.10) and checks that it does not depend on the compactification (Proposition 2.2.11).
- Section 2.8 treats only the iterates of one fixed correspondence C, not products C_t ∘ C_{t′} of different Hecke correspondences.
- Section 4.2 cites [Cas] only for the abstract Hecke algebra map Z[T^+(Q_p)/T(Z_p)] → C_c(K_{p,n}\G(Q_p)/K_{p,n}, Z). That map does not transfer to the integral, normalized cohomological correspondences restricted to S_w with partial supports. Transferring it requires checking that the fibre product of the finite flat formal schemes C_{t,w} and C_{t′,w} over S_w matches C_{tt′,w} integrally, and that the fundamental classes and normalizations compose.
- Proposition 4.2.4 and Lemma 4.3.8 contain the right ingredients: the Igusa description, and trace factors additive on T^+ because the sign of α(w(v(t))) is constant there. They are never assembled into a composition statement.
The step is standard and very likely true, so the defence fails only as a matter of written proof.

4. The final deduction does go through once (b) holds, even with commutativity only up to homotopy. By Proposition 2.5.4, H^i(M^{t-ord}) is a finite Z/p^s-module on which T_t is invertible. Then T_{t′} is invertible on it, because T_t^n = T_{t′}T_{u′} with commuting operators. The t′-non-ordinary factor is a Z/p^s[[T]]-module, so T_{t′} acts nilpotently on any finite-length piece of it. Hence the projection of H^i(M^{t-ord}) to the t′-non-ordinary factor vanishes. Symmetrically, the composite of inclusion and projection between the two direct factors is a quasi-isomorphism.

5. The proposed correction is right and essentially minimal. I add only (a), which follows from Lemma 4.2.11, and the note that (b) is exactly what the sentence "T^+(Q_p) acts" presupposes.

6. What depends on this passage.
- The T(Q_p)-action asserted in the statement of Proposition 4.4.5. Its only justification is this sentence, together with inverting T^{++}(Q_p) on ordinary parts, which also needs commutativity.
- Corollary 4.5.5 (an isomorphism of T(Q_p)-modules).
- The definition of RΓ_w(K^pK_{p,P}) on p. 54 ("the argument of proposition 4.4.5 shows that the ordinary part does not depend on the choice of t") and Proposition 5.2.3 (these complexes lie in D(Z_p[T(Q_p)])).
- Through these, the T(Q_p)-equivariance claims in Theorem 1.4.3 and the adjoint statement in Theorem 5.5.1.
No stated result is shown to be false, so the gap affects the proof only.

sourceIssues.correction:
Replace the parenthetical with the following argument, applied to each w with ℓ(w) = p. Also, "K_p" printed as a subscript should be the superscript K^p. Below, s indexes the truncations mod p^s (this index is written n in Proposition 4.5.8), and n is the level of K_{p,n}, as in Proposition 4.1.13.

(a) Comparison. By Corollary 2.3.11, the right-hand side of Proposition 4.5.8 is lim_s RΓ_{D_{−,w},D_{+,w}}(S^tor_{Z/p^s}, ω̃^κ/p^s). Modulo p^s, the complement of D_{+,w} ∪ D_{−,w} in S^tor is the stratum 𝔖^tor_w (Proposition 4.1.13(2), Corollary 4.1.14). By Lemma 4.2.11, (C_t^tor, S^tor, p_1, p_2, D_{+,w}, D_{−,w}) mod p^s is a dynamic compactification of (ℭ^tor_{t,w}, 𝔖^tor_w) mod p^s, though not necessarily a strict one. The strict dynamic compactification of Proposition 4.4.4 is made of the closures of the stratum, and it maps to this one by a strict map made of closed immersions. So Proposition 2.2.11 (through Lemma 2.2.8) identifies the two cohomologies with partial support, compatibly with the Hecke operators. Theorem 2.5.1(1) then lets one pass between the two orders of support. On 𝔖^tor_w the divisors Z_{i,>w_i} and Z_{i,<w_i} are empty, so Proposition 4.1.13(1) gives Z_i = V(p^{n w_i}) there. So ω̃^κ = p^{n k' Σ_i w_i} ω^κ on 𝔖^tor_w, and this is the same scalar on both sides of the correspondence. Under the resulting identification of ω̃^κ with ω^κ, t̃ therefore corresponds over ℭ^tor_{t,w} to the restriction of t. By Remark 4.3.12 (with w' = w), this restriction is p^{n_w} t_w, and n_w = 0 for w ∈ C(κ).

(b) Case w ∈ C(κ). The operator is t_w. With Lemma 2.4.4(1), the ordinary part of the right-hand side of Proposition 4.5.8 is RΓ_w(K^pK_{w,p,P}, κ) as defined in §4.4 (p. 51). By that proposition, it is also the ordinary part of the w-summand of the E_1 term.

(c) Case w ∉ C(κ). The ordinary part of the w-summand is 0. Since t ∈ T^{++}(Q_p), Remark 4.3.12 gives n_w > 0. Modulo p^s the operator is therefore p^{n_w} t_w, and its s-th power p^{s n_w} t_w^s vanishes. So each level is a module over the polynomial ring Z/p^s[t_w], and in that ring the image p^{n_w} t_w of t is nilpotent. Inverting it gives the zero ring, so the level has zero ordinary part by Definition 2.4.2 (as in case (1) of the proof of Lemma 2.4.3). The limit then has zero ordinary part by Lemma 2.4.4(1). The relation t = p^{n_w} t_w holds only over ℭ^tor_{t,w}, where t_w is defined. So the vanishing has to be read off on the right-hand side of Proposition 4.5.8 and carried over to the E_1-summand by that proposition. This works because Proposition 4.5.8 holds for every w. Its proof (pp. 52–53) uses only Lemma 4.3.14, Corollary 4.4.3, Lemma 2.4.4 and the equality (p) = 𝓘_{Z,>w−1} over 𝔖^tor_w, and it never uses w ∈ C(κ).

Case (c) is what cuts the E_1 term down from all w with ℓ(w) = p to w ∈ C(κ), as Theorem 4.5.2 states. The same argument applies to the cuspidal and Nebentypus variants.

sourceIssues.printed: Corollary 4.5.4. Let κ ∈ X⋆(T)⁺ be such that C(κ) = {w}. There is a canonical isomorphism: RΓ_w(K^p K_{w,p,P}, κ) ≃ RΓ(S^tor, ω̃^κ)^{t−ord} ... Corollary 4.5.5. Let κ ∈ X⋆(T)⁺ be such that C(κ) = {w}. Let ν = −w⁻¹w_{0,M}(κ + ρ) − ρ. There is a canonical isomorphism: RΓ_w(K^p K_{w,p,P}, κ) ⊗ Q_p(−ν) ≃ RΓ(S^tor_{Q_p}, ω^κ)^{ord} ...
sourceIssues.correction: In both corollaries, read "Let κ ∈ X⋆(T)^{M,+} be such that C(κ) = {w}". This is the M-dominant cone k_1 ≥ ··· ≥ k_g. It is written X⋆(T)^{+,M} on p. 34, and κ ranges over it from p. 48 onward ("Let κ ∈ X⋆(T)^{M,+}", just before Proposition 4.3.9).
sourceIssues.reason:
The page image confirms the printed hypothesis: the superscript in both corollaries is a bare "+", with no M.

Conventions (p. 34). X⋆(T)⁺ is the dominant cone "0 ≥ k_1 ≥ ··· ≥ k_g". X⋆(T)^{+,M} is the M-dominant cone "k_1 ≥ ··· ≥ k_g". Also ρ = ½Σ_{α∈Φ⁺} α. P is the stabiliser of ⟨e_{g+1},…,e_{2g}⟩, so the positive roots are e_i − e_j (i < j), −(e_i + e_j) and −2e_i. Summing them gives ρ = (−1, −2, …, −g), which is dominant and regular, as it should be.

On p. 48, C(κ) = {w ∈ ^M W : w⁻¹w_{0,M}(κ+ρ) ∈ X⋆(T)⁻_Q}; the introduction (p. 3) gives the equivalent form −w⁻¹w_{0,M}(κ+ρ) ∈ X⋆(T)⁺.

Take κ ∈ X⋆(T)⁺. Then κ + ρ = (k_1 − 1, …, k_g − g) is strictly decreasing and negative, so it is dominant regular. Since W acts simply transitively on regular chambers, w⁻¹w_{0,M}(κ+ρ) is antidominant only when w⁻¹w_{0,M} = w_0, that is, when w = w_{0,M}w_0. This element lies in ^M W: it is its longest element, of length g² − g(g−1)/2 = g(g+1)/2. So for every κ ∈ X⋆(T)⁺ we have C(κ) = {w_{0,M}w_0} automatically. As printed, the hypothesis "C(κ) = {w}" is therefore empty, and the corollaries only cover the top-degree theory w = w_{0,M}w_0.

Example, g = 1 (checked by direct computation). Here ρ = −1 and ^M W = {1, s}. Every κ ∈ X⋆(T)⁺ (k_1 ≤ 0) has C(κ) = {s}. The weights with C(κ) = {1} are exactly k_1 ≥ 2, which are M-dominant but not in X⋆(T)⁺. So the printed statement does not even contain the degree-0 (classical Hida) control theorem.

The intended hypothesis is clear from the rest of the paper:
- On p. 48, κ is fixed in X⋆(T)^{M,+} before Proposition 4.3.9. The ω̃^κ of Theorem 4.5.2 is defined in that setting.
- Theorem 4.5.2 is the spectral sequence ⊕_{w∈C(κ), ℓ(w)=p} H^{p+q}_w ⇒ H^{p+q}(S^tor, ω̃^κ)^{t-ord}. When C(κ) = {w}, it has a single column and degenerates, for any κ ∈ X⋆(T)^{M,+}. So the proof of the corollaries needs no G-dominance.
- Theorem 1.4.3(4) on p. 5 is labelled "(Classicality in regular weight 4.5.5)". It takes ν ∈ X⋆(T)⁺ and κ = −w_{0,M}w(ν+ρ) − ρ ∈ X⋆(T)^{M_µ,+} for arbitrary w ∈ ^M W. One checks −w⁻¹w_{0,M}(κ+ρ) = ν + ρ, which is dominant regular, so C(κ) = {w}.
- Remark 1.4.5 says point 4) is the case #C(κ) = 1 of point 5), where 5) is stated for κ ∈ X⋆(T)^{M,+}.

The corrected statement follows from Theorem 4.5.2 by the same one-line degeneration argument.

Consequences. As printed, the two corollaries are true but much weaker than intended. They do not support the uses made of them:
- Theorem 1.4.3(4), classicality for every w.
- The interpolation Proposition 1.4.7 (p. 5), which combines the specialisation formula of §5.4 (p. 57) with κ = −w_{0,M}w(ν_alg+ρ) − ρ for arbitrary w.
With the M-dominant hypothesis these results are fine.

review.reason: Confirmed as printed: Corollaries 4.5.4 and 4.5.5 both open `Let $\kappa\in X^\star(T)^+$ be such that $C(\kappa)=\{w\}$', with the plain dominant cone. By p. 34 that cone is $0\geq k_1\geq\cdots\geq k_g$, whereas the weights carrying the automorphic sheaves $\omega^\kappa$ from §4.3 onward are the $M$-dominant ones, $k_1\geq\cdots\geq k_g$, which is where $C(\kappa)$ and Theorem 4.5.2 place $\kappa$; Theorem 1.4.3(4)–(5) and Proposition 1.4.7 also state the corresponding results for $X^\star(T)^{M,+}$. Read with the printed cone the corollaries would exclude most of the weights they are meant to cover, so the omission of the $M$ matters.

sourceIssues.locator: §4.5.6 (proof of Theorem 4.5.2), p. 52: the first display after Lemma 4.5.7. It cites Theorem 2.9.7 (p. 28), whose setup is in §2.9.5 (p. 28). The January 2024 preprint has the same text: §4.5.6 ("proof of the main result") is on p. 50, §2.9.5 on p. 26 and Theorem 2.9.7 on p. 27.
sourceIssues.printed:
p. 52, §4.5.6: "We recall the filtration by closed subsets defined in section 4.1.16: F_{−1} = ∅ ⊆ F_0 ⊆ ··· ⊆ F_{g(g+1)/2} = S^tor_{F_p}, where F_i = ∪_{w,ℓ(w)≤i} Z_{>w−1}." ... "By theorem 2.9.7, we have a spectral sequence: H_c^{p+q}(F̂_p \ F̂_{p−1}, ω̃^κ) ⇒ H^{p+q}(S^tor, ω̃^κ)."
p. 28, §2.9.5: "We now let X be a scheme and we let Z_{−1} = ∅ ⊆ Z_0 ⊆ Z_1 ⊆ Z_2 ⊆ ··· ⊆ X = Z_d be a filtration by closed subschemes." Theorem 2.9.7: "Assume that F ∈ D^−(O_{X,■}). We have a spectral sequence: E_1^{p,q} = H_c^{p+q}(Ẑ_p \ Ẑ_{p−1}, F) ⇒ H^{p+q}(X, F)."
sourceIssues.correction:
Here the X of Theorem 2.9.7 is the Z_p-scheme S^tor = S̃^tor_{K^pK_{p,n}} (p. 42). The filtration ends at F_{g(g+1)/2} = S^tor_{F_p}, which is not X, so Theorem 2.9.7 does not apply as stated. The missing step is to append F_{g(g+1)/2+1} = S^tor. The extended filtration satisfies the setup of §2.9.5. It also satisfies the hypothesis of Proposition 2.9.9, because for the added step the condition p_1^*(S^tor) ⊆ p_2^*(S^tor) holds trivially. Theorem 2.9.7 then gives a spectral sequence, equivariant for t, that converges to H^*(S^tor, ω̃^κ).

Its E_1 page has one extra column: RΓ_c(S^tor_{Q_p}, ω̃^κ) = RΓ(S^tor, j_! j^* ω̃^κ), where j : S^tor_{Q_p} → S^tor. Apply Corollary 2.3.4 with X̄ = S^tor. Let the special fibre S^tor_{F_p} = V(p) play the role of the divisor of §2.3.1, and let multiplication by p : O_{S^tor} → O_{S^tor} play the role of O(−D) → O. Corollary 2.3.4 then gives this column as the derived limit of the tower ··· → RΓ(S^tor, ω̃^κ) → RΓ(S^tor, ω̃^κ), in which every map is multiplication by p. S^tor is proper over Z_p and ω̃^κ is coherent, so RΓ(S^tor, ω̃^κ) is a perfect complex of Z_p-modules, and this derived limit is 0. The extra column vanishes, and the spectral sequence is the one printed.

Equivalently, the printed E_1 terms give a spectral sequence that converges to H^*(F̂_{g(g+1)/2}, ω̃^κ) (first triangle of Lemma 2.9.6, for l = 0, …, g(g+1)/2). By Lemma 2.9.3, with the special fibre defined by the ideal (p), RΓ(F̂_{g(g+1)/2}, ω̃^κ) = lim_n RΓ(S^tor, ω̃^κ/p^n). By the same perfectness this equals RΓ(S^tor, ω̃^κ). The same argument applies to ω̃^κ(−D) on S^tor, and to ω̃^κ(χ) and ω̃^κ(χ)(−D) on S^tor_{Z_p(ζ_{p^n})}, which is proper over Z_p(ζ_{p^n}). Here D is the boundary.
sourceIssues.reason:
The proof of Theorem 2.9.7 needs Z_d = X. With U_l = X \ Z_l, it filters RΓ(X, F) = RΓ_c(U_{−1}, F) by the subcomplexes RΓ_c(U_l, F) for l = −1, …, d−1. The second triangle of Lemma 2.9.6 identifies the graded pieces with the RΓ_c(Ẑ_l \ Ẑ_{l−1}, F). The last piece, RΓ_c(U_{d−1}, F), equals RΓ_c(Ẑ_d \ Ẑ_{d−1}, F) only because U_d = ∅.

In §4.5.6, X = S^tor is a scheme over Z_p, and the filtration of §4.1.16 stops at the special fibre, so U_{g(g+1)/2} = S^tor_{Q_p} is not empty. So the printed E_1 terms are the graded pieces of RΓ(F̂_{g(g+1)/2}, ω̃^κ) = lim_n RΓ(S^tor, ω̃^κ/p^n). This is the cohomology of the p-adic completion. It is not, a priori, RΓ(S^tor, ω̃^κ).

The two can differ, and here it is properness that makes them agree. Take X = A^1_{Z_p}, F = O and the filtration ∅ ⊆ X_{F_p}. The same construction gives H^0 = lim_n (Z/p^n)[T] = Z_p⟨T⟩, but H^0(X, O) = Z_p[T].

In the paper's setting the two do agree. S^tor is proper over Z_p: it is a blow-up (Proposition 4.1.13) of the proper integral toroidal model of §4.1.1. The sheaf ω̃^κ = ω^κ(−k′ Σ_{i=1}^g Z_i) (p. 49) is coherent. So RΓ(S^tor, ω̃^κ) is a perfect complex of Z_p-modules. Now let M be a finitely generated Z_p-module and consider the tower M ← M ← ⋯ in which each map is multiplication by p. Every term of a compatible sequence lies in ∩_n p^n M = 0, so the limit of the tower is 0. Its lim^1 is also 0: for any sequence (a_n), the series m_n = Σ_{k≥0} p^k a_{n+k} converges and satisfies m_n − p m_{n+1} = a_n. By the Milnor sequence, the derived limit of the corresponding tower of perfect complexes vanishes. This is the vanishing of the extra column. Equivalently, RΓ(S^tor, ω̃^κ) → lim_n RΓ(S^tor, ω̃^κ/p^n) is an isomorphism.

One could read X as the formal completion 𝔖^tor of §4.1.5, whose underlying space is the special fibre, but that does not avoid the problem. Theorem 2.9.7 is stated for schemes. Theorem 4.5.2 and Corollary 4.5.4 state the abutment for the scheme S^tor. Corollary 4.5.5 inverts p to reach RΓ(S^tor_{Q_p}, ω^κ), which requires the algebraic cohomology. So on either reading the two cohomologies must be compared. The paper has the tools for this (Lemma 2.9.3, Remark 2.9.4, Corollary 2.3.4), but it never makes the comparison. §4.5.6 does not address the abutment. Neither does the proof of Proposition 4.5.8, which ends on p. 53 and treats only the E_1 terms.

The spectral sequence as stated is true, and the missing argument is short. So this is a gap in the proof, not an error. The step cites a theorem whose hypotheses the filtration does not meet. It also never uses the fact that makes the conclusion hold, namely that S^tor is proper over Z_p. Once the step is added, the proof of Theorem 4.5.2 is complete. The results deduced from it are then also proved: Corollaries 4.5.4 and 4.5.5 and Theorem 1.4.3 (4) and (5) (p. 5). The 2024 preprint has the same text.

review.reason: Confirmed as a gap. §4.5.6 recalls the filtration ending at $F_{g(g+1)/2}=\mathcal S^{\mathrm{tor}}_{\F_p}$ and then says `By theorem 2.9.7, we have a spectral sequence $H^{p+q}_c(\hat F_p\setminus\hat F_{p-1},\tilde\omega^\kappa)\Rightarrow H^{p+q}(\mathcal S^{\mathrm{tor}},\tilde\omega^\kappa)$'. Theorem 2.9.7 is stated for a filtration of $X$ by closed subschemes with $Z_d=X$, and its proof uses that to identify $\mathrm R\Gamma_c(U_{-1},\mathcal F)$ with $\mathrm R\Gamma(X,\mathcal F)$; here the filtration exhausts only the special fibre, while the abutment is the cohomology of the $\Z_p$-scheme. The special fibre is a closed subscheme of $\mathcal S^{\mathrm{tor}}$ cut out by $p$, so the identification needs the completion along it, which is what the formal-completion notation $\hat F$ in the $E_1$ term already signals; but the appeal to Theorem 2.9.7 as stated does not deliver it.

sourceIssues.locator: §4.5.6, proof of Proposition 4.5.8, pp. 52–53 (the sentence at the top of p. 53 that justifies the triangle at the foot of p. 52), citing Corollary 4.4.3 on p. 50. The 2024 preprint has the same text.
sourceIssues.printed: p. 53: "This follows from the property that the original cohomological correspondence factors into p⋆_2 ω̃^κ → O_{C_t^{tor}}((k′ − k) Σ_{i=1}^g p⋆_2 Z_i − Σ_{i=1}^g p⋆_1 Z_i) ⊗ p⋆_2 ω̃^κ → p^!_1 ω̃^κ by lemma 4.3.14, and an application of corollary 4.4.3 (at this place we choose k′ large enough)." The cited Corollary 4.4.3 (p. 50) reads: "Let i ∈ {1, 2}. There exists m ∈ Z≥0 (depending on w and i) such that the canonical map O_{C_t^{tor}} → O_{C_t^{tor}}(m(p⋆_2 Σ_{i=1}^g Z_i − p⋆_1 Σ_{i=1}^g Z_i)) can be factored over p_i^{−1} S^{tor}_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)} through maps: O_{p_i^{−1}S^{tor}_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)}} → O_{p_i^{−1}S^{tor}_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)}}(p⋆_1 D_{w,+} + p⋆_2 D_{w,+}) → O_{p_i^{−1}S^{tor}_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)}}(m(p⋆_2 Σ Z_i − p⋆_1 Σ Z_i))." On p. 50 the locus is defined as "S^{tor}_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)} = ∩_i Z_{i,<w_i+1} ∩ Z_{i,>w_i+1}".
sourceIssues.correction: Corollary 4.4.3 should be stated over p_i^{-1}(Z_{>w−1}), for any closed-subscheme structure on that set, and in particular over V(p_2^{-1}I_{Z,>w−1}·O_{C_t^{tor}}). This set contains p_i^{-1}S^{tor}_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)}. The proof is unchanged except for the support comparison. It only needs supp(p_1^⋆D_{w,+}+p_2^⋆D_{w,+}) ⊆ supp(p_2^⋆ΣZ_i − p_1^⋆ΣZ_i), and this inclusion holds on all of p_i^{-1}(Z_{>w−1}) (see the argument below). Then take k′ ≥ k + m, with m the constant for V(p_2^{-1}I_{Z,>w−1}). This m does not depend on n or on the twist m in D_{−,w}, because every I^{n−1}_{Z,>w−1}/I^n_{Z,>w−1} is killed by I_{Z,>w−1}. No restriction to the complement of p_2^⋆D_{−,w} is needed, and no argument through the limit over m.
sourceIssues.reason:
Checked from the definitions of §4.1, using Z_{i,>j} − Z_{i,<j} = Z_i − V(p^{nj}) and D_i + D_{2g+1−i} = V(p^n), where n is the level. On the open stratum S̃_{=w′} we have Z_i = V(p^{n w′_i}). Hence Z_{>w−1} = ∩_i Z_{i,>w_i−1} contains every stratum S_{F_p,w′} with w′_i ≥ w_i for all i. By contrast, S_{(w−1,w+1)} = ∩_i(Z_{i,<w_i+1} ∩ Z_{i,>w_i−1}) meets only the stratum S_{F_p,w}.

Explicit case, g = 2 and w = (1,1), i.e. Gr_3 multiplicative and Gr_4 étale:
- Z_{1,>0} = D_3 and Z_{2,>0} = D_3 + D_4. So Z_{>w−1} = supp D_3, which contains S_{F_p,(1,2)}, the locus where Gr_3 and Gr_4 are multiplicative.
- Z_2 − V(p^{2n}) = −(D_1 + D_2). So Z_{2,<2} = D_1 + D_2, and this vanishes on S_{F_p,(1,2)}. Hence S_{F_p,(1,2)} ∩ S_{(w−1,w+1)} = ∅.
- D_{+,w} ⊇ Z_{1,<1} = D_2 ≠ 0. So the required factorization is not vacuous.

The sheaves ω̃^κ(−mD_{−,w}) ⊗ I^{n−1}_{Z,>w−1}/I^n_{Z,>w−1} are supported on all of Z_{>w−1}. So "an application of corollary 4.4.3" does not, as stated, give the factorization on the whole support of p⋆_2 of these sheaves. The missing extension is short: either the support argument in (a), or the extension-by-zero argument in (b). For (b) one uses that Z_{>w−1} ∖ D_{−,w} ⊆ S_{(w−1,w+1)}. Here is why. At a special-fibre point x off Z_{i,>w_i}, we have Z_{i,>w_i+1} − Z_{i,<w_i+1} = −Z_{i,<w_i} − V(p^n) near x. If x were not in Z_{i,<w_i+1}, an effective divisor would equal an anti-effective one containing V(p^n), which is impossible at a point where p is not a unit.

This is an omitted argument, not a false statement. The factorization in the proof of Proposition 4.5.8 is applied to p_2^⋆(ω̃^κ(−mD_{−,w}) ⊗ I^{n−1}_{Z,>w−1}/I^n_{Z,>w−1}). This is a module over O/p_2^{-1}I_{Z,>w−1}, so it lives on p_2^{-1}(Z_{>w−1}), where Z_{>w−1} = ∩_i Z_{i,>w_i−1} (§4.1.16). The divisor D_{+,w} of p. 52 is the D_{w,+} of p. 50.

Corollary 4.4.3 only gives the factorization over p_i^{-1}S^{tor}_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)}. Here S^{tor}_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)} = ∩_i Z_{i,<w_i+1} ∩ Z_{i,>w_i−1}. Page 50 prints Z_{i,>w_i+1}, which is a slip: with it the set would not contain S^{tor}_{F_p,w}, which the proof of 4.4.3 requires. So S_{(w−1,w+1)} = Z_{>w−1} ∩ ∩_i Z_{i,<w_i+1}, and this is in general strictly smaller than Z_{>w−1}.

- On S̃_{=w′} one has Z_i = V(p^{nw′_i}). Together with Lemma 4.1.17(1), this shows that S^{tor}_{F_p,w′} ⊆ Z_{>w−1} exactly when w′_i ≥ w_i for all i.
- S^{tor}_{F_p,w′} misses Z_{i,<w_i+1} whenever w′_i > w_i.
- Example: for g = 2 and w = (0,1), the strata w′ = (1,1) and (1,2) lie in Z_{>w−1} but not in S_{(w−1,w+1)}.
- The excess Z_{>w−1} \ S_{(w−1,w+1)} lies in D_{−,w}.

So the sheaves in question are not covered by Corollary 4.4.3 as stated, and no other statement in the paper covers them. For g = 1 the problem does not arise (either D_{w,+} = ∅ or the two sets coincide).

Why this is only a gap. The proof of Corollary 4.4.3 uses two things:
- the scheme is quasi-compact;
- supp(p_1^⋆D_{w,+}+p_2^⋆D_{w,+}) ⊆ supp(E), where E = p_2^⋆ΣZ_i − p_1^⋆ΣZ_i.

The inclusion is what gives f_i^n = h_i g_i; the reverse inclusion is never used. This inclusion holds on all of p_i^{-1}(Z_{>w−1}):
1. By Propositions 4.2.14(1) and 4.2.15(3), the complement of supp E is ∪_{w′} C^{tor}_{t,w′}, where C_{t,w′} = p_1^{-1}S_{w′} ∩ p_2^{-1}S_{w′}.
2. If such a point lies over Z_{>w−1}, then S_{w′} meets every Z_{i,>w_i−1}. This forces w′_i ≥ w_i for all i: otherwise Z_{i,>w_i−1} ≤ Z_{i,>w′_i} by Lemma 4.1.17(1), and Z_{i,>w′_i} misses S_{w′} by definition.
3. Then Z_{i,<w_i} ≤ Z_{i,<w′_i} also misses S_{w′}, so the point lies on neither p_1^⋆D_{w,+} nor p_2^⋆D_{w,+}.

Hence the proof of Corollary 4.4.3 goes through verbatim over the fixed closed subscheme V(p_2^{-1}I_{Z,>w−1}), with a single m that serves all n. Composing O → O(p_2^⋆D_{w,+}) → O(p_1^⋆D_{w,+}+p_2^⋆D_{w,+}) → O(mE) → O((k′−k)E) then gives the claimed factorization. Proposition 4.5.8, Theorem 4.5.2 (item (5) of the introduction) and Corollaries 4.5.4–4.5.5 are unaffected.

On the scheme structure: the paper takes (p) ⊆ I_{Z,>w−1} (last sentence of the proof, p. 53), so these graded pieces are killed by p. The argument does not depend on this in any case.

sourceIssues.locator: §5.1, Remark 5.1.2 and proof of Theorem 5.1.4, p. 53
sourceIssues.printed: Remark 5.1.2, p. 53: "Let t_0 = diag(1_g, p1_g). Let K_{p,P} be a decomposable compact. For n large enough, t_0^{−n} K_{p,P} t_0^{n} ⊆ P′(Z_p)." Proof of Theorem 5.1.4, p. 53: "Also, if the theorem is satisfied by a compact open subgroup K_{p,P}, it is satisfied by any conjugate by t_0 = diag(1_g, p1_g) and for r large enough, t_0^{−r} K_{p,P} t_0^{r} ⊆ K′_{p,P}."
sourceIssues.correction: Remark 5.1.2 should read: for n large enough, t_0^{n} K_{p,P} t_0^{−n} ⊆ P′(Z_p). In the proof of Theorem 5.1.4 it should read: for r large enough, t_0^{r} K_{p,P} t_0^{−r} ⊆ K′_{p,P}. Equivalently, keep the printed exponents and replace t_0 by t_0^{−1} = diag(1_g, p^{−1}1_g).
sourceIssues.reason:
Conventions (§3.1, pp. 33–34). Matrices act on column vectors. P is the stabiliser of ⟨e_{g+1},…,e_{2g}⟩, and x^{−1}Px is described as the stabiliser of x^{−1}⟨e_{g+1},…,e_{2g}⟩. So P is block lower triangular and U_P is the lower-left g×g block. The Borel B ⊆ P is upper triangular on the diagonal blocks, and its unipotent radical is N = N_M·U_P.

The definition of T^+(Q_p) on p. 34 is v(t_{g+1}) ≥ … ≥ v(t_{2g}) ≥ v(t_1) ≥ … ≥ v(t_g). This is exactly the condition that v(t_i) ≥ v(t_j) for every entry (i, j) of N, that is, that n ↦ tnt^{−1} maps N(Z_p) into itself. The dominant cone 0 ≥ k_1 ≥ … ≥ k_g on the same page gives the same picture. With row vectors, B would be upper triangular, and for g ≥ 2 neither condition would cut out the chamber of B or of its opposite.

By Lemma 3.4.3 and the paragraph after it (p. 36), P′(Q_p) has the group structure of P(Q_p), with M(Q_p) acting on U_P(Q_p)(1) by the usual conjugation. Also P′(Z_p) = M(Z_p) ⋉ U_P(Z_p)(1) (Remark 3.4.6).

Computation. t_0 = diag(1_g, p1_g) is a similitude with factor p. It is central in M and lies in T^+(Q_p). For u ∈ U_P and an entry (i, j) with i > g ≥ j, (t_0^{a} u t_0^{−a})_{ij} = p^{a} u_{ij}. So conjugation by t_0^{a} fixes M and scales U_P by p^{a}. Hence t_0^{−n}(·)t_0^{n} enlarges the unipotent part.

The printed inclusions are false. Let K = K_{p,P}. Since K is open in P′(Q_p), U_K = K ∩ U_P(Q_p)(1) is a nonzero compact open subgroup. Then t_0^{−n}Kt_0^{n} ∩ U_P(Q_p)(1) = p^{−n}U_K, and this is not contained in U_P(Z_p)(1) once n is large. So Remark 5.1.2 fails for every K and all large n. The group K′_{p,P} = wK″_pw^{−1} ∩ P(Q_p) is compact, so t_0^{−r}Kt_0^{r} ⊆ K′_{p,P} also fails for all large r.

Example: take g = 1 and w = 1. Then M = T and B = P. K = P′(Z_p) = T(Z_p) ⋉ U_P(Z_p)(1) is decomposable, and K′_{p,P} = P(Z_p). But t_0^{−n}Kt_0^{n} contains the unipotent element with lower-left entry p^{−n}. So both inclusions fail for every n, r ≥ 1.

The corrected inclusions hold. By condition (1), t_0^{r}Kt_0^{−r} = M_K ⋉ p^{r}U_K. By condition (3), M_K lies in the Iwahori subgroup of M(Q_p) with respect to B ∩ M = B_w ∩ M. That subgroup is contained in M(Z_p) and equals wK″_pw^{−1} ∩ M. For r large, p^{r}U_K ⊆ pU_P(Z_p) ⊆ wK″_pw^{−1} ∩ U_P, since elements of pU_P(Z_p) reduce to 1 mod p. Hence t_0^{r}Kt_0^{−r} ⊆ P′(Z_p) and t_0^{r}Kt_0^{−r} ⊆ K′_{p,P}. Conjugation by t_0 also preserves decomposability.

Why this is a misprint and not an error. As printed, both inclusions are false in every case, not only in an edge case. But the intended statement is unambiguous. "For n large enough" can hold only for the conjugation that contracts U_P. The proof of Lemma 3.4.8 (p. 37) conjugates by the same central element diag(1,…,1,p,…,p) of M(Q_p) for exactly this purpose ("to have K_{p,U_P} ⊆ U_P(Z_p)(1)"), without stating a direction. For t_0 ∈ T^+, the map x ↦ t_0xt_0^{−1} fixes M and shrinks U_P ⊆ N (Remark 5.1.3: N_{K_{p,P}} = N_{M_{K_{p,P}}} × U_{K_{p,P}}). The fix is the same change of sign in both places.

Consequences: none. In the proof of Theorem 5.1.4, the theorem holds for t_0^{r}Kt_0^{−r} ⊆ K′_{p,P} by Proposition 4.4.4 and Lemma 2.1.34. It then holds for K, which is the conjugate of t_0^{r}Kt_0^{−r} by t_0^{−r}. The proof invokes invariance under conjugation by t_0, and this applies equally to t_0^{−1}: both lie in T(Q_p) ⊆ M(Q_p), so both commute with t ∈ T_w(Q_p)^{++} ⊆ T(Q_p). The later appeal in the proof of Proposition 5.2.5 (p. 54), "by conjugating by t_0, we may assume that K_{p,P} ⊆ P′(Z_p)", states no direction and is correct in the corrected one.

sourceIssues.printed: Proposition 5.2.3. RΓ_w(K^pK_{p,P}) and RΓ_w(K^pK_{p,P}, cusp) belong to D(Z_p[T(Q_p)]) and are perfect complexes of Z_p[T_w(Z_p)/T_{w,K_{p,P}}]-modules. Proof. This is a consequence of theorem 2.6.10.
sourceIssues.correction:
The one-line proof works only when T_w(Z_p) = T(Z_p) normalises K_{p,P}, so add that hypothesis. Then K_1 = T(Z_p)K_{p,P} is a compact open subgroup with U_{K_1} = U_{K_{p,P}}. By Proposition 3.4.9(5), the map IG_{K^pK_{p,P}} → IG_{K^pK_1} is finite étale and Galois, with group G = K_1/K_{p,P} ≅ T(Z_p)/T_{w,K_{p,P}}. Apply Theorem 2.6.10 on IG_{K^pK_1} to the pushforward of the structure sheaf, and of its twist by (−D) in the cuspidal case. These are flat over (Z/p^s)[G] by Lemma 2.6.11. Use the correspondence of any t ∈ T_w^{++}(Q_p). With this hypothesis, s ∈ T(Z_p) acts by a deck transformation, and the T^+-correspondences give an honest T(Q_p)-action.

This case covers K_{w,p,P}. It is also all that is needed later. The only use of the proposition is Proposition 5.2.7, whose construction does not depend on K_{p,P}; that independence is proved as in Proposition 5.2.5, without Proposition 5.2.3. So one may start from a T(Z_p)-normalised K_{p,P}. Then every (K_{p,P})_n is normalised too, because N(Z/p^n) is T-stable.

For a general decomposable K_{p,P}, the T(Q_p)-structure first has to be defined. It would be the extension of the invertible action of T_w^{++}(Q_p) on the ordinary part, with s ∈ T(Z_p) acting by T_{st}T_t^{-1}. The statement could then be moved across Proposition 5.2.5 from the T(Z_p)-normalised compact T_{w,K_{p,P}}·P′(Z_p)_r (r large), which has the same torus part. That route requires checking that the quasi-isomorphism of 5.2.5 is T_w^{++}-equivariant, which the paper does not state.

The cohomological correspondence must commute with G, and the sheaf must be flat over A[G]. For F = O on IG_{K^pK_{p,P}}, the only available action of G = T_w(Z_p)/T_{w,K_{p,P}} is by deck transformations. That action exists only if T(Z_p) normalises K_{p,P}.

- K = M_K ⋉ U_K;
- an Iwahori decomposition N_{w,K} × T_{w,K} × N̄_{w,K};
- M_K inside the Iwahori subgroup of M, with its own Iwahori decomposition.

So a degree bound for the limit does not follow from cohomological dimension 1.

If it is read as a property of the scheme S̄ \ D_{w,+}, it covers the twisted sheaf automatically. If it is read as sheaf-specific, as in the w = Id case, where it rests on [Lan17] thm. 8.6, then it is unproved for both the untwisted and the twisted sheaf. Proposition 5.6.3 is quoted as Theorem 1.4.3(2) on p. 5. With the correction these statements stand, so only the proof is affected.

sourceIssues.locator: §6.1, proof of Proposition 6.1.7, p. 59
sourceIssues.printed: Proof. We can assume that the support conditions are quasi-compact by lemma 6.1.5. If (U, Z) and (U′, Z′) are two support conditions, then (U ∪ U′, Z ∪ Z′) is also a support condition. We therefore reduce to the situation that U ⊆ U′ and Z ⊆ Z′. Let us assume that U ⊆ U′ and Z = Z′. One treats similarly the case that U = U′ and Z ⊆ Z′.
sourceIssues.correction:
Compare both pairs with the intersection pair (𝒰 ∩ 𝒰′, 𝒵 ∩ 𝒵′), not with the union.

The intersection pair is again a quasi-compact support condition:
- T(closure of 𝒰 ∩ 𝒰′) ⊆ T(𝒰̄) ∩ T(𝒰̄′) ⊆ 𝒰 ∩ 𝒰′;
- T^t(𝒵 ∩ 𝒵′) ⊆ 𝒵° ∩ 𝒵′° = (𝒵 ∩ 𝒵′)°.

Write L for the common limit set. The nested case treated in the proof uses the hypothesis only through one fact: the limit set of the larger pair lies in the smaller pair. That fact is what gives ∩_{m,n} 𝒰′_m ∩ 𝒵_n ∩ 𝒰^c = ∅. Now go in two steps:
- From (𝒰, 𝒵) to (𝒰 ∩ 𝒰′, 𝒵): L ⊆ 𝒰, and L = L′ ⊆ 𝒰′.
- From (𝒰 ∩ 𝒰′, 𝒵) to (𝒰 ∩ 𝒰′, 𝒵 ∩ 𝒵′): the limit set of (𝒰 ∩ 𝒰′, 𝒵) is contained in L, and L ⊆ 𝒵 ∩ 𝒵′.

The same two steps work for (𝒰′, 𝒵′). So both finite slope parts are canonically quasi-isomorphic to that of (𝒰 ∩ 𝒰′, 𝒵 ∩ 𝒵′). In fact every pair in these chains has limit set exactly L, so the nested case applies even in its printed form, with equal limit sets.

The union pair can be used only when the mixed sets 𝒰_∞ ∩ 𝒵′_∞ and 𝒰′_∞ ∩ 𝒵_∞ lie in L, and in general they do not. Here 𝒰_∞ = ∩_m 𝒰_m and 𝒵_∞ = ∩_n 𝒵_n. With this change the statement of Proposition 6.1.7 stands.

The printed text on p. 59 is as quoted: the pair is (U ∪ U′, Z ∪ Z′), with ∪ in both places.

Why the union reduction fails. The proof must compare (U, Z) and (U′, Z′) with the union pair. Its own special case U ⊆ U′, Z = Z′ uses equality of the limit sets: the step "∩_{m,n} U′_m ∩ Z_n ∩ U^c = ∅" needs L′ = L ⊆ U. So the union pair would need limit set L, and nothing guarantees that.
- Since T(Ū) ⊆ U and T^t(Z) ⊆ Z°, the sets U_m and Z_n decrease.
- T commutes with unions.
- For decreasing sequences, ∩_m (A_m ∪ B_m) = (∩A_m) ∪ (∩B_m).
So the union pair has limit set (U_∞ ∪ U′_∞) ∩ (Z_∞ ∪ Z′_∞) = L ∪ (U_∞ ∩ Z′_∞) ∪ (U′_∞ ∩ Z_∞). The hypothesis L = L′ says nothing about the two mixed terms.

Counterexample, checked by direct computation:
- Setup: X̄ = three points {a, b, c}, C̄ = X̄, p̄_1 = p̄_2 = id, so T = T^t = id and every pair of subsets is a quasi-compact support condition. Let (U, Z) = ({a,b}, {a,c}) and (U′, Z′) = ({a,c}, {a,b}).
- Limit sets: both pairs have limit set {a}, but the union pair (X̄, X̄) has limit set X̄.
- Cohomology: for F = O, the finite slope parts are one-dimensional for the two pairs and three-dimensional for the union pair. So neither pair can be compared with the union pair.

In finite discrete models (directed graphs, with U closed under successors and Z under predecessors), the union pair changed the limit set in 1349 of 12662 random instances with L = L′. The intersection pair never did.

The statement itself survives. The intersection pair (U ∩ U′, Z ∩ Z′) always has limit set L, by the compactness argument in the correction, which is the same argument the proof already uses. So this is a gap in the proof, not an error in the result.

Downstream use: Proposition 6.1.7 is not cited by number later. Implicitly, it is what identifies the degree-defined support conditions of Proposition 6.1.10 (used in Theorems 6.2.9 and 6.2.15) with the Hodge–Tate ones of Proposition 6.1.11. Both have limit set S_w^tor. The deductions of Corollaries 6.2.10, 6.2.16 and 6.2.17 from [BP21] go through that identification. Since the proposition holds with the repaired proof, none of these results is affected. The page image of p. 59 shows the text as quoted, with ∪ in both entries of the pair. The 2024 preprint (p. 57) has the same words.

**What the reduction needs.** To pass to nested pairs, the proof must compare (𝒰, 𝒵) and (𝒰′, 𝒵′) with (𝒰 ∪ 𝒰′, 𝒵 ∪ 𝒵′), using the two nested special cases. The nested case (p. 59) needs the limit set of the larger pair to lie in the smaller pair: "we know that ∩_{m,n} 𝒰′_m ∩ 𝒵_n ⋂ 𝒰^c = ∅", which follows from L′ = L ⊆ 𝒰. So the union pair would need limit set L.

**Why that fails.** Since T(𝒰̄) ⊆ 𝒰 and T^t(𝒵) ⊆ 𝒵°, the sequences 𝒰_m and 𝒵_n decrease. T and T^t commute with unions, and for decreasing sequences ∩_m(A_m ∪ B_m) = (∩A_m) ∪ (∩B_m). Hence the limit set of the union pair is L ∪ (𝒰_∞ ∩ 𝒵′_∞) ∪ (𝒰′_∞ ∩ 𝒵_∞). The hypothesis says nothing about the two mixed terms. Replacing 𝒰 by 𝒰_m or 𝒵 by 𝒵_n (Proposition 6.1.4) does not change any limit set, so shrinking first does not help.

**Counterexamples** (checked by direct computation). In both, the conclusion of the proposition holds for the two given pairs, but the union pair has different finite slope cohomology. So neither given pair can be compared with the union pair: the route through the union fails, it is not merely left unproved.
- (a) Take 𝒳̄ = 𝒞̄ = three points {a, b, c}, p̄_1 = p̄_2 = id, so T = T^t = id, and F = O with the identity correspondence. Let (𝒰, 𝒵) = ({a,b}, {a,c}) and (𝒰′, 𝒵′) = ({a,c}, {a,b}). Both are quasi-compact support conditions with limit set {a}, and each finite slope part is 1-dimensional. The union pair (𝒳̄, 𝒳̄) has limit set 𝒳̄ and a 3-dimensional finite slope part.
- (b) Take 𝒳̄ = 𝒞̄ = P^1 over Q_p, p̄_1 = id, p̄_2(z) = z^2, and F = O, so T acts by f ↦ f(z^2). Let (𝒰, 𝒵) = ({|z| < p^{-1}}, {|z| ≥ p^{-1}}) and (𝒰′, 𝒵′) = ({|z| > p}, {|z| ≤ p}). Both pairs have empty support 𝒰 ∩ 𝒵, hence zero cohomology. The union pair has 𝒵 ∪ 𝒵′ = P^1, and on its cohomology the functions constant on each of the two discs are eigenvectors of T with eigenvalue 1. So its finite slope part is non-zero.

In random finite models (a relation on a finite set, with 𝒰 stable under T and 𝒵 stable under T^t) whose two pairs have equal limit sets, the union pair changed the limit set in about 6% of cases. The intersection pair, and the intermediate pair (𝒰 ∩ 𝒰′, 𝒵), never did.

**Defence tried.** No convention in §6.1 makes the union step valid. Nor do the cited [BP21] results. Theorem 5.3.7 of [BP21] concerns one fixed pair. Corollary 5.3.8 is a sandwich criterion (T^{m+s}(𝒰) ∩ (T^t)^n(𝒵) ⊆ 𝒰′ ⊆ T^m(𝒰), and similarly for the supports). It cannot apply to the union pair, because in (a) and (b) the cohomologies really differ.

**The statement survives.** The repair in the correction is sound. That the intersection pair has limit set exactly L follows from the compactness argument already in the proof. That argument gives m0, n0 with 𝒰_{m0} ∩ 𝒵_{n0} ⊆ 𝒰′ ∩ 𝒵′. Now take x ∈ L:
- For each m, write x as the end of a T-chain of length m + m0 that starts in 𝒰. The chain's point at step m0 lies in 𝒰_{m0} ∩ 𝒵_{n0} ⊆ 𝒰 ∩ 𝒰′. So x ∈ T^m(𝒰 ∩ 𝒰′).
- Symmetrically, x ∈ (T^t)^n(𝒵 ∩ 𝒵′) for each n.

So this is a gap, not a false result. The claimed reduction to nested pairs is achievable, but not by the route given.

**Consequences.** Proposition 6.1.7 is not cited by number later. It is the implicit link between two kinds of support conditions:
- the degree-defined ones of §6.1.8 and Proposition 6.1.10, used in Theorems 6.2.9 and 6.2.15;
- the Hodge–Tate-defined ones of Proposition 6.1.11, which are those of [BP21].

Both kinds have limit set the closure of S_w^tor. This identification is what transfers the results to the cohomology of [BP21]: Corollaries 6.2.10, 6.2.16 and 6.2.17, and the remark after Corollary 6.2.10 that yields Theorem 1.5.1. The proposition holds with the repaired proof, so none of these stated results is affected.

sourceIssues.reason: In §6.1.8 the letter n is already fixed as the level: the Shimura variety 𝒮^{tor} has level K_{p,n}, where K_{p,n} consists of the elements of G(Z_p) that reduce to B(Z/p^nZ) (p. 41). This n enters the definition of 𝒰_{≥w−ϵ} and 𝒰_{≤w+ϵ} through the bounds deg H_{g+i}(x) ≥ n(w_i − ϵ) and deg H_{g+i}(x) ≤ n(w_i + ϵ). The proof of Proposition 6.1.9 also says the degrees are 'multiples of n' when equality holds. Items (3)–(4) nevertheless rebind n as an existentially quantified number of iterations of T or T^t, inside sets that themselves depend on the level n. The number of iterations depends on ϵ − ϵ′ and must be allowed to vary with the level held fixed. The clash is explicit in Proposition 6.1.11 and its proof: there (T^t)^n and the index \bar n in ]C_{w,F_p}[_{0,\bar n} run over all iteration counts, while K_{p,n}, π_{HT,K_{p,n}} and U^{op}_{K_{p,n}} in the same formulas refer to the fixed level. The intended meaning is clear and the arguments hold once the letters are separated, so this is a notational slip.

Moreover ∩T^m(π^{-1}_{HT,K_{p,n}}]X_{w,F_p}[) ∩ (T^t)^n(π^{-1}_{HT,K_{p,n}}\overline{]Y_{w,F_p}[}) = \overline{S^{tor}_w}." Consider the Iwahori decomposition K_{p,n} = B_{K_{p,n}} × U^{op}_{K_{p,n}}. We deduce easily that ]C_{w,F_p}[_{m,\bar 0}K_{p,n} ∩ ]C_{w,F_p}[_{0,\bar n}K_{p,n} = ((]C_{w,F_p}[_{m,\bar 0}B_{K_{p,n}}) ∩ (]C_{w,F_p}[_{0,\bar n}U^{op}_{K_{p,n}}))K_{p,n}. Now, by [BP21], coro. 3.3.14, (]C_{w,F_p}[_{m,\bar 0}B_{K_{p,n}}) = ]C_{w,F_p}[_{m,\bar 0} and (]C_{w,F_p}[_{0,\bar n}U^{op}_{K_{p,n}}) = ]C_{w,F_p}[_{0,\bar n} so that finally ]C_{w,F_p}[_{m,\bar 0}K_{p,n} ∩ ]C_{w,F_p}[_{0,\bar n}K_{p,n} = ]C_{w,F_p}[_{m,\bar n}K_{p,n}. □"
sourceIssues.correction:
Below, s denotes the exponent of T^t, because the paper also uses n for the level K = K_{p,n}. After the last displayed identity, add two steps.
(i) Inclusion ⊆. For each m and s, the (m,s)-th set lies in π^{-1}_{HT,K}(]C_w[_{m,\bar s}K). In the coordinates of [BP21] §3.3.6, ]C_w[_{m,\bar s} = w·∏_{α∈w^{-1}Φ^{-,M}∩Φ^-}U°_{α,m}·∏_{α∈w^{-1}Φ^{-,M}∩Φ^+}\overline{U_{α,s}}. A point lying in all of these sets has |u_α| ≤ |p^k| for every k, so u_α = 0 because the valuation is continuous. Hence ∩_{m,s}]C_w[_{m,\bar s} = {w}.
Each ]C_w[_{m,\bar s} = P\PwG_{m,\bar s} ([BP21] coro. 3.3.14) is stable under the open subgroup G_{m,\bar s} ∩ K of K. So for any point x, the sets {k ∈ K : xk^{-1} ∈ ]C_w[_{m,\bar s}} are nonempty, open and closed, and decreasing. Since K is compact, they have a common element. This gives ∩_{m,s}]C_w[_{m,\bar s}K = w·K, and therefore ∩_{m,s}π^{-1}(]C_w[_{m,\bar s}K) = π^{-1}(w·K) = \overline{S^tor_w} by Lemma 4.1.6.
(ii) Inclusion ⊇. Since w ∈ C_w ⊆ X_w ∩ Y_w, the set \overline{S^tor_w} = π^{-1}(w·K) lies in π^{-1}]X_w[ ∩ π^{-1}\overline{]Y_w[}. By the Hecke equivariance of π_{HT,K} ([BP21] thm. 4.5.2), taken as an equality of sets, T(π^{-1}A) = π^{-1}(A·KtK) and T^t(π^{-1}A) = π^{-1}(A·Kt^{-1}K) for every K-stable A. Since wt^{±1}w^{-1} ∈ T ⊆ P, we have w·t^{±1} = w in P\G, so w·K ⊆ w·Kt^{±1}K. Hence \overline{S^tor_w} ⊆ T(\overline{S^tor_w}) and \overline{S^tor_w} ⊆ T^t(\overline{S^tor_w}). By induction, \overline{S^tor_w} lies in T^m(π^{-1}]X_w[) ∩ (T^t)^s(π^{-1}\overline{]Y_w[}) for all m and s.
Surjectivity of the projections of the Hecke correspondence is not enough for (ii). Over each x one needs a point of the correspondence whose other projection stays in \overline{S^tor_w}. Supplying such a point is the role of the equivariance together with w·t^{±1} = w.

The proposition claims an equality: the limit set ∩_{m,n} T^m(π^{-1}]X_w[) ∩ (T^t)^n(π^{-1}\overline{]Y_w[}) equals \overline{S^tor_w}. The proof ends as soon as it has shown that the (m,n)-th set lies in π^{-1}(]C_w[_{m,\bar n}K_{p,n}).
- It never intersects over m and n.
- It never identifies the result with \overline{S^tor_w}: S^tor_w is not mentioned and Lemma 4.1.6 is not invoked.
- It never addresses the reverse inclusion.

Nothing cited fills the gap. [BP21] lem. 3.5.10 (checked on p. 46 of [BP21]) gives only the upper bounds used here, and [BP21] does not state this limit set anywhere.

Defence considered. The missing steps are routine and the stated equality is true: the argument in the correction proves it from Lemma 4.1.6, [BP21] coro. 3.3.14 and [BP21] thm. 4.5.2. But the reverse inclusion does not follow formally from what is written. On p. 60 the paper uses only the inclusion T(π^{-1}A) ⊆ π^{-1}(A·KtK). The reverse inclusion needs the equality form of Hecke equivariance together with w·t^{±1} = w in P\G.

Downstream use. Proposition 6.1.7 needs the two limit sets to be equal. With Proposition 6.1.10, whose limit set is also \overline{S^tor_w}, this identifies the finite-slope cohomology for the support condition (U_{≥w−ε}, Z_{<w+ε}) of Theorem 6.2.9 with the [BP21] cohomology for (π^{-1}]X_w[, π^{-1}\overline{]Y_w[}). Corollary 6.2.10 (Conjecture 5.9.2 of [BP21] in the Siegel case) uses this identification without citing it, and so do the remark after it and hence Theorem 1.5.1. Since the equality holds, none of these results is affected; only the proof of Proposition 6.1.11 is incomplete.

Two notational slips are nearby, neither with mathematical consequence:
- the ∩ in the statement lacks the subscript m,n (compare "∩_{m,n}" in Proposition 6.1.10);
- n is used both for the level K_{p,n} and for the exponent of T^t.

sourceIssues.correction: 𝒵_{>w−ϵ} = \overline{∪_{ϵ′<ϵ} 𝒰_{≥w−ϵ′}}, i.e. the closure of {x : deg H_{g+i}(x) > n(w_i − ϵ) for all i}. This mirrors 𝒵_{<w+ϵ} = \overline{∪_{ϵ′<ϵ} 𝒰_{≤w+ϵ′}}, which is the closure of {deg H_{g+i} < n(w_i + ϵ) for all i}.
sourceIssues.reason:
On p. 60, 𝒰_{≥w−ϵ} is the set of rank 1 points with deg H_{g+i}(x) ≥ n(w_i − ϵ) for all i. As ϵ′ increases the bound n(w_i − ϵ′) decreases, so 𝒰_{≥w−ϵ′} gets larger. The degree is non-negative: on p. 44 it is defined as deg H = v(x) with x ∈ V. So once ϵ′ ≥ max_i w_i, 𝒰_{≥w−ϵ′} is all of 𝒮^{tor}.

As printed, the union over ϵ′ > ϵ is therefore all of 𝒮^{tor}. Even if ϵ′ is kept in ]ϵ,1[, a union of increasing sets over ϵ′ ∈ ]ϵ,1[ equals ∪_{ϵ′<1} 𝒰_{≥w−ϵ′}, which does not depend on ϵ. Either way the printed set cannot be the closed neighbourhood that the name 𝒵_{>w−ϵ} describes. In §4.1 the notation Z_{i,>j} likewise marks the region where the degree is > nj.

With ϵ′ < ϵ one gets ∪_{ϵ′<ϵ} 𝒰_{≥w−ϵ′} = {deg H_{g+i} > n(w_i − ϵ) for all i}. The inclusion ⊆ holds because w_i − ϵ′ > w_i − ϵ. For ⊇, take a rational ϵ′ < ϵ with ϵ′ ≥ max_i (w_i − deg H_{g+i}(x)/n). The companion 𝒵_{<w+ϵ} is correct by the same argument.

The misprint changes nothing. Proposition 6.1.10 and all of §6.2 (for example §6.2.8) use only 𝒰_{≥w−ϵ} and 𝒵_{<w+ϵ}. The symbol 𝒵_{>w−ϵ} does not appear again. The similar-looking Z_{>w−1} = ∩_i Z_{i,>w_i−1} of §4.1.16 (p. 43) and Lemma 4.5.7 is a different object, defined separately on the integral model.

sourceIssues.locator: §6.2.1, Proposition 6.2.3 (2) and (3), second inequalities, p. 61
sourceIssues.printed: Proposition 6.2.3. The following holds: … (2) We have p_1^⋆D_+ ≥ p_2^⋆D_+, p_1^⋆D_{+,ϵ} ≥ p_2^⋆D_{+,ϵ′}. (3) We have p_2^⋆D_− ≥ p_1^⋆D_−, p_2^⋆D_{−,ϵ} ≥ p_1^⋆D_{−,ϵ′}. … Proof. … The second and third point follow from proposition 6.1.9 and lemma 4.2.11.
sourceIssues.correction: Read as inequalities of (Q-)Cartier divisors on C_t^tor, the second halves p_1^⋆D_{+,ϵ} ≥ p_2^⋆D_{+,ϵ′} and p_2^⋆D_{−,ϵ} ≥ p_1^⋆D_{−,ϵ′} are false. Replace them by inclusions of supports (closed subsets): p_1^⋆D_{+,ϵ} ⊇ p_2^⋆D_{+,ϵ′} and p_2^⋆D_{−,ϵ} ⊇ p_1^⋆D_{−,ϵ′}, where 0 < ϵ′ < ϵ is chosen as in §6.2.1. These are the true statements that Proposition 6.1.9 gives. They are also exactly the hypotheses p̄_1^⋆D_+ ⊇ p̄_2^⋆D′_+ and p̄_2^⋆D_− ⊇ p̄_1^⋆D′_− of Proposition 2.10.4, with D_± = D_{±,ϵ} and D′_± = D_{±,ϵ′}. They cannot be strengthened to scheme-theoretic inclusions, because for effective Cartier divisors that is the same as the divisor inequality. The first halves, p_1^⋆D_+ ≥ p_2^⋆D_+ and p_2^⋆D_− ≥ p_1^⋆D_−, are correct divisor inequalities by Lemma 4.2.11. (In the definitions just above, the subscripts w_j should read w_i.)
sourceIssues.reason:
I checked the wording on the page image of p. 61. In the rest of Proposition 6.2.3, "≥" means an inequality of divisors. This holds in (1) (Lemma 4.1.17 (1)), in the first halves of (2) and (3) (Lemma 4.2.11) and in (4) (s·p_1^⋆D_+ ≥ p_2^⋆D_+). Read the same way, the second halves of (2) and (3) are false.

So at a generic point of the special fibre where Z_i = V(p^{nd}), we get Z_{i,<a} = n·max(0, a−d)·V(p) and Z_{i,>a} = n·max(0, d−a)·V(p). Fix w′ ∈ ^M W. On the nonempty open piece C_{t,w′}^tor = p_1^{-1}S_{w′}^tor ∩ p_2^{-1}S_{w′}^tor (Proposition 4.2.4), we have p_1^⋆Z_k = p_2^⋆Z_k = V(p^{n w′_k}) (§4.1.3 and Lemma 4.1.6 with the convention of §3.1, and Proposition 4.2.14 (2)). The blow-up does not change this, because over the ordinary strata the ideals being blown up are generated by powers of p. With D_{+,ϵ} = Σ_i Z_{i,<w_i−ϵ} and D_{−,ϵ} = Σ_i Z_{i,>w_i+ϵ} (the printed w_j is a slip for w_i), we get on C_{t,w′}^tor:
- p_1^⋆D_{+,ϵ} − p_2^⋆D_{+,ϵ′} = −n(ϵ−ϵ′)·#{k : w′_k < w_k}·V(p);
- p_2^⋆D_{−,ϵ} − p_1^⋆D_{−,ϵ′} = −n(ϵ−ϵ′)·#{k : w′_k > w_k}·V(p).

Since ϵ′ < ϵ (§6.2.1), neither difference is effective as soon as w′_k < w_k (respectively w′_k > w_k) for some k. For g = 1, the convention of §3.1 gives w_1 = 1 for w = Id and w_1 = 0 for w_0.
- For (2), take w = Id on C_{t,w_0}^tor. There Z_1 = 0, so p_1^⋆D_{+,ϵ} = n(1−ϵ)V(p), which is strictly less than p_2^⋆D_{+,ϵ′} = n(1−ϵ′)V(p).
- For (3), take w = w_0 on C_{t,Id}^tor. There Z_1 = V(p^n), so p_2^⋆D_{−,ϵ} = n(1−ϵ)V(p), which is strictly less than p_1^⋆D_{−,ϵ′} = n(1−ϵ′)V(p).

In every genus, (2) fails for w = Id and (3) fails for the w with all w_i = 0. The argument does not need nϵ or nϵ′ to be integers. In these examples the supports agree, which is consistent with the set-theoretic inclusions.

Why the inclusions hold. On the adic generic fibre, the complement of the support of D_{+,ϵ} is U_{≥w−ϵ}. Take a point with p_1 outside the support of D_{+,ϵ}. Since T(U_{≥w−ϵ}) ⊆ U_{≥w−ϵ′}, p_2 of that point lies outside the support of D_{+,ϵ′}. The argument for D_− is the same, using T^t(U_{≤w+ϵ}) ⊆ U_{≤w+ϵ′}.

Why nothing downstream is affected. Proposition 6.2.3 is never cited by number. It enters the proof of Theorem 6.2.9 in two places:
- Through Proposition 2.10.4 (p. 30). Its hypotheses are the set-theoretic inclusions p̄_1^⋆D_+ ⊇ p̄_2^⋆D′_+ and p̄_2^⋆D_− ⊇ p̄_1^⋆D′_−.
- Through Theorem 2.11.4 (3) (p. 32). This needs the maps p_2^⋆O(D_+) → p_1^⋆O(D_+) and p_2^⋆O(−D_−) → p_1^⋆O(−D_−), which are the true first halves, together with (4).

No stated result depends on the false divisor inequalities. How to read the symbol. In Proposition 6.2.3, "≥" means an inequality of divisors. That is true in (1) (Lemma 4.1.17), in the first halves of (2) and (3) (Lemma 4.2.11), and in (4), where s·p_1^⋆D_+ ≥ p_2^⋆D_+ with s ∈ ]0,1[ makes sense only for divisors. The paper writes set inclusions of closed subsets as ⊆ or ⊇ (Proposition 2.10.4, §2.11).

Readings that would save the statement, and why they fail:
- Reading the second halves only over C_t^tor \ p_1^⋆D_{+,ϵ}, as in (4), would make them trivial (0 ≥ 0). But (2) and (3) are stated on all of C_t^tor.
- Swapping ϵ and ϵ′ gives p_1^⋆D_{+,ϵ′} ≥ p_2^⋆D_{+,ϵ}, which is a true divisor inequality by (1) and Lemma 4.2.11. But it needs no Proposition 6.1.9, and it gives only the inclusion that is of no use for Proposition 2.10.4.

Setting up the computation (checked by direct computation). Z_i = Σ_{k≤i} D_{g+k} is the degree divisor of H_{g+i}. By Proposition 6.2.2, Z_{i,>a} − Z_{i,<a} = Z_i − V(p^{na}), and the two divisors have disjoint supports. Hence at a generic point of the special fibre where Z_i = V(p^{nd}), we have Z_{i,<a} = n·max(0, a−d)·V(p).

Fix w′ ∈ ^M W. On the open piece C_{t,w′}^tor = p_1^{-1}S_{w′} ∩ p_2^{-1}S_{w′}:
- Each Gr_{g+k} is multiplicative (D_{g+k} = V(p^n)) or étale (D_{g+k} = 0), by §4.1.3, §4.1.8 and the convention for (w_1,…,w_g) in §3.1.
- So p_1^⋆Z_i = p_2^⋆Z_i = V(p^{n w′_i}) (Proposition 4.2.14 (2)).
- The blow-up changes nothing there, because the ideals being blown up are principal.

This gives, on C_{t,w′}^tor:
- p_1^⋆D_{+,ϵ} − p_2^⋆D_{+,ϵ′} = −n(ϵ−ϵ′)·#{i : w′_i < w_i}·V(p);
- p_2^⋆D_{−,ϵ} − p_1^⋆D_{−,ϵ′} = −n(ϵ−ϵ′)·#{i : w′_i > w_i}·V(p).

Since ϵ′ < ϵ (§6.2.1), neither difference is effective as soon as such an i exists.

Concrete cases for g = 1:
- For (2), take w = Id (w_1 = 1). On C_{t,w_0}^tor we have Z_1 = 0, so p_1^⋆D_{+,ϵ} = V(p^{n(1−ϵ)}), which is strictly less than p_2^⋆D_{+,ϵ′} = V(p^{n(1−ϵ′)}).
- For (3), take w = w_0 (w_1 = 0). On C_{t,Id}^tor we have Z_1 = V(p^n), so p_2^⋆D_{−,ϵ} = V(p^{n(1−ϵ)}), which is strictly less than p_1^⋆D_{−,ϵ′} = V(p^{n(1−ϵ′)}).

These opens are nonempty. For example, when H is étale, the quotient by the multiplicative subgroup of order p again has étale image of H. More generally:
- (2) fails whenever some w_i > 0 (compare with the all-étale stratum).
- (3) fails whenever w ≠ Id (compare with w′ = Id).
So for every w at least one of the two fails. In these examples the two supports coincide, which is consistent with the corrected inclusions.

Why the inclusions hold. Let η be a generic point of a component of the special fibre of C_t^tor, and x_η the corresponding rank-1 point. Then η lies in supp p_2^⋆D_{+,ϵ′} if and only if p_2(x_η) ∉ U_{≥w−ϵ′}. By the choice of ϵ′ (Proposition 6.1.9 (1)), this forces p_1(x_η) ∉ U_{≥w−ϵ}, that is, η lies in supp p_1^⋆D_{+,ϵ}. Supports are unions of such components. The argument for D_− is the same, using T^t(U_{≤w+ϵ}) ⊆ U_{≤w+ϵ′}.

What uses the passage. Proposition 6.2.3 is never cited by number. It enters the proof of Theorem 6.2.9 (p. 62) in three ways:
- Through Proposition 2.10.4 (p. 30). This gives t̃ : RΓ_{D_{+,ϵ′},D_{−,ϵ}} → RΓ_{D_{+,ϵ},D_{−,ϵ′}}, whose hypotheses are the set inclusions above.
- Through Theorem 2.11.4 (pp. 31–33), with D″_± = D_{±,ϵ} and D′_± = D_{±,ϵ′}. Here Remark 2.11.2 again invokes Proposition 2.10.4, and the proof uses T : RΓ_{D′_+,D_−} → RΓ_{D″_+,D_−}. Both need only the inclusions. The corresponding hypotheses in §2.11 are printed with p̄_1 and p̄_2 interchanged; this is a separate slip.
- Through Theorem 2.11.4 (3). This needs the maps p_2^⋆O(D_+) → p_1^⋆O(D_+) and p_2^⋆O(−D_−) → p_1^⋆O(−D_−), which are the true first halves, together with (4).

Theorem 6.2.15 is proved "similarly". No stated result needs the false divisor inequalities.

review.reason: Confirmed as an error. Read as inequalities of divisors, which is how `$\geq$' is used in the rest of Proposition 6.2.3 and in Lemma 4.2.11, the second halves of (2) and (3) are false: part (1) of the same proposition gives $D_{+,\epsilon'}\geq D_{+,\epsilon}$, so $p_1^\star D_{+,\epsilon}\geq p_2^\star D_{+,\epsilon'}$ would force the pullback along $p_1$ of the smaller divisor to dominate the pullback along $p_2$ of the larger one, which the cited Proposition 6.1.9 and Lemma 4.2.11 do not give. What those results do give, and what §6.2 uses, is the corresponding inclusion of supports, i.e.\ the dynamical statement $T(\mathcal U_{\geq w-\epsilon})\subseteq\mathcal U_{\geq w-\epsilon'}$ transcribed to divisors. So the two clauses need to be weakened to inclusions.

sourceIssues.locator: §6.2.1, Proposition 6.2.2 (1)–(2) and the paragraph after its proof defining D_±, D_{±,ϵ}, D_{±,ϵ′}, p. 61
sourceIssues.printed: Proposition 6.2.2 (p. 61): "(1) for all 0 ≤ i ≤ g we have effective divisors Z_{i,>w_j} and Z_{i,<w_j} on S̃^{tor} with disjoint support, and Z_{i,>w_j} − Z_{i,<w_j} = Z_i − V(p^{nw_j}). (2) for all 0 ≤ i ≤ g and all η ∈ {ϵ, −ϵ, ϵ′, −ϵ′}, we have effective divisors Z_{i,>w_j+η} and Z_{i,<w_j+η} on S̃^{tor} with disjoint support, and Z_{i,>w_j+η} − Z_{i,<w_j+η} = Z_i − V(p^{n(w_j+η)})." Paragraph after the proof: "We change our notation and let S^{tor} be S̃^{tor}. We let D_+ = Σ_i Z_{i,<w_j}, D_− = Σ_i Z_{i,>w_j}, D_{+,ϵ} = Σ_i Z_{i,<w_j−ϵ}, D_{−,ϵ} = Σ_i Z_{i,>w_j+ϵ} D_{+,ϵ′} = Σ_i Z_{i,<w_j−ϵ′}, D_{−,ϵ′} = Σ_i Z_{i,>w_j+ϵ′}." (There is no comma before D_{+,ϵ′} in the printed text.)
sourceIssues.correction: Replace the subscript w_j by w_i throughout. Then Z_{i,>w_i} − Z_{i,<w_i} = Z_i − V(p^{nw_i}) and Z_{i,>w_i+η} − Z_{i,<w_i+η} = Z_i − V(p^{n(w_i+η)}). The divisors become D_+ = Σ_i Z_{i,<w_i}, D_− = Σ_i Z_{i,>w_i}, D_{+,ϵ} = Σ_i Z_{i,<w_i−ϵ}, D_{−,ϵ} = Σ_i Z_{i,>w_i+ϵ}, D_{+,ϵ′} = Σ_i Z_{i,<w_i−ϵ′} and D_{−,ϵ′} = Σ_i Z_{i,>w_i+ϵ′}. A comma is also missing before D_{+,ϵ′}.
sourceIssues.reason:
At high magnification the page shows the subscript w_j in every place quoted above. The index j is never bound. In the definitions of D_± and D_{±,ϵ}, D_{±,ϵ′} the sum runs over i only. This is the only place in the paper where w_j occurs. §6.2 fixes only w ∈ ^MW and t ∈ T^{++}(Q_p) (p. 61), and w_1, …, w_g is the sequence attached to w at the end of §3.1.

Several parts of the paper require w_i:
(a) Proposition 4.1.13(1) (p. 42) gives Z_{i,>j} − Z_{i,<j} = Z_i − V(p^{nj}) for 0 ≤ j ≤ i. Proposition 6.2.2 says its proof "is identical to the proof of proposition 4.1.13". Taking j = w_i is allowed there, because 0 ≤ w_i ≤ i.
(b) §4.4.1 (p. 50) sets D_{w,−} = ∪ Z_{i,>w_i} and D_{w,+} = ∪_i Z_{i,<w_i}. §4.5.6 (p. 52) recalls "D_{−,w} = Σ_{i=1}^g Z_{i,>w_i} and D_{+,w} = Σ_{i=1}^g Z_{i,<w_i}".
(c) §6.1.8 (p. 60) defines U_{≥w−ϵ} by deg H_{g+i}(x) ≥ n(w_i − ϵ) for all i.
(d) §6.2.8 (p. 62) writes "Z_{<w+ϵ} = ∩Z_{i,<w_i+ϵ}" and "U_{≥w−ϵ} = S^{tor} \ D_{+,ϵ}".

With w_i, the support of Z_{i,<w_i−ϵ} is the locus where deg H_{g+i} < n(w_i − ϵ). So S^{tor} \ D_{+,ϵ} is the locus where deg H_{g+i} ≥ n(w_i − ϵ) for all i, which is U_{≥w−ϵ} of §6.1.8, as §6.2.8 requires. No reading with one fixed j fits the sums over i.

The slip is purely notational and does not affect anything. Everything after it (Propositions 6.2.3–6.2.7 and Theorem 6.2.9, pp. 61–62) uses D_±, D_{±,ϵ}, D_{±,ϵ′} only in the w_i sense, as §6.2.8 makes explicit. The arguments cited for them (Proposition 6.1.9, Lemma 4.2.11, Lemma 4.4.2) are all stated with w_i. No result or proof changes. The published version could not be checked, since it is paywalled; this record refers to the authors' version.
