sourceIssues.locator: §6.2.1, Proposition 6.2.2(2) and its one-line proof, p. 61. The earlier preprint (build of 15 Jan 2024) has the same text.
sourceIssues.printed: Proposition 6.2.2. There exists a blow-up π : S̃^{tor} → S^{tor} satisfying the following properties: ... (2) for all 0 ≤ i ≤ g and all η ∈ {ϵ, −ϵ, ϵ′, −ϵ′}, we have effective divisors Z_{i,>w_j+η} and Z_{i,<w_j+η} on S̃^{tor} with disjoint support, and Z_{i,>w_j+η} − Z_{i,<w_j+η} = Z_i − V(p^{n(w_j+η)}). ... Proof. This is identical to the proof of proposition 4.1.13.
sourceIssues.correction: Choose an integer q ≥ 1 with q·n(w_i+η) ∈ Z for all i and all η ∈ {±ϵ, ±ϵ′}. Read V(p^{n(w_i+η)}) as the Q-Cartier divisor n(w_i+η)·V(p), and read Z_{i,>w_i+η} and Z_{i,<w_i+η} as effective Q-Cartier divisors. When n(w_i+η) ≤ 0, which happens only if w_i = 0 and η < 0, take Z_{i,<w_i+η} = 0, because the difference is already effective. Otherwise, apply Proposition-construction 4.1.11 to the Cartier divisors qZ_i and V(p^{q n(w_i+η)}). Locally this is the blow-up along (f^q, p^{qn(w_i+η)}), where f is a local equation of Z_i. Divide the two resulting divisors by q. Equivalently, keep the two Cartier divisors themselves: they have the same supports, and the identity holds after multiplying by q. The subscripts w_j in (1), (2) and in the definitions of D_±, D_{±,ϵ}, D_{±,ϵ′} should read w_i. This is a separate index slip. The reported correction is right and essentially minimal. The one addition needed is the case n(w_i+η) ≤ 0, where the "apply 4.1.11" form would involve a negative power of p.
sourceIssues.reason:
The model S^{tor} is a scheme over Spec Z_p: in 4.1.1, p. 41, it is defined as a normalisation of a product of the A_{g,d_i} × Spec Z_p. In §6.2.1 the numbers ϵ ∈ ]0,1[∩Q and ϵ′ ∈ ]0,ϵ[∩Q are arbitrary, and the level n is any element of Z_{≥0} (p. 41). Take n = 1. Then for every η ∈ {±ϵ, ±ϵ′} the exponent n(w_i+η) = w_i + η is not an integer, because the w_i are integers and 0 < |η| < 1. So p^{n(w_i+η)} is not a function on S^{tor}, and V(p^{n(w_i+η)}) is not an effective Cartier divisor in the sense of p. 7 (a closed subscheme V(I) with I invertible). Therefore no pair of effective Cartier divisors can satisfy the printed identity. The same happens for any n whenever nη is not an integer. Passing to Z_p(ζ_{p^n}), the ring used for the Nebentypus, does not help: its value group is (1/(p^{n−1}(p−1)))Z, and ϵ is an arbitrary rational.

The proof says it is "identical to the proof of proposition 4.1.13". That proof (p. 42) applies Proposition-construction 4.1.11, which is stated for effective Cartier divisors, to Z_{k+1} and V(p^{nj}) with j an integer. It does not cover a rational exponent. The missing step is to scale by a common denominator q as in the correction. On the blow-up of the ideal locally generated by (f^q, p^{qn(w_i+η)}), where f is a local equation of Z_i, one of the two generators divides the other, and the quotients generate the unit ideal. This gives E_>, E_< with disjoint support, and dividing by q gives the Q-divisors.

This intended reading fits the rest of the paper. The adic definition on p. 60 already uses rational exponents: U_{≥w−ϵ} is defined by |f_{g+i}|_x ≤ |p^{n(w_i−ϵ)}|_x. Rational multiples of divisors also appear without comment in Lemma 4.4.2 ("there exists 0 < s < 1 such that s p_1^⋆Z_{i,<w_i} ≥ p_2^⋆Z_{i,<w_i}") and in Proposition 6.2.3(4) (s ∈ ]0,1[∩Q). Later the divisors D_{±,ϵ} and D_{±,ϵ′} are used only through their supports (U_{≥w−ϵ} = S^{tor} \ D_{+,ϵ}, and cohomology with supports) and through the inequalities of Proposition 6.2.3. Both make sense for Q-divisors, or after replacing each divisor by q times itself. So the statement as printed is not meaningful, and its cited proof does not apply literally, but the repair is routine and no result changes. Why the statement is not meaningful as printed:
- The w_i are integers (bottom of §3.1, recalled before Corollary 4.1.14).
- ϵ is an arbitrary rational in ]0,1[. Theorem 6.2.9 is stated for every such ϵ.
- ϵ′ is not free either. By Proposition 6.1.9(1) the admissible ϵ′ fill an interval ending at ϵ, but that interval need not contain a point of (1/n)Z. For n = 1, no ϵ in ]0,1[ has nϵ ∈ Z at all.
- So n(w_i+η) is in general not an integer.
- S^tor is a scheme over Z_p: it is the normalisation in §4.1, and with a nebentypus the base is Z_p(ζ_{p^n}). A rational power of p is not a function on it, so V(p^{n(w_i+η)}) is not a closed subscheme.
- In the paper, "divisor" always means a closed subscheme, Cartier or locally principal (§2.1.14). The only rational coefficients the paper allows are in the relation D ≤ sD′ of Definition 2.1.15(2). It never defines Q-divisors.
- Every other occurrence of V(p^·) in the paper has integer exponent nj with 0 ≤ j ≤ i: Proposition 4.1.13, its proof, and Lemma 4.2.11.

Why the cited proof does not literally cover it: the proof of Proposition 4.1.13 applies Proposition-construction 4.1.11 "to the divisors Z_{k+1} and V(p^{nj})". Proposition-construction 4.1.11 is stated only for effective Cartier divisors D_1, D_2. So "identical to the proof of proposition 4.1.13" does not apply as written.

The defence, and why it succeeds only as a repair. The intended meaning is clear from §6.1.8, where U_{≥w−ϵ} is defined by |f_{g+i}|_x ≤ |p^{n(w_i−ϵ)}|_x. That is a meaningful condition on rank-one points. The repair described in the correction works:
- Blowing up (f^q, p^m) with m = qn(w_i+η) gives disjoint-support Cartier divisors whose difference is qZ_i − V(p^m).
- Point (3) survives. By the proof of Proposition 4.1.13, Z_i = V(p^{nw_i}) on the open S̃_{=w_1,…,w_g}. There the ideal (f^q, p^m) is generated by a power of p times a unit, so the extra blow-up is an isomorphism over it.

What later uses the passage:
- The divisors D_{±,ϵ} and D_{±,ϵ′} defined just below it on p. 61.
- Proposition 6.2.3(1)–(3). These inequalities follow as in Lemma 4.2.11, either with Q-coefficients or after multiplying by q, which is compatible with Definition 2.1.15(2).
- The open C_t^tor \ (p_1^⋆D_{+,ϵ} ∪ p_2^⋆D_{−,ϵ}) in Proposition 6.2.7.
- Z_{<w+ϵ} and U_{≥w−ϵ} = S^tor \ D_{+,ϵ} in §6.2.8.
- The support conditions RΓ_{D_{+,ϵ},D_{−,ϵ′}} in the proof of Theorem 6.2.9.

All of these use only the supports of the divisors, or inequalities that are unchanged by rescaling. Lemma 2.10.2 and Proposition 2.10.4 need only closed subschemes and containments of supports. The integral model ω̃^κ(χ) = ω^κ(χ)(m(D_+ − D_−)) and Proposition 6.2.3(4) use only D_±, which are built from the integers w_i. So Theorem 6.2.9 and Corollary 6.2.10 are unaffected.

Classification: this is an unjustified step with a routine repair, and no result changes. Hence a gap that affects nothing.

sourceIssues.correction:
(1) Reduction to T^{++}. Replace "as they generate T(Q_p) as a group" with a cone argument. Let λ be a character of T^+ on the finite slope cohomology. For Conjecture 5.9.2 put β = w^{-1}w_{0,M}(κ+ρ)+ρ, and for Conjecture 6.8.1 put β = 0. Let f(t) = v(λ(t)) − ⟨v(t), β⟩. Then f is additive on T^+. Take t ∈ T^+ and t_0 ∈ T^{++}. For every m ≥ 1, v(t^m t_0) = m·v(t) + v(t_0) is regular dominant, so t^m t_0 ∈ T^{++}. Theorem 6.2.9 (resp. 6.2.15(2)), applied with t^m t_0 as the element of T^{++} fixed in §6.2, gives m·f(t) + f(t_0) ≥ 0 for all m, and hence f(t) ≥ 0. Put differently, f(t) = ⟨v(t), v(λ) − β⟩ is a linear form in v(t) that is ≥ 0 on v(T^{++}). The positive multiples of v(T^{++}) are dense in the closed dominant cone, which contains v(T^+), so the form is ≥ 0 on v(T^+).

(2) The cuspidal '+' theories. Before the two corollaries, state the cuspidal analogues of Theorems 6.2.9 and 6.2.15. These are the same statements for ω̃^κ(χ)(−D) and F̃^{ν_A,n}(−D), with the cuspidal higher Hida theory as ordinary part, and they are proved in the same way. Here D is the boundary divisor of the toroidal compactification, as in the definition of cuspidal higher Hida theory in §4.4; it is not one of the divisors D_± of §6.2. Together with the theorems as printed, these analogues give part (1) of [BP21] Conjectures 5.9.2 and 6.8.1 (the bound for characters of T^+ on the '+' theories), for both the non-cuspidal and the cuspidal theories.

(3) Part (2). Add the deduction of part (2) of both conjectures (the bound for characters of T^− on the '−' theories) from part (1), using the Serre duality of [BP21]: Theorems 5.7.1–5.7.2 in the coherent case, and 6.7.1–6.7.2 in the locally analytic case. Put κ^∨ = −2ρ_nc − w_{0,M}κ. The pairing H^i_w(K^p,κ,χ,cusp)^{±,fs} × H^{d−i}_w(K^p,κ^∨,χ^{-1})^{∓,fs} → F is perfect on generalized eigenspaces, and t is adjoint to t^{-1}. So a character λ of T^+ on one side corresponds to a character λ' = λ∘inv of T^− on the other, and v(λ') = −v(λ). Since w_{0,M}ρ = 2ρ_nc − ρ, we have κ^∨ + ρ = −w_{0,M}(κ+ρ). Hence the part (1) bound at κ is exactly the part (2) bound at κ^∨, and conversely ([BP21] Remark 5.9.5). For Conjecture 6.8.1 both bounds are 0, and duality turns v ≥ 0 on T^+ into v ≤ 0 on T^−. Duality pairs cuspidal with non-cuspidal theories, so (2) is needed here. Without it, the printed theorems give part (2) only for the cuspidal '−' theories.

(4) The proof of Corollary 6.2.10 and the sentence before Corollary 6.2.16 should stop describing each conjecture as a statement about T^+ alone.
sourceIssues.reason:
[BP21] is cited as arXiv:2110.10251. Version v1 (19 October 2021) is used here, and its numbering matches every [BP21] reference in §6.2.

What is conjectured. Conjecture 5.9.2 of [BP21] has two parts, and each is asserted for both the non-cuspidal and the cuspidal theory:
(1) every character λ of T^+ on RΓ_w(K^p,κ,χ)^{+,fs} or RΓ_w(K^p,κ,χ,cusp)^{+,fs} satisfies v(λ) ≥ w^{-1}w_{0,M}(κ+ρ)+ρ;
(2) every character λ of T^− on RΓ_w(K^p,κ,χ)^{−,fs} or RΓ_w(K^p,κ,χ,cusp)^{−,fs} satisfies v(λ) ≤ w^{-1}(κ+ρ)−ρ.
Conjecture 6.8.1 makes the same four assertions for RΓ_{w,an}(K^p,ν)^{±,fs} and its cuspidal version, with bounds v(λ) ≥ 0 and v(λ) ≤ 0. By [BP21] Remark 5.9.3, both parts are lower bounds on slopes: part (2) means v(λ(t)) ≥ ⟨v(t), w^{-1}(κ+ρ)−ρ⟩ for all t ∈ T^−. So Theorem 1.4.10 ("The lower bounds on slopes of conjectures 5.9.2 and 6.8.1") claims both parts in full. It is not a narrower statement.

What the proofs cover. The proof on p. 62 describes the conjecture as a statement about t ∈ T^+ only, and so does the sentence before Corollary 6.2.16 on p. 64. Both proofs appeal only to Theorems 6.2.9(3) and 6.2.15(2). Those give a lattice in the cohomology of ω^κ(χ), resp. F̃^{ν,n}, with the '+' support condition (U_{≥w−ε}, Z_{<w+ε}) and with t ∈ T^{++} acting. Propositions 6.1.7, 6.1.10 and 6.1.11 compare this cohomology with the '+' theory of [BP21]. There is no (−D) twist, so this is the non-cuspidal '+' theory. Section 6 contains no '−' support condition, no T^− and no cuspidal sheaf. Remark 6.2.18 uses duality, but only for vanishing. So as written, each proof establishes one of the four assertions of its conjecture: part (1) for the non-cuspidal theory. In the same way, the proof of Corollary 6.2.17 (p. 64) derives the amplitude of M^•_{w,cusp} ⊗ Q_p "from 6.2.15", although 6.2.15 is stated only for the non-cuspidal sheaf. There too the cuspidal case is left implicit.

Duality supplies only some of part (2). The locally analytic pairing of [BP21] Theorems 6.7.1–6.7.2 behaves in the same way as the coherent one. In the coherent case, w_{0,M}ρ_M = −ρ_M and w_{0,M}ρ_nc = ρ_nc, so w_{0,M}ρ = 2ρ_nc − ρ. Hence (−2ρ_nc − w_{0,M}κ) + ρ = −w_{0,M}(κ+ρ). Now take κ^∨ = −2ρ_nc − w_{0,M}κ and s = t^{-1} ∈ T^−. In the form of Remark 5.9.3, the part (2) bound at κ^∨ is v(λ'(s)) ≥ ⟨v(s), w^{-1}(κ^∨+ρ)−ρ⟩. This reads v(λ(t)) ≥ ⟨v(t), w^{-1}w_{0,M}(κ+ρ)+ρ⟩, which is part (1) at κ. Since ρ_nc is W_M-invariant, κ ↦ κ^∨ is an involution of X^*(T^c)^{M_μ,+}, so every weight is covered. However, the pairing matches cuspidal '±' with non-cuspidal '∓'. From the printed theorems it therefore yields part (2) only for the cuspidal '−' theories. Theorems 6.2.9 and 6.2.15 as stated do not cover the cuspidal '+' case of part (1), nor therefore, through duality, the non-cuspidal '−' case of part (2). Both need the cuspidal analogues of those theorems. The paper never states these analogues. They follow by the same argument, because the integral models and the higher Hida theory of §4.4–§5 are also set up for cuspidal cohomology.

The reduction to T^{++}. The stated reason does not justify the reduction. Suppose a lower bound on slopes holds for t_1 and t_2. That says nothing about t_1 t_2^{-1}. And every t ∈ T^+ with v(t) on a wall of the dominant cone has this form with t_1, t_2 ∈ T^{++}: take any t_2 ∈ T^{++} and t_1 = t·t_2. [BP21] §5.9 defines the slope v(λ) of a T^±-character by extending λ to T(Q_p) ("recall that T(Q_p) is generated by the monoids T^±"). So group generation does show that v(λ) is a linear form determined by its values on T^{++}. But the inequality needs one more fact: the positive multiples of v(T^{++}) are dense in the closed dominant cone. The bound then passes to T^+ by linearity and continuity, as in (1) of the correction. The sentence on p. 62 does not say this, and the proof of Corollary 6.2.16 gives no reason at all. The reduction itself cannot be skipped, since §6.2 fixes t ∈ T^{++} (p. 61) and builds its integral models from that choice. So Theorems 6.2.9 and 6.2.15 say nothing directly about t on a wall.

Why only the proof is affected. Later statements use the corollaries at full strength:
- Theorem 1.4.10 (p. 6), and the paragraph after it. That paragraph replaces "strongly small slope" by "small slope" in [BP21] 5.12.3, 6.8.4 and 5.12.20.
- The remark after Corollary 6.2.10 (p. 62). It replaces "strongly small slope" by "small slope" in [BP21] Theorems 5.12.3, 5.12.5 and 5.12.11. All three are stated for both signs ±. Theorems 5.12.3 and 5.12.5 cover cuspidal and non-cuspidal coherent cohomology, and 5.12.11 covers ordinary, compactly supported and interior Betti cohomology. Theorem 1.5.1 is deduced from these on p. 62.
- The remark after Corollary 6.2.16 (p. 64). It improves [BP21] Corollary 6.8.4 and Theorem 6.9.3(2). Corollary 6.8.4 includes a '−' morphism and the cuspidal versions (see [BP21] Remark 6.8.5).
All the missing steps are routine: the cone argument, the cuspidal analogues, and then duality. With them, the two corollaries and all of these consequences hold, so no stated result is lost. Only the written proofs are incomplete.

sourceIssues.printed: Theorem 6.2.9(3): "… the image of RΓ_{𝒵_{<w+ϵ}∩𝒰_{≥w−ϵ}}(𝒰_{≥w−ϵ}, ω^κ(χ))^{int} in RΓ_{𝒵_{<w+ϵ}∩𝒰_{≥w−ϵ}}(𝒰_{≥w−ϵ}, ω^κ(χ))^{≤h} is a ℤ_p-lattice. (Here the superscript ≤ h means the slope ≤ h part for any t ∈ T^{++}(ℚ_p) and h ∈ ℚ. This is a finite dimensional ℚ_p-vector space.)" The proof ends: "That this gives a lattice in the finite slope part of cohomology is a consequence of [BP21] lem. 5.9.10 (which explains how to construct lattices)."
sourceIssues.correction: Replace "a lattice in the finite slope part of cohomology" by "a ℤ_p-lattice in the slope ≤ h part of cohomology, for every h ∈ ℚ". The sentence then reads: "That the image of RΓ_{𝒵_{<w+ϵ}∩𝒰_{≥w−ϵ}}(𝒰_{≥w−ϵ}, ω^κ(χ))^{int} in RΓ_{𝒵_{<w+ϵ}∩𝒰_{≥w−ϵ}}(𝒰_{≥w−ϵ}, ω^κ(χ))^{≤h} is a ℤ_p-lattice for every h ∈ ℚ is a consequence of [BP21] lem. 5.9.10 (which explains how to construct lattices)." More precisely, it follows from the first step of that lemma's proof, which works one slope ≤ h part at a time.
sourceIssues.reason:
The proof's last sentence names a different space from the one in the statement. Theorem 6.2.9(3), as printed on p. 62, is about the slope ≤ h part, and the statement itself notes that this part is a finite-dimensional ℚ_p-vector space. The 2024 preprint stated (3) for the finite slope part (superscript fs) instead. The statement was later changed, but this sentence of the proof was not.

The two spaces differ. Proposition 6.1.4 takes the finite slope part from [BP21], sect. 5.1.1, where it is the projective limit of the slope ≤ h parts over all h. This space is in general infinite-dimensional: already for g = 1 it contains the finite slope overconvergent modular forms of a given weight. So there cannot be a ℤ_p-lattice there in the sense of (3), meaning a finitely generated submodule that spans the space.

The best defence of the wording is that [BP21] Lemma 5.9.10 is itself stated for the finite slope part. It says that the image there is an "open and bounded submodule". On that reading, "a lattice in the finite slope part" can only mean that the projection of the integral cohomology to every slope ≤ h part is a lattice, which is (3) for every h. This is also the order of the argument in the cited proof. It first shows, for each h, that the image in the slope ≤ h part is open and bounded (a lattice, since that part is finite-dimensional), and only then "passes to the limit over h".

So the intended meaning is clear and the mathematics is unaffected. The slope ≤ h form for every h is also all that Corollary 6.2.10 uses, since every eigenvalue of t on the finite slope cohomology occurs in some slope ≤ h part. Theorem 6.2.15(2), whose proof is "similar to the proof of theorem 6.2.9", was changed from the finite slope part to the slope ≤ h part in the same way, and the corrected sentence covers it too. The citation still supplies what the statement needs: the proof of [BP21] Lemma 5.9.10 first shows, for every h, that the image in the slope ≤ h part is open and bounded, and only then passes to the finite slope part. So the intended meaning is clear, and nothing depends on the wording.

sourceIssues.locator: §6.2.11 (Big sheaves), definition of 𝓘𝒲_n, p. 63. The 2024 preprint has the same text (p. 61).
sourceIssues.printed: We let 𝓘𝒲_n → Spa(Q_p, Z_p) be the group defined by 𝓘𝒲_n(C, C^+) = {x ∈ M(C^+), x mod p^n ∈ M_{K_{p,P}}}.
sourceIssues.correction: 𝓘𝒲_n(C, C^+) = {x ∈ M(C^+) : x mod p^n lies in the image of M_{K_{p,P}} ⊆ M(Z_p) in M(Z/p^nZ) ↪ M(C^+/p^nC^+)}.
sourceIssues.reason: x mod p^n is an element of M(C^+/p^nC^+). On p. 37, M_{K_{p,P}} is defined as K_{p,P} ∩ M(Q_p), a compact subgroup of M(Q_p). Since K_{p,P} = wK_{p,n}w^{−1} ∩ P(Q_p) and K_{p,n} ⊆ G(Z_p), this subgroup lies in M(Z_p). So the printed membership does not make sense as written. The intended reading is 'lies in the reduction of M_{K_{p,P}}', parallel to the definition of 𝒯_n one sentence earlier, which inserts T(Z/p^nZ) ↪ T(C^+/p^nC^+) explicitly. The corrected definition is consistent. K_{p,n} is the full preimage of B(Z/p^nZ), so M_{K_{p,P}} contains the kernel of reduction mod p^n and is determined by its image mod p^n. Also M_{K_{p,P}} ∩ T = T(Z_p), so the torus of 𝓘𝒲_n is 𝒯_n, as the text asserts ('with torus 𝔗_n'). This is a mild, common abuse of notation rather than a substantive slip, which is why confidence is only medium that it deserves recording.

sourceIssues.reason: In [BP21] (G. Boxer, V. Pilloni, Higher Coleman theory, arXiv:2110.10251, cited in the bibliography on p. 64), the numbered item 6.3.10 is a lemma, not a section. sourceIssues.locator: §6.2.11, Proposition 6.2.13, p. 63
sourceIssues.printed: Proposition 6.2.13 (p. 63), statement: "The map RΓ_{D_+,D_−}(S^{tor}_{w,Z/p^rZ}, 𝓕_r^{ν_A,n}) → RΓ_{D_+,D_−}(S^{tor}_{w,Z/p^rZ}, 𝓕_r^{ν_A}) induces a quasi-isomorphism on the ordinary part. Moreover, RΓ_{D_+,D_−}(S^{tor}_{w,Z/p^rZ}, 𝓕_r^{ν_A})^{ord} = M_w^• ⊗ A/p^n" (no final period). Proof, same page: "The property that RΓ_{D_+,D_−}(S^{tor}_{w,Z/p^rZ}, 𝓕_r^{ν_A})^{ord} = M_w^•⊗A/p^r follows from the definition. See remark 5.4.3."
sourceIssues.correction: Moreover, RΓ_{D_+,D_−}(S^{tor}_{w,Z/p^rZ}, 𝓕_r^{ν_A})^{ord} = M_w^• ⊗_Λ A/p^r, as in the proof.
sourceIssues.reason: Checked on the page image at high resolution. The statement ends in "A/p^n" and the proof, a few lines below, has "A/p^r". In §6.2.11 (p. 63), n is the analyticity level. It is fixed ("For n large enough, the character ν_A extends to a character 𝔗_n → 𝔊_m × Spf A") and indexes 𝒯_n, 𝔗_n, 𝓘𝓦_n, 𝔅𝔍𝔚_n and K_{p,n}. The index r is the reduction level: "We let 𝓕_r^{κ_A,n} and 𝓕_r^{ν_A} be the sheaves obtained by reduction modulo p^r", and Proposition 6.2.12 holds "for any r ≥ 0". The left side of Proposition 6.2.13 is the ordinary part of the cohomology of a sheaf of A/p^r-modules on S^{tor}_{w,Z/p^rZ}, so its cohomology is killed by p^r. Nothing in the statement ties n to r, so the right side cannot in general be M_w^• ⊗ A/p^n for a fixed n while r varies. The fixed-weight analogue in the proof of Theorem 6.2.9 (p. 62) reduces to the same level as the coefficients: "the ordinary part of these cohomologies further identifies with RΓ_w(K^p, κ, χ)⊗_{Z_p} Z/p^sZ". Theorem 6.2.15(1) (p. 64) defines RΓ(…, 𝔉̃^{ν_A,n})^{int} as lim_r of the mod-p^r cohomologies and identifies its ordinary part with "M_w^• ⊗_Λ A". That is the limit over r of M_w^• ⊗_Λ A/p^r, so it needs the p^r version, which is what the proof of Proposition 6.2.13 states. Remark 5.4.3 (p. 57), cited in the proof, uses n in a different sense (Z_p(ζ_{p^n}) for finite-order characters); that is not relevant here. The ⊗ in the statement is over Λ, as in Theorem 6.2.15(1). This is a one-letter slip in the statement. The intended assertion is given correctly in its own proof and used correctly downstream, so no proof or later result is affected.

sourceIssues.locator: §6.2.11 (Big sheaves), p. 63: the definition of π′, the displays defining 𝔉^{ν_A} and 𝔉^{ν_A,n}, the sentence just before Proposition 6.2.12, and Proposition 6.2.14. Also the proof of Proposition 6.2.14, p. 64. The January 2024 preprint has the same text (p. 61).
sourceIssues.printed:
p. 63: "We also let K_{p,P} = wK_{p,n}w^{−1} ∩ P(Q_p). … The M_{K_{p,P}}-torsor π : 𝔍𝔊_{U_{K_{p,P}}} → 𝔍𝔊_{K_{p,P}} = 𝔖^{tor}_w can be pushed to a 𝔍𝔚_n-torsor π′ : 𝔍𝔊_{U_{K_p}} ×^{M_{K_{p,n}}} 𝔍𝔚_n → 𝔍𝔊_{K_{p,n}}. We let 𝔉^{ν_A} = (π_⋆𝒪_{𝔍𝔊_{U_{K_{p,P}}}} ⊗̂ A)^{B_{K_{p,n}} = −w_{0,M}κ_A}. We let 𝔉^{ν_A,n} = (π′_⋆𝒪_{𝔍𝔊_{U_{K_p}} ×^{M_{K_{p,n}}} 𝔍𝔚_n} ⊗̂ A)^{𝔅𝔍𝔚_n = −w_{0,M}κ_A}. We have a canonical restriction map 𝔉^{ν_A,n} → 𝔉^{ν_A}. We let ℱ_r^{κ_A,n} and ℱ_r^{ν_A} be the sheaves obtained by reduction modulo p^r."
Proposition 6.2.14 (p. 63): "For ε sufficiently small, the sheaf 𝔉^{ν_A,n} extends to a sheaf 𝔉̃^{ν_A,n} over 𝔘̃_{[w−ϵ,w+ϵ]} where 𝔘̃_{[w−ϵ,w+ϵ]} → 𝔘_{[w−ϵ,w+ϵ]} is a further blow-up away from 𝔖^{tor}_w, and moreover for all r > 0 we have cohomological correspondences p_2^⋆ℱ̃_r^{ν_A,n} → p_1^!ℱ̃_r^{ν_A,n} which furthermore factor as p_2^⋆ℱ̃_r^{ν_A,n} → p_2^⋆ℱ̃_r^{ν_A,n}(D_+) → p_1^!ℱ̃_r^{ν_A,n}(−D_−) → p_1^!ℱ̃_r^{ν_A,n}."
Proof (p. 64): "The blow-up 𝔘̃_{[w−ϵ,w+ϵ]} and the sheaf 𝔉̃^{ν_A,n} over 𝔘̃_{[w−ϵ,w+ϵ]} are constructed as in the proof of lem. 6.6.2 of [BP21]."
sourceIssues.correction:
(a) The torsor π′. Read π′ : 𝔍𝔊_{U_{K_{p,P}}} ×^{M_{K_{p,P}}} 𝔍𝔚_n → 𝔍𝔊_{K_{p,P}} = 𝔖^{tor}_w, and make the same change in the subscript of 𝒪 in the display defining 𝔉^{ν_A,n}. That is, replace U_{K_p}, M_{K_{p,n}} and 𝔍𝔊_{K_{p,n}} by U_{K_{p,P}}, M_{K_{p,P}} and 𝔍𝔊_{K_{p,P}}.
(b) The invariance group. In the display defining 𝔉^{ν_A}, the invariance condition is for the Borel subgroup B_M(Z_p) = B ∩ M_{K_{p,P}} of M_{K_{p,P}}, not for B_{K_{p,n}}. This group is the image in M of the group written B_{K_{p,P}} in §5.
(c) The reduced sheaves. Read "We let ℱ_r^{ν_A,n} and ℱ_r^{ν_A} be the sheaves obtained by reduction modulo p^r."
(d) The formal open. Add a definition before Proposition 6.2.14. Use the notation of §6.2.1: S^{tor} now denotes the blow-up S̃^{tor} of Proposition 6.2.2, and 𝔖^{tor} is its p-adic completion. Let 𝔘_{[w−ϵ,w+ϵ]} = 𝔖^{tor} ∖ (D_{+,ϵ} ∪ D_{−,ϵ}). This is the formal open whose generic fibre is 𝒰_{≥w−ϵ} ∩ 𝒰_{≤w+ϵ}.
Also state that the ϵ fixed in §6.2.1 is from now on taken small enough for Proposition 6.2.14, and write ϵ for ε in the first line of that proposition. The smallness is already tacit in the definition before Theorem 6.2.15 and in that theorem.
With this definition, the correspondences live on the modification, lying over 𝔘̃_{[w−ϵ,w+ϵ]}, of the open C_t^{tor} ∖ (p_1^⋆D_{+,ϵ} ∪ p_2^⋆D_{−,ϵ}) of Proposition 6.2.7. No separate statement about this is needed.
sourceIssues.reason:
(1) The base and total space of π′. By §4.1 (p. 40), K_{p,n} is the Iwahori subgroup of G(Z_p) of matrices that reduce modulo p^n into B(Z/p^nZ). It is not contained in P(Q_p). Igusa varieties 𝔍𝔊_{K_{p,P}} are defined only for compact open subgroups K_{p,P} of P′(Q_p) (§3.4.5, pp. 36–37), so 𝔍𝔊_{K_{p,n}} has no meaning.
Nor can K_{p,n} be read as K_{p,n} ∩ P(Q_p). By Lemma 4.1.7 (p. 41), 𝔖^{tor}_w = 𝔍𝔊_{K_{p,P,w}} with K_{p,P,w} = wK_{p,n}w^{−1} ∩ P(Q_p). This is the group K_{p,P} of §6.2.11. Since w is a minimal length representative of W_M\W, w^{−1} sends the positive roots of M to positive roots. So for w ≠ 1 there is a root α of U_P with w^{−1}α < 0. Then K_{p,P} meets U_α in U_α(p^nZ_p), whereas K_{p,n} ∩ P(Q_p) contains U_α(Z_p). Here n ≥ 1, since n is large in §6.2.11.
The symbol U_{K_p} is not defined in §6 either. In §1 (pp. 3, 5) it denotes the unipotent factor of an Iwahori decomposition K_p = U_{K_p} × T_{K_p} × Ū_{K_p} of a subgroup of G(Q_p), which is a different object.
π′ is the push-out of the M_{K_{p,P}}-torsor π along M_{K_{p,P}} → 𝔍𝔚_n, and a push-out keeps its base. So the base is 𝔍𝔊_{K_{p,P}} = 𝔖^{tor}_w and the total space is 𝔍𝔊_{U_{K_{p,P}}} ×^{M_{K_{p,P}}} 𝔍𝔚_n. The text confirms this in three places:
- the "canonical restriction map 𝔉^{ν_A,n} → 𝔉^{ν_A}" needs both sheaves on one base;
- Proposition 6.2.13 takes cohomology of ℱ_r^{ν_A,n} on S^{tor}_{w,Z/p^rZ};
- the proof of Proposition 6.2.14 (p. 64) speaks of "the 𝔍𝔚_n-torsor on 𝔖^{tor}_w".
The subscript in M_{K_{p,n}} does no mathematical harm. With the convention M_K = K ∩ M(Q_p) of p. 37, M_{K_{p,n}} is the depth-n Iwahori subgroup of M(Z_p), that is, the set of m with m mod p^n ∈ B_M. This is the same group as M_{K_{p,P}} = wK_{p,n}w^{−1} ∩ M(Q_p). Indeed, m ∈ M(Z_p) lies in wK_{p,n}w^{−1} if and only if m mod p^n ∈ wBw^{−1} ∩ M, and wBw^{−1} ∩ M = B_M because w^{−1} sends the positive roots of M to positive roots. The notation is still inconsistent with that of π.

(2) The group B_{K_{p,n}} in the definition of 𝔉^{ν_A}. The symbol is defined, but it names the wrong group. The Iwahori decomposition K_{p,n} = B_{K_{p,n}} × U^{op}_{K_{p,n}} on p. 61 gives B_{K_{p,n}} = B(Z_p). The group that acts on the sheaf π_⋆𝒪_{𝔍𝔊_{U_{K_{p,P}}}} over 𝔖^{tor}_w is the structure group M_{K_{p,P}} of π (Proposition 3.4.9(5), p. 37). So the invariance condition must be for a subgroup of M_{K_{p,P}}. B(Z_p) is not one. It is not contained in M(Q_p), and for w ≠ 1 it is not even contained in K_{p,P}. Indeed, for the root α of (1), U_α(Z_p) ⊂ B(Z_p) but w^{−1}U_α(Z_p)w = U_{w^{−1}α}(Z_p) ⊄ K_{p,n}. The intended group is B_M(Z_p) = B ∩ M_{K_{p,P}}, the image in M of B ∩ K_{p,P}. In §5 the corresponding group is written B_{K_{p,P}} and acts through this image: Remark 5.4.3 (p. 57) calls T_w(Z_p) "the diagonal torus of B_{K_{p,P}}". As with the subscripts in (1), K_{p,n} is written where K_{p,P} is meant.

(3) ℱ_r^{κ_A,n}. The sheaves reduced modulo p^r are the two just defined, 𝔉^{ν_A,n} and 𝔉^{ν_A}. The notation ℱ_r^{ν_A,n} is used from then on:
- in both diagrams of Proposition 6.2.12 and its proof;
- in Proposition 6.2.13 and its proof (the map ℱ_r^{ν_A,n} → ℱ_r^{ν_A});
- in Proposition 6.2.14.
The superscript κ_A is a slip, presumably prompted by the weight κ_A = −w_{0,M}w(ν_A+ρ)−ρ that appears in the invariance conditions.

(4) 𝔘_{[w−ϵ,w+ϵ]}. This symbol and its blow-up 𝔘̃_{[w−ϵ,w+ϵ]} occur only in Proposition 6.2.14 and the first line of its proof. They are defined nowhere, and the paper uses no other interval subscript 𝒰_{[·,·]}, U_{[·,·]} or 𝔘_{[·,·]}. The only sets defined by degree conditions are:
- the opens 𝒰_{≥w−ϵ} and 𝒰_{≤w+ϵ} and the closed sets 𝒵_{<w+ϵ} and 𝒵_{>w−ϵ} (§6.1.8, p. 60);
- integrally, U_{≥w−ϵ} = S^{tor} ∖ D_{+,ϵ} and Ẑ_{<w+ϵ} (§6.2.8, p. 62).
The proof cites [BP21] (Higher Coleman theory), Lemma 6.6.2, which does not supply the notation. Its proof builds formal models of π_{HT}^{−1}(U) for affinoid opens U ⊆ ]C_{w,k}[_{n,n}K_p of the flag variety, not for opens cut out by degree conditions.
The statement does not say over which part of C_t^{tor} the correspondences and their factorisation through D_± live.
The phrase "For ε sufficiently small" puts a new condition on the ϵ already fixed in §6.2.1 (p. 61, "Let ϵ ∈ ]0,1[∩Q"). It is also printed with a different glyph (ε, against ϵ in the subscripts). Theorem 6.2.15 uses the same ϵ with no smallness condition. Yet its complex RΓ_{𝒵_{<w+ϵ}∩𝒰_{≥w−ϵ}}(𝒰_{≥w−ϵ}, 𝔉̃^{ν_A,n})^{int} makes sense only when 𝔉̃^{ν_A,n} exists, that is, only for such ϵ.
The intended meaning can be recovered. The reading 𝔘 = 𝔖^{tor} ∖ (D_{+,ϵ} ∪ D_{−,ϵ}) is the one the notation and its uses require. Here D_{+,ϵ} = Σ_i Z_{i,<w_i−ϵ} and D_{−,ϵ} = Σ_i Z_{i,>w_i+ϵ} (p. 61), with Z_i as in §4.1.12 (p. 42). The following checks use Proposition 4.1.13 and Corollary 4.1.14 (p. 42) and the definitions and results on pp. 59–62.
- Generic fibre. Proposition 6.2.2(2) gives Z_{i,>w_i+η} − Z_{i,<w_i+η} = Z_i − V(p^{n(w_i+η)}), with disjoint supports. So off Z_{i,<w_i−ϵ} we have Z_i ≥ V(p^{n(w_i−ϵ)}), and off Z_{i,>w_i+ϵ} we have Z_i ≤ V(p^{n(w_i+ϵ)}). These are the conditions deg H_{g+i} ≥ n(w_i−ϵ) and deg H_{g+i} ≤ n(w_i+ϵ) of §6.1.8. So the generic fibre of 𝔘 is 𝒰_{≥w−ϵ} ∩ 𝒰_{≤w+ϵ}, matching U_{≥w−ϵ} = S^{tor} ∖ D_{+,ϵ} in §6.2.8.
- 𝔘 contains 𝔖^{tor}_w. By Proposition 4.1.13(2) and Corollary 4.1.14 (p. 42), 𝔖^{tor}_w is the open where all Z_{i,>w_i} and Z_{i,<w_i} vanish, so the degrees there are exactly nw_i, that is, Z_i = V(p^{nw_i}). Hence Z_{i,>w_i−ϵ} − Z_{i,<w_i−ϵ} = V(p^{nϵ}) there. Since the two divisors have disjoint supports, Z_{i,<w_i−ϵ} vanishes on 𝔖^{tor}_w, and likewise Z_{i,>w_i+ϵ}. So D_{+,ϵ} and D_{−,ϵ} vanish there, and "extends" makes sense.
- The support in the definition before Theorem 6.2.15 lies in 𝔘. The supports of Z_{i,<w_i+ϵ} and Z_{i,>w_i+ϵ} are disjoint, so Ẑ_{<w+ϵ} = ∩_i Z_{i,<w_i+ϵ} misses D_{−,ϵ}. Hence Ẑ_{<w+ϵ} ∩ U_{≥w−ϵ} is a closed subset of U_{≥w−ϵ} that lies inside 𝔘. By excision, RΓ_{Ẑ_{<w+ϵ}∩U_{≥w−ϵ,Z/p^rZ}}(U_{≥w−ϵ,Z/p^rZ}, ℱ̃_r^{ν_A,n}) is meaningful even though its sheaf lives only on 𝔘̃: it is cohomology on 𝔘̃ with support in the preimage.
- The domain of the correspondences. Only supports matter here. By Proposition 6.2.3(1), supp D_{+,ϵ} ⊆ supp D_{+,ϵ′} and supp D_{−,ϵ} ⊆ supp D_{−,ϵ′}. The choice of ϵ′ in §6.2.1 gives T(𝒰_{≥w−ϵ}) ⊆ 𝒰_{≥w−ϵ′} and T^t(𝒰_{≤w+ϵ}) ⊆ 𝒰_{≤w+ϵ′}. So supp p_2^⋆D_{+,ϵ′} ⊆ supp p_1^⋆D_{+,ϵ} and supp p_1^⋆D_{−,ϵ′} ⊆ supp p_2^⋆D_{−,ϵ}. These are the second statements of Proposition 6.2.3(2) and (3), read as inclusions of supports. Hence supp p_2^⋆D_{+,ϵ} ⊆ supp p_1^⋆D_{+,ϵ} and supp p_1^⋆D_{−,ϵ} ⊆ supp p_2^⋆D_{−,ϵ}. So p_1^{−1}(𝔘) ∩ p_2^{−1}(𝔘) = C_t^{tor} ∖ (p_1^⋆D_{+,ϵ} ∪ p_2^⋆D_{−,ϵ}), which is exactly the open of Proposition 6.2.7. The domain therefore follows from the definition and fits the rest of §6.2.
Shrinking ϵ does no harm. By Proposition 6.1.10 (p. 60), ∩_{m,n} T^m(𝒰_{≥w−ϵ}) ∩ (T^t)^n(𝒵_{<w+ϵ}) is the closure of 𝒮^{tor}_w for every ϵ ∈ ]0,1[∩Q. So by Proposition 6.1.7 (p. 59) the finite-slope parts do not depend on ϵ. The ordinary part is M_w^• ⊗_Λ A for every such ϵ, by Theorem 6.2.15(1), whose input Proposition 6.2.13 does not involve ϵ.

Kind and reach. Each item is a slip of notation, an omitted definition or an omitted standing assumption, and in each case the surrounding text fixes the intended meaning. None is a false statement or a missing argument. The passage is used by the definition before Theorem 6.2.15 and by Theorem 6.2.15 (p. 64). Through these it is used by Corollaries 6.2.16 and 6.2.17, Remark 6.2.18, and Theorems 1.4.3(3), 1.4.9 and 1.4.10 of the introduction (pp. 5–6). None of these involves the misprinted symbols, and each is correct as intended.
